docs.title: Working together across the Nightscout ecosystem — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 35ec9da5a.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, the operators and companies that host or build on Nightscout, and the community. Read after the sponsored maintenance team; leads to the quality system. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion. Written 2026-09-29 against this repository at 2c19f61d. Where it touches conflicts of interest, partner agreements, trademarks or regulatory status, it needs review by the foundation's counsel before any decision rests on it (§8). Nothing here is decided. Rule 10 and §5a were added 2026-10-18 at 0b0d150f.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the sponsored-team proposal. The rules in §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The request
docs.text:
The ecosystem programme says what the shared commons are. The sponsored-team proposal says who would do the work nobody is paid for. This page proposes the rules for working together that both depend on, so that volunteers, app projects, second servers, commercial hosts and researchers can each contribute without any of them gaining control of what the others rely on.

It asks for six decisions (§7). Each borrows a rule another open-source organisation already uses (§4), and each answers a need measured in this repository or dated on a vendor's calendar (§3).

docs.title: 2. Who takes part, and what each needs
docs.text:
party what it needs from the ecosystem what it can contribute people with diabetes and caregivers alarms and data that keep working; control of their own data reports of what breaks; consent to research; donations volunteer maintainers of each project time, review, credit, and the final say over their own project code, review, release judgment, the history of why things are as they are app projects (Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS, xDrip+, followers) a server contract that changes only with notice, and tests that say whether it changed what their apps actually send and expect (the client census covers 40) other servers (Nocturne; any future one) one current description of the contract and tests any server can run, on equal terms a second implementation that tests the description; its own parity evidence commercial hosting providers predictable releases, security fixes on time, and fair treatment beside their competitors engineering time, test infrastructure, money, operating experience at scale researchers and data holders consented, well-described data without taking custody of it studies, methods, aggregate results (nsprobe) the foundation a clear reason to exist that donors and members understand; limited liability the neutral place to hold the shared layers, money and trademarks

The interests overlap more than they conflict. Every party needs the shared contract to stay current and the server to be released on time. The conflicts are about control (who decides what the contract is), credit (whose work is recognised) and advantage (whether any one company or project is favoured). §5 proposes a rule for each.

docs.title: 3. Needs we can predict
docs.text:
Much of the maintenance the ecosystem needs arrives on other organisations' calendars: platform, runtime and hosting dates to the end of 2027, and vendor-cloud changes that arrive with no date. The dated table, read from each vendor's own pages, is evidence §5.

Three things follow:

  • Most of this reaches several projects at once. The Apple and Android changes reach every self-built app; the runtime and hosting dates reach both servers. Preparing once, in public, is cheaper than each project discovering the same change alone.
  • Some of it reaches the people who build the apps, not the projects. Each builder answers Apple's declaration and Google's verification for themselves. What they need is clear, current documentation in time; the projects already publish some (AndroidAPS).
  • None of it can wait for a volunteer's free weekend. The dates are fixed by others. This is the work §4 of the sponsored-team proposal describes.

docs.title: 4. What other open-source organisations do
docs.text: Each rule in §5 borrows from an organisation that already uses it. The rules, quoted from each organisation's own pages, are in PRECEDENTS: rules other organisations use; the sizes, funding and commercial roles of the same organisations are in its main table.

docs.title: 4a. SQLite: paying for assurance, not control
docs.text:
What SQLite sells, and what stays constant across every tier, is in PRECEDENTS: SQLite. For these rules:

  • Transfers: selling assurance rather than influence. Companies that host Nightscout, or build on it under their own quality systems, mostly need evidence for a named release, fixes for the release line they run, and a support horizon they can cite. The ecosystem already produces much of that evidence (the 15.0.9 test matrix, soak runs and client census); what is missing is someone paid to package and keep it.
  • Transfers: a published, sized promise, such as a compatibility promise for the API and a support horizon for each release line, kept only as far as funded people can keep it.
  • Does not transfer: SQLite's "not open-contribution" policy. It works because a salaried team writes all the code. The Nightscout projects depend on volunteer and outside contributions.
  • Does not transfer: the warranty of title. SQLite can offer it because every contributor has signed a public-domain affidavit. cgm-remote-monitor is AGPL-3.0 with many contributors and no such records; a per-release statement of licences and dependencies is the nearest honest equivalent (§8).

docs.title: 5. Proposed rules for working together
docs.text:
1. Decisions go on the public record. Anyone may propose work, a grant or a change to the shared layers. Each proposal gets a public entry, a named reviewer, a response by a published date, and a recorded outcome: accepted, declined with reasons, or returned for changes. Conversations can happen anywhere; the decision is not made until it is on the record (Apache).
  2. Money and staff buy work, not control. Contributions of money, people or infrastructure are welcome from anyone, on published terms that are the same for everyone. No contribution buys a say over what a project merges or what the shared contract says (Apache, OpenStreetMap). Each project's maintainers keep the merge decision.
  3. Providers are listed neutrally, and payment links say who is paid. Where the foundation or a project lists hosting providers or services, it lists every provider that meets published criteria, endorses none (CNCF, OpenStreetMap), and labels any provider run by the project's own maintainers or founders as such. The order is set by published criteria and chosen by people without a stake in the result: alphabetical, rotating, or by the contribution levels of rule 4. Wherever a project's documentation asks for money (a subscription, a donation, a purchase), it names who receives it, and money described as going to the foundation goes to a foundation account.

Both servers' documentation already does part of this:

  • Nightscout's lists nine hosted providers, each linking to its own site for pricing, with no purchase on the documentation domain (docs home, docs/index.md at 9b5afad2, 2026-08-07). It publishes no listing criteria, and its order follows no stated rule; T1Pal, the author's company, is listed first.
  • Nocturne's lists managed instances in a random order on every page load, publishes what a provider must supply to be listed, and labels its one entry, nocturne.run, as "the official managed Nocturne instance, run by the creator of the project" (installation guide, eba84e58). Its documentation pages also carry monthly support subscriptions described as going to the Nightscout Foundation.
  • Contributions are recognised by organisation, every year. A yearly public report of what each organisation contributed (code, review, infrastructure, money, test devices) at published levels (OpenMRS). Commercial success then shows up as help to the commons.
  • One contract, several implementations. The foundation stewards the API description and the conformance tests; servers and apps compete on implementation (openEHR, WHATWG in the sponsored-team proposal §6, Apache on overlap). A change to the contract goes through a recorded problem-report and change-request process (openEHR). Stewarding means hosting the description and tests and running that process. The change requests are decided by the maintainers of the implementations they affect, with no majority from one employer or host (QUALITY-SYSTEM §8.3), so the body that holds the money (rule 2) does not also decide the contract. Any server or hosted offering can publish its conformance results from the same public suite (CNCF).
  • Two labels, never one. If projects adopt maturity levels, each project's maintainers propose their own level against published criteria (CNCF). A maturity level describes the project's organisation and engineering. It says nothing about clinical safety or regulatory status, which is a separate statement each project makes for itself.
  • Data stays with its holder. Shared research runs as aggregate queries that data holders run on their own data (OHDSI; this repository's nsprobe).
  • Assurance can be paid for; the evidence stays public. Companies may pay for release evidence packaged for their own quality systems, fixes on the release line they run, and test runs in their configuration (SQLite). The tests and results that decide a public release stay public, fixes land in the public branches, and the money goes to maintenance. There is one codebase: no separate commercial edition, and no feature held back from people who build and run the software themselves.
  • Everyone discloses. Anyone who decides, reviews or is paid under these rules discloses their commercial ties and any interest in the outcome, and steps back from decisions that affect their own organisation.
  • A second person can review and release. Each repository that other projects or many people depend on has at least two people able to review, merge and release it, and a written path by which a contributor earns those rights, with review by a second person (the xz-utils lesson, PRECEDENTS). In the 12 months to 2026-10-02, pull requests in AndroidAPS (508), xDrip+ (132), nightscout-librelink-up (11), nightguard (6) and three other repositories were each merged by one account (governance today §1).

docs.title: 5a. Read the structure before the motive
docs.text:
Teams that had no channel to agree build what each needs, and the shared data holds both (the Conway's Law case study). Most friction between projects comes from such a boundary, not from what a person intended. The rules below apply to maintainers, contributors, companies and community members alike.

when you see read it first as check before concluding anything else two apps disagree on a field or show different numbers each team wrote what its own app needed, and no one owned the join the quirks registry and each app's source; whether a shared rule existed at the time a long gap between releases releases follow people's available time and outside clocks: toolchains, platforms, hosts the project's own statement; dates do not show causes, and each project's maintainers are the people to say what held a release (ecosystem evidence §3) a pull request or proposal open for a long time review capacity on that boundary is a few people who carry everything else too who can merge there, and what they were releasing at the time a fork a group needed a different pace or direction than one shared channel allowed whether the fork reads and writes the shared contract a company or a paid person involved paid and unpaid roles are both part of the structure their disclosed interests (rule 9), and whether the same requirements apply to them as to anyone a second server or a rewrite a second team implementing the contract whether both pass the same conformance cases (rule 5)
  1. Ask before attributing. A maintainer can usually say in one message what held a release or why a field has its shape.
  2. Argue from the shared contract. State what an app writes, what the contract says and the test that shows the difference; a comparison between two apps or servers does not change either.
  3. State differences as facts about the system. Where your picture of who decides, or of what the code does, differs from the code, say so as a fact about the system, not about people.

docs.title: 6. What would break consensus
docs.text:
• The foundation choosing a winning server or app.
  • A commercial edition that differs from the public one, or evidence that decides a public release kept private.
  • Influence in proportion to money given.
  • Payment decided by one person (Debian's lesson from 2006, PRECEDENTS).
  • Decisions that exist only in private channels.
  • A maturity level read as a statement that software is safe for dosing decisions.
  • Any account of past disagreements in place of measured needs.

docs.title: 6a. How much structure: the options
docs.text:
The rules in §5 are one point on a range. The board and the maintainers can choose less or more structure, and the rules can be adopted one at a time. Each option keeps every project's merge decision with its own maintainers.

option what changes what it costs what it leaves open where it is used 0. Remain informal nothing: proposals, sponsorship and listings are handled case by case, as today (GOVERNANCE-TODAY) no new process outcomes are not on a public record, so readers cannot see how a proposal was handled; no shared rule for companies or for a second server most small open-source projects 1. A transparency layer rule 1 (public proposal record with a named reviewer and a response date) and rule 9 (disclosure); nothing else a public register and someone to keep it; a response for every proposal who decides the shared contract, and on what terms companies take part Apache's "if it isn't on the mailing list, it didn't happen" (PRECEDENTS) 2. Rules for money and listings option 1, plus rules 2–4 and 8: work not control, neutral listings, recognition by organisation, paid assurance with public evidence written policies and a conflict-of-interest policy (counsel, §8) how the shared contract changes OpenStreetMap, CNCF website guidelines, OpenMRS levels, SQLite 3. A cross-project body for the shared contract option 2, plus rule 5: the API description and conformance tests change through a recorded change process, decided by maintainers of the affected implementations with no majority from one employer or host maintainers' time on a standing body; a change-request record maturity labels (rule 6) and research rules (rule 7) can still be added later openEHR change requests, WHATWG, CNCF's technical oversight committee, Python's cap on any one employer

Choosing a lower option now does not rule out a higher one later. CNCF's governance guidance recommends structure by size, from a maintainer council for a single repository with 3–10 maintainers from 1–3 organisations to an elected steering committee or federated subprojects for several repositories with 20 or more maintainers from five or more, and says "Governance should not be more complex than the project" (CNCF blog, 2026-08-26, read 2026-10-02).

docs.title: 7. Decisions requested
docs.text:
For the board:

  1. Which option in §6a to start from. Decisions 1–4 assume option 1 or above.
  2. Adopt rule 1: where proposals are submitted, the response time, and where outcomes are published.
  3. Adopt rules 2, 3 and 9 as policy, with a conflict-of-interest policy that covers board members, maintainers, paid staff and partners (counsel, §8).
  4. Decide whether to offer a partner programme under rules 2–4 and 8, and what a partner contributes and receives.
  5. Under rule 3, who sets the criteria and the order for provider listings in foundation-stewarded documentation, and how payment links that name the foundation are confirmed to reach a foundation account.

For the maintainers of each project:

  1. Whether rules 3, 5–7 and 10, and the practice in §5a, are acceptable to your project, and which of §3's dates your project wants shared preparation for.

For the commercial hosting providers:

  1. What each would contribute under equal published terms: engineering time, test infrastructure (hosted test sites, CI, devices), or money toward the sponsored team; and which assurance under rule 8 (release evidence, fixes on an older line, a support horizon) each would pay for.

docs.title: 8. Points for reviewers to verify
docs.text:
For counsel:

  1. Whether partner agreements under rules 2–4 raise private-benefit issues for a 501(c)(3), and how partner contributions are recorded (donation, sponsorship or contract).
  2. Whether listing providers (rule 3) creates any endorsement or liability exposure.
  3. Whether selling assurance under rule 8 is related or unrelated business income, and what a per-release statement of licences and dependencies may and may not promise, given AGPL-3.0 and many contributors (§4a).
  4. Whether the foundation should say anything to app builders about Apple's medical-device declaration, and if so what; this page gives no regulatory advice, and each builder answers Apple for themselves.

For everyone:

  1. The §4 quotes were read on 2026-09-29; re-read each before quoting. Not used because they could not be verified: an OpenMRS "20+ organisations" figure, and HL7 FHIR connectathon details.
  2. The §3 dates marked "announced" or "estimated" will move; re-check before planning against them.

docs.title: Definition of done: when a change is ready for the apps that depend on it
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 1efa2b753.

What this is: a reference (contributor-facing). Read after work waiting on a person; leads to document control. Applies to every document under docs/00-overview, docs/30-design/{remedial,modernization,tenancy,platform}, docs/60-research/{remedial,modernization,tenancy,programme}, queue/ and reports/reviewer-packets/. Adopted 2026-09-22.

A document is downstream ready when someone who has never read this repository's history — an upstream reviewer, the maintainer deciding a release, an operator, a clinician reviewing a draft — can act on it without asking what changed or whom to believe.

docs.title: The criteria
docs.text:
1. Current facts only. The document says what is true now. It does not narrate how the project came to believe it: no "was X, then Y, now Z" chains, no "an earlier draft said", no "this claim is retracted", no running tallies of past mistakes. A wrong claim is corrected in place. The history is in git.
  2. Dated and anchored. Every measured fact names the date and the commit it was measured against (origin/dev 74fc6619, not "dev"). A count that moves (commits behind, open defects) is either generated by a gate or given with the command that reproduces it.
  3. Provenance marked. Each defect claim says reproduced (run, with a control where the claim is about access or severity) or read-derived (inferred from source, not run). A read-derived fix is a hypothesis.
  4. Status words mean one thing. open · fixed (on a branch, not merged) · merged (in dev, not released) · released (in a tagged release operators run). Nothing is described as fixed for operators until it is released.
  5. Audience declared. The first lines say contributor-facing or user-facing. User-facing text uses plain language, defines jargon, keeps every safety caveat, gives no individual dosing advice, says it is not medical advice, and points to the reader's care team where relevant.
  6. Mechanism, not recipe. A defect that is live on the shipping release is described by mechanism only. No request, payload or pattern that would work against a deployed instance appears in this public repository.
  7. One home per fact. Defect facts live in the backfix register, item state in queue/work-queue.yaml, decisions in the execution plan. Other documents link rather than restate, so there is one place to correct.
  8. Links resolve. make docs-links passes; generated views pass make views-check and make packets-check.
  9. No PII or health data. No names, emails or identifiers from user data, logs or exports; no credentials.
  10. Sendable artifacts are send-ready. A drafted PR body, advisory reply or release note can be pasted as-is: no internal ids a recipient cannot resolve, no notes-to-self, and it is marked draft until a human sends it.

docs.title: Living documents and snapshots
docs.text:
Living documents are kept current and must meet every criterion: the overview pages, the backfix register, the queue and its README, the execution plan, the release-versioning policy, and any drafted outgoing artifact.

Dated research and design documents (a date in the filename) are snapshots. They are not rewritten as the world moves. Each carries a status line under its title stating the date and commit it describes, whether it is current or superseded, and where the current fact lives. Known-wrong claims in a snapshot are corrected in place with a one-line note, not left for the reader to discover.

A series is one living document. When the same deliverable is produced repeatedly — successive test runs of one release candidate, revisions of one plan — it lives in one file with no date in its name. The current version is given in full. Each earlier version is one row in a history table that links to the file at the commit holding it. Checks that the current version did not repeat are carried forward, each naming the tree it ran on. Superseded files are removed from the working tree rather than kept beside the current one. The first such record is the 15.0.9 integration record.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text: It is not a style guide and not a length limit. A long document that meets the criteria is done; a short one that says "see the thread" is not.

docs.title: Document control — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 174c8e8e5.

What this is: a proposal (contributor- and maintainer-facing). Read after the definition of done; leads back to the overview. DRAFT PROPOSAL, requiring review by the maintainer and by a quality-management professional before it is adopted or relied on. Written 2026-09-25 against this repository at eb564053. It is not legal or regulatory advice. It does not claim that the Nightscout Foundation, or any software it stewards, conforms to any standard.

This proposes how the alignment repository controls its documents and records. It is the first procedure of a quality management system (QMS) for the Nightscout ecosystem alignment work. It writes down the practice piloted on 2026-09-25, when 19 superseded files were retired into 5 living ones, and names what is still missing before the practice can be called controlled.

Context that bounds it. The Nightscout Foundation is a 501(c)(3) that stewards open-source automated insulin delivery software. It does not manufacture medical devices or prescribe therapy, and people build and run these tools themselves. The procedure borrows the document-control practices that medical-device quality systems use, because readers of this repository make decisions that can affect people managing diabetes. Borrowing a practice is not a claim of conformity.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
In scope: the programme material from August and September 2026 and everything written after it:

  • docs/00-overview;
  • docs/30-design/{remedial,modernization,tenancy,platform} and the loose design documents of that period;
  • docs/60-research/{remedial,modernization,tenancy,programme};
  • docs/40-migration;
  • queue/, releases/ and reports/.

Out of scope until the maintainer extends it: the January–April 2026 AID research campaign, including the 53 VERIFICATION-* files at the repository root and the loose files in docs/60-research, and the July 2026 telemetry design documents. They stay where they are (maintainer decision, 2026-09-16).

docs.title: 2. Two kinds of controlled information
docs.text:
The procedure turns on one distinction, the same one ISO 13485:2016 draws between documents (§4.2.4) and records (§4.2.5), and ISO 9001:2015 between maintained and retained documented information (§7.5).

a document a record says what is true, decided or intended now what was measured or done at a point in time changes corrected in place whenever the world moves never, once captured file name stable, no date (ROADMAP.md, rc-15.0.9-integration-record.md) dated (manual-lab-15.0.9-rc-2026-09-23.md) examples overview pages, the backfix register, the queue, the execution plan, the versioning policy, a release's contents and decisions, a defect record such as BF-103 a lab run, a soak, a measurement report, a posted PR body, a triage record

A series is one document. When the same deliverable is produced again and again (successive test runs of one release candidate, revisions of one plan), it lives in one undated file. The current version is given in full, and each earlier version is one row in a history table that links to the file at the commit that holds it. This rule is already in the definition of done.

docs.title: 3.1 Identification
docs.text:
Every controlled file opens with a status block under its title. The block states:

  • the audience: contributor-facing, or user-facing;
  • the status: living, or a snapshot with its date; draft requiring professional review where that applies;
  • what it was measured against, as dates and commits (for example origin/dev 4f705217);
  • where the current fact lives, if it lives somewhere else (the queue, the register, a decision record).

Queue items (RT-0, BFQ-47) and register entries (BF-103) are the stable identifiers that documents cite. Proposed, not yet done: a document register (§5) that gives every controlled document an identifier, an owner and a class.

docs.title: 3.2 Revision control
docs.text:
• Git is the revision history. A revision is a commit. Documents carry no change logs, no "was X, now Y" passages and no retraction notes; they are corrected in place.
  • Pushing is a human act. Agents prepare commits locally and stop. The maintainer pushes, so nothing becomes public without a person choosing it.
  • The approved version is the version on main in the public repository. Until pushed, a commit is a proposal.

docs.title: 3.3 Review and approval
docs.text:
class approved by review standard decision records (execution plan, versioning policy, a release's decisions.md) the maintainer, who owns every decision in them each decision is the maintainer's words or is confirmed by them living status documents (overview pages, queue, register, release contents) the maintainer, by pushing the definition of done, ten criteria records nobody after capture; they are reviewed for accuracy when captured reproducible, with the command or harness named, and a control where the claim is about access or severity user-facing text (release notes, operator guidance) the maintainer, plus a reader who is not a developer plain language, every safety caveat kept, no individual dosing advice, not medical advice, points to the care team security- or safety-relevant content the maintainer and a named SECURITY or SAFETY reviewer disclosure rule (§3.8)

Gap: the SECURITY and SAFETY reviewer rows name a kind of reviewer, and for most items no individual is assigned (PROGRAMME-STATUS). Until they are, approval of that content rests on one person.

docs.title: 3.4 The current version is the one a reader finds
docs.text:
• Entry points. The READMEs link to PROGRAMME-STATUS, ROADMAP, NEEDS-A-HUMAN and REVIEWER-ONBOARDING. Each of them points to the one home of each kind of fact.
  • One home per fact. Defect facts live in the register, item state in the queue, decisions in the decision records. Other documents link to them and do not restate them.
  • Generated blocks for anything that moves. Counts, states and orders are generated from queue/work-queue.yaml inside hand-written pages, and make views-check fails when they drift. An example is ROADMAP §1's table of what the next release still waits on.

docs.title: 3.5 Changing a document
docs.text:
A change is a commit that leaves every gate in §3.9 green. A change that supersedes files follows the procedure piloted on 2026-09-25:

  1. Classify each file in the cluster as document or record, and read all of them in full.
  2. Check scope before merging. Files with similar names are not necessarily one series. The adoption roadmap and the 2026-09-09 next-steps discussion were distinct proposals and stayed.
  3. Write the one current document. Give the current version in full. Carry forward, with the tree each ran on, any evidence the current version did not repeat. Re-check each carried-forward claim against the current code before carrying it; one claim in the pilot was already out of date and was dropped.
  4. Move design content that has no other home to the document that owns that topic (for example, tenancy designs to the execution plan) instead of deleting it.
  5. Add a history row for each superseded version, linking to it at a pushed commit.
  6. Rewrite every inbound link, including queue evidence paths, generated views, reviewer packets and copies of posted PR bodies.
  7. Remove the superseded files from the working tree.
  8. Run the gates and show that the link gate goes red on a restored dead link.
  9. Coordinate with every session editing the same files (§3.10).

docs.title: 3.6 Obsolete documents
docs.text:
• A superseded document is removed from the working tree, not kept beside the current one with a "superseded" banner.
  • It stays retrievable: through the history row of its successor, by git show <commit>:<path>, or at a GitHub URL pinned to a pushed commit.
  • Snapshots that quote a removed file (a dated research note citing a line of an old readiness document) keep the citation, repointed to the pinned URL, so the quotation stays checkable.
  • Proposed: a pushed annotated tag at each consolidation (archive/<date>), so retrieval does not depend on remembering a hash. No such tag exists yet.

docs.title: 3.7 Records
docs.text:
• A record is not edited after capture, except to correct a known-wrong claim in place with a one-line note (the definition of done's snapshot rule).
  • A superseded record (an earlier test run of the same candidate) leaves the reader's path. The living document that supersedes it carries its history row, and anything it alone measured.
  • Retention: git retains every record. Proposed: records that are evidence for a release (the integration record, verification records, lab results) are kept retrievable for at least as long as that release is supported. A pushed tag per release would pin them.
  • Health data. Records contain synthetic data only, unless a data holder has agreed otherwise in writing. They contain no names, emails or identifiers from real data, and no credentials.

docs.title: 3.8 External and restricted documents
docs.text:
• Copies of external text (PR bodies as posted, advisory drafts) are records of what was sent, or drafts marked unsent. They follow the live text; they do not replace it.
  • Disclosure rule. The repository is public. A defect that is live on the shipping release is described by mechanism only: no request, payload or pattern that would work against a deployed instance. Security advisory detail is withheld until a release with the fix ships and the advisory is published. The withheld text stays in history at a named commit, and the index of what is withheld is the advisory response pack (not published).
  • Private material, such as BF-72's disposition, is held outside version control. A page that mentions such material says it is withheld under this rule, so a reader does not take a withheld security decision for an unrecorded one.

docs.title: 3.9 Automated controls
docs.text:
gate what it enforces make docs-links every path cited in the groomed material and the queue tooling resolves; the exemptions are named and each carries a reason make views-check every generated block on the overview pages is current make packets-check every reviewer packet is current, and none is orphaned make queue-validate, queue-coverage the queue's schema, and that every open register entry has a queue item make queue-vacuity every runnable gate has a negative control that fails, or a recorded reason why it cannot make queue-check all of the above, for CI

A check is evidence only after it has been seen to fail. Every new gate or generated block introduced during the consolidation was broken on purpose once, to show it goes red.

docs.title: 3.10 Concurrent authors
docs.text:
Several sessions (people and agents) edit the same tree and share one git index.

  • Commit by path (git commit -- <paths>), never the whole index.
  • Announce a multi-file edit to the other sessions before starting, and name the files. Re-read a shared file before editing it.
  • A change containing another author's hunks is committed only when that author agrees, and the commit message names them.
  • A file another session is rewriting is left out of a commit, and the one-line change it needs is handed to that session.

docs.title: 4. The 2026-09-25 pilot
docs.text:
commit retired now a35e7e25 8 run records rc-15.0.9-*-2026-09-2x.md 15.0.9 integration record 8135442f the post-Phase-0 roadmap ROADMAP, generated from the queue; its designs moved into the execution plan bb26a50c 2 BF-103 records, 2 connector profile-sync records, 2 advisory stubs BF-103 record; connector profile sync; the advisory pack README c8945592 the backfix-2 plan and its first integration run 15.0.9 decisions; versioning policy §5.7 (compatibility flags) 238c3da2 2 release-readiness snapshots ROADMAP §1 (what 15.0.9 still waits on, generated) and the release's contents.md; versioning policy §8.3 (why the release order)

19 files retired, 5 living files created, plus new sections in the versioning policy and the execution plan. make queue-check was green after each commit. The pilot also found and fixed three queue items whose recorded blockers or state had fallen behind (RT-0, RT-5, BFQ-47), because the new generated tables made the mismatch visible.

docs.title: 5. Gaps before this can be called controlled
docs.text: gap proposal owner no document register one generated table listing each controlled document: identifier, class, owner, status, path maintainer to approve the shape no named owner per document owner = the person who approves changes to it; the maintainer by default maintainer approval is implicit in pushing record approval of decision records and user-facing text in the commit or PR that carries it maintainer no independent SECURITY or SAFETY reviewer recruit one of each (REVIEWER-ONBOARDING) maintainer 75 dated files remain in the programme directories, many of them snapshots whose facts now live elsewhere classify each as record (keep) or superseded document (consolidate), cluster by cluster agents, maintainer review no pushed archive or release tags tag each consolidation and each release in this repository maintainer the April campaign and July telemetry material out of scope by decision; revisit if outside readers are pointed at it maintainer no periodic review a review of the living documents at each release, checking every fact against the tree it names maintainer training this document and the definition of done are the material; no training record is kept —

docs.title: 6. For the reviewer to verify
docs.text:
• Applicability. Whether the Foundation's role (steward of user-built open-source software, not a manufacturer) makes any QMS obligation apply, or whether this is voluntary good practice only. This draft assumes the latter.
  • Standards mapping. Whether §2 and §3 map correctly onto ISO 13485:2016 §4.2.4 and §4.2.5 and ISO 9001:2015 §7.5. Also, if manufacturers building on this software will cite these documents, whether the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (21 CFR Part 820, which incorporates ISO 13485 by reference and applies from 2026-02-02) or IEC 62304's configuration-management expectations change anything. These references were written from general knowledge and have not been checked against the standards' text.
  • Git as the revision system. Whether commit history on a public host is adequate retention for records, or whether releases need exported, signed snapshots.
  • Approval evidence. Whether a maintainer's push is sufficient evidence of approval, or whether explicit sign-off (a PR review, a signed tag) is needed.
  • Agent authorship. Whether content drafted by AI agents under the maintainer's direction needs its own identification or review step beyond §3.3.
  • Retention period for release evidence (§3.7).

docs.title: The Nightscout ecosystem programme: the stack and four shared commons
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-21 at 59b35119d.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after process models; leads to the sponsored maintenance team. Prepared for the Nightscout project; proposed for Nightscout Foundation stewardship. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion. Written 2026-09-29 against this repository at 37beb699 and cgm-remote-monitor official/dev 7000eb18; reorganised 2026-10-16 at 66403e0f into the stack and four shared commons, adding reports and decision support, research tools, and the controller registrations of decisions D18–D20. The parts on consent, research access, cross-border data, decision support and regulatory terms need review by the foundation's counsel and a privacy, quality or clinical professional before any decision rests on them (§9). Nothing here is decided.

docs.title: 1. What this page is
docs.text:
Several pieces of work are under way or proposed across the Nightscout ecosystem: releases and modernization of cgm-remote-monitor, shared schemas, typed controller registrations and conformance tests, multitenant hosting, a research data commons, report and decision-support prototypes, and new interfaces such as MCP. Each has its own document. This page places them in two views of one programme: the stack, six rows of software that each project builds and runs, and four shared commons that run across every row. For each commons it says what exists, what is proposed, and where it is decided.

It records no decisions and adds no work items. The order of the cgm-remote-monitor work is on the ROADMAP; where it stands is on PROGRAMME-STATUS.

docs.title: 2. The picture
docs.text:
the stack: built and run by each project          the shared commons: stewarded, open to every implementation

 6  Reports and decision support                   A  Shared contract
 5  Followers                                         schemas, quirks, typed controller registrations
 4  Servers: cgm-remote-monitor, Nocturne, hosted  B  Identity, trust and device access
 3  Vendor clouds and connectors                   C  Evidence: research and quality
 2  Controllers: Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS, xDrip+    D  Interfaces for people and agents
 1  Devices: CGMs and pumps                           reports, statistics, MCP
    beside: wearables and health platforms
                                                   under both: shared operations
                                                   complaints and incidents, security, partner and legal, administration

The stack is what runs. Each row is built by its own projects, and the stack census and the quality-system proposal use the same six rows (§2a). The commons are assets that no single app, server or operator is placed to own, and that every row uses: the description of the data that passes between rows, the means of recognising one another, the evidence that the whole works, and the interfaces people and agents read it through. Each commons runs across every row: a registration is written by a controller, stored by a server and read by a follower or a report.

cgm-remote-monitor is one implementation in row 4, and it has its own section (§3) because the commons are extracted from its behaviour: the schemas, the client census and the conformance tests are measured against what cgm-remote-monitor and its clients actually do.

The principle: the foundation stewards the commons and keeps them open to every implementation; each implementation makes its own technical choices. A second server, such as Nocturne, is a second implementation of the same contract, not a competitor for the commons. Stewarding a commons means hosting it and running its change process in public; the implementers decide changes to it (COLLABORATION-MODEL rule 5).

One codebase, two uses. The same open-source releases serve people who build and run their own tools, under the digital rights in DIGITAL-RIGHTS, and companies that host Nightscout or use its release evidence inside their own quality systems. Companies can pay for assurance (packaged evidence, fixes on the line they run, test runs in their configuration), and the evidence that decides each public release stays public (SQLite's model). Commercial offerings can show they track the same contract with the same public conformance suite (CNCF's model). There is no separate commercial edition. Neither use carries a clinical or regulatory claim for the other (COLLABORATION-MODEL rules 6 and 8).

Drawn (idea·one-codebase): with fixes returned, and the second upstream the return edge prevents.

docs.title: 2a. The stack
docs.text:
Measured by the stack census of 2026-09-30 over 62 repositories (evidence §1).

row what it is measured 1 devices drivers that talk to CGMs and pumps over Bluetooth and radio, often through pairing cryptography volunteers had to work out 14 device protocols with 41 independent implementations; no device repository publishes a per-release test report 2 controllers the AID apps that read devices, decide, and write what they did: Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS, xDrip+ each writes its own shapes into the shared collections (§4) 3 vendor clouds and connectors connectors that bring a person's data back out of vendor clouds six code bases log in to Dexcom Share and five to LibreLinkUp; no connector repository publishes a per-release test report 4 servers cgm-remote-monitor (§3), Nocturne, and hosted operators 40 client repositories mapped against 15 parts of the API (evidence §2) 5 followers apps and watches that show another person's data, with alarms read the server's API; counted in the client census 6 reports and decision support reports for people and clinicians, and analysis tools that read a site (§7) listed in evidence §7 beside wearables and health platforms such as HealthKit and Health Connect census §5

Rows 1 and 3 are where data sovereignty starts: the data holder's ability to get their own data, in a form they can compute on, and to hand that job to tools and helpers they choose. The quality-system proposal proposes a shared kit for every row: vector corpora, simulators, fixture suites, a change canary and one record shape. It also proposes how the requirements for it would be agreed.

docs.title: 2b. Sponsoring and operating
docs.text:
Stewarding a commons can mean two different things, and they carry different exposure:

  • Sponsoring: paying for, hosting or convening shared work that others carry out under their own responsibility, such as conformance tests, documentation, an audit or a research pilot.
  • Operating: running a service that other people's data, or their therapy, depends on, and answering for its availability, security and incidents.

The proposal is that the foundation sponsors by default and operates only by a recorded decision that names the operator, its contract, its insurance and its successor. A service whose failure could interrupt someone's treatment, such as an authority that issues credentials for a device, needs an operator with its own contract, security controls, insurance and continuity plan. That operator may be a specialist organisation the foundation contracts with, or one that a manufacturer appoints; the foundation sponsoring the work does not make it the operator. Paying for a shared service also gives no control over any project's roadmap (COLLABORATION-MODEL rule 2).

The difference, drawn: the same service with a named operator in the operator's box, and with the foundation in it (idea·sponsor-or-operate).

docs.title: 2c. Shared operations the commons depend on
docs.text:
The four commons name technical assets. Four kinds of shared operation run underneath them, and none exists yet as shared work:

operation what it covers where it is proposed complaints, incidents and support one intake for reports from users, clinicians, developers and manufacturers; triage into support, complaints and security; investigation records and referral to the responsible manufacturer PARTNER-READINESS §6 security coordination security contacts, private vulnerability reporting, embargoed fixes, an SBOM per release PARTNER-READINESS §8 partner and legal operations agreements with manufacturers, the evidence a manufacturer asks for, the terms that carry data rights PARTNER-READINESS §3–§5 administration funding, insurance, contracts, continuity, published accounts what each activity brings

Each feeds the commons: a confirmed complaint becomes a test vector in commons A or C, a security contact is part of what commons B's trust federation recognises, and an agreement with a manufacturer is what keeps rows 1 and 3 reachable.

docs.title: 3. The reference implementation: cgm-remote-monitor
docs.text:
cgm-remote-monitor is the server most existing sites run, on MongoDB, with its own settings, data and hosting. The work on it runs in three horizons (PROGRAMME-STATUS):

  • Remedial. Defects in what ships to operators today, tracked in the backfix register. 15.0.9 was released on 2026-10-21 (tag v15.0.9, master c6a0d8ed); what is left is in ROADMAP §1.
  • Modernization. A staged release train for the dependency tree and runtime (ROADMAP §2).
  • Multitenancy. A second deployment target for hosting providers, on PostgreSQL. Self-hosted, single-tenant Nightscout on MongoDB stays first-class permanently (decisions D1 and D4, execution plan).

Accepting controller registrations (§4) is queued for it as HUB-REG-CRM, single-tenant first.

What bounds this work is review capacity. The generated reviewer-load table on PROGRAMME-STATUS shows most queue items routing review to the maintainer, and the SECURITY and SAFETY reviewer rows mostly naming no individual (the two constraints). The sponsored-team proposal is the request that addresses this.

docs.title: 4. Commons A — the shared contract
docs.text:
The apps exchange data through the same collections (entries, treatments, devicestatus, profile) without a shared, measured description of what goes in them, and a controller feature that has no shared shape lands in untyped devicestatus. This repository builds the description (collaboration start page):

asset where state schemas, each field graded measured / declared / read-from-code specs/openapi/, specs/nsschema/, specs/jsonschema/generated/ exists; measured over an 11-site corpus, 9 of them Loop quirks, scoped to the vendor versions that produce them specs/quirks/; hub-sync design §3.7 exists; version scoping adopted as D20 per-client mappings with file:line citations mapping/<project>/ exists conformance assertions and replay vectors conformance/, specs/sync/conformance/ exists client census: 40 client repositories against 15 parts of the API consumer impact exists, for 15.0.9 typed controller registrations hub-sync design §3.1 and §3.5–§3.7; specs/sync/ adopted as D18–D20 and specified; well-known declarations for Loop, Trio and AndroidAPS; not implemented in any hub (HUB-REG-CRM not started); the proposal to controller projects is PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS (not started) one write step: _id form, server dates, soft delete, re-send identity, one change event WRITE-CONTRACT in the queue specified; blocked on prerequisites controller descriptions (decomposesTo) proposal adopted as the devicestatus direction by D11; carried forward by the registrations hub-and-spoke adoption path adoption roadmap proposed (ROADMAP §5)

Composition through registrations. Under D18 a controller can declare its own typed definitions (intent kinds, states, transitions, initiators, effect fields and a command contract) composed from the shared primitives, and the hub offers typed API for them. Legacy writers are described by well-known declarations that ship with the hub, so nothing changes for a controller that never registers. D19 separates the immutable, content-addressed definition from each running instance (a phone, simulator, lab rig or agent), which holds a lease and declares whether it is a device or simulated. The roles are fixed: the hub is responsible for observability, the controller for sending data accurately and for syncing and reconciling, and the hub decides nothing about dosing (execution plan §1). The evidence behind D18 is the intent and workflow landscape, which measured where the controllers and hubs disagree about what is active.

With more than one server, this commons is what keeps client apps working on all of them. On 2026-09-23 Nocturne (42275c81) matched the 15.0.9 candidate on the count and filter fixes and differed on eight measured behaviours; its own parity suite runs against Nightscout 15.0.3 (consumer impact §6). The model is the one WHATWG uses: several implementations, one living description, and one test suite any of them can run (sponsored-team proposal §6a).

docs.title: 5. Commons B — identity, trust and device access
docs.text:
What exists. Identity today is per site. In cgm-remote-monitor, API_SECRET and tokens are issued by each site. For the multitenant target, each tenant holds its own root credential (D13), each tenant signs its own tokens (D14), and devices and the data path keep a native per-tenant credential permanently (D17). Whether human identity comes from a shared Ory Kratos pool is held on a proof (T30-ORY-PROOF, D17 row 2). Nocturne implements OAuth dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) with a software_id per app and a bundled directory of known apps (Nocturne 42275c81, KnownOAuthClients.cs).

What is proposed here. Several parties need to recognise one another across sites: people, self-hosted sites, hosting providers, researchers, the projects themselves, and organisations that support the ecosystem. A trust federation would let each keep its own identity provider while presenting verifiable claims ("this person is authenticated by organisation X; X is a recognised participant; this service may read fields A and B for purpose P until date D"). The receiving service decides whether the claims meet its own policy. The foundation would define what counts as recognised participation. It would not hold anyone's passwords.

Existing standards cover most of the mechanism:

standard status what it supplies OpenID Federation 1.0 Final, 2026-02-17 trust anchors, signed entity statements and trust chains for multilateral federations over OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0 RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange Standards Track, January 2020 exchanging one token for another scoped to a downstream service, including delegation RFC 7591, Dynamic Client Registration Standards Track app self-registration with a software_id; Nocturne already uses it GA4GH Passport 1.2.1 current signed "visas" carrying a researcher's affiliation, role, accepted terms and data-access grants between institutions

Where data may go. Joining the federation does not mean data may cross every border. The federation would carry identities, keys, schemas, capabilities, consent references and audit identifiers (a shared control plane). Health data would stay in regional stores that apply their own storage, processing and export rules (regional data planes). An approved analysis could run where the data is and return only permitted aggregates. The European Health Data Space Regulation ((EU) 2025/327) entered into force on 26 March 2025; its secondary-use rules begin applying to most data categories in March 2029. Whether and how it applies to Nightscout data or to the foundation is a question for counsel (§9).

Device access. Where a device accepts only clients its manufacturer has authorised, access depends on an agreement and on credentials issued under the manufacturer's authority. The access tiers (observe and export first), the terms that carry data rights, and the safeguards for credentials are in PARTNER-READINESS §2, §4 and §7; who operates a credential authority is §2b's question.

State. No work item and no decision on the federation. The controller-descriptions proposal §2.2 suggests joining on Nocturne's reverse-DNS software_id, which would be a first shared identifier; the registrations of D18 and D19 use reverse-DNS names too.

docs.title: 6. Commons C — evidence: research and quality
docs.text:
What exists.

  • Data pipeline. tools/ns2parquet/ turns Nightscout exports into Parquet with the normalisation written down. tools/nsprobe lets a data holder run this repository's probes on their own data without sending it anywhere, and the collaboration start page invites that.
  • Release evidence and labs. Release comparison already runs for cgm-remote-monitor: the 15.0.9 candidate was soaked against 15.0.8 and replayed through a lab (quality record). The labs under tools/lab/ and tools/review/journey-lab run on synthetic data, and D19 makes a simulated instance a first-class registration.
  • Research. The 2026 experiment campaign (EXP-001 to EXP-3460) and its 488 snapshot reports are summarised in evidence §7.3. The OREF-INV-003 replication (brief) is the first external study built on the pipeline.
  • Research tools across the ecosystem. Analysis tools are built in several places: oref analysis tools by the author of OREF-INV-003 (insulin kinetics, dynamic ISF, smoothing, exercise, a digital twin), GluPredKit, cgmsim-lib and others, listed without ranking in evidence §7.1. What they can share is a contract more than a codebase: the replication's 18-feature, algorithm-neutral feature set scores on par with the 32-feature oref set under folds grouped by person, and any tool, oref or Loop, can compute it from the same normalised data.

What is proposed. The Nightscout datalake proposal asks the board for a 90-day pilot: a named foundation sponsor, a small advisory group, authority to draft consent and access policies, work with hosting providers on consent brokering, monthly reports and a go/no-go decision, at one of three budget levels. It treats the data lake as the first shared service, not the whole programme. Its pilot outputs include a baseline data-quality report (gaps, source coverage, drift), one conformance or release-comparison report, and governed extracts for two or three external researchers. The quality-system proposal adds the shared kit for every row of the stack.

This commons turns the others from one-off checks into a loop: consented data from many sites shows whether a release changed behaviour, whether an uploader started writing malformed records, or whether two implementations read the same field differently, and the findings return to the servers and to commons A as test vectors and defects.

Terms. This page uses post-deployment safety and quality monitoring. It does not claim that the foundation performs regulatory post-market surveillance (§9).

docs.title: 7. Commons D — interfaces for people and agents
docs.text:
What exists.

  • Reports. cgm-remote-monitor's built-in reports and nightscout-reporter's PDF reports read a site; so do research tools such as the oref digital twin and exercise-eval (evidence §7.1). The hub-sync design §4 records that a clinician cannot get a controller's settings from Nightscout: the digital twin reads them from a screenshot or a preference export.
  • A decision-support prototype. tools/cgmencode/production produces a clinical decision support report: a glycemic summary, the main risks, proposed settings changes with their justification, expected outcomes, and criteria for success and for stopping, comparable across AID and injection therapy and rendered for clinicians (38 test files). Clinical review: not started; it needs one before anyone acts on its output (the boundary below). Its published form is a demonstration on synthetic data (markdown): 90 days generated by tools/cgmencode/synthetic_demo_patient.py with a fixed seed, with no real person's data. On that data the prototype detects no inferred meals, because its metabolic engine takes the absolute value of changes in carbs and insulin on board, and it sets a success criterion that expects time in range to fall after its own carb-ratio change. Runs on real data carry health data and are not published.
  • Statistics and agents. The statistics API proposal specifies an MCP resource provider on top of a documented statistics API (REQ-STATS-005, statistics API proposal). Nocturne ships an MCP component. At least six independent MCP servers read a Nightscout site for an assistant; they differ in transport, in the credential they accept and in whether they expose write tools (evidence §7.1).
  • Intent, action and evidence. What a controller meant to do, what it did, and what it was based on now has a typed home in the registrations of commons A (D18's intent kinds and effect fields; D19's instances and provenance).

What is proposed. The work packages on ROADMAP §5: the report statistics as a tested module with a documented API, a first Svelte report usable as a Web Component, and PDF export for sharing with a clinician. Settings as a first-class, effective-dated resource (hub-sync §4.3) would give reports and clinicians the settings in force at any time.

The boundary. An interface that lets software read and explain data is a different thing from one that takes part in a dosing decision. For agents the split is three ways: develop (writing the software), interpret (reading and explaining a person's data) and act (proposing or starting a therapy change), each needing a different assurance; what exists and what is missing for each is mapped in agents in the ecosystem. A report that proposes settings changes is clinician-facing decision support: it needs clinical review before anyone acts on it, the SAFETY reviewer that the queue does not yet name, and counsel's view of its regulatory status (§9). Anything on the dosing side depends on commons A–C: typed schemas, identity and provenance, and longitudinal quality data.

docs.text: part needs makes possible reference implementation (§3) reviewers and releases the behaviour commons A measures; the sites commons C draws on A shared contract the servers' behaviour, client source code, real data; registrations from controllers several servers and many clients working together; typed homes for controller features B identity, trust and device access commons A's identifiers (software_id, reverse-DNS registrations); D13–D17 for hosted sites; manufacturer agreements governed research access; sites recognising one another; reachable devices C evidence commons B for consent and access; commons A for normalised data release comparison, quality signals and research across the ecosystem D interfaces for people and agents commons A–C reports, decision support and agent interfaces with provenance and a safety boundary shared operations (§2c) funding and named owners the accountability manufacturers, clinicians and users ask for

docs.title: 9. The foundation's role, and points to decide
docs.text:
The two proposals already before the board each cover part of this page:

  • the sponsored-team proposal is about people: review, compatibility and security work on the reference implementation and commons A;
  • the datalake proposal is about the first shared service in commons C.

This page adds the frame that joins them: the four commons and the shared operations are shared infrastructure, stewarded by the foundation and open to every implementation, and support for each implementation is a separate, recorded decision.

For the board:

  1. Which commons the foundation takes on as stewardship, and which it leaves to the projects; and whether it adopts the rule in §2b that it sponsors by default and operates only by a recorded decision.
  2. How a proposal for any commons is submitted, reviewed and answered, and where decisions are published. COLLABORATION-MODEL §5 proposes rules for this and for contributions, provider listings and disclosure, each borrowed from an organisation that uses it (Apache, CNCF, OpenStreetMap, OpenMRS, SQLite; §4 there).
  3. Whether to take the datalake pilot and the sponsored team as separate decisions or as one programme with shared reporting, and whether the shared quality kit of the quality-system proposal belongs in it.

For the maintainers of the ecosystem projects:

  1. Whether the six rows and four commons are the right cut, and which shared assets are missing.
  2. Whether the WHATWG pattern (one living description and shared tests) is acceptable to each server's maintainers, with contract changes through a recorded problem-report and change-request process like openEHR's (COLLABORATION-MODEL §5, rule 5).
  3. Whether each controller project would register its own definitions under D18, and which feature it would register first.

For counsel, and for privacy, quality and clinical professionals:

  1. Whether the EHDS, GDPR or HIPAA apply to data a federation participant holds, and to the foundation as a party that defines participation without holding data.
  2. What consent, de-identification and publication review a research extract needs, in each region that contributes data.
  3. Whether post-deployment safety and quality monitoring avoids implying a regulated post-market role, and what the foundation must not claim.
  4. Whether defining recognised participation in a federation creates any liability for the foundation.
  5. Whether a report that proposes settings changes is clinical decision support software that falls under device regulation, and what clinical review it needs before it is offered to anyone. FDA's Clinical Decision Support Software guidance, issued January 29, 2026, states that software functions that support or provide recommendations to patients or caregivers, rather than to health care professionals, meet the definition of a device.

To verify before this page is quoted: the standards' status and dates in §5 were read from their publishers' pages on 2026-09-29. The datalake proposal's terms in §6 were read from its published page the same day. The census figures in §2a are from 2026-09-30. The review load in §3 is a generated table on PROGRAMME-STATUS; quote the current table, not this page. The FDA guidance in §9 item 11 was read from FDA's published PDF on 2026-10-18, and the MCP servers in §7 were counted the same day.
