docs.title: 4. Remedial: fix what ships
docs.text: The remedial work is not a sequence. It is prioritized by what reaches operators today: the operator-exposure table on PROGRAMME-STATUS lists the queue items for defects that are present on 15.0.8. A fix reaches operators only in a release, so each merged fix joins the next step on the release train.

docs.title: 5. Proposals
docs.text:
These are proposals for discussion with other projects and maintainers. None is scheduled in the queue.

Cross-project adoption (hub and spoke). This is a proposal to the controller projects (AAPS, Loop, Trio) and to Nightscout as the hub. Each phase is useful even if the next never happens:

  1. A schema for controller settings documents in the existing v3 settings collection.
  2. Two one-symbol fixes, one in Nocturne and one in NightscoutKit, that stop dosing records being discarded.
  3. A catalogue of controller registrations shipped with the hub.
  4. A read-only sync contract.
  5. Therapy effects, then batched writes, then decomposition.

Nothing in it requires a Loop protocol change. Detail and evidence: adoption roadmap.

Product direction after the modernization baseline. This is a discussion between the maintainers. It proposes these work packages once the modernization branch is accepted:

  • bringing the connector's source in-tree;
  • extracting the report statistics into a tested module and exposing them through a documented API;
  • a first Svelte report (Daily Stats), also usable as a standard Web Component;
  • PDF export for sharing with a clinician;
  • vendor test fixtures shared across projects.

Library and implementation choices are open. Detail: modernization review and proposed next steps.

A shared quality kit for the whole stack. A proposal to every project: vector corpora for device protocols, simulators, fixture suites and a change canary for vendor clouds, a conformance suite any server can run, and one record shape for every test run, built in four stages. It also proposes how requirements that touch several projects are agreed. Detail: quality-system proposal, measured by the stack census.

docs.title: 6. What bounds all of it
docs.text:
Review capacity, not engineering. Most queue items route to the maintainer, and the SECURITY and SAFETY review rows do not name a person. The current split is on PROGRAMME-STATUS. Onboarding for reviewers is in REVIEWER-ONBOARDING.

Generated from queue/work-queue.yaml by tools/queue/emit_views.py. Manifest measured_at 2026-09-27, against cgm-remote-monitor-official 7000eb18 and this repository at 18cdcce0. Every state above is a claim about what the gates will say — make queue-status is the measurement.

docs.title: A sponsored maintenance team for the Nightscout ecosystem — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 174c8e8e5.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after the ecosystem programme; leads to working together. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion. Written 2026-09-27 against this repository at de46efc1 and cgm-remote-monitor official/dev 295f1177; revised through 2026-10-02. The facts it relies on are on the evidence page, and the comparisons in perspective. Where it touches employment, contracting, tax or the foundation's exempt status, it needs review by the foundation's counsel and accountant before any decision rests on it (§9). Nothing here is decided.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under this proposal. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The request
docs.text:
Fund a small, fulltime, paid team whose job is to keep the Nightscout ecosystem's shared software reviewed, released and working with the apps that depend on it. The team works alongside the volunteer maintainers and contributors, answers to the foundation for the time it is paid for, and takes no authority away from any project.

Long-standing maintainers of the ecosystem projects have asked the foundation for this. [To confirm before this is shared: whether the maintainers who made the request agree to be named here.]

docs.title: 1a. What is at stake
docs.text:
The facts this section relies on are on the evidence page; the history is in HISTORY.

Open-source AID has published evidence behind it. It improved time in range over pump therapy in a randomised trial and, in real-world comparisons, matched or exceeded commercial systems on time in range, with differences in time below range that matter for some people (evidence §6, with each study's caveats).

The assets grew in the open, over more than ten years, across 62 repositories from device drivers to vendor-cloud connectors, most of them in GitHub organisations run by volunteers or under personal accounts (evidence §1). A foundation taking stewardship responsibility for these assets is how the software behind that evidence keeps working, and how new evidence can be built on it.

Today the cost falls on people with diabetes and individual maintainers. Their own time pays for the review, releases, vendor changes and security response of §3. After the xz-utils backdoor in 2024, CISA wrote that "the burden of security shouldn't fall on an individual open source maintainer" (PRECEDENTS: histories). Full-time stewards funded by the foundation would move that cost off the people the software serves.

Better evidence needs a shared commons. Which system does better, for whom and in which circumstances (children, pregnancy, exercise, different pumps and sensors, different settings) is the question the published studies cannot yet answer. The Nightscout datalake proposal is the route to that evidence. It proposes consented data from many sites, governed research extracts, and a methods-review step before any clinical claim is published. Its current pilot outputs are a data-quality report, a release-comparison report and extracts for two or three researchers. Its research agenda lists comparative outcome studies across systems as a later use of the same commons, with what a comparison needs before it is published: a registered protocol, a design that accounts for who chooses which system, aggregate results only, and review by the maintainers of each system compared. The OHDSI network's rule (data stays at each site; only aggregate results are shared, PRECEDENTS) is one tested model. The team in §4 keeps the software and records such studies rely on; it does not run the studies or make clinical claims.

docs.title: 2. Why now
docs.text:
The ecosystem depends on one shared server. Many other apps read and write their data through it, and a change there reaches every one of them; a second server implements the same API (evidence §2).

Releases have come in long gaps, here and across the ecosystem. Every main project has had gaps of similar length in the same years, and in cgm-remote-monitor the number of people committing fell before releases slowed (evidence §3). A gap in one project's history, read on its own, says little about the diligence of the people who maintain it. Set beside the others and the contributor counts, it reads as the same work carried by fewer people. Each project's maintainers are the right people to say what held their releases (§9).

Important work can wait for years. The MongoDB 5 driver upgrade was first proposed in 2022 and shipped in 2026, while hosting providers retire old database versions on their own schedule (evidence §3).

Much of the coming work is already dated. Between now and the end of 2027 the ecosystem meets Apple's medical-device status declaration, Xcode 27, Android developer verification for all installations, Node 22 and Heroku-22 end of life, and MongoDB 7.0 end of life, each on the vendor's calendar, not a volunteer's (evidence §5).

2026 shows what steady attention produces. Five releases so far this year, and a 15.0.9 candidate built, tested and recorded in four weeks (how 15.0.9 was made).

docs.title: 3. Where the time goes
docs.text:
Much of the engineering in 2026 was done with AI coding agents under a maintainer's direction. That changed what limits progress. Writing a fix is now the cheap part. The steps that still need a person are the ones this proposal would fund: review, specialist security and safety review, decisions, hand checks, checks on real client systems, dependency-alert triage and the backlog (evidence §4; the current review load is the generated table on PROGRAMME-STATUS).

Today all of this depends on a few people. Some of them are paid for part of their time by the commercial hosts they work for, on terms each host sets, and those arrangements differ in scope, availability and the compliance obligations each host carries. No one is paid to do this work for the ecosystem as a whole, on published terms, with a public report. When those few people's time runs short, the work waits.

docs.title: 4. What the team would do
docs.text:
A starting shape. The board and maintainers would settle the final one.

role what it does why it is needed Release and review lead reviews pull requests, keeps the release process running on a published schedule, tags releases with the maintainers review and release are where work waits (§3) Ecosystem compatibility engineer keeps the census of client apps current; runs the real-system checks with Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS and xDrip+ builders; turns what clients actually send into tests; watches the vendor clouds the connectors log into and keeps a connector test lab that any server can use a server change reaches every client (§2), and a vendor change reaches every server (§6a) Quality and security lead (part time at first) triages security reports and dependency alerts, keeps the defect register and test records, is the named reviewer for security and safety items the SECURITY and SAFETY items in the reviewer-load table name a kind of reviewer, and most name no individual

Beyond cgm-remote-monitor, the stack census estimates a shared quality kit for the device drivers and vendor-cloud connectors at 167–388 person-weeks one-time and 0.4–0.7 of a full-time engineer after that (estimates, with their assumptions). The quality-system proposal sets out what that kit contains and which parts volunteers can do alone.

Out of scope for the team:

  • It does not decide what a project accepts. Each project's maintainers keep the merge decision.
  • It does not change project governance or licences.
  • It does not give therapy or dosing advice.

docs.title: 5. How it fits with volunteers
docs.text:
• Maintainers keep authority. The team proposes and reviews; each project's maintainers decide what merges, as now.
  • Paid time goes to the work volunteers find hardest to sustain: review queues, release chores, compatibility testing, security triage. New features stay open to everyone.
  • Everything happens in public. The team works in the same repositories, issue trackers and chat as everyone else, and publishes a short monthly report.
  • The team makes it easier to contribute. Reviews happen faster, and the release schedule is published, so a contributor knows when their fix will ship.

docs.title: 6. How other open-source organisations do this
docs.text:
How Zig, the Haskell Foundation, CNCF, WHATWG, W3C, the PSF, the Sovereign Tech Fellowship, OpenStreetMap and SQLite fund and staff their work is in PRECEDENTS: how other organisations fund and staff the work, read from each organisation's own pages and IRS Form 990 summaries. What this proposal takes from them:

  • Where paid staff exist, the volunteer or project maintainers keep technical authority; §5 keeps it so here.
  • Money tied to one sponsor or a few donors is the usual weak point; option C and E (§7) spread it.
  • The smallest organisations that pay for code (Zig, the PSF residencies) spend almost all of it on engineering; §4 is three engineering roles.
  • Companies that build on the commons pay for work and assurance, not for control, and commercial offerings prove they track the same upstream with the same public tests; the rules that would keep it so here are in COLLABORATION-MODEL §5.

docs.title: 6a. More than one server
docs.text:
Nightscout is no longer the only server that speaks its API. Nocturne is a second implementation, with its own design and visual language, so for operators it is an alternative, and choosing it is each operator's decision (evidence §2).

A second server makes this proposal more necessary, not less:

  • Client apps depend on behaviour, not on which server provides it. The two servers already differ on eight measured behaviours, and Nocturne's parity suite targets an older Nightscout. A shared, current description of the API and a test suite that any server can run keep the apps working on both. This is the WHATWG pattern in §6: several implementations, one living standard, and shared tests.
  • Building a server and keeping one current are different jobs. Volunteers built both servers. Keeping them current includes work whose timing neither project sets: the vendor clouds that the CGM and pump connectors log into. When a vendor changes its service, glucose data stops arriving at the site until a fix ships. Both servers carry connectors for the same vendors, so each vendor change reaches both (evidence §5). A second server adds implementations of this work; it does not remove the work or let anyone schedule it. A connector test lab and one person watching the vendor clouds (§4) would serve both.
  • The existing sites still need maintenance. Moving to another server is a migration each operator chooses. Until they choose it, their site needs the releases, security fixes and driver upgrades described in §2.
  • The roles in §4 serve the whole ecosystem. The compatibility engineer and the quality and security lead would keep the client census, the conformance tests and the security triage open to every implementation.

docs.title: 7. Options
docs.text:
option what it is first-year cost trade-off A. Release and review lead only one person, fulltime [board to fill in] smallest step; one person is still a single point of failure B. The three roles in §4 two fulltime, one part time [board to fill in] covers review, compatibility and security; needs sustained funding C. Grant-funded fixed term option A or B for 12–18 months from a grant per grant tests the model before a long-term commitment; ends when the grant ends D. No change volunteers, and the part-time paid arrangements individual hosts make (§3) none to the foundation keeps today's pattern of long release gaps; the requirements others ask of the server (release schedule, security response, vendor changes) stay with whoever has time E. Companies pay for assurance hosts and companies that build on Nightscout buy release evidence for their own quality systems, fixes on the release line they run, or test runs in their configuration, on published terms (collaboration rule 8); the money funds A or B depends on demand evidence and fixes stay public, so free users get the same releases; needs buyers, and adds the counsel questions in COLLABORATION-MODEL §8

Option E can be combined with A, B or C. The board fills in the costs (§9). For reference, the Sovereign Tech Fellowship pays €64k–€82k a year for an employed two-year post, and Zig paid $460,625 to its contractors and one employee in 2024 (§6).

docs.title: 8. How we would know it works
docs.text:
Measured the same way as the 15.0.9 record, and reported every quarter:

  • time from a pull request opening to its first review, and to merge or close;
  • time from a merge to the release that ships it;
  • releases per year, and whether they follow the published schedule;
  • the open-issue and open-PR backlog, and the age of the oldest items;
  • how many client apps are checked against each release on real systems;
  • how many security reports are acknowledged and resolved within the published window.

docs.title: 9. Points for reviewers to verify
docs.text:
For counsel and the accountant:

  1. Whether the team members are employees or contractors. This affects classification, taxes, benefits and jurisdiction, since the maintainers do not all live in one country.
  2. Whether paying developers who also volunteer on the same projects raises any private-benefit or conflict-of-interest issue for a 501(c)(3). What conflict-of-interest policy would cover it?
  3. Whether restricted grants or corporate sponsorship impose conditions that could affect project independence, and how to disclose them.
  4. How work paid for by the foundation is licensed and owned, so that it stays under each project's existing open-source licence.
  5. The figures in §6 come from the organisations' pages and ProPublica 990 summaries (the Zig figures were re-read from the source on 2026-09-27). Confirm each against the underlying 990 before quoting it. Not verified: WHATWG editors' employment, and whether the Haskell Foundation merger has completed.

For the board:

  1. Cost ranges for options A–C, which funding sources to approach, and whether to test demand for option E with the hosting providers (COLLABORATION-MODEL decision 6).
  2. Who the team reports to, and how the maintainers take part in hiring and reviews.

For a clinician or clinical researcher:

  • Whether §1a summarises the four studies fairly, including their comparators, the time-below-range difference in the Canadian study and the selection of participants; whether other studies (for example of Trio, or head-to-head comparisons published since) belong beside them; and what study designs a comparative analysis on the research commons would need before any result is published.

For the maintainers:

  1. Whether the three roles in §4 are the right ones.
  2. Whether the success measures in §8 are the right ones.
  3. For the AndroidAPS, Loop, Trio and xDrip+ maintainers: whether §2's release gaps and contributor counts describe their projects fairly, and what held their releases.

Assumptions this draft makes:

  • the foundation can hold restricted funds for this purpose;
  • the maintainers would take part in hiring;
  • the team would work in public, like any other contributor.

docs.title: Why organise: an accountable party for the ecosystem, and why now — proposal
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 060287245.

What this is: a proposal (part 3 of the overview, recommendations; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after partner readiness; leads to the work itself, starting with reviewer onboarding. DRAFT PROPOSAL for discussion. Living page, written 2026-10-17. It draws together evidence from partner readiness, what we believe, and how it works, the vendor note and the evidence page. Its characterisations of law are drafts for the foundation's counsel, and of regulation for a regulatory professional, before anything rests on them (§9). Nothing here is decided.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the related proposals. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The claim
docs.text: Open-source diabetes software reaches devices and vendor clouds today through routes that no one in the ecosystem is accountable for and no one can renew. Newer devices move the key to the manufacturer, and access has already been lost or delayed for whole device generations. Every route that could replace today's, for more than one person or for any command, needs a party that can sign an agreement, take complaints, hold insurance and answer for a service. No such party exists in the ecosystem today. Organising one takes years, and the dates that matter fall in 2027.

docs.title: 2. How access works today
docs.text:
The access ladder places each device line by how much an open app depends on its manufacturer. Each placement was read in the drivers' code on 2026-10-17 and is recorded in tools/structure-diagrams/access/devices.yaml.

step what an open app needs device lines who is accountable for the access A the protocol, plus what the person has: a code, a serial, the device itself Omnipod Eros and DASH, Medtronic 5xx/7xx, Tandem t:slim X2 and Mobi, Dana RS/i, Medtrum Nano, Dexcom G6, Libre 1/2, Eversense E3, Accu-Chek SmartGuide no one; the protocol was worked out by volunteers B the manufacturer's own app running alongside G7 passive mode, Medtronic 640G/670G and several CGMs through companion apps no one; it lasts while the manufacturer's app tolerates it C a credential through the person's own account Eversense 365 the manufacturer's service, at its discretion D the device checks the app Dexcom G7, Libre 3, MiniMed 780G, Omnipod 5 no one; open apps present credentials the manufacturer did not issue to them E readings sealed for the manufacturer's cloud none found; not looked for —

Open Omnipod 5 support currently depends on a community-run certificate service. A service that therapy depends on needs a named operator, a contract, insurance and a successor (programme §2b).

Beside the devices, the vendor-cloud path that Nightscout's connectors use logs in as the person, under terms that ban unauthorised apps, and it breaks when the cloud changes (evidence §5). The legal cover in the US is the copyright exemption for device data: a defence for data access only, renewed every three years, which does not cover commands or the distribution of circumvention tools (vendor note §3.4).

What each path's loss would mean, for the person and for caregivers, is in partner readiness §1.

docs.title: 3. Access already lost or delayed
docs.text:
The access-loss log dates 34 events from public commits, issues and vendor pages: 11 on devices and 23 on vendor clouds.

Devices.

  • Medtronic pumps after the Paradigm series were never openly controllable. The 530G (2013), the 600 series (read only, through companion apps or CareLink) and the 770G/780G have no open control driver; the 780G work that began in 2026 is a proof of concept "not for therapy". The openly controllable Paradigm family was the subject of an FDA cybersecurity communication in 2019 that recommended replacing it (read through press coverage).
  • Access to newer generations arrived years late, through volunteer reimplementation. From clearance or first launch to open support:
  • Omnipod DASH: 32 months to the first AndroidAPS code, 55 months to a Loop release.
  • Dexcom G7: 5 months to direct pairing in xDrip+, 47 months to Loop's development branch. Loop and Trio releases still listen alongside Dexcom's app.
  • Libre 3: up to 27 months, on Android.
  • Omnipod 5: 49 months, on a development branch only.
  • Some routes were removed. Abbott sent GitHub takedown notices for patched-app projects in 2019 (two), 2021 and 2023 (two).

Vendor clouds.

  • 23 breakages since 2020: LibreLinkUp 8, Tandem 6, CareLink 4, Dexcom Share 3, Glooko 1, and Dexcom's channel to Sugarmate 1. Eleven were fixed in at least one connector within seven days. Five are unfixed or only partly mitigated, including CareLink's move to a new sign-in that blocks automated logins (2026). Nightscout's own connector took 11 months to follow LibreLinkUp's October 2025 change that another connector met before the deadline, and its Glooko source was broken for about 15 months.
  • The one restoration that came through an agreement went to a company. When Dexcom closed the channel Sugarmate used in November 2021, Sugarmate's data came back through Dexcom's partner API within weeks in the US. Its Nightscout bridge, which had no agreement, never came back.
  • The next change is already shipping. LibreLinkUp's app 5.0 (April 2026) uses a new interface whose responses connectors cannot read. The older interface still works, and no date for switching it off has been found.

No source records how many people any of these events reached (§8).

docs.title: 4. Where newer devices are going
docs.text:
Manufacturers' own systems are moving setup online. From their public documents, read 2026-10-17 (cloud-pairing census):

  • Every phone app read for a current CGM line needs a manufacturer account at first setup: Dexcom, Abbott, Eversense, Roche and Sibionics. Dedicated receivers and readers are documented without one. On the pump side, the MiniMed Mobile, Tandem, Omnipod 5 and CamAPS FX (YpsoPump) apps and controllers also start with an account sign-in.
  • Three lines say the setup or pairing step itself needs the internet: Dexcom ONE+, Eversense 365, and CamAPS FX.
  • One manufacturer documents a credential its app delivers for another's device. Beta Bionics' iLet app "loads certificates required to enable Dexcom G7 features"; where they come from is not stated. A partner's product meets the G7 app check with certificates its own app loads; open software meets the same check with a credential no one issued to it (§2).

What a manufacturer's app needs at setup does not decide whether an open app can reach the device: "account at setup" appears on step A and step D alike. What the record shows is the direction: accounts and online steps at setup, and app checks met by partners through issued certificates. How many devices still on sale sit on step A, and for how long, is not known (§8).

docs.title: 5. Every replacement route needs an accountable party
docs.text:
route what it requires for whom it works a written agreement with a manufacturer (tiers A–C, partner readiness §2) a legal entity, named contacts, security response, complaint handling, insurance, and terms both sides sign (§3–§5) everyone the agreement covers the FDA's interoperable routes (iCGM, ACE pump, iAGC) a manufacturer with a quality system, and contracts that assign complaint duties (vendor note §2); Tidepool, a non-profit, took this route from 2020 to 2023 (precedents) users of the cleared product credentials issued under the manufacturer's authority an operator with its own contract, security controls, insurance and successor (partner readiness §7) everyone the operator serves a vendor's published developer route Dexcom's is the only one found: a registered developer, five people for an individual, a non-negotiable agreement beyond that, and readings one to three hours late (vendor note §1.2) display and research; not automated insulin delivery an EU Data Act request by a third party the person names an organisation that meets Art. 6's conditions and the GDPR (vendor note §5.3) EU users; data only an EU Data Act request by the person for their own data nothing institutional one person at a time, in the EU; data only; untested for CGM data

The last row is the one route that needs no organisation, and it carries data only, in one jurisdiction. The requirements in the other rows are the same for anyone who meets them; a non-profit has no advantage in meeting them (what each activity brings §5).

docs.title: 6. Why now
docs.text:
when what what it means for access to 2027-10-28 the 10th triennial rulemaking decides whether the device-data exemption continues (vendor note §3.4) renewal comments are stronger with dated, counted cases (§3); none are recorded in that form today since 2026-09-12 the EU Data Act's design duty for connected products placed on the market from that date (vendor note §3.1) devices launching now are the first that must be designed for access; the right is untested for diabetes data early 2027 Apple requires health apps to declare whether they are a regulated device (evidence §5) reaches every person who builds an app under their own developer record 2027 Android developer verification extends to all installs (evidence §5) reaches every AndroidAPS and xDrip+ builder 2026–2027 MiniMed separated from Medtronic (2026-10-15); Diabeloop's algorithm on twiist for a 2027 US launch (vendor note §1.4, §1.7) partner terms are being set between companies now lead time the one regulated route a community project took ran 2020–2023 a start in 2026 lands near 2029

Interpretation. None of these dates is a crisis on its own. Together with §2–§4 they mean that the routes in §5 take longer to open than the routes in §2 are likely to last, and the dates by which evidence and an accountable party would help fall in 2027.

docs.title: 7. What organising means here
docs.text:
Organising does not mean the foundation running devices' credentials or anyone's therapy. The proposals already before the board divide the work by role:

  • The foundation sponsors and oversees. It pays for, convenes and sets the rules for shared work, and operates a service only by a recorded decision that names the operator, its contract, its insurance and its successor (programme §2b). A credential service needs an operator of its own; issuance has standing only under the manufacturer's authority (partner readiness §7).
  • An accountable counterparty signs. A manufacturer agreement needs a legal entity with named contacts, security response, complaint handling and insurance. In practice that is usually a company; the foundation's role is the oversight layer above it (what each activity brings §5; drawn in 2·agreement and 2·controller-operator).
  • The projects keep their code and their roadmaps. Paying for shared work buys no control over any project (collaboration rules rule 2).

The steps that cost little and produce the evidence the rest depends on can start now (partner readiness §8):

  1. a shared intake that records each access loss: the device or cloud, the date, how long it lasted and how many people and projects it reached;
  2. a security contact and private vulnerability reporting for each project;
  3. one EU Data Act request, made by a person for their own real-time CGM data, to learn how a manufacturer answers;
  4. one tier A request to one manufacturer, to learn what it requires;
  5. the readiness dossier of partner readiness §3, kept current.

An accountable counterparty, its insurance, and any agreement follow from what those steps show.

docs.title: 7a. What the FDA has asked for, and an entity that takes it on in stages
docs.text:
What the record shows. The FDA's statements to and about the community, gathered in process models, 0·diy-status, name the same things from 2014 to now. The 2014 pre-submission meeting with Nightscout contributors recorded that device regulations apply, that "some entity be responsible for assuring the safety and effectiveness of the device and that postmarket safety is adequately monitored", and that the FDA believed the requirements could be met "even with non-traditional methods of development"; it asked for a gap analysis and a follow-up meeting. It asked whether update tracking would scale to 10,000 or 50,000 users, and three questions: who checks that changes are tested against the design, who collects details when things go wrong, and who is ultimately responsible. In 2016 an FDA official said such systems fall under FDA jurisdiction, that enforcement is based on risk, with one person low and thousands higher, and that responsibility for adverse events and failures is the agency's biggest concern. Payment was not named as a factor; scale and responsibility were. The communities now number, by the Foundation's estimate, 10,000 or more people, perhaps up to 60,000: the scale the 2014 question named.

Discretion is not the only limit. Even if the FDA's use of discretion never changes, devices are moving to checks that the app reaching them holds a credential the manufacturer issued or authorised (step D, §2), and the credentials that meet those checks go to partners (§4). On those devices open software works today only by presenting credentials the manufacturer did not issue to it, a route no one is accountable for and no one can renew (§2). The routes that can last are those of §5, and each of them asks for what the FDA and manufacturers have already asked for: a responsible party, complaint and adverse-event handling, change control and security response. The community has treated meeting these requirements as a cost to avoid. For devices that check the app, meeting them is the route that can last.

The proposal. Enforcement discretion is not a permission, and it can change. It does leave time in which the factors the FDA named, an accountable party, complaint and adverse-event handling, change control, and the reach of updates, can be put in place by an entity before any route of §5 requires them, and before more devices close the routes of §2. The proposal is that a legal entity takes these on in stages, each with a recorded start, a scope and a condition for moving on or stopping. It is the 2014 gap analysis, carried out:

stage what the entity does what it does not do moves on when 0. shared functions, no entity yet a shared complaint intake with severity triage (partner readiness §6); a MedWatch link on each project's pages, as the FDA welcomed in 2014; a measure of how many people run each version hold anyone's responsibility; distribute builds the intake has run long enough to show volume and kinds of report 1. incubation becomes the named party for the shared functions, for the projects that opt in; writes and publishes the gap analysis against the quality-system, complaint and reporting requirements; answers platform declarations such as Apple's early-2027 regulated-device question where it holds the developer record take over any project's code or roadmap (collaboration rules rule 2); claim that discretion covers what it does the gap analysis is reviewed by a regulatory professional, and each participating project has chosen a route 2. a route per project for each project that chooses one: a manufacturer agreement (partner readiness), a submission on the interoperable routes, as Tidepool did from 2020 to 2023 (precedents), or staying DIY with the shared functions choose for a project the route is open, or the project declines it

The entity can be a company or a non-profit; the requirements are the same for either (what each activity brings §5). The foundation's part follows programme §2b: it can sponsor stage 0 and oversee the entity, and it operates only by a recorded decision.

Options.

  • No change. Each project and person carries the position as today. The 2014 and 2016 questions stay unanswered as the communities grow, and each device that checks the app is reachable only through a credential no one issued to the open software (§2).
  • Stage 0 only. The foundation sponsors the shared functions. No entity takes responsibility, so the FDA's central question, who is responsible, is not answered.
  • Stages 0 and 1. An incubating entity, with stage 2 decided project by project later.
  • All three stages for one project first, chosen with its maintainers, before any others join.

What it would not change. It does not make a personal build exempt, it does not lower any requirement of §5, and it does not by itself obtain a credential: a manufacturer still decides whether to issue or authorise one (partner readiness §7). Whether taking on these functions changes how the FDA weighs its discretion, and in which direction, is for a regulatory professional (§9); so is whether the entity takes on a manufacturer's duties by doing so.

docs.title: 8. What this page does not show
docs.text:
• When today's open devices leave supply. End-of-sale and coverage dates for the step A devices have not been collected. They set how long the routes in §2 last.
  • How many people each loss reached. No outage has been counted (§7, step 1).
  • How the FDA would view an incubating entity. No meeting since 2014 is on record here, and the 2014 follow-up meeting and gap analysis are not known to have taken place.
  • Whether manufacturers would agree. No request by the foundation or the projects is on record; whether one was ever made should be confirmed with the maintainers.

docs.title: 9. Points for reviewers to verify
docs.text:
• The law in §2, §5 and §6 is summarised from the vendor note; its own review points (vendor note §7) apply here, in particular the device-data exemption's scope (points 6, 7 and 16) and the Data Act's reach to CGM data (points 1–4).
  • The step placements in §2 were read in code, not run against devices.
  • §7a: whether an entity that takes on complaint intake, triage and update tracking for DIY projects (a) changes how the FDA weighs enforcement discretion, and in which direction, (b) takes on a manufacturer's duties under 21 CFR 803, 806 or 820 by doing so, and (c) can answer Apple's regulated-device declaration for apps built under its developer record; and whether a new pre-submission is the way to raise the gap analysis with the FDA. The FDA record §7a relies on is listed with its own review points in process models, 0·diy-status.
  • The dates in §6 come from the evidence page and the vendor note; re-read them before the page is quoted outside the ecosystem.

docs.title: Mission: aligning data across the Nightscout ecosystem
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at c10adf924.

What this is: a reference (contributor-facing). Read after reviewer onboarding; leads to programme status.

docs.title: What Alignment Is
docs.text:
Alignment is a coordination effort to establish shared semantics, schemas, and conformance criteria across multiple Automated Insulin Delivery (AID) systems and their supporting infrastructure.

The goal is to enable:

  • Interoperability: Data from any AID system (Loop, AAPS, Trio) can be understood and processed by any compliant server (Nightscout, Tidepool, etc.)
  • Traceability: Every piece of AID data can be traced from its origin through transformations to its final representation
  • Consistency: The same concepts (profiles, overrides, treatments, etc.) mean the same thing across all systems

docs.title: What Alignment Is Not
docs.text:
• A replacement for any existing project's internal data model
  • A mandate that projects must change their implementations
  • A single source of truth that overrides project-specific decisions

Instead, alignment provides:

  • A reference schema that projects can map to
  • Conformance tests that verify correct mapping
  • Documentation that explains the rationale behind semantic choices

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This workspace covers:

Area In Scope Out of Scope Data semantics Event types, fields, relationships UI/UX decisions Schemas JSON Schema, OpenAPI definitions Internal storage formats Conformance Test scenarios, assertions Performance benchmarks Mapping How each project interprets specs Implementation guidance

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Alignment is successful when:

  1. A new AID event type can be defined once and understood by all projects
  2. Data exported from one system can be imported into another without loss of semantic meaning
  3. Gaps and ambiguities are explicitly documented rather than discovered through bugs

What this is: a measurement (part 1 of the overview, observations; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after governance today; leads to part 2, perspective. Living page, assembled 2026-10-02 against this repository at e3d7b65c; §7 added 2026-10-16 at 66403e0f; §7.1's agent tools and MCP servers checked 2026-10-18 at 5a9a49cc. Each section names the date and the source or command of its figures; where a figure lives in a generated table or a record, this page links to that one home instead of copying it. docs.title: 1. What the ecosystem consists of
docs.text:
The stack census of 2026-09-30 listed 63 repositories (62 distinct; one fork is kept level with its upstream), from device drivers to vendor-cloud connectors, servers, followers and reports:

  • 56 of the 62 had commits in the last year, by 219 distinct human authors.
  • 13 of the 63 listings are held under personal GitHub accounts; most of the rest sit in GitHub organisations run by volunteers.
  • 14 device protocols have 41 independent implementations; for 10 of them no two implementations test against the same bytes.
  • Six code bases log in to Dexcom Share and five to LibreLinkUp.
  • There are more than 35,000 test declarations across the stack. CI runs tests in 14 of the 62 repositories, and no device or connector repository publishes a per-release test report.
  • In 25 of the 56 repositories with human commits in the year, one author made 80% or more of them. This describes where the knowledge sits, not the quality of the work.

Per-layer and per-repository figures, and the method, are in the census record.

docs.title: 2. What depends on the shared server
docs.text:
Client apps. Nightscout is a secondary display for CGM and pump data, and it is also where many other apps read and write that data. The 15.0.9 client survey mapped 40 client repositories against 15 parts of the API (consumer impact). Loop, Trio, AndroidAPS, xDrip+, caregiver apps, watch faces and reporting tools rely on how the server behaves.

A second server. Nocturne (nightscout/nocturne) is a second implementation of the API, in .NET with PostgreSQL, with its own web interface and visual language. xDrip+ ships an uploader for it (adoption roadmap). Its typed event model is used as a reference in this repository's data-model work (primitive coverage). On 2026-09-23 Nocturne (42275c81, v0.2.x) matched the 15.0.9 candidate on the count and filter fixes and differed on eight measured behaviours; its parity suite runs against Nightscout 15.0.3 (consumer impact §6).

Existing sites. Operators run cgm-remote-monitor on MongoDB, with their own settings, data and hosting. A move to another server is a migration each operator chooses.

docs.title: 6. Published clinical evidence for open-source AID
docs.text:
Abstracts read on PubMed, 2026-09-30. A clinician or clinical researcher should check this summary before it is relied on.

study design what it found caveats the authors state or the design implies CREATE (Burnside et al., NEJM 2022;387:869–881) randomised controlled trial, 97 children and adults, 24 weeks; AndroidAPS 2.8 with the OpenAPS 0.7.0 algorithm against a sensor-augmented pump time in range rose from 61.2% to 71.2% with AID and fell from 57.7% to 54.5% in the control group (adjusted difference 14 percentage points, 95% CI 9.2–18.8); no severe hypoglycaemia or DKA in either group the comparator was a pump without automation, not a commercial AID system; two AID participants withdrew because of connectivity issues Loop observational study (Lum et al., Diabetes Technol Ther 2021;23:367–375) prospective, real-world, 558 adults and children, 6 months time in range rose from 67% to 73%; time below 54 mg/dL fell slightly people who chose to start Loop themselves; no control group Canadian comparison (Wu et al., Diabetes Technol Ther 2025;27:517–526) prospective, observational non-inferiority study, 26 open-source and 52 commercial AID users, 12 weeks open-source non-inferior on 24-hour time in range (78.3% against 71.2%) open-source users spent more time below 3.9 mmol/L (3.9% against 1.8%, "yet within the recommended range"); not randomised Systematic review (Knoll et al., Diabet Med 2022;39:e14741) 21 real-world studies, 2018–2021 improvements "observed in open-source and commercially developed AID systems alike" real-world studies; most were of one commercial system

Open-source AID improved time in range over pump therapy in one randomised trial. In real-world comparisons it matched or exceeded commercial systems on time in range, with differences in time below range. No randomised head-to-head trial against commercial AID systems is among the studies read here. The people in the real-world studies chose these systems themselves; the authors of one comparison describe them as "a very selected group of people" (Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology, 2024). Which system does better, for whom and in which circumstances is a question these studies do not answer.

docs.title: 7.3 The 2026 experiment campaign
docs.text: From January to July 2026 this repository ran numbered experiments, EXP-001 to EXP-3460 (ls tools/cgmencode | grep -oE '_[0-9]{4}\.py$' | sort | tail -1), on Nightscout data held in the workspace and not in the repository: glucose forecasting, event detection, a supply-and-demand decomposition of glucose, insulin pharmacodynamics, settings extraction and therapy analysis. Its 488 reports are in docs/60-research/, with an index and an overview of 2026-04-07. The reports are snapshots: each gives results as of its date, and later experiments revised some of them. The largest revision concerns evaluation. Cross-validation that shuffled rows mixed each person's data across training and test folds; with folds grouped by person, every feature set compared scores a 4-hour hypoglycaemia AUC of 0.67 to 0.69 (EXP-2519, replication brief).

docs.title: 8. Limits of this page
docs.text:
• The release and contributor tables are from 2026-09-29 and the clones named; author counts are by email, so one person under two addresses counts twice.
  • The maintenance-time rows dated 2026-09-27 are a snapshot; the generated tables they link to are current.
  • Vendor dates marked "announced" or "estimated" will move.
  • Nothing here measures user numbers, installations or outcomes beyond the studies cited.
  • The agent-tool and MCP-server rows of §7.1 are read from READMEs and source on 2026-10-18; none was run against a site.

docs.title: 4. The shared documentation's provider listing
docs.text: The Nightscout documentation's "Nightscout as a Service" section lists nine hosted providers, each linking to its own site (nightscout/nightscout.github.io, branch source, docs/index.md, last changed at 9b5afad2 on 2026-08-07). Its introduction: "If you want to save time and avoid the need to maintain a DIY solution, you have many providers." Providers are added by pull request; the two most recent additions (#247, 2026-03-13, and #249, 2026-05-24) were merged with no review recorded. The repository publishes no criteria for being listed and no rule for the order. The first entry is the company founded by this repository's author.

docs.title: 5. Where the foundation's statements and the repositories differ
docs.text:
• The FAQ says the code "will continue to be available under a GPL". The repositories in §1 carry AGPL-3.0, GPL-2.0, GPL-3.0, MIT and BSD licences, and four carry no licence file; two of the MIT repositories (Trio, minimed-connect-to-nightscout) are in the nightscout organisation.
  • The purpose statement on the homepage begins "support the creation of technological solutions"; the about page says "open source technology projects".
  • One board member is "President" on the leadership page and "(Chair)" on the FAQ.

docs.title: 6. Where we looked and found nothing
docs.text:
• Foundation decision records. The 18 pages linked from nightscoutfoundation.org, its awards page, and the 24 non-blog paths in its sitemap.xml: no meeting minutes, annual reports, financial statements, decision records, grant policy or sponsorship policy. The resource-request page names no committee members and no review criteria.
  • Financial filings. ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer has no Form 990 data for EIN 47-2130306.
  • Repository governance files. As in §2, searched at the root, .github/ and docs/ of each of the 20 repositories and through GitHub's community-profile endpoint.
  • Provider listing criteria. The documentation's provider section and every .md file in that repository, searched for listing criteria or instructions.
  • A shared body for decisions that cross projects. None is named on the foundation's pages or in the governance files above.

docs.title: 7. What only the foundation can supply
docs.text:
These are not public, or not readable without signing in. The page records them as open, not as absent:

  1. Whether the bylaws and the conflict-of-interest policy are meant to be public, and if so a readable copy.
  2. Who sits on the resource-request committee, what it weighs, and where its decisions are recorded.
  3. How spending is approved, and whether a yearly summary of income and spending is published.
  4. Which domains, accounts, repositories and marks the foundation holds, and which belong to individuals or other organisations.
  5. How a sponsorship or partnership is agreed, and where it is recorded.

docs.title: 5. Where sources differ, and what is not established
docs.text:
Sources that differ.

  • When the foundation began. Its FAQ gives incorporation in October 2014; the IRS exemption is dated April 2015. These are different events, incorporation and the IRS ruling; no state filing was read.
  • First commit and repository date. Several repositories carry history older than the repository itself: cgm-remote-monitor (code from 2013, repository 2014), AndroidAPS (code 2016, nightscout repository 2020), minimed-connect-to-nightscout (code 2015, nightscout repository 2020) and Trio (FreeAPS X history from 2021, repository 2024). The tables give both dates; neither is a founding date.
  • The ACE pump date. The FDA press release and original order are dated 2019-02-14; a letter of 2019-12-03 corrects that classification order.
  • The #WeAreNotWaiting origin. D-Data calls its 2013 meeting the hashtag's birthplace; the foundation's homepage describes the foundation as the movement's beginning. This is a difference in characterisation, not in dates.

Not established from a primary source, so not dated above: the origin of the name Nightscout and its first public announcement; when Dexcom Share and Abbott LibreLinkUp launched; when mLab shut down entirely (only the Heroku add-on removal is sourced); Azure's free-tier history for Nightscout.

docs.title: Accountability thresholds: the duties each activity brings
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 1efa2b753.

What this is: an analysis (part 2 of the overview, perspective; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after precedents: how other organisations are funded, staffed and governed; leads to who controls what. Living page, written 2026-10-16 against this repository at faafc57c as "Accountability as an organisation grows"; widened and retitled 2026-10-17 to cover every entity in the control structures, not only the foundation. It sets out which duties arrive with each asset an organisation holds and each activity it takes on, how mature programmes put those duties in place, and the conditions under which a US nonprofit takes on new legal, financial and insurance duties. Where it interprets, it says so. It makes no request. The evidence for §4 is in two research notes of 2026-10-17: Apple's developer program and vendor programmes and data rights.

It is a draft that needs review by the foundation's accountant (§6), counsel and an insurance broker (§3, §4, §5) and, for anything touching insulin delivery, a regulatory professional, before anything rests on it. Thresholds and terms were checked on 2026-10-16 and 2026-10-17 against the publishers' pages or secondary summaries, as §9 lists; confirm each against the primary source and the jurisdictions that apply. It describes conditions in general and says nothing about what the foundation files, holds or has insured today; those are among the facts only the foundation can supply.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text: A common prompt for an organisation to review its duties is the amount of money it handles. Money is one trigger among several, and for this ecosystem not the most important one. What an organisation must have in place follows from what it holds and what it does: reading someone's glucose data, hosting it for others, issuing a credential for a pump, commanding insulin delivery, signing with a manufacturer, taking money. This page lists those triggers and the duties each brings, for any entity in the proposed structure (the foundation, a hosting operator, a credential authority, a controller operator), so that the duties a proposal would bring can be seen before it is adopted rather than after.

docs.title: 2. The pillars
docs.text:
Interpretation. The duties group into nine pillars. A pillar is triggered by what an organisation does, not by what it is called. Eight are read from the way Apple's developer program apportions accountability (Apple note §6.1); the ninth, governance and oversight, is the nonprofit's own.

pillar what it answers 1. identity and standing who is accountable, and can they sign a contract 2. allocation of liability who answers for harm, up to what, and with what insurance 3. regulatory role which regulator sees whom as the manufacturer, for which intended use, under what quality system 4. privacy and data protection consent, purpose, disclosure, retention, breach notice 5. credentials and revocation who may act, for how long, and how access is withdrawn safely 6. release verification what is checked before software reaches someone else 7. money tax, filing, payments, consumer law, paying people 8. continuity and exit what happens to the people already relying on it when the organisation stops 9. governance and oversight board duties, conflicts of interest, a public record, and any rules the organisation sets for others

docs.text:

docs.title: 4. How mature programmes put the pillars in place
docs.text:
Facts as cited; the lessons are interpretation.

  • Apple prices flat and scales scrutiny by what the app does. The $99 annual fee is the same for every app and waived for nonprofits that sell nothing. What grows with an app's characteristics is review depth, approvals and declarations: medical apps get greater scrutiny and must link any clearance (guideline 1.4.1); dosage calculators must come from an approved entity or be approved (1.4.2); healthcare apps "should be submitted by a legal entity that provides the services, and not by an individual developer" (5.1.1(ix)); from 2026-03-26, health and medical apps in the US, EU and UK must declare whether they are a regulated medical device. The agreement caps Apple's liability at $50 and takes an indemnity from the developer. The fee does not visibly fund insurance; the identity checks and the fee make each account accountable, which fits Apple's report of 193,035 developer accounts terminated in 2025, 192,702 of them for fraud (Apple note §4–§5).
  • Apple's personal-use tier is a revocable licence. A free account can build for its own devices with 7-day profiles, 3 devices and 3 apps each, for "personal, non-commercial use". It carves personal use out of almost every organisational duty, but it rests on a licence Apple can withdraw, and its expiry has no defined safe state: Apple disclaims life-critical use.
  • Dexcom offers one agreement on the same terms to everyone, with tiers by scale. A registered developer can serve up to five people with data delayed one hour in the US and three hours elsewhere; beyond that comes "a standard, non-negotiable Data Licensing Agreement" and Dexcom's review; real-time access is by invitation (vendor note §1.2). No other pump or CGM maker publishes a developer programme.
  • The FDA's interoperable routes expect contracts. The decision summaries for the first ACE pump and iAGC describe the manufacturer's plan for sharing interface specifications as covering contracts and who handles complaints and adverse-event reporting (vendor note §2).

Interpretation: across the three, identity comes before access, the price is the same for everyone, scrutiny scales with the activity, and liability moves to whoever acts. Credentials are issued for a stated time and can be revoked. For a device that delivers insulin, the programmes found do not supply what partner readiness §7 asks for: previously authorised, safely bounded operation that continues when a credential service is unreachable.

docs.title: 5. The same requirements for anyone
docs.text:
Interpretation: the author's view, tested against the evidence in §4 and in the vendor note §5.2.

The requirements are the same for anyone who takes on an activity: in the US any organisation may meet them by fulfilling all of them, and in practice that means a legal entity with a quality system and contracts, usually a company. The FDA routes are open to any manufacturer that meets the special controls, and Tidepool, a nonprofit, took the same 510(k) route a company would (precedents). Dexcom's agreement is standard and non-negotiable. Washington's health-data act does not exclude nonprofits. Apple's only nonprofit concession is a fee waiver.

A nonprofit therefore has no advantage in meeting the requirements of §3. Its role is a layer of oversight, at one level of governance, over the companies that build on a shared commons: CNCF certifies vendors' offerings against one upstream with the same public tests, and the Open Home Foundation binds its commercial partners by contract, without either carrying those companies' own regulatory duties. That role is pillar 9, and it answers the community's need for a party that is not one of the competitors.

On the engineering side, the cost is falling for everyone: coding agents are used for increasingly ambitious projects, device connectivity among them (the author's observation; no source read measures it). That lowers the cost of building an integration. It does not change who is authorised to use one: device authentication, app attestation and issued credentials are met by an entity and its agreements, which is the structure drawn in 1·proposed, 2·agreement and 2·controller-operator.

Both ideas, drawn small (single ideas):

docs.title: 6. A US nonprofit's own thresholds
docs.text: The money and staffing conditions that bring the foundation itself new filing, tax and employment duties, whatever activities it takes on.

docs.title: 6.1 Money
docs.text:
condition what it brings gross receipts normally above $50,000 the annual return moves from the Form 990-N e-Postcard to Form 990-EZ gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or total assets of $500,000 or more the full Form 990. Its Part VI asks whether the organisation has a written conflict-of-interest policy, a whistleblower policy and a document-retention policy, whether the board reviewed the return, and whether it keeps minutes of board and committee meetings at the time they happen asking for donations from residents of a state that requires registration charitable-solicitation registration and annual reports in that state (Colorado is one) revenue above a state's audit level, where registered financial statements reviewed or audited by an independent accountant: in New York, a review between $250,000 and $1 million in revenue and an audit above $1 million; in California, an audit at $2 million $1 million or more of federal awards spent in a fiscal year a Single Audit under 2 CFR 200 Subpart F (the threshold rose from $750,000 for fiscal years beginning on or after 2024-10-01)

Interpretation: at six figures, the money triggers are mostly about filing and disclosure. The return becomes the public record of the governance practices in Part VI.

docs.title: 6.2 Paying people
docs.text: condition what it brings paying anyone for work deciding whether each person is a contractor or an employee, which follows how the work is controlled, not what the agreement calls it paying someone with influence over the organisation (a director, officer, founder or their family) the excess-benefit rules (Internal Revenue Code §4958). docs.title: 8. What this frame does not show
docs.text:
• It is not legal, tax, insurance or regulatory advice. It lists conditions to raise with professionals.

  • Insurance terms vary by policy. The cover named in §3 is what is usually considered, not what any policy includes.
  • Apple's and Dexcom's reasons are inferred. §4 reads mechanisms from public terms; what either company intends, or what its fees pay for, is not in the sources read.

docs.title: The Nightscout ecosystem: a case study in Conway's Law
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 35ec9da5a.

What this is: a case study (part 2 of the overview, perspective; how the overview is organised): how the ecosystem's teams explain the shape of its software and data contract, and where that points to ways to unify and move forward. For the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after process models; leads to part 3, starting with the ecosystem programme. Living page, written 2026-10-18 against this repository at 0b0d150f. Every fact is taken from a page linked beside it, which gives its own date and source; the Conway readings are interpretation and are marked as such.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the related proposals. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else.

docs.title: 1. The frame
docs.text:
Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organisations which design systems "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations" (Conway, "How Do Committees Invent?", Datamation, April 1968, read 2026-10-18). Where two teams talk, the interface between their parts is agreed; where they do not, each side builds what it needs and the system holds both.

The Nightscout ecosystem fits the frame closely. Each of the 20 repositories measured in governance today §1 decides what it merges and releases, no shared body for decisions that cross projects is named (§6), and the Nightscout hub is where their data meets. This page reads the observations of part 1 and the drawings of control structures and process models through that frame.

docs.title: 2. The chronology, by kind of team
docs.text:
Rows from the chronology; the drawing is generated from tools/structure-diagrams/history/timeline.yaml, whose rows are checked against it.

Interpretation. Each section of the chronology adds a kind of team that writes to the hub:

chronology section teams that begin writing to the hub what each brought to the data §1, 2012–2014 one group building both the uploader and the display the first shapes (entries with sgv, treatments with eventType), set before there was a second team §2, 2015–2019 closed-loop communities around their own hardware, language and chat (Loop, OpenAPS, AndroidAPS) a device-status block per family (loop, openaps) §3, 2020–2024 forks (FreeAPS X, iAPS, Trio), followers, and bridges per vendor cloud a record-id convention per app; readers that must handle every writer §4, 2025–2026 a second server implementing the same API (Nocturne) a second implementation of one contract, which needs the contract written down

Trio shows the pattern inside one row. It uses the same LoopKit CGM managers as Loop, discards the manager's syncIdentifier and sends a random id of its own (identifier format research §1). Shared code did not carry a shared contract once the teams were separate.

This is a genuine fork, not a deprecation." Interpretation. A schemaless store and a server that keeps what it is sent let every team ship without waiting for another, which suited an ecosystem with no cross-project decision body. The cost of agreement moved to the readers: every follower, report and research tool carries code for each writer it has met. The entries shape that every uploader shares (with small deviations such as QUIRK-ENTRIES-001) is the one set before a second team existed.

docs.text:
The drawing's sources are in its input, tools/structure-diagrams/inputs/1-teams.yaml; the same set, with its own notes, is on process models.

question as believed (inferred) as the repositories show how the code mirrors it who decides for the ecosystem the foundation, or Nightscout as one project each of 20 repositories decides alone; the foundation supports, convenes and recognises (governance §1, §3) no shared schema owner; each writer's code is its own specification who knows which controller wrote a record the hub nobody: there is no registration code; readers infer it from the document's shape the display plugins look for loop or openaps (3·registration) whether a sent command was applied the hub tracks it one development-only AndroidAPS path returns an acknowledgement with an id; elsewhere success shows as a later record and failure as a free-text note each controller team built its own command path and reply who runs shared operations someone of 20 repositories, none has a SECURITY policy of its own; 4 have private vulnerability reporting; reports arrive in five chat systems (2·shared-infra) no project's CI runs a shared conformance suite what an automated agent is a separate actor a shared credential, indistinguishable from the person who shared it no delegation grant in the code

Interpretation. The hub's model of "which controller" is the set of block names its display plugins look for, one per controller family that had a plugin written. A controller that reuses an existing name (Trio and AndroidAPS writing openaps, as oref0 does) inherits the name of the family it came from and does not show as a separate system. A caregiver who reads a sent command as an applied one acts on the believed structure; the STPA analysis places hazards in exactly that kind of gap between a controller's model and the system.

Coding agents lower the cost of engineering (cgm-remote-monitor's 2026 commits include agent-written ones, ecosystem evidence §4). Every edge in the tables above is still a decision between people or organisations.

docs.title: 6. Inverse Conway: specifications shaped to their owners
docs.text:
The "inverse Conway manoeuvre" designs the system so that each part matches a team able to keep it. The platform specifications already cut their layers this way: "Each boundary falls where the reader, the rate of change or the review differs" (platform index). Controller-owned definitions (D18, D19) move the meaning of a controller's data from the hub's plugins to the team that writes it; the hub routes and records and never doses; version-scoped quirks (D20) write the existing habits down, per version, so a team can retire its own.

Each layer's natural owner, and whether that owner is engaged today, is tabled on the platform index. Interpretation. A contract drafted in one repository fits that repository's habits best; the manoeuvre works when the controller teams hold L2 and L3 in practice, through review of the parts that describe their data and a route to change them. A single central schema committee would add a team boundary the ecosystem has never had; owned declarations at the edges match a federation of independent teams.

docs.title: 7. What it implies for sustaining the ecosystem
docs.text: Interpretation. If the design follows the communication structure, the structure is what has to be sustained: a recorded channel for changes to the shared contract (collaboration rule 5), a second person able to review and release each widely used repository (rule 10), a shared conformance suite and a release record with a bug-to-test rule (quality system §3), a security contact per project (partner readiness §8), paid time for shared operations as a named service (sponsored team, ecosystem programme §2b), and an entity able to hold agreements with manufacturers under the same requirements as anyone (partner readiness, accountability thresholds §5).

docs.title: 8. Reading intent
docs.text: When two apps disagree on a field, a release is late or a proposal waits, the frame suggests asking who would have had to talk to whom for it to come out differently, before asking why someone chose it. The working rules that follow from that are in working together §5a.

docs.title: 9. What this frame does not show
docs.text:
• Causes. The chronology gives dates, not causes; each project's maintainers are the people to say what held a release (ecosystem evidence §3).
  • Agreement that happens without a channel. Shared shapes exist where one team set them first (§3), and teams agree informally in ways no repository records.
  • Whether a different structure would have shipped as much. The arrangement described here let independent teams release for thirteen years; the frame describes its cost, not an alternative's.

docs.title: When a DIY ecosystem becomes infrastructure: what other communities did
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 1efa2b753.

What this is: an analysis (part 2 of the overview, perspective; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after the perspective index; leads to precedents: how other organisations are funded, staffed and governed. Living page, written 2026-10-02 against this repository at e3d7b65c. It offers a frame for reading the observations and sets other communities' experience beside them. Where it interprets, it says so. It makes no request; the author's recommendations are in part 3. Every outside quote was read at its source on the date given; re-read before quoting.

docs.title: 1. The question
docs.text:
Open source describes rights: to use, study, change and share software. It says nothing about whether the work of keeping that software current is paid. Many people's picture of open source is still of volunteers working in their spare time, and for most projects that picture is accurate: in Tidelift's 2024 survey of maintainers, 60% described themselves as unpaid hobbyists (histories annex §B9).

Some communities have reached a point where they changed how parts of their work are organised and paid for. This page asks what those points had in common, and which of those conditions can be measured for the Nightscout ecosystem.

docs.title: 2. No single threshold
docs.text:
None of the communities below adopted a rule such as "past a number of users, pay maintainers". They changed after conditions accumulated, often made visible by one event. The conditions recur across the cases, and in this page they are called gravity: what a project accumulates that makes its work harder to leave to whoever has time. The term is this page's, not a standard one.

kind of gravity what accumulates what the Nightscout observations show dependency other software relies on behaviour staying compatible 40 client repositories mapped against 15 parts of the API; a second server implementing the same API (evidence §2) assets code, schemas, test suites, protocol knowledge, documentation 62 repositories, more than 35,000 test declarations, 14 device protocols with 41 independent implementations (evidence §1) deadlines set by others platform, runtime and vendor dates that arrive regardless of anyone's free time ten dated platform and runtime events to the end of 2027, and vendor-cloud changes the connectors have had to follow since 2020, with no date to plan against (evidence §5) concentration important work resting on few people in 25 of 56 active repositories one author made 80% or more of the year's commits; cgm-remote-monitor had 11 to 18 authors a year from 2021 to 2025; review in its work queue routes mostly to one maintainer (evidence §1, §3, §4) safety and security consequences of a mistake beyond inconvenience Nightscout is a secondary display for CGM and pump data, with alarms; the backfix register's operator-exposure table counts defects present in the shipping release (PROGRAMME-STATUS) commercial use businesses that depend on dependable releases hosted providers listed in the Nightscout documentation; paid part-time arrangements set by individual hosts (evidence §4); revenue and site counts not measured institutions researchers, regulators, manufacturers and nonprofits interacting with the work published trials and observational studies (evidence §6); a nonprofit's FDA clearance built on DIY Loop (history) users people affected by failures who never meet the maintainers not measured: no count of sites or users exists in this repository jurisdictions identity, consent, hosting and data rules that differ by country not measured: no count of sites by country; the regulatory questions are listed for counsel in ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §9

Interpretation: on the dimensions that can be measured from this repository, the ecosystem has accumulated each kind of gravity. Two dimensions, users and jurisdictions, have no measurement here, and claims about them should wait for one.

docs.text:
Each row was read at its source on 2026-10-02 unless it says otherwise. Fuller histories on one template are in PRECEDENTS.

The Linux Foundation: "The idea that open source just happens in someone's basement is a myth. As the software has grown more complex, so has the need for full time developer support." (LF, 2014); folded into OpenSSF in 2020 funded developers, audits and test infrastructure for critical projects the projects' own maintainers and governance Linux kernel companies came to depend on it. "Seventy-five percent of all kernel development is done by developers who are being paid for their work" (LF report, 2012) most development, by employers' staff the maintainer hierarchy decides what merges OpenStreetMap Foundation "Given that volunteer work has not proven to be sufficient in the past, support through paid development is necessary"; "An all volunteer Board has proven insufficient to execute on all Foundation needs" (Strategic Plan) core-systems work and full-time system monitoring, under a Hiring Framework that avoids "paid leadership or decision-making positions" working groups, so that "the overall course of the OSMF is driven by community members as opposed to a paid body of staff" Django Software Foundation review and ticket backlog; after a pilot, "a full-time, ongoing Django Fellow" from March 2015 (DSF, 2015-03-06) triage, review and release chores feature work and technical decisions Python Software Foundation review and security load on volunteer core developers; Developers-in-Residence from July 2021, each seat funded by a named sponsor (Alpha-Omega and Bloomberg among them, PSF) triage, review, build monitoring, security response the elected Steering Council Home Assistant / Open Home Foundation a founder-linked company had paid the maintainers for years; in 2024 a nonprofit took ownership, "funded by commercial partner fees and donations", supporting "more than 50 full-time employees" (structure) the staff working on foundation projects contributions from the wider community Germany's Sovereign Tech Agency public dependence on open infrastructure; set up "on the basis of a decision by the German Bundestag" (about); "A total of €33.6 million has been invested in 96 technologies" (newsletter, November 2025) maintenance and security work in the projects it funds each project's own governance

Interpretation: across these cases the paid work was mostly operations, security, triage, review and release, and technical authority stayed with community bodies. Several communities wrote down how they would keep it that way before or as they hired.

docs.title: 4. The concerns these communities recorded
docs.text:
The worry that paid work changes a volunteer community is not peculiar to Nightscout, and some communities wrote their concerns down. When OpenStreetMap's board introduced its hiring framework in 2020, the risks it listed included (osmf-talk, 2020-05-06):

  • "Paid work can have a chilling effect on volunteering."
  • "Paid staff has other incentives than volunteers."
  • "Paid staff has more power to set direction of the project than a volunteer, if only because of the amount of time they have."

The volunteer-only view, in its strongest form, and the rules other projects used to reconcile it with paid work, are in QUALITY-SYSTEM §8.2 and the histories annex §E. Debian's 2006 experiment in paying release managers, and what that project drew from it, is in PRECEDENTS.

docs.title: 5. What this frame does not show
docs.text:
• It does not show that paid work is needed. It shows which conditions other communities faced when they chose it, and which of those conditions are present here. Whether and how to respond is a decision, and the proposals in part 3 are one author's answer.
  • It does not show that volunteer work is failing. Most maintainers in the wider open-source world are unpaid, and the 2025–26 release record across the ecosystem was more frequent than the years before it (evidence §3).
  • Size differs. Every community above is larger than this ecosystem, or funded at a scale this ecosystem is not. Their structures may transfer; their budgets do not (PRECEDENTS).
  • Two dimensions are unmeasured (§2): users and jurisdictions.

docs.title: What the table shows
docs.text:
• No precedent matches on size and stakes together. Debian has about five times as many voting developers (1,030) as the ecosystem had human authors in a year (219); CNCF and W3C count organisations as members (728 and 335+), each employing engineers. None of them carries clinical outcomes. Their structures transfer; their funding scale does not.
  • Every organisation that pays people keeps technical authority with the maintainers, whether the money comes from donors (Zig, OpenStreetMap), sponsors (PSF), members (CNCF) or customers (SQLite, curl).
  • Commercial support adds to the commons where the codebase stays single. SQLite sells assurance on the same releases free users get; CNCF certifies commercial offerings against the same upstream with the same public tests; Debian keeps paid support outside the project and reports it monthly. The collaboration model's rules 2, 5 and 8 draw on these.
  • Regulated and DIY tracks can coexist when each carries its own label (Tidepool Loop).
