docs.title: SQLite: paying for assurance, not control
docs.text:
SQLite is public domain, free to anyone, and built into phones, browsers and aircraft ("Airbus confirms that SQLite is being used in the flight software for the A350 XWB family"). Its developers are employed by one small company, Hwaci, and paid from what companies with their own quality and legal obligations buy. Read from sqlite.org on 2026-09-29:

what is sold what the buyer gets source consortium membership, $150K a year on the support page ($120,000 on the member page) 23 staff-days a year, bug fixes back-ported to any version "no matter how old", regression tests run in the member's own configuration consortium, support technical support, $8K to $85K a year priority support for versions up to a year old support test runs on the customer's hardware and build options evidence for the customer's own quality system; the test harness was built to support the avionics standard DO-178B, and every release since 2009 meets 100% MC/DC coverage support, TH3 a "warranty of title", $6,000 once indemnity for legal departments; "all proceeds … are used to fund continuing improvement and support of SQLite" copyright

What stays constant across every tier: "technical control and direction of SQLite remains with the SQLite architect and developers … [it] does not fall under the governance of any single company" (consortium). Free users get the same releases, tested the same way. The developers publish a quality management plan modelled on DO-178B, and they "plan as if we will be supporting SQLite until 2050" (long-term support).

  • Check before quoting: SQLite's own pages disagree on prices (above), and the site makes no medical-device quality claim; "medical devices" appears only as an example of where SQLite fits (when to use).

docs.title: Transitions, on one template
docs.text: Each case answers the same eight questions, so they can be compared with one another and with the observations. Sources are those in the histories annex §B unless a line links its own; outside quotes were re-read at the source on 2026-10-02 where they first appear on this site in INFRASTRUCTURE-TRANSITION.

docs.title: OpenSSL, 2014–2024
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. A cryptography library maintained by volunteers; before April 2014, "two primary developers, both of whom were volunteers, and no decision-making process" (LWN, 2016).
  2. What depended on it. Encrypted connections in a large share of servers and devices; not measured in the sources read.
  3. Pressure. Heartbleed, disclosed April 2014. Its foundation "typically receives about US$2000 a year in outright donations".
  4. Response. The Linux Foundation's Core Infrastructure Initiative funded "two, fulltime core developers" and an audit; the project wrote release, security and support policies and required review of all code. In 2024 it became a foundation and a corporation as "two independent but co-equal entities".
  5. Stayed with the community. The project's own decisions, through its committees.
  6. Became paid. Two developers per funded role, then more from donations.
  7. Still disputed or hard. Not found in the sources read; the 2024 split is recent.
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: money turned into a working project through named roles plus written policies. Does not: the scale of dependence and of funding.

docs.title: OpenStreetMap Foundation, 2020–2023
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. A volunteer mapping community with a volunteer board.
  2. What depended on it. The map data and the foundation's own servers, which need "full-time system monitoring to ensure availability" (Strategic Plan).
  3. Pressure. "Given that volunteer work has not proven to be sufficient in the past, support through paid development is necessary"; "An all volunteer Board has proven insufficient to execute on all Foundation needs" (Strategic Plan, 2023).
  4. Response. A Hiring Framework, introduced to the members in May 2020, and then paid work on core systems and full-time monitoring.
  5. Stayed with the community. Working groups, so that "the overall course of the OSMF is driven by community members as opposed to a paid body of staff"; the framework avoids "paid leadership or decision-making positions".
  6. Became paid. Core-systems development and system monitoring.
  7. Still disputed or hard. The board listed the risks in public before hiring: a "chilling effect on volunteering", different incentives, and paid staff's greater power to set direction (osmf-talk, 2020-05-06).
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: writing down, before hiring, what paid staff may and may not decide. Does not: OSM's size and its own hosted service.

docs.title: Debian: Dunc-Tank (2006) and paid long-term support (2014–)
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. A volunteer project that pays none of its members; about 1,000 voting developers in 2006 and 1,030 in 2025.
  2. What depended on it. Debian's users, and the long-supported releases companies run.
  3. Pressure. A release to deliver (Etch, planned for December 2006, shipped 2007-04-08), and security support that lasted three years.
  4. Response. 2006: an independent group, with the project leader on its board, paid two release managers for a month each. From 2014: long-term support run by Freexian as a separate service, funded by sponsors outside the project, with monthly public reports.
  5. Stayed with the community. All of Debian's own decisions; the 2006 resolution said the experiment "is not the result of a decision of the Debian Project".
  6. Became paid. Long-term security support beyond the project's own term.
  7. Still disputed or hard. Dunc-Tank drew a recall vote (which failed) and a protest statement; the lesson drawn in 2019 was "don't let the DPL decide alone who gets paid".
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: paid work as a separate, named, reported service; never one person deciding who is paid. Does not: Debian's size.

docs.title: Home Assistant and the Open Home Foundation, 2018–2025
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. A community home-automation project.
  2. What depended on it. Its users and device integrations; not measured in the sources read.
  3. Pressure. Not stated in the sources read as a single event; for years "a significant portion of Nabu Casa's revenue was used to pay the salaries" of maintainers.
  4. Response. 2024: a nonprofit foundation took ownership, "funded by commercial partner fees and donations"; each partner must "contribute a majority of its profit from selling licensed products"; in 2025 the staff working on foundation projects moved to the foundation.
  5. Stayed with the community. Contributions from the wider community, under the foundation.
  6. Became paid. "more than 50 full-time employees".
  7. Still disputed or hard. Not found in the sources read.
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: a founder-linked company paying maintainers, formalised as a foundation with a published rule for partners; it took six years. Does not: the revenue scale.

docs.title: Python Software Foundation Developers-in-Residence, 2021–
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. A volunteer core team with an elected Steering Council.
  2. What depended on it. Python's users and its package index; not measured in the sources read.
  3. Pressure. Review, triage and security load on volunteer core developers.
  4. Response. From July 2021, paid residents, each seat funded by a named sponsor (PSF).
  5. Stayed with the community. Technical decisions, through the Steering Council.
  6. Became paid. Triage, review, build monitoring and security response.
  7. Still disputed or hard. Each seat lasts only as long as its sponsor.
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: the nearest model to paid review and release work beside volunteers. Does not: the number of sponsors Python can draw.

docs.title: Tidepool Loop, 2020–2023
docs.text:
1. Starting condition. DIY Loop, built by volunteers, run by people who build it themselves.
  2. What depended on it. People using Loop, and later a manufacturer's product.
  3. Pressure. Not stated as a single event in the sources read.
  4. Response. A nonprofit, Tidepool, took the software through FDA 510(k) clearance (submitted 2020-12-17, cleared 2023-01-23) with its own paid team and a community observational study; the clearance "can now become a predicate device".
  5. Stayed with the community. DIY Loop continued alongside.
  6. Became paid. The regulated track: Tidepool's team, and later Sequel's twiist system, which incorporates the cleared technology. On 2026-01-13 Diabeloop and Sequel announced that Diabeloop's DBLG2 algorithm will also be integrated into twiist, with a US launch expected in 2027 (Diabeloop, 2026-01-13, read 2026-10-17); Abbott's partner page still lists the "twiist Automated Insulin Delivery (AID) System Powered by Tidepool" on 2026-10-17.
  7. Still disputed or hard. Not found in the sources read.
  8. Transfers / does not. Transfers: regulated and DIY tracks can coexist, each with its own label. Does not: a regulatory route is a choice for each project, not something a foundation does for it.

docs.title: Process models: what we believe, and how it works
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 35ec9da5a.

What this is: a map (part 2 of the overview, perspective; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after who controls what; leads to the Conway's Law case study. Living page, written 2026-10-17; 1·teams added 2026-10-18. Companion to control structures, whose conventions, legend and icons apply here. Every node and edge comes from a source cited under the drawing; where a panel is inferred or proposed, it says so.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the related proposals. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else. Operators in the drawings are roles, not named companies.

docs.title: How to read these drawings
docs.text:
Every controller in an STPA structure acts on a process model: its belief about the system it controls. Many hazards come from the gap between that model and how the system actually behaves. Each set below draws one structure three times on one layout, so the boxes line up and the lines that appear, disappear or change their label are the finding.

  • Policy questions are drawn as believed (the community's own reading), as it works today and as it is emerging.
  • The ecosystem's own designs are drawn as believed (what clients, operators and people assume), as it works today (cited to code) and as proposed (cited to the decision or proposal; nothing in a proposed panel is built unless it says so).

Teal dashed lines are authority: where a party's right to act comes from (a law, an exemption, a licence). Purple dash-dot lines are discretion: control another party exercises at its own choice (terms, enforcement, revocation). The other lines and the icons are as in the legend and icon key.

set question panels 1·authority where DIY and open-source authority to act comes from believed, actual, emerging 0·diy-status under what regulatory status a DIY build runs believed, actual, emerging 1·data-rights how data gets out, and how others are let in believed, actual, emerging 1·access-paths who holds the key on each path between device, phone, cloud and site believed, actual, emerging; and a ladder 1·hosting who answers for a site run for someone else believed, actual, emerging 1·teams who decides the shared data contract believed, actual 3·identity who is who on a hub, and who may do what believed, actual, proposed 1·federation one sign-in across regional zones, with zero-trust access believed, actual, proposed 3·registration who writes to the hub, and where a command goes believed, actual, proposed 2·data-commons how Nightscout data reaches research believed, actual, proposed 2·shared-infra the shared operations, and who runs them believed, actual, proposed

docs.title: 1·authority: where the authority to act comes from
docs.text:
As believed. The community's own reading of its protections: open-source licences, the DMCA medical-device data exemption, interoperability rights (DIGITAL-RIGHTS, overview). In this picture the person's authority runs straight from the law to their own device and data, and no one else's choices sit between them.

As it works today. The same rights, read precisely, and the discretion they leave standing. The DMCA exemption covers data access only and is a defence renewed every three years; DIY looping "remains in a legal gray area", and the community operates partly on "the practical reality that manufacturers have generally not pursued enforcement" (DIGITAL-RIGHTS, implications). Five discretion edges reach the person or the projects: a manufacturer's firmware and cloud changes, its takedown notices (Abbott, 2019), cloud terms that ban "unauthorized third-party applications" (Dexcom consumer terms §5.11, vendor note §1.2), the FDA's 2019 warning against unauthorised devices (history), and a phone platform's signing licence, 7 days on a free account and revocable (Apple note §1.1). Regulators' requirements reach manufacturers, including premarket cybersecurity for connected devices under FD&C Act §524B, in effect since 2023-03-29 (FDA, cybersecurity, read 2026-10-17).

As it is emerging. Two changes are under way at once. Newer devices authenticate the app as well as the person. The community's Omnipod 5 driver presents a controller certificate and signs pod commands (OmnipodKit 928bb79, read 2026-10-17; vendor note §1.6); where that certificate comes from is not described here, and whether the driver runs against a real pod was not checked. The app check is already on two CGM lines: Dexcom G7 and Libre 3 ask for a client credential after the person's code or NFC scan, and the open implementations carry a fixed one that the manufacturer did not issue to them (xdripswift c268542, Juggluco 75399d7, LibreLoop 150d2b1, read 2026-10-17). Tandem pairs with a code shown on the pump, and no app credential was found (pumpX2 6fa9459). Why device-level controls tighten and do not loosen is not settled by any source read. One reading, for counsel and regulatory review: §524B and the FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance ask manufacturers to show how device interfaces authenticate those that connect, which leaves a manufacturer little reason to keep an unauthenticated path (vendor note §7). And in the EU, the Data Act (applying since 2025-09-12) turns part of the data right from a defence into a duty: the manufacturer must share device data at the person's request, real-time where feasible, including with a third party the person designates (vendor note §3.1). The drawing combines what exists on some devices and in one jurisdiction; it is not a forecast for any one device or market.

Interpretation. Properties of the emerging landscape, read from the three drawings:

  1. Where a device checks the app, access is bound to identity. A credential is issued to a known party and can be renewed or withdrawn; knowing the protocol is no longer enough.
  2. Authority is delegated, and its withdrawal is the issuer's. Whether revocation follows a published process or the issuer's discretion is decided by the agreement (partner readiness §4).
  3. Rights move from defences to duties, for data first. The Data Act obliges sharing data; no law found obliges a manufacturer to accept commands from another party's software.
  4. The designated third party has to be an entity that can meet the requirements: privacy, security, and the terms the manufacturer's credentials carry (what each activity brings §5).
  5. Requirements flow down by contract. Cybersecurity and quality duties sit with the manufacturer, and reach anyone holding its credentials through the agreement.
  6. Authorisation becomes the binding constraint. The engineering gets cheaper for everyone; who is authorised to use it does not. This is a reading of the direction. Where the person holds the pairing secret (Tandem, Dana, Medtrum, Dexcom G6), engineering is still the constraint, and it has been met. Where the device checks the app (Dexcom G7, Libre 3, MiniMed 780G, Omnipod 5), open access today rests on credentials the manufacturer did not issue to the projects, which new sensors or firmware could stop accepting.

The characterisations of law here are summaries for discussion, drafts for counsel to review, and not legal advice.

docs.title: 0·diy-status: under what status a DIY build runs
docs.text:
Draft for review by regulatory counsel. This section summarises published sources for discussion; it is not legal or regulatory advice, and it does not say what any regulator will or will not do.

People who build and run open-source automated insulin delivery (AID) software for themselves act under a regulatory status that the community describes one way and regulators have described only in part. The drawings keep four positions apart, because that is where the status can change: a person building for themselves, a project publishing source code, anyone handing out built apps, and anyone running the software for someone else.

As believed. The projects' own pages say the software is not approved and that the person who builds it carries the risk: "not approved for therapy by any government organization" and "You take full responsibility for building and running this system and do so at your own risk" (LoopDocs, read 2026-10-17); "not CE or FDA approved for therapy" (Trio README). The AndroidAPS FAQ gives the community's fullest reading: under EU rules a system of class IIa or IIb is a medical device needing a CE mark, distribution "even giving away for free" is covered, and "Building a medical device for yourself is the only way to use the app within these regulations" (AAPS FAQ, read 2026-10-17). The repository's suggested disclaimer says the software "is NOT a medical device" (DIGITAL-RIGHTS, disclaimers). In this picture regulation reaches manufacturers and people who hand out built apps, and stops short of the person and of published source.

As regulators have spoken. On 2019-05-17 the FDA warned patients and clinicians against "unapproved or unauthorized devices", noting that "patients may choose to create these systems", and said it is "aware of manufacturers illegally marketing unauthorized devices" (FDA, read 2026-10-17; history). No published FDA document was found that addresses an individual building such software for their own use, and none that exempts it. FDA officials have addressed it in conference presentations and in discussions with the Nightscout Foundation (reported by the Foundation; no recording, slides or minutes were located): Courtney Lias of the FDA said at the June 2016 D-Data ExChange (DDATA), held back to back with the ADA Scientific Sessions, that "it looks like distribution is happening"; the FDA does not treat DIY or personal distribution as exempt or permitted; and "the absence of money exchanged" is not one of the triggers the FDA uses to decide whether distribution is happening.

The earliest record is a pre-submission meeting between Nightscout contributors and the FDA on 2014-10-08 (Q141084). Its minutes, published by Nightscout contributors with the pre-submission supplement, record that "Medical Device regulations are applicable to the Nightscout project"; that the FDA "doesn't have a bias against the open source route"; that "a key tenet of device regulation is that some entity be responsible for assuring the safety and effectiveness of the device and that postmarket safety is adequately monitored"; that the FDA believed Nightscout could meet applicable requirements "even with non-traditional methods of development"; and that the FDA asked for a gap analysis and a follow-up meeting (minutes, read 2026-10-19). The raw notes taken at the meeting add an FDA attendee asking, of how Nightscout tracks and pushes updates, "Will this scale to 10,000 or 50,000 users?", and the FDA's three questions: who is responsible for testing changes against the design, who collects details "when things go wrong", and who is "ultimately responsible if things go really wrong"; asked whether there were "red lines" to avoid, the FDA said it would consult internally (raw notes, read 2026-10-19).

A second account was published from the same week of meetings: diaTribe's report of 2016-06-27, written around the ADA Scientific Sessions, does not say at which meeting she spoke, and says that "according to the FDA's Dr. Courtney Lias, systems like OpenAPS do fall under the FDA's jurisdiction, though the Agency enforces its authority based on risk – a single individual using OpenAPS presents a low risk, while thousands using the system presents a higher risk"; that "the FDA may not choose to spend resources on someone building a system for their own personal use"; and that the agency's "biggest concern" is responsibility: "who will catalog and report any adverse events, and who is responsible if something goes wrong" (diaTribe, archived copy of 2025-07-23, read 2026-10-19).

US device duties attach to establishments and distribution: registration (21 CFR 807), premarket notification "before ... the introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce for commercial distribution" (807.81(a)), where commercial distribution is defined as a device "held or offered for sale" (807.3(b)); the registration exemptions in 807.65 list no class for a person making a device for their own use (eCFR 807, read 2026-10-17). Separately, 21 U.S.C. 331(a) prohibits introducing an adulterated or misbranded device into interstate commerce with no sale condition (LII, read 2026-10-17). No published source read says whether publishing source code, or handing out a built app free, is either of these; the FDA officials' statements above treat free sharing as distribution.

What the community does around a personal build. Each person still builds and runs their own copy, which spreads operator responsibility across individuals. The activity around that step has changed since 2014, when a person compiled the code on their own computer. By the Foundation's account (2026-10-19), the community now:

  • publishes browser builds: the person forks a repository, adds their account secrets, and a GitHub Actions workflow builds the app and uploads it to TestFlight, with no local Xcode (Loop, Trio, xDrip4iOS, LoopFollow, LoopCaregiver; TestFlight distribution §1.2);
  • runs regular Zoom and other online workshops, in several formats, where people build the software together, and holds live events;
  • coordinates documentation sites that direct people to free tiers, trials and other resources from many companies;
  • promotes the software publicly, on social media and through foundations that describe themselves as sponsoring or being the centre of the activity, and offers it free with a few steps left to the person.

These are the activities FDA officials have described as looking like distribution. The number of people using DIY AID has also grown: by the Foundation's estimate (2026-10-19, not measured here), the AndroidAPS, Loop and Trio communities number 10,000 or more people, perhaps up to 60,000, against the 18 of OpenAPS's first 40 users whose data diaTribe reported in 2016.

The regulated route exists: the iCGM, ACE pump and iAGC special controls (cloud layer §2.2), and Tidepool Loop, cleared by 510(k) K203689 on 2023-01-23 as an iAGC, beside the continuing DIY project (precedents). In the EU, the MDR's in-house exemption (Article 5(5)) is for health institutions: "an organisation the primary purpose of which is the care or treatment of patients", and a device used "outside the health institution's legal entity ... cannot be in-house" (MDCG 2023-1, January 2023, not legally binding, read 2026-10-17). No MDR provision for an individual's own build was found. No MHRA statement on DIY AID was found (search, 2026-10-17).

As it is emerging. Three developments reach the positions differently. FD&C Act §524B (premarket cybersecurity, in effect 2023-03-29; guidance issued 2025-06-27) applies to "a person who submits an application or submission" for a cyber device (FDA, cybersecurity; LII 21 U.S.C. 360n-2, both read 2026-10-17), so it reaches the regulated route directly. FDA officials have described the cybersecurity work as closing unintended-use paths while the FDA exercises discretion (reported by the Foundation, as above). Apple, from 2026-03-26, requires health and medical apps in the US, EEA and UK to declare whether they are a regulated medical device; a "Yes" needs an EU SRN or FDA owner/operator number, and existing apps must declare "by early 2027" (Apple note §1.7). And the ACE and iAGC decision summaries record interface plans covering contracts and "who is responsible for investigating and reporting complaints", which is a route for an operator under contract with a manufacturer; no manufacturer was found to publish a route for a third party (vendor note §2). The regulated form of running it for others is drawn in 2·controller-operator. A proposal that responds to the FDA's stated concerns is in why organise §7a.

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. The status turns on distribution, and payment does not decide it. Every published duty found attaches to placing on the market, distribution or a premarket submission. The US prohibition (331(a)) has no sale condition, and FDA officials have said the absence of money is not a trigger they use and that the community's practice looks like distribution. No published source settles whether publishing source code alone is distribution.
  2. Device regulation has been said to apply since 2014; enforcement is by discretion. The 2014 pre-submission minutes record that device regulations apply to Nightscout. In 2016 an FDA official said systems like OpenAPS fall under FDA jurisdiction and that the agency may not spend resources on someone building for their own use. Its published line since is the 2019 warning. The EU's only exemption found is for health institutions. Low enforcement priority is not an exemption or a permission.
  3. Scale and responsibility are the factors named, not payment. In 2014 the FDA asked for one responsible party and whether updates would reach 10,000 or 50,000 users. In 2016 it weighed risk by how many people use a system (one person low, thousands higher) and named responsibility for adverse-event reporting and failures as its biggest concern. Community use has grown from tens of people in 2016 to an estimated tens of thousands.
  4. The person's own step has shrunk; the shared activity around it has grown. In 2014 the person compiled the code. Today the person forks a repository and runs an automated build, often in a workshop, following coordinated documentation, with the software promoted and offered free. Those shared activities, not the final build step, are what FDA officials have said look like distribution.
  5. The community's beliefs differ by project. One project reads EU rules as reaching free distribution of built apps; others say only "not approved". The beliefs agree that the person carries the risk.
  6. Running it for others has a regulated form and no published DIY form. The regulated form is a submission and, for interoperable devices, a contract that assigns complaint duties.
  7. New requirements reach the distributor first. §524B and app-store declarations bind whoever submits or publishes. No new published requirement names the self-builder; FDA officials describe the cybersecurity work as closing unintended-use paths, with discretion in how the FDA acts.

Not drawn: the EU AI Act, because whether it reaches a rule-based controller was not determined; the UK's own device regulations, which were not read. The characterisations of law here are drafts for regulatory counsel, not advice; no enforcement intent is inferred beyond what the sources say.

docs.title: Points for a regulatory professional to verify
docs.text:
1. Whether publishing AID source code (no binaries, no sale) is "introduction or delivery for introduction into interstate commerce" of a device under 21 U.S.C. 331(a) or 21 CFR 807, given FDA officials' informal view that the community's practice looks like distribution; and whether workshops, coordinated build documentation, automated build workflows and public promotion by projects or foundations are distribution, promotion or labelling of a device.
  2. How free distribution of a built app is treated under 807.3(b) ("held or offered for sale") and 331(a), given FDA officials' statement that the absence of money is not a trigger they use.
  3. Whether an individual building for personal use is a "manufacturer" under 21 CFR 807.3(d) or 820.1, given that 807.65 lists no exemption for that case.
  4. MDR Article 2 definitions of "manufacturer", "placing on the market" and "making available on the market", read from EUR-Lex (not reachable on 2026-10-17); whether "commercial activity" covers free supply by a hobbyist or project, as the AAPS FAQ reads it.
  5. Whether any MDR provision or national rule addresses a patient's own build; MDCG 2023-1 covers only health institutions.
  6. The MHRA's position, if any, and the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002 on own-use builds.
  7. Whether the FDA's 2019-05-17 notice remains current, and whether any later FDA statement on DIY or open-source AID exists.
  8. A citable record (slides, minutes, recordings or correspondence) of the FDA officials' statements reported here, starting with Courtney Lias's DDATA 2016 talk (no transcript or video was found as of 2026-10-19; diaTribe's report of the same week is the nearest published account): that DIY or personal distribution is not exempt, that the community's practice looks like distribution, that the absence of money is not a trigger, and that the cybersecurity work aims to close unintended-use paths. The 2014 meeting has published minutes and raw notes; the 2016 jurisdiction, risk and responsibility statements are in diaTribe's report. Also whether the FDA holds its own record of the 2014 meeting, whether the follow-up meeting or gap analysis took place, and whether the FDA answered the "red lines" question.
  9. Whether the 2016 risk-based position (one person low risk, thousands higher) is still the FDA's approach, and how it applies at the community's current scale.
  10. Whether a person or entity running AID software for others (including paid builders or hosted controllers) is a manufacturer, and whether 807.65(i) (service through "a previously manufactured device") could ever apply.
  11. Whether a legal entity that supports DIY users (for example by incubating projects, running shared build infrastructure, or taking on adverse-event intake) changes how that risk-based discretion applies, and in which direction.
  12. Whether §524B's "cyber device" definition could reach an unsubmitted DIY build (the statute attaches it to a submitter).
  13. Whether answering "No" to Apple's regulated-device declaration is accurate for a DIY AID app, and what that answer implies in each market.

docs.title: 1·data-rights: getting data out, and letting others in
docs.text:
As believed. The data rights primer names five rights: access, export, share, delegate and audit. Sharing is to be "on your terms, with the scope you choose" and "revocable when circumstances change" (primer; DIGITAL-RIGHTS, overview). In this picture data runs from the vendor cloud to the person's own site, and the person decides who sees it.

As it works today. US rights are a copyright exemption (a defence, not a duty to provide access), HIPAA (the US health-privacy law) access to what a clinic holds, and state privacy laws (vendor note §5.2). A manufacturer's consumer terms can forbid automated access and "unauthorized third-party applications" (Dexcom §5.11, vendor note §1.2). The ecosystem's real-time data comes from follower services and device protocols the vendors do not document for this use (§1.9). The site's connector is configured with the person's vendor username and password (nightscout-connect README, read 2026-10-17). The vendor's own routes go elsewhere: MiniMed shares with "up to five care partners" and uploads to the clinic (§1.4). On the site, read access is one setting. As documented, the default role readable (*:*:read) lets anyone with the address view everything unless the owner sets denied (cgm-remote-monitor 15.0.8 README, AUTH_DEFAULT_ROLES). Beyond that, sharing means handing over the API secret or a token. There are no scoped, expiring grants (configuration and delegation §5.3).

As it is emerging. The EU Data Act has applied since 2025-09-12. It gives the user access to product data "continuously and in real-time" where feasible (Art. 4). It also lets "a user, or a party acting on behalf of a user" have the same data sent to a third party (Art. 5), free of charge to the user. The third party may use it only for the agreed purposes (Art. 6) (vendor note §3.1). The European Health Data Space adds proxy services, so that a person can authorise someone else to reach the records clinics hold (Art. 4(2), §3.2). Scoped, revocable delegation for hubs exists only as a design: grants with scopes, constraints and expiry (authority model, "not implemented"). The drawing combines one jurisdiction's law with an unbuilt design; it is not a forecast for any market.

Interpretation.

  1. The route out of the vendor cloud is the person's own login. Today's real-time path depends on the vendor tolerating it, not on a duty to provide it.
  2. Delegation is shared credentials. Revoking one helper means changing what everyone holds.
  3. The law that creates a duty is European, and covers data only. It obliges sharing on request with a designated party. No law found obliges accepting commands.
  4. Two kinds of proxy are emerging. EHDS proxy covers clinic records, and a Data Act third party covers device data. Neither yet reaches a self-hosted hub's own followers.

The characterisations of law here are summaries for discussion, drafts for counsel to review, and not legal advice. Points to check: whether CGM values are in the Data Act's scope (Recital 15); the Art. 4(2) health-and-safety carve-out; whether a US non-profit can be a designated third party; and the current HIPAA rule for directing records to a third party (45 CFR 164.524) (vendor note §7).

docs.title: 1·access-paths: who holds the key on each path
docs.text:
As believed. Every path is open to software that knows the protocol, and the data is the person's to share (DIGITAL-RIGHTS, overview; primer).

As it works today. Pump paths are mostly open because the secret they need is one the person holds: a code shown on the pump, a serial, or the device itself (device-layer census; DanaKit e157a86, MedtrumKit ef866fa, pumpX2 6fa9459). The CGM paths split. Dexcom G6 needs only the transmitter's ID (CGMBLEKit ea224e7). Dexcom G7 and Libre 3 check the app as well, and the open implementations present a fixed client credential the manufacturer did not issue to them (xdripswift c268542, Juggluco 75399d7, LibreLoop 150d2b1, read 2026-10-17). Two pumps check the app too. The MiniMed 780G's open connectors authenticate as the manufacturer's own mobile app, using that app's key database, after the person starts pairing from the pump (OpenMinimed Documentation 73a7811); both connectors say they are proofs of concept, not for therapy. The open Omnipod 5 driver presents a controller certificate whose source is not described here (OmnipodKit 928bb79; vendor note §1.6). Eversense 365 takes a different route: the open driver signs in to the manufacturer's service with the person's own account to get the device's certificate, so the manufacturer's service is in the path though no check of the app was found (EversenseKit e1bb6fa; its predecessor, the E3, has no link security). The cloud path runs on the person's own login and the vendor's tolerance, and breaks when the cloud changes (evidence §5).

As it is emerging. Two closures are possible on the device side: an app check that stops accepting the credentials open software presents, and readings sealed end to end for the manufacturer's cloud. The second was not looked for in the census (vendor note §5.1). On the cloud side the EU Data Act adds a duty to share, and the US has none (vendor note §3.1).

Interpretation.

  1. The key, not the encryption, decides access. Every device on step A uses authenticated or encrypted links, and open implementations work with all of them.
  2. Each step up moves the key towards the manufacturer. On step B the open app depends on the manufacturer's app staying installed; on C, on the manufacturer's service answering the person's sign-in; on D, on the device continuing to accept the credential the open app presents; on E no app on the phone can read the data at all.
  3. Step D is in use today, not only emerging. Every device on it works with open software only through credentials the manufacturer did not issue to the projects: fixed ones carried in the open code (Dexcom G7, Libre 3, MiniMed 780G), and for Omnipod 5 a controller certificate whose source is not described here. A sensor, pump or firmware change that stops accepting them would close the path for every open implementation at once, and whether carrying such a credential is lawful is a question for counsel (vendor note §7).
  4. Loss on the device side and on the cloud side reach different people. The device side stops automation for the person; the cloud side stops remote following for caregivers (partner readiness §1).

The drawing and ladder are at mechanism level only. The ladder's data and generator are tools/structure-diagrams/access/devices.yaml and access_charts.py.

docs.title: 1·hosting: who answers for a site run for someone else
docs.text:
As believed. Nightscout is "software you run yourself", written for "the person who runs a Nightscout site: for themselves, for their child, or for someone they care for" (operator upgrade path §1). The licence is AGPL-3.0 and the code comes "WITHOUT ANY WARRANTY" (cgm-remote-monitor README.md, licence section). Here the person who runs the site is the person who relies on it.

As it works today. Many sites are run by a hosting operator for a subscription. The shared documentation lists nine providers, added by pull request, with no published criteria and no rule for the order. Its introduction reads "If you want to save time and avoid the need to maintain a DIY solution, you have many providers", so the listing presents upgrades and upkeep as the operator's job (GOVERNANCE-TODAY §4). What each operator promises on availability, security and exit is in its own terms, which were not read for this drawing. Health-data law is already in force: the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (16 CFR 318, amended 2024) sets breach notice for health apps outside HIPAA (the US medical-privacy law), and Washington's My Health My Data Act reaches "any legal entity", non-profits included (vendor note §3.5–3.6). Whether either reaches a given operator is a question for counsel.

As it is emerging. The duties follow the activity, whoever does it. "Hosting or processing anyone's health data" brings a privacy notice, retention rules and breach response; "operating a service that people's data or therapy depends on" brings availability, security and incident duties and a continuity plan (what each activity brings §3). Three changes are proposed, not adopted. The collaboration model's rule 3 lists every provider that meets published criteria and labels any run by the project's own maintainers or founders (COLLABORATION-MODEL §5). Commercial offerings would show they track the shared contract with the same public conformance suite, CNCF's model (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §2). And the multitenancy design takes bulk hosting as its target, with one operator running many tenants while "self-hosted single-tenant stays first-class permanently" (D1, with per-tenant credentials in D13; execution plan §1); adopted, not released.

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. The licence disclaims the software's warranty; it does not disclaim the operator's duties. "As is" covers the code. The duties of hosting and operating attach to whoever does them.
  2. The person who relies on a site and the person who runs it come apart. The believed picture has one box doing both jobs. Today the operator runs the site and the person pays for it.
  3. The listing is the ecosystem's only lever over hosting, and it has no criteria. Today it adds providers case by case. The emerging picture makes listing conditional on published criteria and public tests, without the foundation taking on an operator's own duties (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §2b: sponsor by default, operate only by a recorded decision).
  4. Multitenancy concentrates the duty. One operator answers for every tenant at once.

Caveat. The characterisations of law here are drafts for counsel, not legal advice. Points to check: whether the FTC rule and state health-data laws reach a hosting operator, and which state laws beyond Washington apply; whether listing providers creates endorsement or liability exposure (COLLABORATION-MODEL §8).

docs.title: 1·teams: who decides the shared data contract
docs.text:
As believed (inferred: the assumptions the next panel tests). One project decides, the hub knows each writer, and someone runs the shared operations.

As the repositories and code show. Each of 20 repositories decides what it merges and releases; the foundation supports projects by resource request, runs events and gives awards; no shared body for decisions that cross projects is named (governance §1, §3, §6, measured 2026-10-02). The hub has no registration code and tells controllers apart by the loop or openaps key (3·registration). Writers send their own shapes: the quirks registry holds 20 entries in four collections (specs/quirks/*.yaml at 0b0d150f), and five apps use five record-id conventions (identifier format research §1). Intake and registry have no named runner (2·shared-infra).

Interpretation. The organisation and the data contract have the same shape: where no team owns a join, the hub keeps every side of it. The set is read through Conway's Law in the case study.

Caveat. Counts are as measured on the dates given; re-measure before quoting.

docs.title: The ecosystem's designs: believed, actual, proposed
3·identity: who is who on a hub, and who may do what
docs.text:
As believed (inferred). The README describes API_SECRET only as "a secret passphrase that must be at least 12 characters long". Client apps ask for it to upload, and people share it with apps and caregivers (authority model, "The Credential Dilemma"). Read this way, the secret is an upload password.

As it works today (read-derived, cgm-remote-monitor 15.0.8; the lines are unchanged on dev). A request with no credential gets the default roles (index.js:161-169), readable unless the operator changes it (settings.js:39). A matching API secret grants *, every permission (index.js:173-180), including managing subjects and roles (endpoints.js:38-98). An access token resolves to its subject's roles plus the default roles (index.js:222-238). A token can be exchanged for a JWT that lasts 8 hours (enclave.js:58-59). Each subject's token is derived from the API secret, so changing the secret replaces every token (storage.js:187-193). The seven default roles are at storage.js:140-148. This is the access model as the code and the README document it. It is not a security assessment of any release, and it does not show how well each part of the server enforces it.

As proposed (hosted, TENANCY_MODE=multi; self-hosted single-tenant keeps API_SECRET, D1). The decisions are in the execution plan §1, §2.8 and §2.9: - D13: there is no deployment-wide secret. Each tenant holds its own root credential, which the hosting operator mints through ns-admin. That port is unreachable from outside (D7), and the owner can rotate the credential. - D14: a per-tenant signing key. - D16: three listeners. ns-tenant-admin is a second socket inside ns-api, decided 2026-10-16. - D17: devices keep a native credential, "never Ory". Ory Kratos for people is adopted in principle and gated. Ory Hydra, for delegated access by third-party apps, is deferred.

A controller registration is bound to the subject that created it, "never the token". The owner may retire, block, release or transfer it (hub-sync design §3.5). Bindings made with the API secret move to the tenant root credential (walk-through 2026-10-16, row 12, commit 66403e0f). None of the proposed boxes is built.

Interpretation.

  1. One secret is both a key and the root of trust today. It grants every permission and every token derives from it.
  2. The proposal separates the hoster, the owner and the data path into separate credentials and separate sockets.
  3. Identity moves from a shared secret to a subject. Registrations and tokens attach to who created them.
  4. Delegation to people or agents is still undecided. Hydra is deferred, and the grant model is a design.

docs.title: 1·federation: one sign-in across regional zones
docs.text:
Identity today belongs to each site, and each hosting operator has its own sign-in. The programme proposes a trust federation instead: each party keeps its own identity provider, the foundation defines what counts as recognised participation, and health data stays in the zone whose law applies to it. Zero trust means no request is trusted because of where it comes from: every call carries a credential that is checked, scoped to what it may do, and short-lived.

As believed (inferred: no survey exists). Each site is its own island, kept safe by a private secret; sharing means giving the secret to apps and people one trusts. The setup reads this way: one API_SECRET per site, and Nightscout deliberately holds no usernames or passwords of its own (ADR-003).

As it works today. "Identity today is per site": API_SECRET and tokens are issued by each site; in the multitenant target each tenant holds its own root credential and signing key (D13, D14), and devices keep a native per-tenant credential permanently (D17) (programme §5; and 3·identity above). Each hosting operator runs its own sign-in, and the providers are listed with no published criteria (governance §4). One server, Nocturne, registers apps with OAuth dynamic client registration (RFC 7591) against a bundled list of known apps. The programme records "no work item and no decision on the federation".

As proposed. The trust federation of programme §5: each party keeps its own identity provider and presents verifiable claims; the receiving service decides whether they meet its policy; the foundation "would define what counts as recognised participation. It would not hold anyone's passwords." The standards exist: OpenID Federation 1.0 (final 2026-02-17) supplies trust anchors and signed entity statements, and OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) supplies scoped, downstream and delegated tokens. The federation would carry identities, keys, schemas, consent references and audit identifiers as a shared control plane, while health data stays in regional stores under their own rules. The council of members is the governance form of the 2026-01-31 draft community identity-provider proposal (Option A, a federated council), drawn here as roles: a zone operator may be a hosting company, or a national or informal group, recognised on the same published criteria as every other member. None of this is built or decided.

Two precedents show the governance at scale: - TEFCA, the US Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement: separately operated health information networks, each designated after an application and onboarding, sign one Common Agreement that sets baseline legal and technical requirements and a governing approach; a Recognized Coordinating Entity, the Sequoia Project, coordinates under contract with the federal government (healthit.gov, read 2026-10-17). "Individual access services" is one of its exchange purposes. - eduGAIN, the interfederation of national research and education identity federations: each federation keeps its own members, signed metadata is aggregated and exchanged, and a steering group with one representative per federation approves policy, new members and suspensions (Wikipedia, read 2026-10-17; edugain.org refused the request, so re-check there before quoting).

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. The foundation's role is recognition, not operation. It publishes the criteria and signs statements about members; it holds no passwords and runs no zone (the §2b sponsor-or-operate split applied to identity).
  2. The same criteria for every member. A hosting company and a national or informal group meet one published standard, the "same requirements for anyone" of what each activity brings §5.
  3. Identity is shared; data is not. The control plane crosses zones; health data stays where its law applies.
  4. Zero trust replaces "the secret is private". Each request carries a scoped, short-lived credential, so a helper or agent can be given exactly what it needs and lose it alone.
  5. Governance is visible. A council approves policy, members and suspensions, so recognition and its withdrawal follow a published process rather than one party's discretion.

Caveat. The federation is a proposal; whether the foundation can act as a trust anchor, and what liability recognition carries, are questions for counsel.

docs.title: 3·registration: who writes to the hub, and where a command goes
docs.text:
As believed (inferred: the assumptions the next panel tests). The hub knows which controller wrote a record, an agent acts as an agent, and a command that was sent was applied.

As the code works today (cgm-remote-monitor a8888f0d, read-derived). There is no registry (no registration code under lib/). Readers re-derive the controller from the document's shape, by whether a devicestatus has a loop or an openaps key (lib/plugins/loop.js:50, lib/plugins/openaps.js:82, lib/plugins/iob.js:100-101), so Trio and AndroidAPS, which both write openaps, look the same, and the free-text device string is unreliable (control-plane supersession map §3.2–§3.3). Access is a shared secret or tokens with default roles; the Loop relay permission is held only by admin (lib/authorization/storage.js:140-148, lib/api2/notifications-v2.js:19). Only one development-only AndroidAPS path records a command and returns an acknowledgement with an id; elsewhere success shows as the resulting record and failure as a free-text Note (technical loops §3.3–§3.4, landscape §6). An automated agent holds a credential someone shared and is indistinguishable from them; delegation grants are "not implemented" (authority model).

As decided (D18–D20): specified, not built. D18: well-known declarations ship with the hub for today's writers, and controllers own typed registrations; the hub is responsible for observability, the controller for sending accurately and reconciling, and the hub records composition results rather than computing them (plan §2.6.1). A registration is bound to the subject that created it, not to a token; the owner may block, retire, release or transfer it, never edit it (hub-sync §3.5). D19 separates the definition (what data means, identified by its content hash) from the instance (one connected copy with a lease and device or simulated provenance per role). Each role has one source of record, an overlap is flagged, and a command goes only to the live device command sink, or is refused no-command-destination; that role needs the product's binding or the owner's transfer (plan §2.6.2, hub-sync §3.6). D20 scopes quirks to the versions that produce them and splits the client-assigned identifier from the hub-assigned _id (hub-sync §3.7). An agent would register its own instance; role types are open "so roles such as proposing versus acting can be added for agents" (D19 rule 5). Open: the command API, proposed in the commands specification and not decided, the contract per tenancy mode (SPEC-REG-MODES), the first hub (HUB-REG-CRM), the proposals to Nocturne and the controllers, all not started (queue); and how an agent is scoped, limited and revoked, which no decision covers.

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. Identity moves from inference to declaration, and the declaration is bound to a subject.
  2. The hub routes and records; it never doses. One source of record per role and one command destination decide where data and commands go, not what the controller does with them.
  3. Requested and applied become separate records, though the command record is not yet specified.
  4. The owner gains a control the code lacks: acting on one registration without rotating a secret everyone shares.
  5. An agent stops being a borrowed identity once it registers; its scope is still open.

Caveat. Read from code and design pages, not run; every proposed box is implemented in no hub.

docs.title: 2·data-commons: how Nightscout data reaches research
docs.text:
As believed. What each party says it needs: people want "control of their own data" and offer "consent to research"; researchers want "consented, well-described data without taking custody of it" (COLLABORATION-MODEL §2).

As it works today. Data reaches research by two routes. In the first, a person hands over an export or a readable token (a credential that lets a program read their site), and a researcher converts it one site at a time: tools/ns2parquet/ns_fetch.py reads a site address and token from an environment file (lines 36–81; read from code). This repository's schema corpus is 11 consenting sites, with every recorded value passed through one redaction step (typed-schema evidence §1.3). tools/nsprobe reverses the direction: a data holder runs the probes on their own machine and only counts leave it, with at least three sites behind any named value (nsprobe README; MIN_SITES = 3 at tools/nsprobe/privacy.py:34). In the second route, the foundation's Nightscout Data Transfer (2017) moves a site's data to Open Humans, a research-data platform, and on to data commons there (history). The OpenAPS Data Commons page says members "may remove your data … at any time", that data already given to researchers "may have already been shared", and that raw data is accessed by the volunteer administrators and the projects they authorise (Open Humans, read 2026-10-17). Ethics (IRB) review, consent and withdrawal terms, and data-use agreements are a duty of research with identifiable data (what each activity brings §3); no shared record of such review was found in the sources read.

As proposed. The datalake proposal asks the board for a 90-day pilot (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §6). Participants opt in through foundation-approved consent with a revocation and deletion path. Hosting operators may offer that opt-in at sign-up. A contracted implementation team runs intake and normalisation. A foundation sponsor and advisory reviewers decide consent, access and publication, and the foundation "remains accountable" (proposal, board draft, "operating flow" and "consent model"; bewest/ns-data-proposal at 18df3a0). Its roadmap lists federated analysis as a later expansion candidate, not a pilot output. That follows OHDSI's pattern: "data remains at the site … Only aggregate results are shared" (PRECEDENTS; ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §5, "where data may go"). The proposal names legal, privacy and methods review, not IRB review.

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. Consent today is per route, not per person. No one record shows a person where their data went.
  2. Withdrawal stops future use, not copies already shared. This is true of today's commons. The proposal adds a deletion path; it does not say what happens to extracts already delivered.
  3. Two directions compete: pooling, or analysis where the data is. The pilot pools consented exports in one governed store. nsprobe and the OHDSI pattern keep data with its holder and move only aggregates.
  4. The proposal separates sponsor from operator, the §2b split applied to research, and puts consent collection with hosting operators, which joins this drawing to 1·hosting.

Caveat. The characterisations of research ethics and privacy here are drafts for an ethics or privacy professional and for counsel, not advice. Points to check: whether the pilot needs IRB review, and under which institution; and what consent, de-identification and publication review an extract needs in each region (ECOSYSTEM-PROGRAMME §9, point 8).

docs.title: 2·shared-infra: shared operations, and who runs them
docs.text:
As believed (inferred): someone is doing each shared operation.

As measured today. Of 20 repositories (2026-10-02), none has a SECURITY policy of its own and 4 have private vulnerability reporting on; reports arrive in Discord, Facebook, Zulip, Gitter and GitHub; the provider listing changes by pull request with no published criteria; the foundation's resource-request page names no review criteria; no cross-project body is named (governance §2–§6). No named security contact, complaint workflow, SBOM or build-provenance record was found (partner readiness §3). The conformance suite lives in this repository: 85 vector files, an oref0 runner, and AndroidAPS and Loop runners not implemented (conformance/; tools/conformance_suite.py:43-55). This repository's CI runs Python syntax and spec validation; the suite and the queue gates run by make, outside CI. The 15.0.9 run records are the nearest thing to release evidence (quality system §4.1).

As proposed. Four shared operations, "none exists yet as shared work" (programme §2c); two are drawn, with the conformance kit, registry and documentation. The foundation sponsors by default and operates only by a recorded decision naming the operator, its contract, insurance and successor (§2b). One intake takes three streams and refers reportable events to the responsible manufacturer; intake is not legal responsibility (partner readiness §6). Security contacts and private reporting per project "can start at once" (§8). The registry, the credential authority and hosting are kept apart (§7); the foundation would define recognised participation (programme §5). The quality kit gives one run record and a suite any server can run; each project decides whether to join (quality system §4–§5). No change to documentation is proposed.

Interpretation. Properties the three panels show:

  1. Two operations have no runner today. Registry and intake have no edge in the actual panel.
  2. What exists is engineering, held in one repository; the operational evidence mostly does not.
  3. Sponsoring and operating are different edges: funding to projects, control of a service others depend on to a named operator, by decision.
  4. The intake closes two loops: regression tests back to projects, referrals out to manufacturers.

Caveat. Counts are as measured on the dates given; re-measure before quoting. Whether operating an intake creates duties for the foundation, and how referrals meet a manufacturer's reporting duties (21 CFR Part 803), are drafts for counsel and a regulatory professional, not advice.

docs.title: Who controls what: the ecosystem's control structures, today and proposed
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-19 at 35ec9da5a.

What this is: a map (part 2 of the overview, perspective; how the overview is organised), for the Nightscout Foundation board, the maintainers of the ecosystem projects, and the community. Read after accountability thresholds; leads to process models. Living page, written 2026-10-16, relabelled 2026-10-17; 1·agents listed 2026-10-18. Drawings to follow and discuss the overview's proposals with: who controls whom, what comes back, and where money flows. Every node and edge comes from a page linked under the drawing; nothing here is a new finding. The drawings marked proposed show a proposal for discussion, not a decision.

Author's interests: the author maintains cgm-remote-monitor, founded a company that hosts Nightscout commercially, and could be a candidate for paid work under the related proposals. The collaboration rules §5 would apply to that company and to the author like anyone else. Operators in the drawings are roles, not named companies.

docs.title: How to read the drawings
docs.text:
The drawings follow the convention of STPA (system-theoretic process analysis) control structures. Whoever controls sits above what they control. Control actions run down the left of each loop and the feedback that tells a controller what happened runs up the right. A loop with no feedback edge is a loop whose controller cannot see the result of what it does.

An icon at the left of each box says what the box does: a factory for a manufacturer, a civic building for a legislature, scales for a regulator, one figure for a person and two for people, a key for a credential authority, a phone for an app. The key lists every icon. The icons are from Lucide (ISC licence), copied into tools/structure-diagrams/icons/ with their licence.

Every drawing is labelled level · subject. The level is where the drawing sits in the hierarchy, from society down to software and devices; the subject is a short name that stays the same as drawings are added beside it.

level what sits at it drawings 0 · society legislatures, regulators and the sector around AID in general 0·sector; 0·diy-status* 1 · ecosystem the ecosystem's organisations and how they connect 1·today, 1·proposed (and six stakeholder views); 1·authority*, 1·data-rights*, 1·hosting*, 1·federation*, 1·teams*; 1·contract (drawn on the Conway's Law case study §3); 1·agents (drawn on agents in the ecosystem §1) 2 · one organisation or agreement one entity, one agreement, one programme 2·agreement, 2·controller-operator; the precedents 2·sqlite, 2·cncf, 2·apple; 2·data-commons*, 2·shared-infra* 3 · technical process one loop in software and devices 3·controller, 3·hub-sync, 3·delegation, 3·person-loop; 3·identity*, 3·registration* idea one idea from the argument, drawn small idea·sponsor-or-operate, idea·one-codebase, idea·same-requirements, idea·oversight-layer, idea·tiers, idea·credential-lifetime, idea·complaints, idea·designated-third-party

* Drawn three times on one layout (believed, actual, and emerging or proposed) on the companion page Process models: what we believe, and how it works.

A box marked [zoom: 2·agreement] is drawn in more detail in that drawing. Markers are used only where the link between two drawings would not be obvious otherwise: 0·sector's commons is the whole of 1·proposed; 1·proposed's credential authority is where the agreements of 2·agreement reach the projects; its regulated controller operator is 2·controller-operator; the people at the bottom of 1·proposed, and the controller app in 2·controller-operator, run the loop drawn in 3·controller. The levels are views of one system, not separate systems, so the same box can appear at several levels: the credential authority is in 1·proposed, 2·agreement and 3·person-loop.

Drawings that span more than one kind of boundary carry horizontal bands: legal (law, regulation and the authorities that make them), social (organisations, agreements and people) and technical (software and devices). The bands show where accountability crosses from one to the next.

docs.title: 0·sector
docs.text: The two columns follow Leveson's sociotechnical form: development on the left, operations on the right. The commons sits between them because it is both: specifications and release processes on one side, documentation and hubs that people use on the other.

docs.title: 1·today
docs.text:
Sources: how decisions are made today §1, §3 and §4; partner readiness §1 and §3. What the drawing shows by its gaps:

  • No edge joins a project or the foundation to a manufacturer. Projects reach devices through protocols volunteers worked out (a data edge, not an agreement).
  • No complaint or incident route leaves the ecosystem. Feedback from people reaches projects as issues and logs, and stops there.
  • The only funding edges are the foundation's support to projects and subscriptions to hosted providers.

docs.title: 1·proposed
docs.text:
Sources: ecosystem programme §2b (the foundation sponsors by default and operates only by recorded decision); partner readiness §2 (tiers A, B and C), §6 (complaint intake) and §7 (registry, credential authority and hosting kept apart); precedents (Tidepool Loop: a regulated track beside the DIY one).

What changes against today: each new edge to a manufacturer runs through a named legal entity. The foundation signs for tier A, observe and export. Tier B and C relationships go to an operator with its own contract, insurance and successor: a credential authority, or a regulated controller operator as Tidepool was for Loop. The DIY track keeps its own edges to people. Complaints and incidents gain a route back to the manufacturer; that route is drawn one level down, in 2·agreement, and the person's own loop in 3·controller, so that this drawing carries one idea: who holds which agreement. The manufacturer is drawn above the foundation because in this drawing it grants access; that is the direction of control, not a ranking.

docs.title: The same drawing, from each stakeholder's side
docs.text:
Each view greys out everything that does not touch the stakeholder. The layout does not change, so the views can be laid side by side.

view what this stakeholder controls what reaches them as feedback a person with diabetes or a caregiver which releases, hosted hubs and devices they use, and whether to pay a host releases, hosted hubs and a cleared app; their complaints and their own loop are in 2·agreement and 3·controller a project maintainer releases to people conformance results go up; credentials and tests come down from bodies the project does not run a Nightscout-as-a-service operator the hosted hubs subscriptions; hub conformance is proposed, not existing a manufacturer agreements, credential authority, clearance submissions a readiness dossier from the foundation and submissions from any regulated operator; forwarded complaints are in 2·agreement. None of this exists today the foundation board sponsorship of shared operations the tier A agreement and nothing else; it operates nothing in this drawing a regulator clearance of manufacturers and of any regulated controller operator adverse events and submissions; the DIY track has no edge to a regulator

The "feedback" column is read from the drawing; it is where the stakeholders are likely to disagree, and where the drawing should be corrected if it is wrong.

docs.title: 2·agreement
docs.text: Source: partner readiness §4 (terms that carry data rights), §6 (complaints in both directions) and §7 (three roles kept apart; separating request from effect). The registry says who qualifies, the credential authority issues credentials, and the client release is hosted or built by someone else again. The client's commands to the device are requests; what comes back is the state the device applied, the split the hub-sync architecture already makes.

docs.title: 2·controller-operator: Loop-as-a-service
docs.text:
A proposal for discussion. Sources: the special controls for interoperable automated glycemic controllers (iAGC, 21 CFR 862.1356), integrated CGMs (iCGM, 862.1355) and alternate controller enabled pumps (ACE, 880.5730), as summarised in the stack census cloud layer; history and precedents for Tidepool Loop, cleared as an iAGC on 2023-01-23 (K203689); partner readiness §2 (tier C) and §7.

What makes this a different drawing from 2·agreement:

  • The operator is the legal manufacturer of the controller. It answers to the regulator for one validated release and its updates. The DIY track continues beside it, as DIY Loop did beside Tidepool Loop.
  • One codebase. The cleared release is a validated build of the same open-source releases, not a separate edition (programme, "One codebase, two uses": SQLite sells assurance on the releases free users get; CNCF certifies vendors against one upstream). Fixes and validation evidence from the regulated track return to the shared codebase, drawn as a proposed edge. The reason for the edge: without it the regulated track becomes a second upstream, and the open project and the operator compete for the same fixes and the same maintainers' time.
  • The interfaces are regulated on both sides. The iAGC controls ask for validated interface specifications, secure authentication (pairing) and a process for sharing and validating the interface with connected devices. The ACE pump and iCGM controls ask the device side for the same. The pump and CGM manufacturers' edges to the operator are therefore agreements, not protocols worked out by volunteers.
  • The controller's inputs and outputs are restricted. Under the iAGC regulation it takes glucose only from iCGMs and commands only ACE pumps, unless the regulator determines otherwise. An ACE pump must fall back safely when it loses the connection.
  • Feedback has a record. The regulation asks for a record of critical events. Together with complaints, it returns to the operator and from there to the regulator, which the DIY loop in 1·today does not have.

The drawing does not settle who operates such an entity, whether the foundation sponsors it (programme §2b: sponsoring does not make the foundation the operator), or how the return edge works when a fix to the open codebase has not yet been validated for the cleared release. The regulatory summary above paraphrases the regulations; it is for regulatory counsel to confirm against the current text and any device-specific clearance.

docs.title: The technical loops
docs.text: Contributor-facing in detail; summarised here for every reader. Three loops in software and devices, drawn from the source code of Loop, Trio and AndroidAPS (AAPS) and the Nightscout server. The detail, with file and line references, is in the technical loops note (read 2026-10-17 from the revisions it lists; read from the code, not run on a device). The design pages they serve embed the same drawings.

docs.title: 3·controller
docs.text: The classic STPA loop: a controller (the app and its algorithm), an actuator (the pump), the controlled process (the body's glucose and insulin) and a sensor (the CGM), with the person supervising. All three apps command short temporary basal rates of up to 30 minutes, and automatic or manual boluses; they stop dosing when the newest glucose reading is too old (15 minutes in Loop, 12 in Trio, 7 in AAPS, each read from the code; Loop and Trio rechecked at LoopWorkspace v3.14.9 and Trio v1.0.2 on 2026-10-17). What each app does with a failed or uncertain pump command, and how the person can open or close the loop, differ; the note's §1.3 compares them. This is a description of how the software is built, not advice on using it; settings are for each person and their care team.

docs.title: 3·hub-sync
docs.text: The hub in the middle: who writes each kind of record (glucose, treatments, device status, profiles) and who reads it. What a controller says it applied and what someone asked for are kept apart, the split the hub-sync architecture makes.

docs.title: 3·delegation
docs.text: How a caregiver, or an automated agent acting for the person, sends a command (a remote bolus, carbs, a temporary target, an override) to the controller. Measured gaps (note §3): the hub keeps no record of a command with an id and an acknowledgement, except in AAPS's development branch; a reply reaches the sender only where the sender supplied a return path; "success" means the pump accepted the command, not that delivery finished; and an automated agent looks the same as whoever shared the credential with it. The proposed command record and acknowledgement are drawn in 3·registration, as proposed.

docs.title: 3·person-loop
docs.text: Source: partner readiness §7, "no single point of failure for therapy". The credential authority is the only node above the person that can reach the loop, and the drawing puts it outside the loop: the app holds a grant that stays valid offline within bounds, so the authority being unreachable does not stop the loop. What the bounds are is for each manufacturer to define and validate; the drawing does not describe how any released system behaves.

docs.title: Precedents at level 2
docs.text:
drawing precedent maps onto the shape it shows 2·sqlite SQLite 1·proposed, foundation and shared operations companies buy assurance through one small company; no edge runs from a buyer to the developers 2·cncf CNCF 1·proposed and 2·agreement, conformance and registry many vendors certified against one upstream by the same public tests 2·apple Apple Developer Program 2·agreement and 3·person-loop, credential authority a platform owner enrols developers, issues signing credentials that expire, and approves special entitlements

Source: precedents, SQLite, read from sqlite.org 2026-09-29.

Source: precedents, funding and rules rows (charter, TOC process, conformance and KCSP pages, read 2026-09-29 and 2026-10-01).

Source: TestFlight distribution infrastructure §1, §3 and §4. Self-built apps put one developer account, and its yearly certificate, on every person who builds; App Store apps put one account on the publisher. That is the trade a credential authority in 2·agreement makes too: who holds the credential decides who answers for it and whose renewal can lapse.

docs.title: Single ideas
docs.text: Leveson's figures are crisp partly because each carries one idea. These drawings take one idea from the overview's argument and draw it with as few boxes as it needs, in two or three panels on one layout.

docs.title: idea·sponsor-or-operate
docs.text: The same service, drawn twice. The only change is who sits in the operator's box, and with it where uptime, incidents, complaints and claims arrive. Sponsoring passes money down and reports up; operating passes control down and makes every incident the foundation's. The programme proposes that the foundation sponsors by default and operates only by a recorded decision naming the operator, its contract, insurance and successor (programme §2b); the duties that operating brings are listed in what each activity brings §3.

docs.title: idea·one-codebase
docs.text: One project's releases serve both people who build their own and an operator, with no separate edition (programme, "One codebase, two uses"; SQLite's and CNCF's models in precedents). The second panel is what the proposed return edge prevents: a fork, after which the open project and the operator compete for the same fixes and the same maintainers' time (2·controller-operator).

docs.title: idea·same-requirements
docs.text: The requirements do not change with the kind of organisation; meeting them usually takes a legal entity. Evidence: the FDA routes are open to any manufacturer and Tidepool, a nonprofit, took the same 510(k) route; Dexcom's agreement is standard and non-negotiable; Washington's health-data act does not exclude nonprofits; Apple asks healthcare apps to come from a legal entity (what each activity brings §5).

docs.title: idea·oversight-layer
docs.text: A nonprofit's role is oversight: published criteria, listing and certification, applied the same way to every company, with results returned in public. Each company keeps its own legal and regulatory duties; the nonprofit does not take them over (CNCF, the Open Home Foundation, TEFCA and eduGAIN in precedents; what each activity brings §5).

docs.title: idea·tiers
docs.text: The same relationship three times, one agreement per tier, each adding lines: observe and export; configure and coordinate; control insulin delivery. The tiers are this repository's terms for technical risk, not FDA classifications; the recommendation is to ask for tier A first and separately (partner readiness §2).

docs.title: idea·credential-lifetime
docs.text: One credential in three states, each with a defined safe state. A credential service must not be able to stop insulin delivery by being unreachable; revocation follows a published process, and must leave a person's devices in a defined safe state (partner readiness §4 and §7). The bounds and safe states are for each manufacturer to define and validate; the drawing states requirements, not the behaviour of any released system.

docs.title: idea·complaints
docs.text: One intake for support, complaints and security, routing each report to the party legally responsible. It closes two loops: regression tests back to the projects, and referrals out to the manufacturer, whose own reporting duties stay its own (21 CFR Part 803). Intake is not legal responsibility (partner readiness §5 and §6).

docs.title: idea·designated-third-party
docs.text: In the EU since 2025-09-12, the person decides who receives their device data, and the data holder must send it there; the recipient is bound to the agreed purposes (vendor note §3.1). This is a draft summary of the law for counsel to review, not legal advice. The drawing is also embedded in DIGITAL-RIGHTS, beside the Data Act entry.

docs.title: What the drawings do not show
docs.text:
• Legal relationships in detail. An edge labelled "agreement" stands for terms that partner readiness §4–§5 lists; which party is the manufacturer for which function, liability and intellectual property are for counsel and are not drawn.
  • Sizes and amounts. Edges show that money flows, not how much.
  • Every participant. Clinicians appear only in 0·sector; the support community and hubs other than Nightscout are not drawn.

docs.title: Changing a drawing
docs.text: The drawings are generated. Each one's source is a YAML file in tools/structure-diagrams/inputs/, with nodes placed by level and column, edges typed as control, feedback, funding or data, and optional stakeholder views. Edit the YAML and run python3 tools/structure-diagrams/render.py. The renderer places every box on a grid and routes lines at right angles, with each control and feedback pair drawn as two parallel lines, in the manner of Leveson's control structures. It replaced a Graphviz renderer on 2026-10-17 after the grid layout lab measured both; the earlier diagram tool lab compared the off-the-shelf tools.

docs.text:

This document analyzes the 69% divergence found in conformance testing between AAPS algorithm outputs and vanilla oref0, based on 85 test vectors extracted from AAPS ReplayApsResultsTest fixtures.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Metric Value Total test vectors 85 Passed 26 (31%) Failed 59 (69%) Errors 0

Root Cause: The divergence is NOT caused by differences between vanilla AAPS and oref0. It is caused by AAPS's Dynamic ISF and AutoISF extensions that are not present in oref0.

AAPS Algorithm Variant Tests Pass Rate Divergence OpenAPSSMBPlugin 16 94% Minimal (1 failure) OpenAPSAMAPlugin 3 67% Low (1 failure) OpenAPSSMBDynamicISFPlugin 44 18% High (36 failures) OpenAPSSMBAutoISFPlugin 22 5% Very High (21 failures)

Conclusion: The core oref0 algorithm (OpenAPSSMBPlugin) is effectively identical in AAPS and oref0. The divergence comes from AAPS-specific ISF calculation extensions.
