Purpose: Document how BabelBetes standardizes multi-source clinical diabetes data and how this pattern informs multifactored FactsLoader design in the AID audition system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
BabelBetes provides a data standardization toolkit for 9 clinical trial datasets (~500,000 subject-days of paired CGM, basal, bolus). Its core insight is factor-aware extraction: complex real-world signals (insulin delivery, CGM artifacts, closed-loop modes) are decomposed into independent factors, reconciled at extraction time, and validated against strict schemas.

This directly parallels our multifactored phenotype synthesis (EXP-2886: stack × brake × counter-reg, all orthogonal |ρ|<0.32).

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: The four major open-source AID systems use fundamentally different approaches to carb absorption modeling. Loop uses predictive curve-based models that project expected absorption, while oref0/AAPS/Trio use reactive deviation-based models that infer absorption from glucose changes.

docs.title: CGM Data Sources Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-17 at 03a869a26.

This document provides comprehensive analysis of how CGM (Continuous Glucose Monitor) data flows from sensors to Nightscout entries, covering data sources, calibration, follower modes, and data provenance across xDrip+ (Android), xDrip4iOS, Loop, AAPS, and Trio.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
CGM data originates from hardware transmitters and flows through a chain of software components before reaching Nightscout. Understanding this flow is critical for:

  1. Data provenance - Knowing where glucose values came from
  2. Calibration accuracy - Understanding which calibration was applied where
  3. Deduplication - Preventing duplicate entries from multiple uploaders
  4. Latency - Understanding delays introduced by each layer

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text: Aspect Finding Primary Producer xDrip+ Android is the most common CGM data producer with 20+ data source types iOS Producers xDrip4iOS and Loop CGMManager plugins handle Dexcom/Libre transmitters Calibration Diversity Only xDrip+ Android has pluggable calibration (5+ algorithms); others use native/OOP Follower Latency Nightscout follower: real-time; LibreLinkUp: 1-3 min; Dexcom Share: ~5 min Provenance Gap Calibration source and algorithm are not tracked in Nightscout entries

Status: Living Document Last Updated: January 2026 Purpose: A plain-language guide to data rights in diabetes care for patients, caregivers, clinicians, developers, and policymakers

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This document provides an accessible introduction to data rights in the context of diabetes technology. It complements the Digital Rights and Legal Protections document (which covers legal frameworks) and the Progressive Enhancement Framework (which covers technical architecture).

Modern diabetes care is increasingly data-driven. Continuous glucose monitors generate readings every few minutes. Insulin pumps log every dose. Automated systems make decisions based on patterns, predictions, and real-time signals. This data doesn't just describe care—it drives care.

If data drives care, then people with diabetes must have clear rights to control, share, and act on their data.

docs.title: Dexcom G6/G7 BLE Protocol Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at 5a9a49cc1.

This document provides a comprehensive specification of the Dexcom G6 and G7 Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) protocols, reverse-engineered from open-source implementations.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Dexcom G6 and G7 continuous glucose monitors use Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to communicate with mobile devices. The protocol consists of:

  • BLE Service Discovery: Standardized Dexcom service UUIDs
  • Authentication: Challenge-response using AES-128-ECB (G6) or J-PAKE (G7)
  • Message Exchange: Opcode-based command/response pairs
  • Data Integrity: CRC-16 CCITT (XModem) checksums

Key Differences G6 vs G7: | Aspect | G6 | G7 | |--------|----|----| | Authentication | AES-128-ECB challenge-response | J-PAKE (Password Authenticated Key Exchange) | | Connection Slots | 2 (allows xDrip + Dexcom app) | one per display type (phone, watch, receiver, pump, …), so a phone and a watch each hold their own; see G7 slots (corrected 2026-10-18; previously "1 (exclusive connection)") | | Glucose Opcode | 0x30/0x31 or 0x4E/0x4F | 0x4E/0x4F only | | Calibration | Factory + user calibration | Factory calibration only | | Warmup Period | 2 hours | 27 minutes |

docs.title: DiaBLE Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-28 at b2d818131.

This document provides a comprehensive analysis of DiaBLE, an iOS/watchOS CGM reader application that supports Abbott Libre and Dexcom sensors with Nightscout integration.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
DiaBLE is a Swift-based iOS/watchOS application developed by gui-dos that provides direct BLE communication with CGM sensors. Unlike most CGM apps that focus on a single sensor family, DiaBLE supports both Abbott Libre (1/2/3) and Dexcom (G6/G7) sensors, making it a valuable research platform for protocol analysis.

Key Differentiators:

Feature DiaBLE xDrip4iOS Loop/Trio Libre 1/2 Direct ✅ NFC + BLE ✅ Via bridges ❌ Bridge only Libre 3 Support ⚠️ Partial ⚠️ Cloud only ⚠️ Cloud only Dexcom G7 ⚠️ App-dependent ⚠️ App-dependent ⚠️ App-dependent Apple Watch ✅ Native ❌ ❌ Nightscout Upload ✅ SGV only ✅ Full ✅ Full Treatment Logging ❌ ✅ ✅ AID Integration ❌ ✅ (Trio) ✅

Nightscout Integration Pattern:

  • Producer Only: DiaBLE uploads SGV entries to Nightscout but does not consume or create treatments
  • API Version: v1 only (api/v1/entries)
  • Auth Method: SHA1-hashed API secret in header
  • Data Source: Uses sensor type name as device identifier (e.g., "Libre 3", "Dexcom G7")

docs.title: Entries Collection Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-17 at 9b191334b.

This document provides comprehensive field-by-field mapping of glucose data across AID systems (Loop, AAPS, Trio) and data uploaders (xDrip+) to the Nightscout entries collection.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Nightscout entries collection stores all glucose observations: - SGV (Sensor Glucose Values): CGM readings - MBG (Meter Blood Glucose): Fingerstick calibrations - CAL: Calibration records

Each system has its own internal glucose data model that must be translated to/from Nightscout's format.

docs.title: Data Flow Patterns
docs.text:
System Primary Role Upload Download xDrip+ Producer (CGM data source) Yes (primary) Rare Loop Consumer (uses for predictions) No (consumer only) Yes (via Share/NS/CGMManager) AAPS Consumer (uses for predictions) Yes (rebroadcast) Yes Trio Consumer (uses for predictions) No (consumer only) Yes (via Share/NS/CGMManager)

Key Insight: xDrip+ is often the authoritative glucose producer, while Loop/AAPS/Trio are primarily consumers. Loop and Trio do not upload CGM entries to Nightscout—they receive glucose data from CGM apps (via CGMManager plugins) or download from Nightscout/Share. AAPS may rebroadcast readings it receives. This creates potential for duplicate records when multiple uploaders (xDrip+, AAPS, Spike) upload the same readings.

docs.title: g7sim Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-17 at 38395a913.

Contributor-facing. Measured 2026-10-17 at LoopKit/g7sim 7c039de5 (2026-10-12; the GitHub default branch main had the same head on 2026-10-17). Other repositories cited: LoopKit/G7SensorKit next-dev e17129d (2026-10-15) and main dd91f46 (2026-10-03); LoopKit/LoopWorkspace next-dev 1561bff0 (2026-10-15), dev c1f55970 and main 548b3324 (read through the GitHub API); LoopKit/NightscoutService ace20b0f (2026-10-14, the LoopWorkspace next-dev pin); nightscout/Trio dev and main (G7SensorKit pointer read through the GitHub API on 2026-10-17); LoopKit/pod a491a5e (2026-10-12); jwoglom/trio-test-harness c3c1bfe (2026-10-17); mickeyl/ImpossiBLE 58fe38d (the pin in g7sim's build script); JohanDegraeve/xdripswift c268542e; NightscoutFoundation/xDrip 9898cb8e0; xdrip-js/xdrip-js dev e301273; j-kaltes/Juggluco db70dc1. Disclosure level: cryptography is named by family only. This page contains no keys, constants, test vectors or handshake byte sequences.

g7sim is a Go program that plays the sensor side of a Dexcom G7, ONE+ or Stelo for CGM software under development. The client it was built against is LoopKit/G7SensorKit's direct-connection code, which is on G7SensorKit's next-dev branch and not on its main. g7sim has two transports. The first is a real Bluetooth LE peripheral on Linux, built on a vendored paypal/gatt HCI stack. The second, impossible, serves an app running in the iOS Simulator over ImpossiBLE's JSON-over-Unix-socket CoreBluetooth replacement, so no radio is needed. It models the sensor's advertising schedule, display slots, lockout, readings (warm-up, expiry, a 24-hour backfill store, calibration offset), the identity certificate chain, and the iOS behaviours that decide whether a backgrounded app wakes for a reading. The project describes itself as "for development use only — not a Dexcom product", unaffiliated with Dexcom, Inc., emitting "only simulated, made-up data".

Item Value How it was measured Repository LoopKit/g7sim, MIT, Go gh api repos/LoopKit/g7sim History 17 commits, 2026-10-09 to 2026-10-12; GitHub repository created 2026-10-10 git log at 7c039de5 Size 5,407 lines of Go outside third_party/ (26 files) wc -l $(git ls-files '*.go' \| grep -v third_party) Packages main (transports, HTTP API, web UI), g7 (sensor model, protocol handler, crypto), suspend, cmd/impossible-mux tree Tests 33 func Test in 8 files, no t.Run subtests; 4 functions loop over 11 table cases go test -v ./... (§5) Test result 4 packages ok, 33 PASS, 0 FAIL; also clean under -race and go vet Go 1.23.0, linux/amd64, offline CI none: no .github/ in the tree, and gh api repos/LoopKit/g7sim/actions/workflows returns total_count 0 2026-10-17 Builds linux/amd64, linux/arm (GOARM=6, Pi Zero class) and darwin/arm64 cross-builds succeed GOOS=… go build Client it targets G7SensorKit direct connection (next-dev); Loop built from LoopWorkspace next-dev §6, §7

docs.title: 1.1 Sensor identity and models
docs.text:
A sensor is created with -fresh, or from the web UI or POST /new, and is persisted in a JSON state file (g7state.json by default). The state holds the serial, the 4-digit pairing code, the model, the activation time, the session parameters, the display slots and their keys, the identity certificate, the calibration and the stored readings (g7/state.go).

  • Models. g7, oneplus and stelo differ only in the advertised name prefix, which is the only thing G7SensorKit uses to tell them apart (g7/state.go:34-36).
  • Presets. The 10- and 15-day presets carry the session length, warm-up, algorithm version and maximum lifetime that a real sensor reports in its extended-version reply. The values come from captured replies (g7/state.go:43-57). -lifetime and -warmup override the preset lengths. A 12-hour grace period is added after the rated lifetime (GracePeriod).
  • Address and peripheral identity. The BLE transport advertises from a random static address derived from the serial. The Simulator transport derives a stable peripheral UUID from the serial (impossible.go, peripheralID). Each new sensor is therefore a new peripheral to iOS, and a restarted g7sim is the same one.
  • Identity certificate. A real G7 streams an X.509 P-256 certificate chain during pairing and signs the display's key-challenge nonce with its leaf key (ECDSA P-256). g7sim mirrors this with its own fixed dummy CA. The CA's signing key is in the source by design: a marker that the data is simulated, not a secret (g7/identity.go:16-24). G7SensorKit next-dev pins that dummy CA as a second trust anchor and classifies a sensor as genuine, simulated or unverified (§6.3).

docs.title: 1.2 Advertising schedule
docs.text:
The timing model is g7.MeasuredTiming() (g7/sensor.go:43). The README attributes it to sniffer and scanner measurements of a real G7, recorded in LoopKit/Loop docs/G7_MUTE_INVESTIGATION_2026-09.md at b930fe17. That file exists at that commit (checked through the GitHub API, 2026-10-17). In outline:

  • A reading every 300 s from activation, and a burst of adverts shortly after each one.
  • The burst ends early once every held display has collected the reading. It runs longer while a held display is missing. A short "bare" advert that admits only the phone is repeated at four minute marks while the phone's slot is held and it missed the reading.
  • A display slot stays held for 15 minutes after it was last seen. Held slots set bits in a types-in-use byte in the manufacturer data.
  • A client that has collected the current reading is refused for the rest of that window: by address when its link comes up, and by display type at its challenge.
  • Four rejections in a row stop all advertising for 10 minutes.
  • A sensor that no phone has paired with advertises continuously, so a phone can find it at any time (g7/sensor.go:210).

A difference the README states itself: a real sensor refuses a served client at the link layer, whereas g7sim lets the link come up and closes it within milliseconds. iOS reports that as a connect followed by a disconnect.

docs.title: 1.3 GATT layout and protocol handler
docs.text:
Both transports serve the same table: the CGM service with control, authentication, backfill and certificate characteristics plus one notify-only characteristic, and a second vendor service with two characteristics, under a 16-bit advertised service UUID (ble.go, impossible.go:122-139). Writes to characteristics with no protocol role are logged and acknowledged.

g7/handler.go runs one goroutine per link and reads the exchange as a straight-line sequence. The README says this mirrors G7SensorKit's G7Authenticator.run(). The first write on the authentication characteristic selects the path:

  • Fresh pairing. A three-round EC-JPAKE exchange on P-256 over the 4-digit code. Then an AES-128 challenge in each direction under the derived key, the certificate phase (the identity chain from §1.1), a key-challenge step in which the sensor signs the display's nonce and checks the display's signature, and a finalize/bond exchange.
  • Reconnect. Straight to the AES challenge with the key stored for that display type. A wrong answer is a rejection that counts toward the lockout. With no stored key (the slot was forgotten), the sensor answers with random bytes, so the client's own check fails and it re-pairs with the code.

After authentication the session answers the control requests: current glucose, backfill over a time range, two version replies, and calibration (set and bounds). It hangs up after 6 s without a request (sessionIdle, g7/handler.go:20).

Where the emulated sensor is more permissive than the client's own model of a real sensor:

  • The sensor does not act on its verification of the client's J-PAKE round proofs. SetClientRound returns a verdict, and keyExchange discards it (g7/handler.go:153,155). A wrong code still surfaces at the AES challenge, as it does with a real sensor.
  • G7SensorKit's tests record a constraint that the real sensor places on the client's third round (G7JPAKETests.swift, testRound3UsesTheFixedRandomizer). g7sim does not check it. A client that broke that constraint would pair with g7sim and fail against a real sensor.
  • The display-signature check in the key-challenge step is logged and not enforced: "Advisory for now (logged, not enforced) so a verification quirk cannot block pairing" (g7/handler.go:295).

docs.title: 1.4 Readings model
docs.text:
g7/glucose.go and g7/sensor.go:

Aspect Behaviour Cadence One reading per 300 s since activation. Missed readings are generated on the next tick, so the store has no gaps. Glucose modes sine (default: 120 mg/dL ± 50, 240-minute period), fixed, and walk (a mean-reverting random walk with Gaussian noise). Output is clamped to 40–400 mg/dL and rounded. Trend The difference from the previous reading per minute, rounded to 0.1. It is present only when the previous reading exists and had glucose. Warm-up and expiry Algorithm state "warm-up" before the warm-up time and "expired" after the session length (rated lifetime plus 12 h). Neither carries glucose. Forced states algorithmState in the glucose mode replaces the computed state, for example a temporary sensor issue or a failed sensor. Any state other than OK carries no glucose. Backfill store The last 24 × 12 = 288 readings (keptReadings, g7/state.go:32). Calibration Calibration shifts later readings by the difference between the entered value and the stored reading nearest the calibration time (Calibrate). Bounds are reported back to the client.

docs.title: 1.5 iOS behaviours modelled for the Simulator
docs.text:
These run only with -transport impossible (impossible.go, suspend/suspend.go):

  • Discovery and connect follow the advertising schedule. The app sees the sensor only while it advertises, and a pending connect waits for the next advert. A connect is also held for the kCBConnectOptionStartDelay the app passes, "as iOS does" (7c039de5).
  • Wake-path check. When a reading starts advertising and the app has no pending connect, no scan and no live link, g7sim logs NO WAKE PATH with a running count. On a phone, the backgrounded app would sleep through that reading.
  • Suspension (-suspend). g7sim follows runningboard's suspend and resume verdicts from the simulator's log (xcrun simctl spawn … log stream) and stops the app process with SIGSTOP while it is suspended. Every message g7sim then sends the app resumes it for 10 s (SIGCONT), as bluetoothd's wake assertion does.
  • Termination and relaunch (-relaunch). When the app's socket closes with a connect or scan lodged, g7sim holds those requests, as bluetoothd does. At the next reading it relaunches the app through simctl launch with ImpossiBLE injected, and hands the requests back as a state restoration at the app's first call. POST /force-quit makes the app's end a user force-quit instead, which drops the held requests. The README lists four ways this differs from iOS: foreground relaunch, the order of the restore callback, a restored peripheral that is still connecting, and live links being closed rather than kept.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-09-16 at 1a10007b4.

This glossary defines terms as used within this alignment workspace. Projects may use different terminology internally; see the mapping notes for project-specific translations.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
A collection of settings that define how the AID algorithm should behave. Includes basal rates, ISF, CR, and targets.

In Nightscout, profiles are stored in a store object with named profiles (e.g., "Default", "Weekend").

See also: Override, Profile Switch

docs.title: Profile Switch
docs.text: A treatment event that changes the active profile. In Nightscout, this is represented as a treatment with eventType: "Profile Switch".

docs.title: Override
docs.text:
A temporary modification to profile settings. Overrides have a defined duration and can affect one or more profile parameters.

Key properties: - name: Human-readable identifier - duration: How long the override is active - target_range: Modified target glucose range (if any) - insulin_sensitivity_factor: Modified ISF (if any) - overall_insulin_needs: Percentage modifier (e.g., 110% = more aggressive)

Nightscout mapping: Stored as treatments with eventType: "Temporary Override" or "Temporary Target".

docs.title: Supersede
docs.text:
When one event replaces or cancels another. An override that supersedes another means the new override takes effect and the previous one is no longer active.

Important: Supersession is not deletion—the original event still exists in history but is marked as superseded.

Nightscout gap: Currently no superseded or superseded_by fields exist (GAP-001).

docs.title: Treatment
docs.text:
Any user intervention or system event related to diabetes management. Includes insulin doses, carb entries, profile switches, notes, and device events.

In Nightscout, treatments are stored in the treatments collection with an eventType field indicating the type.

docs.title: Entry
docs.text: A glucose reading from a CGM device. In Nightscout, entries are stored in the entries collection with sgv (sensor glucose value) and direction (trend arrow) fields.

docs.title: DeviceStatus
docs.text: Current state of a controller, pump, or uploader. Contains loop/algorithm state, pump status, and connectivity information.

docs.title: Glucose Unit Conversion Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-04-10 at 5207f64d0.

This document provides a comprehensive cross-project analysis of how glucose units (mg/dL vs mmol/L) are handled for ingestion, storage, algorithm processing, and display across all major apps in the Nightscout AID ecosystem.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text: Every app in the ecosystem stores glucose internally in mg/dL. Conversion to mmol/L is performed exclusively at the display layer based on user preferences. All Nightscout API traffic (entries, treatments, devicestatus) uses mg/dL. However, the conversion factors differ across projects (ranging from 18 to 18.0182), creating minor rounding inconsistencies.

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
1. Universal mg/dL storage — all 10+ apps store glucose in mg/dL
  2. Display-only conversion — mmol/L is never persisted; it is computed at render time
  3. Conversion factor divergence — 6 distinct constants used across the ecosystem (see §4)
  4. No API-level unit negotiation — Nightscout APIs accept and return mg/dL only; no Accept-Units header or unit field on entries
  5. Threshold auto-conversion — Nightscout and oref0 use heuristics (value < 20 or < 50) to detect mmol/L in user-configured settings

docs.title: Insulin Curves Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-31 at bad5d277c.

This document provides a comprehensive cross-system analysis of insulin activity curves used by AID (Automated Insulin Delivery) systems. Understanding insulin curves is fundamental to IOB (Insulin on Board) calculations and prediction accuracy.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Key Finding: All major AID systems (Loop, oref0, AAPS, Trio) share the same exponential insulin model formula. oref0 explicitly credits Loop as the source. However, IOB values are not directly comparable without accounting for:

  • Delay offset: Loop includes a 10-minute delay before insulin activity; oref0/AAPS/Trio assume immediate onset
  • Peak time differences: Same-named presets use different peaks (e.g., AAPS Lyumjev = 45 min, Loop Lyumjev = 55 min)

Notable Exception: xDrip+ uses a different linear trapezoid model with support for multiple insulin types including long-acting insulins not modeled by AID systems.

docs.title: Libre Sensor Protocol Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-31 at 54324fb52.

This document provides a comprehensive specification of Abbott Libre sensor protocols (Libre 1, 2, 2+, 3, 3+), reverse-engineered from open-source implementations.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Abbott Libre continuous glucose monitors use NFC and/or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to communicate with mobile devices. The protocol complexity varies significantly by sensor generation:

  • Libre 1/Pro: NFC-only, unencrypted FRAM, requires transmitter bridges for continuous monitoring
  • Libre 2: NFC + BLE, encrypted FRAM and BLE data, proprietary crypto
  • Libre 2 Gen2 (US): Enhanced security with session-based authentication
  • Libre 3/3+: BLE-only, fully encrypted with ECDH key exchange, cloud-dependent decryption

Key Protocol Differences:

Aspect Libre 1/Pro Libre 2 Libre 2 Gen2 Libre 3/3+ NFC Access Unencrypted Encrypted FRAM Session-based Pairing only BLE Streaming No (via bridges) Yes (encrypted) Yes (session keys) Yes (AES-CCM) Encryption None XOR cipher Session crypto ECDH + AES Warmup 60 min 60 min 60 min 60 min Max Life 14 days 14 days 14/15 days 14 days IC Manufacturer TI (0x07) TI (0x07) TI (0x07) Abbott (0x7a)

docs.title: Libre 3 Protocol Readiness Report
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-07-16 at 2b8a1a5e1.

Updated: 2026-07-16 Prior report: 2026-01-29 "eavesdrop only" gap analysis Focus: Loop next-dev, Trio PR #1275, DiaBLE, LibreLoop, and LibreCRKit

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The January report is now stale. It correctly described the then-visible ecosystem state: Libre 3/3+ direct BLE access was blocked for most open-source apps, with LibreLinkUp cloud polling or eavesdrop/Juggluco-style approaches as the practical options. The July 2026 source evidence shows a new active direct-reader lane:

  • Loop next-dev has a LibreLoop/LibreCRKit integration path and has been receiving frequent Libre 3 stability updates, including backfill, reconnect, sensor-failure UI, and status handling.
  • Trio PR #1275 adds Libre 3/3+ as a CGM plugin by wiring LibreLoop, LibreCRKit, and LoopAlgorithm through Trio's existing PluginManager / PluginSource path.
  • DiaBLE remains the strongest protocol-research reference. Its README now advertises Libre 3 Direct-To-Watch via Messina while still warning that direct Apple Watch BLE is prototype-stage and background operation remains unresolved.

The core protocol conclusion should shift from "no known legal/direct solution" to "active direct-reader implementations exist, but protocol provenance, long-term compatibility, and app-readiness evidence need verification before treating this as a stable ecosystem baseline."

Aspect January 2026 Status July 2026 Evidence Current Assessment Direct BLE Marked blocked for third-party apps Loop next-dev integrates LibreLoop/LibreCRKit; Trio PR #1275 integrates the same lane Active implementation lane, not yet broadly released NFC Activation/pairing only No evidence of retrospective glucose reads via NFC Still activation/pairing only Cloud fallback LibreLinkUp was the practical path nightscout-connect now hardens LibreLinkUp regions, patient selection, version/product knobs, and current+graph reads Still important fallback and bridge path Backfill Cloud/API dependent in prior report LibreLoop commits include Libre 3 backfill fixes, ATT 0xFD, and 24h cold-start/relaunch test criteria in Trio PR #1275 Direct-reader backfill is now a readiness claim needing validation Alerts/status Not integrated into AID UI Loop next-dev and Trio PR #1275 surface sensor lifecycle/status highlights and LibreLoop alerts Near-readiness UI integration

docs.title: Loop Automatic-Bolus SMB Gating — Code Deep Dive (EXP-2990)
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-04-23. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Date: 2026-04-23 Audience: open-source AID code authors (Loop, LoopAlgorithm, AAPS, Trio). Scope: trace, in source, every gate in the Loop / LoopAlgorithm auto-bolus path that can drive SMB delivery to ~zero at low–normal BG (70–100 mg/dL). Map each gate to the observed >99% peer-suppression pattern in our cohort (Loop_AB_ON peers c, d, e, g vs outlier i — EXP-2987). What this is NOT: not a runtime trace; not a per-user therapy recommendation; not an oref0/oref1 comparison. We document Loop's gates only, in the version pinned in workspace.lock.json.

docs.title: 1. Source path under analysis
docs.text:
The Loop auto-bolus dose decision flows:

LoopDataManager.swift  ── computes inputs
   └─> predictedGlucose.recommendedAutomaticDose(...)
         └─> insulinCorrection(...)             // DoseMath.swift
         └─> recommendAutomaticDose(...)        // LoopAlgorithm.swift
                  └─> InsulinCorrection.asPartialBolus(...) // DoseMath.swift

with the per-cycle dose fraction supplied by either ConstantApplicationFactorStrategy (legacy) or GlucoseBasedApplicationFactorStrategy (GBAF, opt-in).

Executive Summary: YES—multifactored design + BabelBetes pattern directly mitigates collider bias (C7 from deconfounding toolkit) and enables stratified deconfounding by keeping orthogonal signals isolated through extraction.

docs.title: The Core Problem: Counter-Causal Reasoning
docs.text:
In AID systems, the controller intervenes on the very variables we want to measure:

Reality:         low_brake_ratio → high_hypo_risk
                                 ↓
                           AID suspends basal
                                 ↓
Observed outcome: low_hypo_count (despite high risk)

Collider bias (C7): Observed hypo rate is negatively correlated with brake_ratio because the AID suspension collapses the pathway. Naive analysis concludes "low brake = fewer hypos" (WRONG; actually high risk, well-protected).

Memory reference: EXP-2888 leverage validation showed hidden_leverage did NOT predict severe_fraction (ρ=-0.17, p=0.48) because AID protection masked the signal. Solution: counterfactual simulation (EXP-2889), not observed-outcome validation.

docs.title: Nightscout Telemetry and Observability Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-01 at 66c337cd9.

Date: 2026-07-16

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Nightscout needs a telemetry and observability plan that helps maintainers make stability, compatibility, release, and infrastructure decisions without turning sensitive diabetes software into a broad analytics product. The practical answer is not one vendor SDK. It is a separated architecture with clear governance:

  1. Community usage telemetry: a small, public, versioned, locally aggregated feature census for estimated active installations, release adoption, enabled capabilities, and coarse feature use.
  2. Diagnostic observability: optional or tightly sampled metrics, traces, uptime, exceptions, and performance signals for maintainers and operators.
  3. Operational logging: local or operator-directed structured logs for incident response on one deployment.
  4. Research and data operations: a distinct consent-governed data commons path for clinical, product, or machine learning analysis.

This separation is the main unifying design choice. It lets different stakeholders support the same infrastructure while keeping their motivations distinct: maintainers get release stability evidence, the Foundation gets public installation and adoption reports, operators get diagnostics, researchers get a separate consent pathway, and privacy advocates get a narrow default schema with opt-out and payload preview.

docs.title: Nightscout Write Purification Compatibility Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-09-09 at 0adbca4b1.

Date: 2026-09-02

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Nightscout stored-XSS mitigation that purifies write payloads for data collections is expected to have low compatibility impact for typical mobile and edge clients. The reviewed clients model Nightscout treatment metadata as plain strings, JSON objects, or stringified JSON payloads; no reviewed upload path intentionally uses HTML markup in notes, enteredBy, reason, foodType, profile names, or treatment event metadata.

The main asymmetry to close is server-side consistency: mutable Nightscout data writes should receive equivalent purification whether they arrive through API v1 REST, API v3 REST, or legacy WebSocket write paths. Output escaping remains necessary because older stored records and non-purified historical data may still be rendered.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Nocturne uses hard delete (removes records from database) while cgm-remote-monitor uses soft delete (sets isValid: false). This difference affects:

docs.title: Omnipod DASH Pod Simulator (LoopKit/pod) Deep Dive
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-17 at 5e265927f.

Contributor-facing. Measured 2026-10-17 at LoopKit/pod a491a5ea (2026-10-12; 183 commits; GPL-3.0; GitHub lists it as a fork of randallknutson/pod). Other repositories cited: loopandlearn/pod ec13f460 (2025-12-05), randallknutson/pod main 12c54c2 (2022-12-06), jwoglom/faketandem 34c9401 (2026-10-17), loopandlearn/OmnipodKit main 4e923d7 (2026-09-19), dev 928bb79 (2026-10-13) and next-dev c21a077 (2026-10-14), LoopKit/OmniBLE 29358d5 (2026-05-29), nightscout/AndroidAPS dev 7e1d537d49 (2026-09-23) and master 598e2eb39c (2026-08-02), LoopKit/LoopWorkspace f841285 (2026-09-19) with NightscoutService fe075ef (2026-09-17), nightscout/Trio e41c9db37 (dev, 2026-09-22), LoopKit/g7sim 7c039de (2026-10-12), jwoglom/trio-test-harness c3c1bfe (2026-10-17); this repository at d9167f59 (2026-10-16).

Repository: LoopKit/pod Language: Go (module path github.com/avereha/pod, go 1.15 in go.mod, dependencies vendored) Purpose: the pod side of Omnipod DASH: a program that a Loop or Trio phone (or an app in the iOS Simulator) pairs with, primes and runs as if it were a pod Source: externals/pod/

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
• pod plays the pod in the Omnipod DASH protocol. It pairs, runs the session cryptography, decodes the controller's commands, keeps pod state (reservoir, delivered insulin, pod progress, delivery flags, alerts, fault, age) and builds status responses from that state.
  • Two transports: a BLE peripheral on a Linux Bluetooth adapter (a Raspberry Pi in the README), and, since 2026-10-12, an iOS Simulator transport over ImpossiBLE's Unix socket, so an app in the iOS Simulator on a Mac talks to it with no radio.
  • A control panel and JSON API on port 8080 (GET /status, POST /command) set the reservoir and pod age, raise alert slots, set or clear a pod fault code, and crash the process on the next state-changing command, before or after it is applied.
  • The pod advertises a fault or a firing alert the way a real pod does (2nd service UUID C00A / C005, plus manufacturer data), hangs up after 3 minutes without a command, and since 2026-10-12 hangs up, rather than exiting, on a message it cannot use.
  • Tests: 7 test functions in 5 files at a491a5e, all passing (§7). A GitHub Actions workflow runs go test ./... on pushes and PRs since 2026-05-23.
  • Lineage: randallknutson/pod → LoopKit/pod → loopandlearn/pod. LoopKit/pod is where PRs merge. loopandlearn/pod's main is an older LoopKit/pod commit with no commits of its own (§2).
  • Not modelled: basal and temp-basal insulin draw from the reservoir, the delivery rates themselves, alert timers, pod-side rejection of commands, battery, transport-level faults, a controllable clock (§4).
  • jwoglom/faketandem shares this repository's root commit. The mechanisms compare in §8.
  • pod's own hex literals and test hex appear almost nowhere in the DASH driver test suites (§9).
  • The iOS Simulator path needs OmnipodKit's ImpossiBLE detection, which is on OmnipodKit next-dev and not in the OmnipodKit that LoopWorkspace and Trio pin: 928bb79 on their dev, 043b91d in Loop v3.14.9 and Trio v1.0.2 (§10).

Concept Loop AAPS Nightscout eventType Override TemporaryScheduleOverride N/A Temporary Override Temp Target (part of override) TemporaryTarget Temporary Target

docs.title: Record identity in cgm-remote-monitor: _id, identifier and time keys
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-26 at 9ea0af8cd.

Contributor-facing. Living reference, as of 2026-10-18. Pinned to cgm-remote-monitor 15.0.8 (92d08342, the shipping release) and dev (fade2299, the 15.0.9 candidate). Queue item DOCS-RECORD-IDENTITY. It describes what the code does today; it proposes nothing.

Every claim is marked [M] measured or [R] read. Measured claims come from tools/lab/record-identity (results 2026-10-18: both refs, MongoDB 7.0.43, UUID_HANDLING at its default) and, where cited, from tools/lab/v3-identifier-immutable. Read claims cite lib/ paths at the ref named. When this page and the code disagree, the code wins; re-run the lab before quoting a cell for a newer ref.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
A Nightscout record has two ids. _id is MongoDB's storage key; the server serves it as 24 hex characters and, on v1, a client may send its own 24-hex value. identifier is the client's sync identity: API v3 matches on it everywhere, v1 matches on it only for treatments, and the socket does not match on it at all. When neither is sent, each path falls back to a time key (entries sysTime + type, treatments created_at + eventType), and devicestatus has none, so every POST adds a record. The paths disagree in the details that matter to an uploader: whether a 24-hex _id is stored as an ObjectId or as a string (15.0.8: ObjectId on v1 entries and treatments, string on v1 devicestatus, profile and food, on the socket and on API v3; dev: ObjectId everywhere except API v3), whether _id or identifier wins when both are sent (v1 treatments: identifier, and the sent _id is dropped), and whether the reply names the stored _id (not after a v1 treatments time-key match, on either ref). dev removes most of 15.0.8's _id failures (#8758): a re-sent devicestatus no longer fails its batch, an entry re-sent under another _id no longer fails, and string-stored ids are found by every v1 and socket lookup.

collection path a client's _id match key on write, in order the reply's _id 15.0.8 vs dev entries v1 POST (one object or an array; one ordered bulkWrite) 24-hex → ObjectId [M]; any other string → identifier (if none) and dropped, server assigns [M] sysTime + type only; _id and identifier are not match keys [M] inserted: the new _id; matched: 15.0.8 none [M], dev the stored _id [M] another _id at a stored time: 15.0.8 500 "immutable field _id", dev 200 and keeps the stored _id [M] entries v1 GET /entries/<hex>, find[_id], find[identifier]; DELETE /entries/<hex> hex → ObjectId; UUID → identifier or _id under UUID_HANDLING [R] — — dev also matches a hex stored as a string [R]; DELETE is a hard delete on both [M] entries v3 POST / PUT / PATCH / GET / DELETE {identifier} a body _id is stored as sent: 24-hex as a string [M treatments, R entries] identifier; then date + type against a record with no identifier [R] identifier, never _id [M] same on both [R], except that dev accepts a v1 record's first device at the same time [M treatments] entries socket dbAdd / dbUpdate / dbRemove stored as sent on 15.0.8 (24-hex as a string) [M]; dev stores 24-hex as ObjectId [M] none: every dbAdd inserts [M] the inserted document; [] on a duplicate _id [M] update/remove by _id only treatments v1 POST (always an array; preBolus items one by one) 24-hex → ObjectId [M]; other string → identifier (if none), dropped [M]; dropped when identifier is also sent [M] identifier (or a UUID-shaped legacy _id equal to it); else _id; else created_at + eventType [M]; dev adds client ids and amounts to the last (BF-121) [M] inserted: new _id; identifier match: stored _id [M]; time-key match: none on both [M] same carbs at one time + eventType, other amount: 15.0.8 overwrites, dev keeps both [M] treatments v1 PUT as POST [R] as POST [M] stored _id [M] dev removes a string twin of the matched hex _id [R] treatments v1 GET find[_id], find[identifier] hex → ObjectId; UUID → identifier or _id, compared exactly (case kept) [M] — — dev also matches a hex stored as a string [R] treatments v1 DELETE /treatments/<id> hex or UUID as above; any other string matches only a stored _id [M] — — hard delete on both [M] treatments v3 POST / PUT / PATCH / GET / DELETE {identifier} body _id stored as sent, 24-hex as a string [M] identifier (or a hex _id with no identifier); then created_at + eventType against a record with no identifier [R] identifier, never _id [M] v1 record re-sent through v3 at the same time: 15.0.8 400, dev 200 [M] treatments socket dbAdd / dbUpdate / dbRemove 15.0.8 stored as sent (24-hex as a string, UUID as a string) [M]; dev 24-hex → ObjectId, other strings as sent [M] NSCLIENT_ID, else created_at + eventType (exact, then ±2 s by amount); never identifier [M] the stored or inserted document 15.0.8 dbUpdate/dbRemove by a hex _id stored as a string answer success and change nothing; dev finds it [M] devicestatus v1 POST (array; insertMany) 24-hex: 15.0.8 stored as a string, dev ObjectId [M]; any other _id → 400 [M] none on 15.0.8 [M]; dev: a re-sent 24-hex _id is answered with the stored record and not written [M] the _id stored [M] re-sent _id: 15.0.8 500, earlier items kept, later items lost; dev 200, all stored [M] devicestatus v1 GET find[_id]; DELETE /devicestatus/<hex> hex → ObjectId [R] — — a hex stored as a string by 15.0.8's POST: 15.0.8 finds 0, deletes 0; dev finds and deletes it [M] devicestatus v3 POST / PUT / PATCH / GET / DELETE {identifier} body _id stored as sent [R] identifier; then created_at + device against a record with no identifier [R] identifier [M] same on both [M] devicestatus socket dbAdd as sent (15.0.8), 24-hex → ObjectId (dev, every collection: storeIdAsObjectId, lib/server/websocket.js:575-588 @fade2299) [R] NSCLIENT_ID, else created_at (exact) [M] the stored or inserted document [M] — profile v1 POST / PUT / GET / DELETE /profile/<hex> 24-hex: 15.0.8 POST stores a string, PUT looks up the ObjectId [M]; dev ObjectId [M]; any other _id → 400 [M] POST: none (insertMany); PUT: _id [R] the document [R] 15.0.8 PUT after POST adds an ObjectId copy beside the string one (BF-99); dev one record [M] profile v3 {identifier} body _id stored as sent [R] identifier; then created_at [R] identifier [R] — profile socket dbAdd as sent (15.0.8) [R] NSCLIENT_ID, else startDate, then replaces the match [R] the document [R] — food v1 POST / PUT / DELETE /food/<hex> 24-hex: 15.0.8 POST stores a string, PUT looks up the ObjectId [M]; dev ObjectId [M]; any other _id → 400 [M] _id only (server-assigned when absent) [R] the document [R] 15.0.8 PUT after POST adds an ObjectId copy (BF-100); dev one record [M] food v3 {identifier} body _id stored as sent [R] identifier; then created_at [R] identifier [R] — food socket dbAdd as sent (15.0.8) [R] none: inserts [R] the inserted document [R] —

API v3 GET of any collection answers identifier, and a record stored without one shows its _id hex as its identifier; _id itself is never in a v3 reply [M for treatments; R for the rest] (normalizeDoc, lib/api3/storage/mongoCollection/utils.js:12-18 @15.0.8).

docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-01-31 at b6ef8b351.

Deep Dive Document | Created: 2026-01-31 Source: Ready Queue #3 (aid-algorithms.md #6) Files Analyzed: ~2,336 lines across Nightscout sync components

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Trio implements a unidirectional upload-only sync architecture with Nightscout, fundamentally different from Loop's bidirectional approach. Key findings:

  1. Upload Pipelines: 7 throttled upload channels (carbs, glucose, pump history, etc.)
  2. Fetch Filtering: Excludes data from Trio, AndroidAPS, iAPS, Loop via enteredBy filter
  3. Identity Tracking: Local isUploadedToNS flag, NO syncIdentifier↔objectId mapping
  4. Profile Sync: Includes APNS push token and override presets in profile upload
  5. Delete Operations: Uses find[id][$eq] query, relies on local id field

Contributor-facing. Measured 2026-10-17 at jwoglom/trio-test-harness c3c1bfe7 (2026-10-17; first commit 2026-09-19; 73 commits, 71 of them non-merge). No licence: the repository has no LICENSE or COPYING file and no licence statement in any file (§14). Other repositories cited: nightscout/Trio e41c9db37 (dev, 2026-09-22), LoopKit/LoopWorkspace f841285 (2026-09-19), LoopKit/g7sim 7c039de (2026-10-12), LoopKit/pod a491a5e (2026-10-12), jwoglom/faketandem 34c9401 (2026-10-17), jwoglom/pumpX2 f13ccf96 (2026-09-28); this repository at d9167f59 (2026-10-16).

Repository: jwoglom/trio-test-harness Language: Python (35 files, 9,986 lines), shell wrappers, Markdown prompts and Claude Code skills Purpose: build, install, drive and screenshot the Trio iOS app (and Loop with --app loop) from any branch, PR or submodule PR, on the iOS Simulator or an iPhone, and turn the run into an HTML report or a PR comment Source: externals/trio-test-harness/

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
• The harness takes a Trio or Loop PR, branch or submodule PR (for example a TandemKit PR), checks it out, builds it with xcodebuild, installs it, launches it past onboarding, adds the app's built-in CGM and pump simulators, and records every step as a screenshot plus a JSON line.
  • A coding agent (Claude Code) then exercises what the PR description says, using only the harness CLI, and a second, separate agent pass picks the screenshots that show the change and gives a verdict (works, broken, inconclusive).
  • Three targets: the iOS Simulator (simctl + WebDriverAgent), a jailbroken iPhone over VNC and SSH (rooted-vnc), and any iPhone through macOS iPhone Mirroring (iphone-usb). An Xcode-signed install path covers non-jailbroken phones (install only).
  • CI is one manually dispatched GitHub Actions workflow on self-hosted macOS runners. A local web UI runs the same stages on the operator's Mac.
  • External device emulators (g7sim, pod, faketandem) are not attached at this commit. A faketandem stress lane existed in this repository for seven minutes on 2026-10-01 and was moved to a separate repository; the build options it uses remain (§8).
  • Nightscout is never configured. Onboarding pre-seeding skips it, the onboarding walk taps "Skip Nightscout Setup", and Trio keeps the Nightscout URL in the iOS Keychain, which no harness command writes. A harness run as shipped therefore produces no Nightscout uploads and checks nothing on a server (§9).
  • The harness has no tests of its own at this commit (§10).

docs.text: Living document, last changed 2026-03-18 at 79ee9ee0d.

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
Risk Assessment: 🟡 MEDIUM ✅ CONFIRMED

AAPS demonstrates robust ObjectId compatibility through its dual-format _id handling pattern. The app: - ✅ Treats _id as opaque string values (NOT parsed/validated) - ✅ Preserves original _id format from Nightscout (string → string passthrough) - ✅ Will work transparently with both MongoDB 3.x hex strings and 5.x ObjectId objects - ✅ Properly stores and retrieves _id via nightscoutId field in InterfaceIDs

Key Difference from Loop: Unlike Loop (requires string-only _id responses), AAPS has NO assumptions about _id format.

Correction (2026-10-16, SPEC-REG-AMEND; source read at Trio e41c9db37, corpus measured with make schema-quirks). The statement that Trio's id maps to _id holds for the carbs and temporary-target models, not for NightscoutTreatment: CarbsEntry.swift:29 and TempTarget.swift:50 encode case id = "_id", while NightscoutTreatment.swift:62 encodes case id with no key, so a treatment built as NightscoutTreatment is sent with its UUID in the member id, not _id. cgm-remote-monitor does not read id: it matches such a treatment by created_at + eventType (write contract treatment-fallback-key; lib/server/treatments.js:383-405 at crm-write 239f8c25). docs.title: devicestatus field reference
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-09-11 at 4d0538709.

Source spec: specs/openapi/aid-devicestatus-2025.yaml Evidence: reports/schema-census/devicestatus.census.json Corpus: 702,254 documents from 11 Nightscout sites across 2 snapshots (2026-04-01, 2026-04-26).

Documents is the share of corpus documents carrying the field; sites is how many independent Nightscout instances were seen to write it. The second number matters more: one busy site can make a single client's private field look common.

Sensitivity is the derived label (secret, identifying, quasi-identifying, descriptive) that projections strip by; see specs/sync/sensitivity.yaml. It is derived from the redaction policy and the census, not asserted, and an unlabelled field defaults to identifying.

Handled by lists projects whose source code serializes the field, from reports/schema-census/attribution.json. It is source evidence, not document provenance: a project that reads a field looks identical to one that writes it, and names too generic to attribute are left blank.

This corpus is Loop-dominant (see the census site_documents). A field marked universal here is universal in this corpus, which is not the same as universal across the ecosystem.
