docs.title: Evidence coverage of the primitive catalogue
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-11. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a measurement (contributor-facing). Read after typed schemas; leads to devicestatus and profile replay. Snapshot — describes 2026-09-11. Status: current — the catalogue it assesses is specs/sync/primitives.yaml; the rules built on it are maintained in the records specification. Corrected 2026-10-18: §2's per-primitive table predates the catalogue's regrading; the totals (84 measured, 50 declared) stand, and the current per-primitive counts are generated in the records specification §3 (for example ApsSnapshot 23 measured and 2 declared, not 14 and 11). Current decisions: execution plan §1.

Date: 2026-09-11.

Short answer: no, we had not done it — five documents referenced a set of primitives and none defined them. It is now built, and the evidence supports 63% of it with measurement, 37% by declaration only, and names 19 fields nothing carries at all.

docs.title: 1. What was actually missing
docs.text:
Before this change, the artifacts in this series named 15 primitives — every registration says decomposesTo: [Bolus, CarbIntake, TempBasal, ...] — and defined none of them. ControllerSettings was referenced as a resource by all three registrations and had no schema. The settings blocks were bare field-name lists: no types, no units, no ranges, no semantics.

So the composition story had a hole in the middle. Decomposition was measured (99.86% of treatments route), the sync contract referenced primitives, the effects model sat beside them — and "what is a Bolus" had no answer in this repository.

Two artifacts close it:

specs/sync/primitives.yaml 16 primitives, 134 fields, each field graded by what backs it specs/sync/controller-settings.schema.json 19 typed settings, effective-dated, build-versioned. This is roadmap phase 1, which five documents asked for and none wrote

docs.title: 2. How much evidence there actually is
docs.text:
Every field carries a grade, because "we have primitives" and "we have evidence for primitives" are different claims:

Grade Count Meaning measured 84 (63%) A wire path in the corpus populates it, or Nocturne's own decomposer maps it from a path the corpus carries declared 50 (37%) A typed model declares it; this corpus shows no source. Real, unverified proposed 19 more We are asking for it. No shipped model has it

Per primitive:

Primitive Fields measured declared PumpSnapshot 13 11 2 ApsSnapshot 25 14 11 SensorGlucose 14 8 6 TherapySettings 18 8 10 Bolus 13 6 7 TempBasal 14 6 8 BGCheck 5 4 1 UploaderSnapshot 6 4 2 StateSpan 8 4 4 CarbIntake 5 2 3 DeviceEvent 2 2 — Note 3 2 1 the four schedules 8 4 4

docs.title: 2.1 The grading was wrong twice before it was right
docs.text:
Worth recording, because the first number was 45/134 and publishing it would have understated the evidence by a third:

  1. V4 renames on the way in. SensorGlucose.Mgdl is fed by entries.sgv; BasalSchedule.Entries by profile.store.{}.basal[]. Name-level matching scores a rename as "no evidence" — precisely where the model is doing its job.
  2. A generic-name filter suppressed real matches. programmed, duration and delivered are in the corpus on 10 sites and were being discarded for being common words.

The fix was to stop guessing and read Nocturne's own decomposer assignments — Iob = ds.OpenAps.Iob?.Iob, Entries = ConvertTimeValues(profileData.Basal). The model states where each value comes from; combining that statement with the corpus is far stronger evidence than either alone. That recovered 39 fields, and the remaining generic matches are flagged low_confidence rather than silently counted.

docs.title: 3. Where the evidence is strong, and where it is not
docs.text:
Strong — build on it now

  • The shape. All 16 primitives exist as typed classes in a shipped implementation, and 99.86% of real treatments route into them by eventType alone. The decomposition is not speculative.
  • Device and decision state. PumpSnapshot 11/13 and ApsSnapshot 14/25 measured — the two primitives an observability or replay consumer reaches for first.
  • Observations. SensorGlucose and BGCheck are well grounded.

Weak — do not claim confidence

  • TherapySettings at 8/18. The settings primitive is the one the physician complaint is about, and it is the least grounded of the large ones, because the corpus was collected through /api/v1/ and settings mostly are not there.
  • The four schedules at 4/8. Their ProfileName and Entries shape is right; the ScheduleEntry interior is unexamined.
  • Anything AAPS. No AAPS closed-loop site in the corpus. Every AAPS statement in this series is read from source.

Absent — 19 fields nothing carries

Including automaticBolusApplicationFactor (scales every automatic Loop dose), carbAbsorptionModel, maxIob, microBolusAllowed and flatBGsDetected. These are not modelling gaps; they are publication gaps, and they are the content of the settings schema.

docs.title: 4. The settings schema — phase 1, written
docs.text:
specs/sync/controller-settings.schema.json: 19 settings, generated from the dosing-input map so it cannot claim more than was measured.

Status today Count Fields recorded 4 dia, maxBasalRate, maxBolus, units partial 4 dosingStrategy, maxBasal, recommendationType, suspendThreshold derivable 1 maxDailyBasal absent 10 automaticBolusApplicationFactor, carbAbsorptionModel, gradualTransitionsThreshold, includePositiveVelocityAndRC, maxActiveInsulinMultiplier, maxIob, microBolusAllowed, recommendationInsulinModel, useIntegralRetrospectiveCorrection, useMidAbsorptionISF

Three design decisions worth arguing with:

  • Every setting is optional, and absent is not a default. A controller publishes what it has; "not published" is information a replay needs, and collapsing it into a default value is how a replay silently becomes fiction.
  • controller.version is required. Algorithm behaviour changes between releases, so a setting without a build cannot be replayed against the right code.
  • Eleven inputs were deliberately excluded as per-cycle state rather than configuration — flatBGsDetected, the meal-detection slopes, the IOB components, and the effective sensitivity and carb ratio, whose scheduled forms belong to the schedule primitives. The boundary is stated in the generator rather than implied, because it is exactly the kind of line that drifts.

docs.title: 5. So: enough evidence, with high confidence?
docs.text:
Honestly graded:

Question Answer Enough to name the primitives? Yes. All 16 exist in a shipped implementation and the routing is measured Enough to define their fields with confidence? For 63%. The rest is declared-but-unobserved, and labelled as such Enough for high-fidelity replay? No, and the catalogue now says exactly why: 10 settings no controller publishes, plus 8 oref0 run-state inputs Enough for observability? Mostly yes — the device and decision primitives are the best-grounded, and the obligations profile states the floor Enough to unify the proposals? Yes, structurally. The catalogue is the missing referent; every other document in this series pointed at it

The useful way to read 63% is not as a shortfall but as a map: it says which parts of a decomposition could be built today against real data, and which would be building against a model unverified against data. Those are different risks and they were previously indistinguishable.

docs.title: 6. What would raise confidence most, in order
docs.text:
1. Collect a corpus through /api/v3/. A large share of declared is an artefact of v1 collection — the metadata envelope and anything v3-only is structurally invisible. This is a fetcher change, not a negotiation.
  2. One AAPS closed-loop site. It would convert every AAPS claim in this series from source-derived to corroborated.
  3. Any controller publishing a settings document. Ten absent settings become measurable the moment one does.
  4. Examine ScheduleEntry. The schedules' interior is the largest unexamined structure.
  5. Ask Nocturne whether the decomposer assignments are the intended mapping, rather than inferring them from source.

docs.title: 7. Reproduce
docs.text:
make schema-primitives   # -> specs/sync/primitives.yaml
make schema-settings     # -> specs/sync/controller-settings.schema.json
make schema-dosing       # the input map both are generated from

Tests pin the parts that would rot silently: that every primitive a registration names is defined, that every field is graded with a reason, that the decomposer assignments still parse, that the settings schema still requires a build version, and that per-cycle state stays out of it.

docs.title: Typed schemas for Nightscout, measured against stored documents
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-09-10. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a measurement (contributor-facing). Read after the records specification; leads to primitive coverage. Snapshot — describes 2026-09-10. Status: current — the measurements stand. Current decisions: execution plan §1.

Date: 2026-09-10. Companion to Nightscout multitenancy: evidence and options (§6.4 in particular) and to the x-aid-extensions convention proposal.

The deliverable is evidence, plus the tooling that produced it, so that any of it can be re-derived or disputed.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
The multitenancy discussion's §6.4 recommends one source of truth for a field's type, with validators, an ODM schema and column types generated from it. That recommendation has an unchecked precondition: the spec has to match the data. It does not.

Measured over 1,968,464 real documents from 11 consenting Nightscout sites, against specs/openapi/aid-*-2025.yaml:

# Finding Evidence 1 entries.date is declared integer and is fractional in 61.5% of values, on 9 of 11 sites. 13-digit epoch milliseconds with 1–4 decimal places. A generated type: integer validator would reject the majority of real CGM traffic §4.1 2 treatments.carbs is null in 95.8% of documents and treatments.insulin in 60.7%, both declared as a bare number. Nullability is not an edge case here, it is the common case §4.2 3 treatments.timestamp is declared integer and is a string in 100% of its occurrences; profile.mills is declared integer and is a string in 99% of documents. These are not near-misses, they are wholly wrong declarations §4.2, §4.4 4 Strict vs. permissive is now a measured number, not a preference. Against the 2025.1.0 specs, additionalProperties: false rejected 93.5% / 63.4% / 100% / 100% of live documents per collection. That was spec debt, not bad data: applying the corrections in §9 drops it to 6.4% / 15.2% / 10.5% / 0.0%, and the residue is exactly the single-site vendor fields §5, §9 5 Validation is not a throughput problem. Compiled validators run at 85,000–330,000 documents/second on one core. At 10,000 tenants each writing one entry per five minutes — 33 documents/second — validation costs about 0.03% of one core §6 6 The analysis pipeline has already drifted from the wire. tools/ns2parquet never mentions entries.isCalibration (62% of documents, 10 sites), treatments.amount (46%, 10 sites), treatments.unabsorbed (35%, 10 sites) or profile.loopSettings (99%, 10 sites), and reads carbs/insulin without accounting for their majority-null reality §7 7 Nocturne independently built tolerance for exactly the two type conflicts this corpus shows. Its FlexibleLongConverter rounds a fractional JSON number into long and parses a numeric string, which is precisely what findings 1 and 3 require of a reader. Convergent evidence from an unrelated codebase §8

The recommendation this supports is narrow and sequenced:

  1. Correct the specs against the evidence — done, in this change. specs/openapi/aid-{entries,treatments,devicestatus,profile}-2025.yaml are now at version 2025.2.0, with every corrected or added field carrying an x-aid-evidence block pointing at the census record that justifies it. Reconciliation against the corpus now reports zero type conflicts and zero constraint violations in all four collections, where it previously reported eight and four. These are spec bugs, fixed independently of any decision about tenancy, ODMs or storage engines.
  2. Adopt tolerant at the write boundary, not strict. It rejects nothing in the corpus, drops nothing on storage, and asks no shipped client to change. Even after the corrections, strict still rejects 6–15% of entries, treatments and devicestatus traffic, because single-site vendor fields remain undeclared by design (§10).
  3. Treat x-aid-extensions as a forward-looking convention with a measured migration cost, not a validator to switch on. Its rejection rate is the size of the client migration it asks for, and that number is now known rather than assumed.

docs.title: 1. What was measured, and what it cannot tell you
1.1 The corpus
docs.text:
Snapshot Layout Sites 2026-04-01 externals/ns-data/patients/<site>/raw/ 11 2026-04-26 externals/ns-resync-2026-04-26/raw/<site>/ 11 Collection Documents Observed paths Declared paths entries 896,589 19 27 treatments 369,419 41 47 devicestatus 702,254 166 117 profile 202 66 45 settings (/api/v1/status) 11 115 —

Sites appear only as the single-letter pseudonyms the original collection pass assigned. No site URL, hostname or token is read by any tool in this pipeline.

docs.title: 1.2 The three limits that matter
docs.text:
The corpus is Loop-dominant, and contains no AndroidAPS closed-loop site at all. Nine of eleven sites are Loop (100% of their device statuses) and one is Trio (98%, having previously run Loop). The eleventh runs no closed loop: its device statuses carry only uploader battery, its treatments are Carbs, Bolus and BG Check with automatic never true, and its entries come from xDrip4iOS and LibreLinkUp. Ten of eleven report an Insulet Dash pump.

An earlier revision of this document described that eleventh site as AndroidAPS, on the strength of its devicestatus.device string. That was wrong: the device string there identifies the uploading phone, not a controller, and the treatment record shows no automated dosing. Every statement about AndroidAPS in this series is therefore source-derived — from its own wire models — and none of it is corroborated by data. A field marked "universal" in this report is universal in a Loop-dominant corpus, which is not the same as universal across the ecosystem. This is why the model never promotes an observation into a write requirement (§3.3): requiring a field because Loop always sends it would reject AAPS and xDrip documents that this corpus is too thin to speak for.

The corpus was collected through /api/v1/. tools/ns2parquet/ns_fetch.py fetches /api/v1/entries.json and siblings, which do not return the API v3 metadata envelope. The absence of identifier, srvCreated, srvModified, subject, isValid, isReadOnly, modifiedBy and app from the census is a property of the collection method, not evidence that clients never write them. The reconciliation reports these separately from genuinely unobserved fields rather than blaming the spec for them.

Two snapshots 25 days apart are not a longitudinal study. They catch what two points in April 2026 contained. A field that appeared in May, or that a client stopped writing in March, is invisible here.

docs.title: 1.3 Privacy
docs.text:
The corpus is real health data from consenting sites. tools/nsschema/redact.py is the single chokepoint every recorded value passes through. Field names, types, counts and numeric ranges are recorded; a value is recorded only if it survives all five checks below, and is then masked for digit runs, emails, URLs and hex tokens.

Each check exists because the one before it was demonstrably insufficient, on this corpus, during this work:

# Check What got through without it 1 Identifying-name denylist, exact names — 2 Cardinality cap (>60 distinct values → drop) — 3 Value-shape rejection: timestamps, clock times, timezones, reverse-DNS bundle identifiers, any non-ASCII character Profile-edit timestamps to the millisecond; Apple Developer Team IDs inside Loop bundleIdentifier values; users' own override-preset emoji; timezones; individual insulin schedule times 4 Name-suffix denial (*Id, *Identifier, *Token, *Name, *Url, *Serial, …, ignoring trailing digits) extendedSettings.loop.apnsDeveloperTeamId; settings.frameName1, whose name no exact list would have contained 5 Cross-site corroboration (a value must be written by ≥3 independent sites) Two people's first names, from one site's frameName1/frameName2 dashboard labels — ordinary-looking tokens that match no shape rule at all Small-sample numeric suppression (<20 observations → no min/max) One site's exact event timestamp, as a mills field's min and max

Check 5 is the structurally important one, and it was the last to be found. A collection with few documents has no effective cardinality cap: settings holds one document per site, so every string in it is per-site free text that a 60-value cap never reaches. Corroboration replaces pattern-matching with a property: a shared vocabulary term is by definition used by more than one site; a person's own text is not. Three sites rather than two, because two installs sharing a value can simply be two builds by the same person — which is exactly how the Apple Developer Team ID survived a two-site threshold.

The rule has a real cost, and the census records it rather than hiding it: distinct_value_count and values_withheld are reported per field, and the reconciliation now separates enum_unverifiable from constraint_violations. A declared enum may still be incomplete in ways this corpus deliberately cannot show — treatments.eventType had 14 distinct values observed and 6 publishable — and saying so is more useful than a clean-looking zero.

Every rule is asserted in tools/nsschema/test_nsschema.py (96 tests), and a sweep over every committed artifact for personal-shaped values, single-site values, small-sample numeric extremes and site URLs returns zero.

None of the leaked material was needed to know a field is a string.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The same policy, pointed at files already in the repo
docs.text:
redact.py protects what this pipeline emits. It cannot protect what was committed before it existed. tools/nsschema/scan_pii.py applies the same rules in reverse to any JSON file — reporting paths and categories, never values, because a report about a leak should not be a second copy of it:

make schema-scan-pii                       # the ns2parquet fixtures
make schema-scan-pii FILES='path/to/*.json'

Run against tools/ns2parquet/fixtures/ it reports live personal data in committed test fixtures — APNs deviceToken values, Loop bundleIdentifier values carrying Apple Developer Team IDs, override-preset names and symbols, pump identifiers, timezones and exact timestamps. Those fixtures predate this work and are already published; remediating them is a maintainer decision, not something this pipeline should do silently, and it is raised here rather than fixed. The scanner exists so the question can be asked of any file, repeatably.

docs.title: 2. Method
docs.text:
graph LR
    CORPUS[("Raw documents<br/>11 sites x 2 snapshots<br/>~2.5 GB JSON")]
    SPEC[/"specs/openapi/<br/>aid-*-2025.yaml"/]
    CENSUS["census.py<br/>type unions, per-site and<br/>per-document presence,<br/>numeric ranges"]
    REDACT{{"redact.py<br/>every value passes here"}}
    DIFF["diff.py<br/>undeclared / unobserved /<br/>type conflicts / constraints"]
    MODEL["model.py<br/>reconciled model<br/>+ recorded policy"]
    JS["JSON Schema x 8<br/>(write|read) x<br/>(permissive|tolerant|<br/>extension-bag|strict)"]
    MG["mongoose Schemas"]
    TS["zod + TypeScript"]
    AR["Arrow wire schemas"]
    DOC["field reference (md)"]
    REPLAY["replay.js<br/>Ajv over the whole corpus"]

    CORPUS --> CENSUS --> REDACT --> DIFF
    SPEC --> DIFF --> MODEL
    SPEC --> MODEL
    MODEL --> JS & MG & TS & AR & DOC
    JS --> REPLAY
    CORPUS --> REPLAY

    style REDACT fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#a1791b,color:#111
    style MODEL fill:#d4edda,stroke:#2c7a3f,color:#111

Reproduce any number in this document:

make schema            # census -> reconcile -> model -> emit -> impact -> drift
make schema-test       # 96 unit tests, including the redaction policy
make schema-verify     # committed artifacts still match their model

make schema-census takes about four minutes over ~2.5 GB of JSON; everything downstream of it is seconds.

docs.title: 3. How evidence becomes a schema decision
3.1 Tiers count sites, not documents
docs.text:
One busy site can contribute a quarter of a collection. Tiering is therefore driven by the number of independent sites a field appears on, with document frequency as a secondary signal:

Tier Rule Schema commitment universal every site, ≥95% of documents safe to require on read core ≥60% of sites, ≥10% of documents typed, optional common ≥3 independent sites typed, optional vendor 1–2 sites but written in ≥80% of their documents the population x-aid-extensions is about sparse 1–2 sites, inconsistently document, do not type rare <10 documents in the whole corpus document only

docs.title: 3.2 Type unions are preserved, not flattened
docs.text: integer and number are counted separately throughout, because JSON Schema type: integer rejects 1.5 and this corpus contains fields where the majority of values are fractional. Where a spec declares integer and the data is fractional, the model widens to number and records why; where a field holds genuinely different types by client, the union survives into every emitted artifact rather than being resolved by guesswork.

docs.title: 3.3 Read and write are different contracts
docs.text:
A Nightscout document does not have one schema. _id is present in 100% of returned documents and is never sent by a client. Conflating the two produces a validator that either rejects legitimate writes or lets consumers assume a field that is sometimes absent. Every artifact is therefore emitted in a write and a read profile.

Write requirements are deliberately not derived from evidence, for the reason in §1.2: sgv, sysTime and utcOffset are universal in this corpus, and the model marks them candidate_required_write rather than requiring them, because "Loop always sends it" is not "a client must send it."

docs.title: 3.4 An enum is a closed set, and observation cannot close one
docs.text: The model never creates an enum from observed values; it only extends an enum the spec already declares. An earlier version did create them, and devicestatus.loop.version promptly acquired a spurious enum of the eight Loop versions that happened to appear — which then rejected 81.8% of live device statuses in the replay. Observed values are still carried, as x-observed-values documentation.

docs.title: 4. Findings, by collection
docs.text: Every number below was measured against the 2025.1.0 specs, and is what motivated the corrections in §9. The specs in this repo are now at 2025.2.0; re-running make schema-reconcile against them reports zero type conflicts and zero constraint violations, so these tables are the record of what was wrong, not a description of the current specs.

docs.title: 4.1 entries — the timestamp is not an integer
docs.text:
Path Declared Observed Impact date integer integer 345,332 · number 551,257 61.5% of values rejected by the declared type, across 11 sites direction enum of 9 also NONE enum incomplete trend undeclared integer, 71.6% of documents, 10 sites core field missing from the spec isCalibration undeclared boolean, 61.9%, 10 sites core field missing from the spec trendRate undeclared number, 46.0%, 10 sites core field missing from the spec glucose undeclared 1 site, 86% of its documents vendor field scale, slope, intercept declared never observed calibration fields no client in this corpus writes

The date finding was verified independently of the census, by scanning raw bytes for "date": and counting values containing a decimal point: 399,739 of 649,840 (61.5%) in the 2026-04-01 snapshot alone, ranging from 0.0% on two sites to over 99% on five. The shape is consistently a 13-digit epoch millisecond value with 1–4 fractional digits — sub-millisecond precision leaking into a field the ecosystem treats as an integer. This is the same class of defect as Trio #1476, and it is not confined to one client.

docs.title: 4.2 treatments — null is the common case
docs.text:
Path Declared Observed Impact carbs number null 353,734 · integer 10,656 · number 5,029 95.8% of values are null insulin number null 224,268 · number 142,360 · integer 2,791 60.7% of values are null timestamp integer string, 311,648 occurrences 100% wrong type eventType enum of 28 also Bolus, Carbs enum incomplete type enum Normal/Priming/SMB normal case mismatch, 130,257 documents amount undeclared 45.7% of documents, 10 sites core field missing from the spec unabsorbed undeclared 35.3%, 10 sites core field missing from the spec userEnteredAt undeclared 10 sites cross-client, low volume insulinNeedsScaleFactor, correctionRange undeclared 9 and 7 sites cross-client override fields id undeclared 1 site, 90% of its documents vendor field

carbs and insulin are present in 100% of documents on all 11 sites and null in most of them — Nightscout writes the key regardless. A generated type of number is not a near-miss here; it is wrong for the majority case, and it is the kind of wrongness that surfaces as a crash in a consumer that trusted the type.

docs.title: 4.3 devicestatus — 65 undeclared paths, and the pump subtree is missing
docs.text:
166 observed paths against 117 declared. The undeclared set splits cleanly:

  • Cross-client, undeclared: pump.bolusing, pump.pumpID, pump.secondsFromGMT, pump.suspended, pump.manufacturer, pump.model, uploader.timestamp — each on 10 sites, 84–85% of documents. Seven core fields absent from the spec.
  • Single-vendor subtrees: 40-odd openaps.suggested.*, openaps.enacted.* and openaps.iob.* paths, all on the one Trio site. Real, but this corpus cannot distinguish "Trio-specific" from "the corpus only has one openaps site" — see §10.
  • One type conflict: openaps.iob.lastTemp.duration, declared integer, fractional in 97.2% of its values.

docs.title: 4.4 profile — the whole Loop subtree is undeclared
docs.text:
Path Declared Observed mills integer string in 200 of 202 documents (99%) store.{}.carbs_hr number string in 99% store.{}.delay integer string in 99% units enum mg/dl, mmol mg/dL, mmol/L store.{}.units undeclared present in 100% of documents, all 11 sites loopSettings.* undeclared 26 paths, 10 sites, 99% of documents

loopSettings is the attribute-flattening camp from the x-aid-extensions proposal, measured: an entire 26-path subtree that ten of eleven sites write into every profile document and that no spec in this repo describes.

The units enums are also mutually inconsistent within our own specs: aid-entries-2025.yaml declares [mg, mmol], aid-profile-2025.yaml declares [mg/dl, mmol], and the data contains mg/dL, mg/dl and mmol/L. No single declared enum matches any other, or the data.

docs.title: 5. Strict vs. permissive, measured
docs.text:
Every document in the corpus was replayed through compiled Ajv 8 validators for each policy — 1,968,464 documents × 8 policies. Rejection rate, write profile (read differs by <0.2 points), against the 2025.1.0 specs:

Collection permissive tolerant extension-bag strict entries (896,589) 0.00% 0.00% 6.44% 93.48% treatments (369,419) 0.00% 0.00% 15.19% 63.43% devicestatus (702,254) 0.00% 0.00% 14.94% 100.00% profile (202) 0.00% 0.00% 0.99% 100.00%

What each policy means:

  • permissive — types and enums checked, additionalProperties: true. Closest to Nightscout today, plus type checking.
  • tolerant — every field the corpus has ever shown, typed where its clients actually write it, additionalProperties: false. Only genuinely novel fields are rejected.
  • extension-bag — core fields at the top level, weakly-evidenced vendor fields required to live under x-aid-extensions, additionalProperties: false.
  • strict — only what the spec declares, additionalProperties: false everywhere.

That permissive and tolerant both reject nothing is the load-bearing result. It says the reconciled model is a faithful description of the corpus — if it were not, these columns would not be zero — and it says a closed-world schema is adoptable today at the tolerant level, with no client changing anything.

docs.title: 5.1 What strict actually rejects
docs.text:
strict fails not because live data is malformed but because the spec is incomplete. Its top causes are precisely the undeclared-but-core fields of §4:

Collection Dominant cause Share of documents entries trend 71.6% treatments amount 45.7% devicestatus uploader.timestamp, pump.pumpID, pump.bolusing, pump.secondsFromGMT, pump.suspended 85.1% each profile store.{}.units (100%), loopSettings (99%) —

docs.title: 5.1a The same measurement after the corrections
docs.text:
The §9 corrections were applied and the replay re-run, unchanged in every other respect:

Collection strict, 2025.1.0 strict, 2025.2.0 What still fails entries 93.48% 6.44% glucose, 1 site treatments 63.43% 15.21% id (1 site, 90% of its documents), units, remoteAddress, mills, endmills, durationType devicestatus 100.00% 10.52% the openaps.* subtree, 1 site profile 100.00% 0.00% nothing

Reconciliation against the corrected specs reports zero type conflicts and zero constraint violations in all four collections. profile is now fully described: every path in 202 real documents is declared.

This is the load-bearing confirmation that the 93–100% figures were spec debt rather than data quality. It also shows where the honest limit is: strict and extension-bag now report identical rates, because the only remaining rejections are single-site vendor fields — precisely the population §3.1 declines to promote into a typed core schema on the evidence of one site, and precisely what x-aid-extensions exists to give a home.

docs.title: 5.2 Storage and return are not symmetric
docs.text:
Rejection is one reading of "strict". The other is strip-unknown: accept the document, silently discard fields the schema does not name. Measured as undeclared top-level values per policy:

Collection Under strict, values dropped Documents affected entries 1,667,406 838,093 (93.5%) treatments 236,075 234,340 (63.4%) profile 200 200 (99.0%)

Under permissive the same numbers are 57,722 / 56,105 / 0 — the vendor fields of §4. Under tolerant, zero: nothing observed is dropped.

The distinction matters because the two failure modes are visible in different places. Rejection is loud and lands on the uploader; stripping is silent and lands on whoever reads the data months later. For a storage-and-return boundary, the tolerant policy is the only one of the four that neither rejects nor drops anything in this corpus.

docs.title: 6. Validation cost
docs.text:
Compiled Ajv, single-threaded, all errors collected (a production validator would short-circuit on the first and be faster):

Collection permissive tolerant strict entries 328,788 docs/s 315,365 275,971 treatments 149,598 135,999 157,601 devicestatus 119,798 106,041 84,793 profile 65,541 71,162 91,553

The multitenancy discussion flags per-document validation as a candidate CPU sink at N tenants × ingest rate (EXP-MT-013). At 10,000 tenants each writing one entry every five minutes, ingest is ~33 documents/second. Against 100,000 documents/second, validation is roughly 0.03% of one core. Even three orders of magnitude of headroom off, it is not the bottleneck. This does not settle mongoose's casting cost at ingest (EXP-MT-046), which is a different measurement.

docs.title: 7. The analysis pipeline has already drifted
docs.text:
tools/ns2parquet/ is the fifth independent declaration of the document model, and the one furthest from review. make schema-drift checks it against the measured wire model. Fields whose name appears nowhere in the pipeline source:

Field Tier Documents Sites entries.isCalibration core 61.9% 10 treatments.amount core 45.7% 10 treatments.unabsorbed core 35.3% 10 profile.loopSettings core 99.0% 10

Plus two type risks: treatments.carbs and treatments.insulin are read without accounting for being null in 96% and 61% of the documents that carry them.

The check is deliberately at name level. An earlier, stricter version that looked only at .get() and subscript access reported sysTime, startDate, mills and defaultProfile as dropped — all four are read, through a varargs helper (_parse_ts(doc, 'created_at', 'startDate', 'mills')) that the narrower analysis could not see. A field whose name appears nowhere cannot be being read; a field whose name appears might only be in a comment. The check under-reports rather than over-reports, by design.

This is not an argument for regenerating ns2parquet. Its normalization is deliberate semantic work — unit conversion, controller detection, SMB inference — that a schema cannot express. It is an argument for the drift check running in CI.

docs.title: 8. Cross-check against Nocturne
docs.text:
Nocturne (pinned at cb43fae5) arrives at the same two conclusions from the other direction, without having seen this corpus:

  • Fractional timestamps. Entry.date carries [JsonConverter(typeof(FlexibleLongConverter))], and FlexibleNumberReader.ReadLong falls back from TryGetInt64 to TryGetDouble plus rounding. A fractional date — finding 1, 61.5% of values — is absorbed rather than rejected.
  • Type unions on timestamps. The same reader parses a numeric string, which is exactly finding 3 (profile.mills is a string in 99% of documents).
  • Extension data. DeviceStatus.ExtensionData ([JsonExtensionData]) captures unknown top-level keys, matching the extension-bag camp the x-aid-extensions proposal recommends.
  • mills-first timestamp chain. Entry documents its mills → date → dateString fallback explicitly, with a comment noting that AAPS reads date alone with no fallback.

Two independent efforts — a C# reimplementation and a census of 2 million documents — converging on the same tolerance requirements is stronger evidence than either alone. It also suggests the right question for the spec is not "which type is correct" but "which types must a conforming reader accept", which is a different and more useful thing to write down.

docs.title: 9. Spec corrections — proposed, applied, and re-measured
docs.text:
Each is a change to specs/openapi/aid-*-2025.yaml, justified by a number above, and independent of any decision about tenancy, ODMs or storage engines. All thirteen have been applied and the specs bumped to 2025.2.0; every corrected or added field carries an x-aid-evidence block naming the census record behind it, and each spec's description carries a changelog. §5.1a is the re-measurement.

# Spec Change Justification 1 entries date: integer → number 61.5% of values, 11 sites 2 entries direction: add NONE observed 3 entries add trend, trendRate, isCalibration 10 sites each 4 treatments carbs, insulin: allow null 95.8% / 60.7% 5 treatments timestamp: integer → string (or a union) 100% of occurrences 6 treatments eventType: add Bolus, Carbs observed 7 treatments type: accept normal or normalise case at the boundary 130,257 documents 8 treatments add amount, unabsorbed, userEnteredAt, insulinNeedsScaleFactor, correctionRange 7–10 sites each 9 devicestatus add pump.{bolusing,pumpID,secondsFromGMT,suspended,manufacturer,model}, uploader.timestamp 10 sites each 10 devicestatus openaps.iob.lastTemp.duration: integer → number 97.2% of values 11 profile mills, store.{}.carbs_hr, store.{}.delay: accept string 99% of documents 12 profile add store.{}.units; reconcile the three different units enums across specs 100% of documents 13 profile describe loopSettings (26 paths) 10 sites, 99% of documents

docs.title: 9.1 Three of these are a widening, and should not stay one
docs.text:
Items 1, 5 and 11 were applied as type unions, which keeps every real document valid but encodes an ambiguity rather than resolving it. The useful contract is probably two-sided: "a conforming reader MUST accept these types", with a narrower "a conforming writer SHOULD emit" beside it. That is what Nocturne's flexible converters implement in practice (§8), and it is not expressible as a single type: keyword. The applied specs say so in prose — entries.date reads "a conforming reader MUST accept a fractional value; a conforming writer SHOULD emit a whole number" — but prose is not checkable, and a x-aid-writer-type companion keyword would be.

Item 7 (treatments.type accepting lowercase normal) and item 12 (three mutually inconsistent units enums across our own specs) are the same shape of problem: the widening keeps readers working while leaving the underlying disagreement in place. Both are ecosystem questions to raise alongside the x-aid-extensions proposal — which the §5 numbers now give a migration cost — rather than spec edits to make unilaterally.

docs.title: 9.2 Two fields were marked sensitive, not merely typed
docs.text: profile.loopSettings.deviceToken is an APNs credential and profile.loopSettings.bundleIdentifier embeds the builder's Apple Developer Team ID. Both are now described as values not to log, display or copy into derived data. They reached an intermediate version of this pipeline's own output before the value-shape redaction of §1.3 caught them, which is a fair indication of how easily they travel.

docs.title: 10. What is not measured
docs.text:
• Whether the openaps.* subtree is Trio-specific. One Trio site and one AAPS site cannot separate "this client writes it" from "only one site runs this client". Needs more AAPS and Trio sites.
  • Whether the undeclared pump.* fields are Loop-specific. Same problem, inverted: 10 of 11 sites are Loop.
  • Anything about xDrip, LibreLink, or non-Dash pumps. Ten of eleven sites report Insulet Dash.
  • API v3 documents. The corpus is v1 (§1.2). The v3 metadata envelope and identifier semantics are unmeasured here.
  • food, activity, entries of type cal. cal entries do not appear in the corpus at all despite being a declared EntryType.
  • mongoose's casting cost at ingest rate (EXP-MT-046) — §6 measures JSON Schema validation only.
  • Whether the generated mongoose schemas behave correctly against a live MongoDB. They are generated and reviewable; they have not been run.
  • Enum completeness for values written by fewer than three sites. The corroboration rule of §1.3 withholds them by design; enum_unverifiable in each reconciliation names the affected fields and how many values were withheld. Closing this needs either more sites or a separate, non-publishing check.

docs.title: 11. What was built
docs.text:
All under tools/nsschema/, with 96 unit tests:

Artifact Location Per-field census, 5 collections reports/schema-census/*.census.json Spec reconciliation reports/schema-census/*.reconcile.json Strictness impact measurement reports/schema-census/impact.json ns2parquet drift check reports/schema-census/ns2parquet-drift.json Reconciled model (the source of truth) specs/nsschema/*.model.json JSON Schema 2020-12, 8 variants each specs/jsonschema/generated/ mongoose Schemas specs/generated/mongoose/ zod schemas + inferred TypeScript types specs/generated/typescript/ Arrow wire schemas specs/generated/arrow/ Human-readable field reference docs/10-domain/field-reference/ Corrected specs, 2025.2.0, with x-aid-evidence specs/openapi/aid-*-2025.yaml

Every artifact below specs/nsschema/*.model.json is generated from it and nothing else, which is what makes §6.4's "one source, four consumers" checkable: make schema-verify fails if any committed artifact has drifted from the model.

docs.title: 12. References
docs.text:

  • x-aid-extensions convention proposal
  • Nightscout modernization review and proposed next steps
  • Tooling evaluation: keyv, mongoose, zod, WASM
  • tools/nsschema/README.md — pipeline, commands, privacy policy
  • Nocturne cb43fae5: src/Core/Nocturne.Core.Models/Entry.cs, Serializers/FlexibleNumberConverters.cs, DeviceStatus.cs

docs.title: Partial acceptance: binding an approval that accepts part of a plan
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-18. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

What this is: a prototype and assessment (contributor-facing). Read after the command queue and planning note (§3, and §5 decision 4) and the command journeys (PL1.3, PL5.3 and "Specification needs"); it compares three ways a hub could bind an approval that accepts some elements of a proposed plan, runs them against the same hand-authored cases, and recommends one for the commands specification. Snapshot — describes 2026-10-18. Status: proposed.

The question. The maintainer decided on 2026-10-18 that an adjustment is a new proposal, but that a plan may be accepted in parts, with the approval naming what it accepted. CM13 today binds an approval to the hash of the whole proposal and makes one command whose payload is the proposal's, byte for byte, and CM10 has the controller recompute that one hash. The journeys listed "partial acceptance: the approval names elements; a hash rule for the accepted subset" as a specification need. The maintainer asked whether this could be prototyped and assessed for what serves the ecosystem better.

docs.title: 1. What was built
docs.text:
file what it is tools/nsschema/prototypes/partial_acceptance.py the three variants as small decision functions (hub approval, command binding, controller check) and one scenario runner: propose, approve with an acceptance, deliver with optional tampering in transit, controller check, enact tools/nsschema/prototypes/test_partial_acceptance.py runs every case against every variant, two invariants, and a generated sweep specs/sync/prototypes/partial-acceptance/ 11 cases, each with expectations per variant written from the rules before the code was run

The plan payload. {"frame": {...}, "elements": [{"id", "content"}, ...]}. The frame holds what every element shares (days, end date, confirmation rule); each element is one separately acceptable part. The cases use the PL1 plan: an eating-soon temporary-target element and a meal element. The numbers in the cases are placeholders. All hashes are CM1's: SHA-256 over the RFC 8785 canonical JSON (negotiate.canonical_json).

The variants.

the proposal carries the approval sends the hub checks the command carries the controller checks V1 hash per element the whole hash, a frame hash and a hash per element the frame hash and each accepted element's id and hash each id exists, each hash equals the proposal's the frame and the accepted elements, a frame hash and a hash per element the frame hash; no element twice; no element without a hash; no hashed element missing; each element's hash V2 hash of the accepted subset the whole hash the accepted subset (frame and elements) each id exists, each element's canonical content equals the proposal's the frame and the accepted elements in the proposal's order, and one hash over them one hash, as CM10 V3 no partial the whole hash the whole hash (CM13 as written) a strict subset is refused partial-not-supported; the hash equals the proposal's the proposal's payload and hash one hash, as CM10

Shared by all three: an approval closes its proposal (CM13: only open changes), records the accepted and declined element ids, and makes one command; the proposer cannot approve its own proposal (CM14); the controller decides each commandId once (CM21). Routing, tenants, expiry and basedOn are left out: they do not differ between the variants.

Decided for the prototype: accepting the rest later. In V1 and V2 a person who accepted part of a plan and later wants the rest cannot approve the same proposal again; it is approved and refused proposal-closed. The rest comes back as a new proposal, which is decision 4's rule for adjustments, and keeps one proposal to one approval to one command. The person cannot approve a proposal they made (CM14), so the proposer, or another party, proposes it again.

docs.title: 2. Cases
docs.text:
Each case runs against every variant; only: on a step limits it to the variants that need it (V3's reject and new proposal).

case scenario V1 V2 V3 accept-all both elements accepted; the command delivered twice enacts both; second delivery ignored same same accept-one PL1.3: eating-soon accepted, meal declined one command with eating-soon; meal recorded declined same partial-not-supported; reject, new proposal, approve, enact accept-unknown-element an id the plan lacks; nothing accepted; a plan with an id twice unknown-element; nothing-accepted; duplicate-element same hash-mismatch; partial-not-supported; duplicate-element accept-altered-content the approver's display holds a larger meal, then a later end date hash-mismatch twice same same transit-altered-element an element changed between hub and controller, whole and part refused hash-mismatch same same (whole only) transit-dropped-or-duplicated an accepted element dropped; an element sent twice missing-element; duplicate-element hash-mismatch twice same as V2 reordered-keys the display and the delivery hold every key in another order; then the accepted elements listed in reverse approves and enacts; reverse order approved same approves and enacts; reverse order refused hash-mismatch declined-added-in-transit the declined meal added to the command in transit refused unbound-element refused hash-mismatch same as V2 (after a new proposal) declined-built-in-by-hub a faulty hub builds the command from the whole proposal and binds it to what it built enacts the declined meal enacts the declined meal the fault has no subset to get wrong; enacts eating-soon concurrent-approvals the person and a caregiver approve different parts in turn first makes one command; second proposal-closed same same, both accepting the whole accept-rest-later eating-soon accepted, the meal wanted a week later second approval proposal-closed; new proposal for the meal same reject, new proposal, then a third proposal for the meal

Invariants, checked on every case and on a generated sweep (every acceptance of the two elements, from none to both, against nine tamperings and none, in each variant):

  1. the controller never enacts an element that no approval named;
  2. every enacted element's content hash equals the hash its approval named.

The faulty-hub case is excluded from the invariant run and has its own tests: in V1 and V2 it breaks invariant 1 with exactly ("unnamed", "c1", "meal"), and in V3 it breaks neither.

docs.title: 3. Results
docs.text:
cd tools && python3 -m pytest -q nsschema/prototypes: 126 passed (0.28 s). 11 cases × 3 variants for steps and for final state (66), invariants on 10 cases × 3 variants (30), 3 faulty-hub tests, the sweep in 3 variants, and 24 structural and non-vacuity checks. Every hand-authored expectation held on the first run.

Weakenings, each applied to partial_acceptance.py, run, and restored from a copy (126 passed after the last restore):

weakening red W1 V1 controller: no unbound-element check 4: declined-added-in-transit V1 steps, final state and invariants; the V1 sweep W2 V2 hub: no comparison of element content 2: accept-altered-content V2 steps and final state W3 an approval leaves its proposal open 35: the final state of every case with an accepted approval, and the steps of concurrent-approvals and accept-rest-later W4 the hash over raw JSON instead of canonical JSON 11: reordered-keys in all three variants (steps, final state, invariants) and the sweep in all three W5 no CM21 check at the controller 3: accept-all steps in all three variants W6 V1 hub: no per-element hash check 2: accept-altered-content V1 steps and final state

W2 and W6 turn red only through the case expectations: nothing reaches the controller in that case, so the invariants have nothing to check. They would catch it on delivery, because the approval's named hash and the enacted content's hash would differ.

A composition, run once. V1's approval form and hub check with V2's command binding and controller check (the recommendation in §5) reproduced V2's expectations on all 11 cases. It was run as a one-off script, not as a fourth variant in the test file.

docs.title: 4. Assessment
docs.text:
V1 hash per element V2 hash of the accepted subset V3 no partial tamper in transit detected: altered, added, dropped and duplicated elements, and an altered frame; the refusal names which check failed detected, all as hash-mismatch detected, as hash-mismatch a hub that builds the wrong subset not detected: the controller gets the payload and the hashes from the same hub (CM10's limit) not detected, for the same reason nothing to build: the command is the proposal what the approver sees and sends the elements; the client computes and sends a frame hash and one hash per accepted element the elements; the client sends the accepted content back, and the hub compares the whole plan; to decline part, the approver rejects and waits for a new proposal controller burden a frame hash, a hash per element and five checks (13 lines in the prototype); the controller must know the element grammar one hash over the payload (1 line), CM10 unchanged; a smaller plan is an ordinary payload one hash, CM10 unchanged hub complexity 18 lines, 5 checks; per-element hashes stored on the proposal 20 lines, 5 checks 6 lines, 2 checks audit record accepted ids with their hashes, comparable one by one with the proposal's; declined ids accepted and declined ids and one subset hash; per-element hashes are recomputed from the stored subset a rejected proposal and an unrelated new one; the link between them is not recorded PL1 (lunch plan) PL1.3 in one step; PL1.2's required reviews stay on the one proposal same PL1.3 needs the agent to propose again, and the required reviews again PL3 (a week of overrides) the second parent can decline one day of five same a new proposal of four days; PL3.3's adjustment is a new proposal in all three PL5 (clinician, at the visit) one setting accepted at the visit; reviews attached weeks earlier still apply same the clinician proposes again during the visit, and the earlier reviews are on the old proposal CM21 one command per approval, so one commandId per accepted set; accepting the rest later is a new proposal and a new commandId same one command per proposal the mirror the controller can report a hash per held element, and the mirror can show each element as held as approved the mirror compares one hash for the held plan same as V2 conflict with decision 4 none none it does not allow partial acceptance

No controller computes a payload hash today (commands §8): each checks its own sender authentication. Any variant adds hashing to every controller that takes plans. V2 and V3 add exactly what CM10 already asks; V1 adds per-element hashing and five checks, and ties the controller's check to the plan's element grammar.

Unsafe control actions.

UCA V1 V2 V3 UCA-PROP-003: an approval creates a command whose payload differs from the one approved a new path: the hub builds a subset. The approval-to-command check (invariant 1 at the hub) covers a correct hub; a faulty one is not detected at the controller (declined-built-in-by-hub) same as V1 unchanged: CM13's byte-for-byte rule UCA-PROP-004: an approver misreads a payload's meaning not addressed by any binding. Partial acceptance makes each element a unit the approver reads and decides on, so the element's kind needs a declared shape for a display to render same unchanged UCA-CMD-007: the payload a controller receives differs from the one sent covered, with a reason per check covered covered

What the prototype does not model. Elements that depend on each other: declining an eating-soon target can change whether a meal element is still what the person wants, and a plan may need to say which elements can be accepted alone. Approver signatures, which are what would close the faulty-hub gap in V1 and V2. Whether a later proposal for the declined part joins the held plan or runs as a second plan (plan supersession, open in the journeys).

docs.title: 5. Recommendation
docs.text:
Bind the command to the hash of the accepted subset (V2), and have the approval name each accepted element by id and hash (V1's approval form). The hub checks the named hashes against the proposal's per-element hashes, records accepted and declined ids with their hashes, builds the command from the accepted elements in the proposal's order, and binds it to one hash. The controller recomputes one hash, as CM10 already asks, and sees an ordinary plan with fewer elements. This composition reproduced V2's expectations on all 11 cases.

Why. Partial acceptance serves PL1.3 and PL5.3 in one step and keeps required reviews on the proposal the reviewers read, which V3 cannot. Between V1 and V2, the controller is the expensive side: none computes a hash today, and V2 asks it for one hash where V1 asks for one per element plus four structural checks tied to the plan grammar. V1's approval form gives a small approval message and an audit record that compares element by element, at no cost to the controller.

The tradeoff. The controller's refusal says hash-mismatch without naming the element, and the hub gains a subset-building step that the controller cannot check (UCA-PROP-003's new path). That step needs its own conformance cases and the invariant "a command made by an approval carries exactly the elements it named" at the hub.

What would change it.

  • Toward V1's binding: controllers that enact a held plan element by element and refuse one element while keeping the rest; then a per-element hash is the unit the controller needs.
  • Toward V3: element dependencies that make most partial acceptances unsafe, or plans not reaching any controller for some time, in which case CM13 as written costs nothing now.
  • Toward an approver signature in any variant: a hub not trusted to build the subset, which CM10 already names as the limit of a hash carried by the same hub.

docs.title: 6. For the specification
docs.text: If adopted, CM13 gains: an approval of a plan names each accepted element's id and hash and the frame's hash; ids must exist and be distinct, and at least one is accepted (422 nothing-accepted, 422 duplicate-element, 409 unknown-element, 409 hash-mismatch); the command's payload is the frame and the accepted elements in the proposal's order, with its own payloadHash; the proposal records accepted and declined ids; a later approval is refused proposal-closed. The cases under specs/sync/prototypes/partial-acceptance/ would move to specs/sync/conformance/commands/ in that format once the plan object (commands §9 item 3) is specified.

docs.title: Release allocation: what goes in 16.0.0, what follows, and in what order
docs.text:
Record

Record as of 2026-10-27. A point-in-time document; it is not kept up to date.

Contributor-facing. Snapshot, 2026-10-27: cgm-remote-monitor official/dev 8dbb60c2, re-anchored for §0, §3.5 and Q13–Q16 at ca1652d6 the same evening, official/master c6a0d8ed (= v15.0.9), open PRs read with gh pr list and gh pr view the same day. The work items are those of the living next-gen platform plan; the release's own state is in releases/cgm-remote-monitor-16.0.0. The versioning rules quoted are those of the semver policy §2. Recommendations are proposals for the maintainer; nothing here is decided until §5 says so.

The maintainer asked four questions on 2026-10-27:

  1. Given the progress toward multitenancy, how much of the storage seam should go into the current release, if any?
  2. Does including the other roadmap features help multitenancy?
  3. How should the releases and schedule for client identity, formal schemas, API v4 and multitenancy be managed against each other?
  4. Where are the open questions and the briefs for understanding each scenario?

§1 answers in brief, §2–§4 give the reasoning, §5 lists the open decisions, and §6 holds the scenario briefs. B6 and Q12 answer a follow-up the same day: whether prototypes should ship in 16.0.0 as alpha.

Re-anchored the same evening at official/dev ca1652d6 (merge of #8858, 22:29Z). Between 8dbb60c2 and ca1652d6 ten PRs merged: #8864, #8866, #8859, #8868, #8856, #8861, #8863, #8870,

docs.text:
• How much more of the seam goes in 16.0.0: none, beyond what is on dev. The behaviour-neutral slices that every single-tenant site runs (ST-FILTER, ST-READS, ST-WRITES, ST-COUNT-ONEPATH) are merged, so the soak value B6 argued for is already being collected. Every storage item left (§3.5) either changes what clients see (WC-STEP-PATCH, ID-BATCH), changes a safety-relevant computation (ST-VIEWS: the page, plugins and alarms), or is reached only by multi mode (ST-V3-DECOUPLE, PLAT-SERVE, ST-HARNESS, ST-PG). None of them improves 16.0.0 for a self-hoster, and each would spend the short quiet period the pre-tag definition of done asks for (RT-16-RELEASE, item 4, decided 2026-10-27). Recommendation: dev takes only release fixes until the tag (Q1 (a), now Q13). D-EVENT was deferred by the maintainer the same evening (Q9); ST-EVENT stays tied to WC-STEP-PATCH in 16.2.0.
  • Does including other roadmap features help multitenancy: not by being in 16.0.0. The one indirect benefit, real traffic on the interface before PostgreSQL depends on it (§4.2), is now bought by M1. What shortens the path from here is decisions and a reopened dev: D-T30, D-LOOP-ID's remaining items, the identifier and schema rules that fix the PostgreSQL keys and columns, and ST-V3-DECOUPLE for serve api. Registration and v4 reads stay parallel work.
  • Schedule: tag 16.0.0 as soon as its four pre-tag items are met; then one theme per minor. The fastest route to a multi-mode preview is to release 16.0.0 and reopen dev, not to load it. The revised themes are in §4.3 (16.1.0 one executable, serve api and registration off by default; 16.2.0 write(intent), the commit event and identity on every path; 16.3.0 or later the multi preview; 17.0.0 enforcement). Client identity and formal schemas run ahead of tenancy because they fix its tables; v4 publishes in pieces, unstable until shared.
  • Open questions and briefs: Q13–Q16 in §5 and B7–B9 in §6 are new this evening.

docs.title: 1. The answers in brief
docs.text:
• Storage seam in 16.0.0: in, if it meets the entry bar with time left on dev before the tag (decided by the maintainer 2026-10-27, Q12). #8854 (the write boundary) is on dev and ships. The three seam slices in review (#8861 ST-FILTER and ST-READS, #8863 ST-WRITES) are measured to change no behaviour, so no rule of the versioning policy needs them in a major. The first recommendation was to hold them to 16.1.0 to keep the soak small (§3). The soak is informal (§2.1): whatever is on dev is run by people who use it as a nightly, so B6's measured checks decide, and the slices then need time on dev and targeted cohort checks before the tag. Building to the bar is worth doing either way, because it prepares the work that follows.
  • What 16.0.0 should still take is the work whose behaviour change belongs at a major boundary or that fixes a live defect: #8859 (re-send matching and the null-removes rule), #8856 (BF-193, write logging), #8864 (the IOB pill on reconnect), #8866 (two CI test faults), #8858 (API docs held to the routes) and the BF-72 and BF-161 advisory fixes. #8862 (one executable) goes in only if it merges before the tag with time on dev (Q2).
  • The other roadmap features help multitenancy unevenly. Identity and formal record schemas are on its critical path: they fix the keys and columns of the PostgreSQL tables. PLAT-ENTRY and PLAT-SERVE are on it too. Registration, statistics and the v4 typed paths are parallel work that joins tenancy later through HUB-REG-CRM-SEAM. Their benefit to tenancy is indirect: each one that ships in a single-tenant minor puts the storage interface under real traffic on MongoDB before PostgreSQL depends on it.
  • Order the tracks by what they fix for the next one: identity first (it fixes keys), schemas second (they fix columns and validation), the storage interface alongside both, then PostgreSQL and tenancy on top. API v4 is published in pieces as each piece's contract settles; registration first, typed record paths after the identity decisions.
  • Releases follow themes, not dates. A minor ships when a theme's checks pass and it has soaked. Everything single-tenant operators can opt into (registration, the storage interface, v4 reads, multi mode itself) is additive and fits minors. The changes that refuse or migrate existing data (a unique identifier index, validation on by default, bounding v1 queries) collect for 17.0.0.

docs.title: 2.1 How 16.0.0 is soaked (maintainer, 2026-10-27)
docs.text:
The soak is informal. Anything on dev is run by people who follow it as a nightly, so merging to dev starts exposure; there is no separate soak start. When a change needs a specific behaviour checked, the maintainers ask for it, or look for the cohort that exercises it (one uploader, one follower app, mmol/L users, a hosting provider). RT-16-RIG-SOAK is met by those reports. Two consequences for this plan:

  • The deadline for anything entering 16.0.0 is the tag, less the time on dev its cohort checks need; it is not a soak start date.
  • A change merged to dev early gets more exposure than one merged late, so a change that is going into 16.0.0 should merge as soon as its measured checks pass.

docs.title: 3. How much of the storage seam goes in 16.0.0
3.1 What the versioning policy asks
docs.text:
The policy classifies a release by its loudest change (R3) and says a version number is not a substitute for a test. Applied to the seam:

change ladder consequence ST-FILTER, ST-READS, ST-WRITES no question 1–13 answers yes: same records, same bodies, same stored documents patch-class; can ship in any later release PLAT-ENTRY question 9 (a new executable and subcommands is added); the image's start changes form but every measured start path is unchanged minor-class PLAT-SERVE question 9 (a new start mode) minor-class Registration S0–S5, off by default question 9 (endpoints added) minor-class #8859 null removes a field; identifier matching on v1 entries and devicestatus question 10 (a re-send that made a duplicate now matches; a null that was stored now removes the field) minor-class at least; it changes what clients see, so it belongs where client notes are already being written WC-STEP-PATCH, ID-BATCH question 10 (reply shape and per-item results) minor-class ID-UNIQUE-INDEX questions 4 and 5 (a duplicate that was accepted is refused or merged; existing databases with duplicates need cleaning) major WRITE_VALIDATION on by default question 4 (inputs a real client sends that return 2xx today would return 4xx) major D8 bounding of v1 queries question 3 (a parameter's effect narrowed) major

Nothing in the seam slices needs 16.0.0. The items that need a major are not ready, and none of them is in review.

docs.title: 3.2 What including the slices would cost
docs.text:
Written before the maintainer said the soak is informal (§2.1). With no soak start to restart, the cost below becomes exposure time: slices merged late get less of it.

16.0.0 is already 890 commits and 855 files past v15.0.9 (contents, Identity). Its remaining gates are a soak and live delivery checks, which measure time on real sites, not lines of code. Every merge to dev after a soak starts changes what the soak measured. The three slices add about 3,000 lines over every v1 read and write path. Their matrices say they change nothing, and the soak is where that claim is tested on real rigs, so they cost the soak either a restart or a gap.

docs.title: 3.3 What holding them costs
docs.text:
• The stacked chain (#8861 → #8863 → #8865) keeps dev merged in rather than rebased. A week of holding costs one dev merge per branch; #8861 and #8863 are 0 commits behind dev today.
  • Tenancy work above WC-STEP-PATCH does not start until ST-WRITES is on dev. ST-EVENT (decision D-EVENT) is a decision, not code, and can be settled while the slices wait.

docs.title: 3.4 Recommendation
docs.text: Hold #8861, #8863 and #8865 until 16.0.0 is tagged; merge them to dev the day after, in stack order, and ship them in 16.1.0. This needs one rule for dev between now and the tag (Q1). The soak has not started, so B6 states the one condition under which they go into 16.0.0 instead: an entry bar met before it starts. Decided 2026-10-27 (Q12): that condition applies; the slices are built to the bar and go in if they meet it. Outcome: the bar was met and #8861, #8863 and #8870 merged to dev the same afternoon (84fac457, 9668b179, 7abe1cf6), after #8859 and #8856 in the agreed order.

So the morning's question (how much of the seam goes ahead of multitenancy into 16.0.0) is answered by what merged: the part every single-tenant site exercises went in; the part only multi mode needs waits for the minors, where it can ship as alpha without holding the tag.

docs.title: 4. How the tracks depend on each other
4.1 Which features shorten the path to multitenancy
docs.text:
The multitenant target (D1–D3) is PostgreSQL with row-level security behind the same storage interface, with tenant resolution and per-tenant credentials. Its critical path in the plan:

ST-WRITES → WC-STEP-PATCH → ST-HARNESS → ST-PG ─────────────────────────┐
T30-RESEARCH (D-T30) → T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG ───────────────────────────────┼→ TEN-RESOLVE → T30-WIRING → TEN-LAB
PLAT-ENTRY → PLAT-SERVE ───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
track on the critical path? why Storage slices yes ST-PG is an implementation of the interface they build Client identity (ID-FIRST-MATCH, ID-UNIQUE-INDEX) yes, for the schema the PostgreSQL key for a client record is (tenant, collection, identifier); settling identifier format, scope and immutability before the tables exist avoids migrating them. D-LOOP-ID's six questions are the slowest input, because they wait on another project's answer Formal record schemas (records spec, indexedFields, OpenAPI) yes, for the columns D11 emits only declared indexed fields as columns and keeps the rest in JSONB; the declared set comes from these schemas WRITE_VALIDATION rules partly WC-STEP-PATCH moves the rules into write(intent); whether they reject by default is a separate, major decision PLAT-ENTRY, PLAT-SERVE yes hosted roles (D5) are nightscout serve <roles> Tenant configuration surface (D-T30) yes the per-tenant settings table (D15) cannot be written until the maintainer approves which settings a tenant owns Registration S0–S5 no single-tenant, no storage work; joins tenancy at HUB-REG-CRM-SEAM, after ST-PG Registration S3 (typed writes) no, but shares WC-STEP-PATCH applied by the same write step tenancy uses API v4 statistics no read-only, computes over the interface API v4 typed record paths no; deferred decision 12 of the v4 page waits on the identity decisions

So the features that help are the ones that fix the shape of stored data (identity, schemas) and the process shape (PLAT-*). Registration and v4 reads are parallel; bundling them into a tenancy release would make that release larger without making it earlier.

docs.title: 4.2 The indirect benefit: real traffic on the interface
docs.text: Multi mode depends on the storage interface being correct under every client the 12-site corpus and the 67-shape replay describe. Each single-tenant minor that routes more paths through the interface (16.1.0: v1 reads and writes; 16.2.0: write(intent)) puts that code on MongoDB under real uploaders before PostgreSQL relies on it. That argues for shipping the storage slices early and separately, not for bundling features with tenancy.

docs.title: 4.3 Proposed release themes
docs.text:
Each row ships when its checks pass and it has soaked; no dates are proposed. The version class is the loudest row's (R3).

release theme contents class 16.0.0 modernization, the write boundary, one read and write path what is on dev ca1652d6 (M1 included: #8859, #8856, #8861, #8863, #8870, #8864, #8866, #8868, #8869, #8858 merged 2026-10-27), plus BF-72, BF-161 and any release fix found in the quiet period; #8862 only if Q2 (a) and Q13 allow it major (already) 16.1.0 one executable, hosted roles as alpha, registration readable #8862 and #8865 (one executable, serve api) with ST-V3-DECOUPLE; #8857 off by default (D-REG-FLAG); SPEC-ID-AMEND; the OpenAPI description of what 16.1.0 serves, including the registration paths minor 16.2.0 write(intent) and identity on every path WC-STEP-PATCH, ST-EVENT, ID-BATCH, ID-FIRST-MATCH where it changes no outcome, ST-HARNESS; ST-VIEWS if its alarm checks pass; REG-S3 behind its flag; v4 statistics reads minor 16.3.0 or later multi mode, preview ST-PG, T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG, TEN-RESOLVE, T30-WIRING behind TENANCY_MODE=multi; TEN-LAB passes with its control; single-tenant unchanged minor for self-hosters 17.0.0 contract tightening ID-UNIQUE-INDEX with a duplicate-cleaning step, ID-FIRST-MATCH where it changes outcomes, WRITE_VALIDATION default (if decided), D8 v1 query bounds, any v4 path promoted from unstable major

Two consequences:

  • Multitenancy does not wait for 17.0.0. Multi mode is a new deployment target behind a setting a self-hoster never sets, so for the single-tenant surface it is additive (question 9). Its maturity for hosting is a separate label (preview, then supported), set by TEN-LAB and a hosted soak, not by the version number.
  • 17.0.0 is where identity is enforced, not where it starts. Identifier matching starts in 16.0.0 (#8859) and spreads in 16.2.0; the unique index that makes it a guarantee is the major.

Milestones proposed by session -2e (2026-10-27); M3 and M4 adopted as plan items the same day (maintainer): ST-V3-DECOUPLE and ST-VIEWS. A finer split of the storage and tenancy work, from its route census of dev 2dc0c1bc (129 routes and 7 socket events):

milestone contents exit check release row M0 route census done — M1 one read and write path: every REST and socket record read and write, and count, through the storage interface (#8861, #8863, the count commit, ST-COUNT-ONEPATH) the census finds no direct driver call in lib/server or lib/api 16.0.0 (Q12) M2 write(intent), then the commit event (D-EVENT deferred until it exists) 16.2.0 M3 API v3 decoupled from v1 and the cache (the cause of serve api's 81 failing suites in #8865) 16.1.0 or 16.2.0 M4 computed views without a resident ddata before multi M5 backend-selectable harness and PostgreSQL 16.3.0 or later M6 tenant resolution, per-tenant credentials, realtime, the hosted lab, as a preview 16.3.0 or later

M3 is ST-V3-DECOUPLE and M4 is ST-VIEWS in the next-gen plan (adopted 2026-10-27); the other milestones map onto existing items.

docs.title: 4.4 API v4 and formal schemas across releases
docs.text:
• v4 ships in pieces, marked unstable until its contract is shared. Registration is already under /api/v4/ in #8857. Each v4 path is served as unstable (declared in the capability document) until REG-PROPOSE and D-NOCTURNE-ID settle what the shared contract says. Promotion from unstable to stable is additive; changing an unstable path is not a semver event if the capability document says it is unstable (Q7).
  • Formal schemas are a per-release product, not a release. #8858 holds the API docs to the routes with a test; the alignment repository's OpenAPI and nsschema are re-vendored when it merges. Each release's OpenAPI describes what that release serves. Enforcing a schema on writes (validation on by default) is the only schema step with a major's consequences.

(a) per path in the capability document; (b) a /api/v4-unstable prefix; (c) no marker (a): the capability document is already the place a client reads what the hub serves REG-PROPOSE Q8 WRITE_VALIDATION default (a) stays off; (b) log in a minor; (c) reject in 17.0.0 (b) then (c), after #8841's open items (contents, item 7) 17.0.0 contents Q9 D-EVENT: commit event per call or per driver operation per the plan's decision card Deferred, maintainer 2026-10-27: no shape adopted; the event stays counts-only and internal; reopened when WC-STEP-PATCH's WriteResult.items[], a named first subscriber, the BF-164 websocket cursor re-measure and a count of replica-set sites are in hand. A read after the write is not adopted (no precedent) ST-EVENT, the change feed Q10 D-T30: approve the tenant configuration surface walk through the DECISION sections start once 16.0.0 is tagged, after re-measuring the 277 settings on dev T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG, TEN-RESOLVE Q11 Review capacity #8857, #8859, #8861, #8862, #8863 and #8865 add 17,794 lines against their bases (§2) review in theme order (16.1.0 first), one stacked chain at a time every row of §4.3 Q12 Put prototypes in 16.0.0 to soak them as alpha? Decided, maintainer 2026-10-27: the seam slices go into 16.0.0 if feasible and B6's entry bar is met with time on dev before the tag (§2.1); building them to that bar is worth doing whether or not they ship, because it prepares the work that follows. Components that ship before they are mature are labelled alpha in the release notes. Still open: Q12a B6 the soak start, BFQ-72 Q12a If the slices ship, how is an alpha label made meaningful for code on the default path? Decided, maintainer 2026-10-27: option (a). The slices are default on in the single-tenant release, named in the release notes as new internals, with the rehearsed revert as the fallback. Once verified, exercised on dev and released, that code is trusted for what single-tenant sites run. The alpha label belongs to the multitenant bindings only: serve roles, tenant resolution and scope, per-tenant credentials, and the PostgreSQL backend. Trust covers the paths real clients exercise; code no single-tenant site runs (the filter tree's SQL translation, the tenant binding the interface carries, rarely used endpoints without a cohort check) does not inherit it — the release notes' wording Q13 Does the quiet period start now, at ca1652d6? (asked 2026-10-27 evening) (a) yes: dev takes release fixes only (BF-72 and BF-161 at publication, fixes for what the cohorts report, CI and docs); feature PRs stay draft. (b) take #8862 first, then start. (c) keep merging until the alarms and cohort checks are done (a): M1 is on dev, so what is left in review is 16.1.0 work (§3.5), and every merge restarts what the quiet period measures; (b) only if the image's new start is wanted in the major the tag date; #8862, #8865, #8857 merge dates Q14 Who asks the cohorts, and when? (a) now, one request per cohort in B6's table, naming M1 and #8859 as what changed; (b) after the alarms check (a): the cohort confirmations are pre-tag item 2 and the slowest, because they wait on other people RT-16-RIG-SOAK Q15 #8865's base (a) retarget to dev now and merge dev in, still draft; (b) close it and reopen with ST-V3-DECOUPLE (a), by the maintainer; re-measure serve api after PLAT-SERVE, ST-V3-DECOUPLE Q16 When does dev reopen for 16.1.0 work? (a) the day 16.0.0 is tagged; (b) a release/16.0.0 branch for fixes, dev reopened earlier (a), as Q1 (a); (b) only if the quiet period runs longer than about two weeks every 16.1.0 row

docs.title: 6. Scenario briefs
docs.text: Each brief states what the scenario is, who it reaches, and what to measure before choosing it.

docs.title: B1. 16.0.0 with the seam held (recommended)
docs.text:
• What happens. dev takes only #8859, #8856, #8864, #8866, #8858 and the two advisory fixes; the soak runs; the tag follows; the seam chain merges the next day.
  • Who it reaches. Operators get the modernization and the write boundary. Uploaders (AndroidAPS, Loop, Trio, xDrip+) see #8859's re-send matching and the null-removes rule, which the client notes list.
  • Measure first. The soak and live delivery checks (RT-16-RIG-SOAK, RT-16-LIVE-ALARMS); the 67-shape client replay on the candidate with #8859 merged.

docs.title: B2. 16.0.0 with the seam included
docs.text:
• What happens. #8861 and #8863 merge to dev as soon as their checks pass (now the decided path, Q12). 16.1.0 starts from a dev that already routes v1 through the interface.
  • Who it reaches. The same as B1, plus every v1 read and write on every site going through new code.
  • Measure first. The write-contract matrix, the HTTP and v1 read diffs and the client replay on the merged tree; dev users exercise them from the merge (§2.1). The gain is about one release of lead time for tenancy; the cost is less time on dev for the rest of 16.0.0's changes to be told apart from the slices if something regresses.

docs.title: B3. Identity first
docs.text:
• What happens. After 16.0.0, the next work is SPEC-ID-AMEND, the Loop reply (D-LOOP-ID) and the six ID-*-DECISION items, with WC-STEP-PATCH built to them.
  • Who it reaches. Controller authors: Loop (syncIdentifier), Trio (id), AndroidAPS (keeps the server's identifier). Nocturne, through D-NOCTURNE-ID.
  • Measure first. ID-DUP-MEASURE (duplicates by identifier across the corpus) and the replay of each controller's re-send.
  • Why it comes first. It fixes the PostgreSQL key and the v4 typed paths; an answer that arrives after the tables exist is a migration.

docs.title: B4. Tenancy first
docs.text:
• What happens. ST-PG and TEN-RESOLVE are built before the identity decisions, with identifier as an unconstrained column.
  • Who it reaches. Hosted tenants only; self-hosters are unaffected.
  • Risk. The unique key and the typed record paths are decided later, against tables that hold data. It also puts PostgreSQL behind an interface that has had no release under real traffic.
  • When to choose it. If a hosting partner needs a dated preview before the identity answers arrive; then TEN-LAB is labelled preview and ID-UNIQUE-INDEX is a migration step in the plan.

docs.title: B5. Registration and v4 as their own minors
docs.text:
• What happens. #8857 ships in 16.1.0 off by default; v4 statistics in 16.2.0; typed paths when decision 12 is settled.
  • Who it reaches. Controller authors who opt in; Nocturne, as the second hub the contract is proposed to.
  • Measure first. The conformance cases against a booted server (35 pass, 88 mapped, 0 fail at 3be98536); flag off is byte-identical to dev.
  • Effect on tenancy. None until HUB-REG-CRM-SEAM; registrations are per tenant (AU6), so the store gains a tenant column when ST-PG lands.

docs.title: B6. Prototypes in 16.0.0, labelled alpha (asked 2026-10-27)
docs.text:
Decided, maintainer 2026-10-27: the seam slices go in if feasible and the entry bar below is met; components that ship before they are mature are labelled alpha (Q12, Q12a).

The question: if a prototype of every REST API behind the storage interface, and a prototype of multi mode, exist within days, are they worth shipping in 16.0.0 with their status noted, so the release soaks them; and how does that weigh against releasing as soon as the candidate is ready?

  • The candidate is not ready to release now, so the choice is what is on dev long enough before the tag. Unmet on 2026-10-27: the real-rig soak (not started), the live delivery check, the BF-72 and BF-161 fork fixes, #8859 (needed in 16.0.0, draft), #8866 (dev CI red until it merges) and master's protection (#8824 blocked). The soak is informal (§2.1): dev users exercise whatever is merged, so a change merged sooner is soaked longer.
  • The two prototypes behave differently in a release.
