docs.title: 2. Where a command goes
docs.text: A command names a channel (registration §9). It goes to the live device instance holding command-sink on that channel, on the command's tenant. A command that names no product for a channel that is not shared goes to the one product that declares that channel; when more than one product declares it, it is refused 409 ambiguous-command-destination, and naming the product resolves it. "Declares" reads every product's current registration and stored definitions, in any state. With no holder, or a channel no product declares, the command is refused 409 no-command-destination. The hub never routes to a lapsed former holder, a simulated command sink, or the product's latest instance. Which instance may hold the sink is authority §6.

docs.title: 3. Commands today
docs.text:
Read from cgm-remote-monitor at the 15.0.8 release (92d08342), dev (fade2299) and the multitenancy seam branch (81a1f6ce), 2026-10-18; "run" marks what was executed.

One path carries a command. POST /api/v2/notifications/loop (lib/api2/notifications-v2.js, line 17 at 15.0.8, 21 on dev) hands a request to lib/server/loop.js, which sends an APNs push to Loop.

what the hub does permission notifications:loop:push; of the default roles only admin holds it, so a caller needs API_SECRET, an admin token or a custom role (lib/authorization/storage.js:232-238 on dev) commands four eventType values: Temporary Override, Temporary Override Cancel, Remote Carbs Entry, Remote Bolus Entry; anything else is refused "Unhandled event type" (loop.js:67-110 on dev; run) payload the command's fields, remote-address, notes, entered-by, sent-at, expiration five minutes ahead, and otp only when the sender gave one (loop.js:61-126); no command id, nonce or signature, and no limit on an amount beyond "greater than zero" the one-time password forwarded, never checked; checking it is the controller's destination the device token and bundle id in the latest profile's loopSettings (loop.js:31-47); Trio publishes its token at the profile's top level, so this path does not reach Trio credentials the deployment's LOOP_APNS_KEY, LOOP_APNS_KEY_ID and LOOP_DEVELOPER_TEAM_ID, read only when ENABLE includes loop; without it, or with it but no LOOP_* variable set, extendedSettings.loop is never created and the route fails with a TypeError at loop.js:16 (run without ENABLE, all three commits; read for the second case, lib/server/env.js:281 on dev) what is stored nothing: neither file writes to a store, and the careportal's submit hook replaces its treatment write, so no treatment is stored either response 200 when APNs accepted the push (loop.js:139-141 on dev); it says nothing about delivery, the password or enactment outcome none: no route, collection, socket event or field records that a controller received, accepted, refused or enacted a command

Senders are the careportal's Loop plugin (lib/plugins/loop.js:110-180 on dev) and the NightscoutKit fork LoopCaregiver uses, for overrides, bolus and carbs when its newer remote-command option is off; LoopCaregiver sends closed-loop and automatic-bolus changes to /api/v2/remotecommands whatever the option, a route neither cgm-remote-monitor nor Nocturne implements. Trio, LoopFollow and AndroidAPS do not call this route.

Everything else is data. Temporary Target, Profile Switch and Announcement treatments are stored and broadcast like any other record; a controller that downloads treatments may act on them by its own rules, and the hub does not know whether it did. AndroidAPS dev writes signed command envelopes and acknowledgements to the API v3 settings collection; the hub stores them as documents and reads none of them. What each controller does with these paths is in state and intent §7.

Under TENANCY_MODE=multi, on the seam branch:

  • the request is bound to its tenant (lib/server/tenant-middleware.js:263-272), but nothing on the APNs path reads the binding: ctx.loop is built once per process (lib/server/bootevent.js:229), so the key, team id and device lookup are the deployment's, against one process-wide copy of the loaded data;
  • multi requires PostgreSQL, and the PostgreSQL store at that commit implements only entries (lib/storage/postgres-storage.js:127-133), so no tenant's profile or treatments can be stored;
  • socket emissions go to the bound tenant's room and are withheld when no tenant is bound (lib/server/socket-tenancy.js:157-170,255-267). The dataUpdate and alarm events come from the process-wide load cycle and are withheld; storage events from an API v3 request reach their tenant.

CM19 and CM20 are written against these two facts: a signal from the load cycle reaches no one under multi, and the only push credential today is the deployment's.

docs.title: 4. The command record (proposed)
docs.text:
# rule CM1 The hub records a command before it sends it. A command the hub accepts is stored as a record: commandId (assigned by the hub), its tenant, channel, the product named or inferred, the destination's instanceId and definitionId as routed, the payload exactly as received, payloadHash (sha256: over the payload's RFC 8785 canonical JSON, the rule D19 uses for definition ids), the initiator in the form state and intent S8 gives it, the subject that sent it, proposalId and the proposal's basedOn when it came from an approval (§6), createdAt, expiresAt and state. A command refused at routing (§2) is recorded as not-routed, with its reason, and never sent. CM2 Routed once. The destination is fixed when the command is accepted; it is never re-routed to a later holder, which would enact a request its sender addressed to another device. If the destination lapses or loses its role while the command is pending, nothing was handed over, whatever signals were sent (CM27), and the command becomes undeliverable. If that happens after it was fetched, the controller has it: the command keeps its state, and the destination's report is accepted (CM7). CM3 An expiry is required. A command without expiresAt, or with one not after the request's time, is refused 422 expiry-required; one more than the hub's commands.maxExpirySeconds after the request is refused 422 expiry-too-long. Times are the hub's. A command at or past its expiry is never signalled or fetched. At its expiry a pending command becomes expired, because nothing was handed over; a fetched command becomes unconfirmed, because the controller may have enacted it; an acknowledged command keeps the controller's state. A hub never reports a command that may have been enacted as expired or undeliverable, which a sender would read as safe to send again. CM4 Re-sending a request. A sender may give a requestId. Within a tenant and subject, a second command with the same requestId, channel, product as the request names it (naming none differs from naming the one that would be inferred) and payloadHash returns the first command and its current state; with any of them different it is refused 409 request-id-reused. Without a requestId, every request is a new command. CM5 The hub does not judge. The hub checks only that the channel accepts commands, the routing, the expiry, the size (a payload over the hub's commands.maxPayloadBytes of canonical JSON is refused 413 payload-too-large) and the sender's permission (403 not-authorised without api:commands:create). It never checks a dose, a limit or the therapy state, and it never changes the payload. CM6 Tenant isolation. A command's tenant is the tenant its request resolved to. Routing, sending, fetching, proposals, reports and reads see only that tenant: a command, proposal or instance from another tenant is 404, as one that does not exist is, so a request never reveals that it exists. CM24 The outstanding list. For a channel, the hub lists every proposal that is open and every command that is not final, with its sender or proposer, initiator, createdAt, expiresAt and state, and the times of the dose and carb records for the channel's products that reached the hub since the earliest of them, and, under destinations, each live holder of the channel's sink with its fetch bound (CM30). A reply that accepts a command or an approval carries the list of the other items when there are any. Anyone holding api:commands:read, api:commands:create or api:proposals:read on the tenant may read it, so a follower can see the queue without acting on it; anyone else is 403 not-authorised. CM25 Cancel. The sender of a command, or the subject acting for the person (CM14), may cancel it; anyone else is 403 not-authorised. A pending command becomes cancelled, which is final, and is never sent or fetched. A command already fetched or acknowledged stays in its state with cancelRequested (202): the destination's fetches carry the cancel until it reports (CM26), and the controller, deciding the command once (CM21), refuses it with reason cancelled if it has not decided it yet. A command with a final state is 409 already-final.

Order of checks. Where more than one refusal applies, the first wins: another tenant (404), then the sender's permission and ownership (403), then the request's own content (413, 422), then state (409). Among an approval's 409s the order is: the proposal's state (proposal-expired, proposal-closed), hash-mismatch, routing, destination-changed, state-changed, doses-since. A signal checks the binding (withheld), then the command (expired, then nothing-waiting when no fetch would return it or its cancel, CM26), then the transport (no-live-transport, then no-tenant-credential). Without the capability's commands member every path in CM32 is 404 (CM31).

States. The hub sets pending, not-routed, fetched, unconfirmed, undeliverable, expired and cancelled; only the destination sets acknowledged, succeeded, failed and refused (§5).

state set by means pending hub accepted and routed; not yet fetched, whatever signals were sent (CM27) not-routed hub refused at routing (§2); its reason is recorded fetched hub the destination instance read it with its own credential (CM18); a receipt, not an outcome; returned again by each fetch until the controller reports (CM26) unconfirmed hub fetched, with no outcome, and its expiry passed. It may have been enacted (CM3) undeliverable hub the destination lapsed or lost its role before it fetched the command (CM2) expired hub its expiry passed before the destination fetched it (CM3) cancelled hub its sender or the person cancelled it before anything was handed over (CM25) acknowledged controller received; validating or enacting succeeded controller enacted failed controller accepted but not enacted, such as a pump that did not respond refused controller declined by the controller's own checks

succeeded, failed, refused, not-routed, undeliverable, expired and cancelled are final; the hub sets the last four only for a command that was never fetched. A signal, fetched and unconfirmed are never reported as success or as failure.

The same states as a diagram. Blue states are set by the hub, green by the destination's reports; the bold ones are final. A report may skip acknowledged (CM9).

Only the destination's reports set acknowledged, succeeded, failed or refused, and a report replaces fetched or unconfirmed.

docs.title: 5. Outcomes (proposed)
docs.text: # rule CM7 Only the destination reports. An outcome report names the commandId and is accepted only from the bound subject of the destination the command was routed to, whether or not that instance still holds the role; any other subject is refused 403 not-registration-owner. The report carries state (acknowledged, succeeded, failed or refused; any other is 422 invalid-state), the payloadHash the controller computed over the payload it received, a reason when refused or failed, and, when enacted, the identity of the record that shows the effect (how the link works is open, §9 item 9; effect-link prototype) (identity). A reported hash that differs from the command's is recorded as reported, with the record marked as a mismatch; the hub does not refuse it, because the report is evidence of what the controller did. CM8 Reasons. A refusal or failure reason is one of hash-mismatch, expired, not-accepted (the controller's acceptance preference is off, S10), limit (a limit the controller enforces), doses-since (CM23), cancelled (CM25) or {value: other, controllerTerm}; a bare unknown string is refused 422 invalid-reason. The hub records the reason and does not interpret it. CM9 One outcome. After a final state, a further report is refused 409 already-final. A report on an unconfirmed command is accepted and replaces it: that state is the hub's inference, and the controller's report of what it did is better evidence. acknowledged may precede a final state and may be skipped. CM10 The controller checks the hash. Before enacting, the controller recomputes payloadHash over the payload it received and refuses hash-mismatch when it differs from the hash the command carries. It also refuses a command past expiresAt by its own clock. These checks are the controller's, as all validation is (D18). The controller receives the payload and the hash from the same hub, so the check detects a payload changed in transit or storage; it does not show that a hub, or anything acting as one, delivered what an approver approved, and it does not authenticate the sender. Binding an approval to a payload end to end needs a signature by the sender or approver. Authentication between sender and controller, such as Loop's one-time password, Trio's shared secret or AndroidAPS's per-client signature (§8), stays the controller's, and the hub carries it unread. CM23 The controller checks doses since. Before it enacts a dose or carbs, the controller compares the doses and carbs it holds since the command was made, and refuses doses-since when its own rule says the command is no longer wanted. The rule and its threshold are the controller's, as all validation is (D18); Trio's refusal when boluses since reach 20 % of the request is one such rule (§8).

docs.title: 6. Proposals and approvals (proposed)
docs.text:
propose → (evaluate) → approve | reject | withdraw | expire → command (§4) → outcome (§5)
# rule CM11 A proposal. A proposal names the proposing instance, the target channel and, when known, the target product and instanceId; the payload and its payloadHash, under CM5's size limit; basedOn, the state version of the target product that the proposer read, required (422 based-on-required); and expiresAt, under the same limits as CM3. The hub routes the proposal when it is made (§2) and records the destination with its definitionId: a proposal with no destination is refused as a command would be, with nothing recorded; a named instanceId on another tenant, or none at all, is 404 (CM6); and one that is not the destination is refused 409 destination-changed. Its states are open, approved, rejected, withdrawn and expired; only open changes. A proposal is read by its tenant's subjects holding api:proposals:read or api:commands:create. CM12 Who may propose. The sender holds api:proposals:create, and the proposing instance is its own and holds a granted propose role on the channel: an other role that the hub's capability document lists as proposing (registration §9); a hub grants only roles it lists. Without the permission it is 403 not-authorised; an instance that is not the sender's is 403 not-registration-owner; without the role it is 403 role-not-granted. Reading confers neither: a readable credential, or a tool holding one, cannot propose. CM13 An approval binds to one payload. An approval names the proposalId and the payloadHash it approves. A hash that differs from the proposal's is refused 409 hash-mismatch; a proposal past its expiry is refused 409 proposal-expired; one that is not open is refused 409 proposal-closed. The approval routes again: with no destination it is refused as a command would be (§2), and when the destination differs from the one recorded at the proposal it is refused 409 destination-changed, because the proposer read one device's state and the change would reach another. A refused approval leaves the proposal open and creates no command. An accepted approval creates one command (CM1) whose payload is the proposal's, byte for byte, with the same hash, proposalId and basedOn set, and the proposal's expiresAt. CM14 Who may approve. The approver holds the permission to send the command itself (api:commands:create), else 403 not-authorised; approving is sending. When the proposing instance's propose role is an agent's, the subject that proposed cannot approve it (403 self-approval); a person may approve a proposal they made from their own app. Rejecting needs the same permission. Withdrawing is the proposer's, and also the person's: the subject the tenant marks as acting for the person whose therapy it holds may withdraw any proposal. The tenant owner sets that mark on a subject, on the owner's listener, as part of subject and role configuration; the hub reads it from the subject when it checks a withdrawal, a cancel (CM25) or an approval, and a client cannot assert it in a request (maintainer, 2026-10-26). Either by anyone else is 403 not-authorised. How a capability document marks a propose role as an agent's is open (§9). CM15 Based on. An approval is refused 409 state-changed when the target product's state version at the hub, at the time of approval, differs from the proposal's basedOn. This checks the hub's record of what the controller reported, the way an etag does; it does not tell the approver that the controller's own state is unchanged, which only the controller's own validation can (D18); the controller is given basedOn but cannot recompute it, because it versions the hub's record. CM16 Evaluations are evidence. Anyone who may read the proposal (CM11) may attach an evaluation: a risk check, a second model's opinion, a request for review. An evaluation never changes the proposal's state and never approves. CM22 Doses since the proposal. An approval is refused 409 doses-since when a dose or carb record for the target product reached the hub after the proposal was made and by the time of approval. The proposer could not have seen it, as basedOn (A12) does not cover doses or carbs. It is the hub's record, limited by the controller's upload lag; the controller's own check is CM23. A refused approval leaves the proposal open.

docs.title: 7. Delivery in each mode (proposed)
docs.text:
# rule CM17 The record is the command. The hub's record (CM1) is what states, outcomes and audit refer to, and only a fetch (CM18) hands a command over. A fetch-now signal (CM27) carries none of the record. CM18 Fetch. The destination reads the commands waiting for it (CM26) with its own credential. This works the same in both modes, because the request is bound to the tenant; it is the path a hub must offer, and the only one by which a payload and its hash reach a controller. A fetch returns only commands whose destination is that instance; a fetch naming an instance that is not the credential's own is 403 not-registration-owner, and an instance that no longer holds the role gets an empty list. CM19 Signals only inside a bound request. A fetch-now signal (CM27), on the socket or by a platform push, is sent only inside a request already bound to the command's tenant, such as the request that accepted the command, the approval or the cancel, or a later request from the destination. Under TENANCY_MODE=multi, nothing is sent from a context with no tenant bound, such as the load cycle; a signal there, or one bound to another tenant, is withheld (withheld), and the command waits for the destination's fetch (CM29). Under single the one tenant is always bound. CM20 A platform push is a signal sent with the tenant's credential. A platform push carries only a fetch-now signal (CM27) and is sent with a credential the command's tenant holds, never the deployment's. Without one, no platform push is sent (no-tenant-credential), and the destination fetches on its cadence (CM29). CM21 Enacted once. Delivery is at least once: a fetch returns a command again until the controller reports (CM26), a reply can be lost after the hub recorded the fetch, and a signal can arrive twice or after the fetch it asked for. Every fetch carries each command's commandId. The controller decides each commandId once: it records the id when it first enacts or refuses the command, keeps that record across restarts until expiresAt by its own clock, and answers any later delivery of the id without enacting it and without a second outcome report. A sender who sends again without the same requestId makes a new command (CM4), which this rule does not catch. CM26 Fetched until reported. A fetch returns every command routed to the fetching instance that is pending or fetched, while the instance holds the role and before the command's expiry. The first fetch moves it to fetched; later fetches return it again until the controller reports (acknowledged or a final state) or it expires, when it becomes unconfirmed (CM3). A cancel requested after hand-over (CM25) is carried under cancels, in place of the command, by every fetch until the controller reports after it. A fetch reply that never reaches the controller delays a command and never loses it; CM21 makes the repeats harmless. CM27 A signal says only "fetch now". While a command or a carried cancel waits for a destination (CM26), the hub may send that instance a fetch-now signal. The signal goes to the destination instance only, over a live transport it listens on (CM28), and carries nothing beyond its event: no payload, no payloadHash, no commandId, no channel. It names no command because the fetch that follows returns every waiting command anyway, so an id would give the controller nothing, while each signal passes through the transport's operator (a platform push service or a broker), which an id would let count and time one person's commands. A forged signal causes at most one extra fetch with the controller's own credential. A signal changes no state: a signalled command stays pending until fetched, and becomes expired or undeliverable if it never is. A signal is a hint: lost, late or repeated, it delays a command and never loses or duplicates one, because the fetch bound (CM29) still holds. None is sent for a command at or past its expiry (expired) or when nothing waits (nothing-waiting). CM28 Live transports. The capability's commands.liveTransports lists the transports the hub sends signals on, an open vocabulary: socket (Socket.IO on the hub's existing listener, sync-transport T16), apns, fcm, or {value: other, controllerTerm}, such as a message broker. A controller declares the transports it listens on in its registration: the liveTransports of its commands[] entry whose transport is nightscout-commands. The hub signals by the first transport the destination lists that the hub also lists; with none in common no signal is sent (no-live-transport), and the controller fetches on its cadence. A controller moves from polling to a live transport by adding the transport to its registration; it keeps fetching. CM29 The fetch bound. A destination fetches at least once per controller cycle: within cadence.nominalSeconds of its last fetch, deferred by at most cadence.maxDeferralSeconds, so its fetch bound is the sum of the two. It may declare a tighter bound, fetchIntervalSeconds on its nightscout-commands entry; the bound is then the shorter of that and the cycle. A bound under the hub's commands.minFetchIntervalSeconds is raised to it. A signal (CM27) can bring a fetch sooner and never lengthens the bound. CM30 The fetch bound is shown. The reply that accepts a command or an approval carries fetchWithinSeconds, the destination's fetch bound (CM29), so a sender sees how soon the command can be fetched without a signal. The outstanding list (CM24) carries, under destinations, each live holder of the channel's sink with its fetchWithinSeconds. A command whose expiresAt is no more than the fetch bound after the request is accepted unchanged and flagged mayExpireUnfetched, in the reply and on the record: the hub does not judge an expiry within CM3's limits (CM5), and a command never fetched expires harmlessly (CM3). A live transport does not clear the flag, because a signal is a hint.

From proposal to outcome, with the checks each step makes:

sequenceDiagram
  accTitle: From proposal to outcome
  accDescr: An agent instance proposes a payload with the state version it read. The hub routes and records the proposal; evaluations attach as evidence. A person or delegate approves the payload's hash; the hub refuses when the hash, the destination, the state version or doses since differ, leaving the proposal open, and otherwise records one command and returns the destination's fetch bound and what else is outstanding. The hub may send the controller a fetch-now signal that carries nothing; the command reaches the controller only by its fetch, with its id and hash. The controller checks the hash and expiry, decides the command once and checks doses since, then reports. A cancel before hand-over is final; after it, a request the controller decides.

  participant H as Hub
  participant A as Approver (person or delegate)

  H-->>P: 201 proposalId, routed and recorded
  Note over H: evaluations attach as evidence (CM16)

docs.title: 7.1 Discovery and paths (proposed)
docs.text:
# rule CM31 The capability member. The capability document's commands member (registration §4) is present only when the hub offers the command record. It carries the paths (href, fetch, and proposals when the hub takes proposals), maxExpirySeconds (CM3), maxPayloadBytes (CM5), liveTransports (CM28) and minFetchIntervalSeconds (CM29). Without it the hub serves none of CM32's paths (404), and a controller offers no hub command path and keeps the transports it has (§8). A controller reads it when it reads the capability document: at launch and after a controller release. CM32 Paths. The operations of §4–§7 are served on the data listener (ns-api, or single; maintainer, 2026-10-26) at the paths below, each bound to the request's tenant (CM6) and answered as the rules state. Request and reply members are in the tables that follow; a member not listed is ignored, as in the grammar (G1). operation method and path rules send a command POST /api/v4/commands CM1–CM6, CM30 the outstanding list GET /api/v4/commands?channel=<channel> CM24, CM30 read a command GET /api/v4/commands/{commandId} CM6 cancel POST /api/v4/commands/{commandId}/cancel CM25 report an outcome POST /api/v4/commands/{commandId}/reports CM7–CM9 fetch (the destination) GET /api/v4/instances/{instanceId}/commands CM18, CM26 propose POST /api/v4/proposals CM11, CM12 read a proposal GET /api/v4/proposals/{proposalId} CM11 approve POST /api/v4/proposals/{proposalId}/approve CM13–CM15, CM22, CM30 reject POST /api/v4/proposals/{proposalId}/reject CM14 withdraw POST /api/v4/proposals/{proposalId}/withdraw CM14 attach an evaluation POST /api/v4/proposals/{proposalId}/evaluations CM16

The capability's commands.href is /api/v4/commands, commands.fetch the URI template /api/v4/instances/{instanceId}/commands, and commands.proposals /api/v4/proposals; a hub may serve them elsewhere and says so there. Since 2026-10-26 (maintainer) the instance resource itself is /api/v4/instances/{instanceId} (registration §7, amendment), so the fetch is a sub-resource of the instance it serves.

Send (POST /api/v4/commands) and approve (POST …/approve):

member in states channel send the channel (§2) product send optional; the product, {vendor, product} (§2, CM4) payload send the payload, stored exactly as received (CM1, CM5) expiresAt send required (CM3) requestId send optional (CM4) initiator send, approve as state and intent S8 gives it payloadHash approve the hash approved (CM13) commandId, state reply 201 the command recorded (CM1); pending fetchWithinSeconds reply 201 the destination's fetch bound (CM30) mayExpireUnfetched reply 201 true when the command expires within that bound (CM30); absent otherwise outstanding reply 201 the other open proposals and commands on the channel and the doses since, when there are any (CM24)

A re-send with the same requestId answers 200 with the first commandId and its current state (CM4); a refusal answers its status and code, with commandId for a command refused at routing (CM1).

The outstanding list (GET /api/v4/commands?channel=): proposals[] and commands[], each with its id, sender or proposer, initiator, createdAt, expiresAt and state; dosesSince[]; and destinations, a map from each holder's instanceId to {fetchWithinSeconds} (CM24, CM30).

Fetch (GET /api/v4/instances/{instanceId}/commands):

member states commands[] each waiting command (CM26): commandId, channel, payload, payloadHash, expiresAt, initiator, and proposalId and basedOn when it came from an approval cancels[] each carried cancel (CM25, CM26): commandId

Report (POST /api/v4/commands/{commandId}/reports): state, payloadHash, reason when refused or failed, and when enacted the identity of the record that shows the effect (CM7); the reply is 200, or the refusals CM7–CM9 name.

Cancel (POST /api/v4/commands/{commandId}/cancel): no members; 200 with state: cancelled, or 202 with the command's state and cancelRequested: true (CM25).

Propose (POST /api/v4/proposals): proposer (the proposing instance's instanceId), channel, product and instanceId when known, payload, basedOn and expiresAt (CM11); 201 with proposalId. Reject and withdraw take no members and answer 200; evaluations take the evaluation and answer 201 (CM16).

What a mode changes beyond these, such as the storage key and the credential kinds a command record names, is the registration contract per mode (SPEC-REG-MODES, not written).

docs.text:
The same, for every app the corpus holds and every layer: compatibility.

Read from Loop (c30b5c89, NightscoutService 2cef489), Trio (0b29cd534), AndroidAPS (7e1d537d49, dev), LoopCaregiver (2305718) and LoopFollow (4a74b781), 2026-10-18; nothing was run.

A hub keeps it as it is or retires it; bringing it under these rules needs Loop to register LoopCaregiver "Remote Commands 2" (experimental, off by default; closed-loop and automatic-bolus changes always) expects /api/v2/remotecommands, which neither cgm-remote-monitor nor Nocturne implements one-time password none on the record the record's _id Pending → InProgress → Success or Error the closest to CM1 and CM7: its states map to pending, acknowledged, succeeded, and failed or refused; who may change a status is not stated, and no Loop build in the checkouts reads it LoopFollow → Loop or Trio (direct APNs) no; the device token is read from the hub's profile as above; Trio encrypts the whole payload with a shared secret Loop: as above; Trio: ±600 s around the sender's time, fixed, no expiry field none a reply push to the sender; a Note on failure outside the hub; a hub sees only the resulting records AndroidAPS client control (dev, not released) the settings collection carries it; the hub reads none of it HMAC per paired client, a strictly increasing counter ±5 min and validUntil (unbounded by default; its senders set 8 s, 60 s or 5 min) the counter signed Executing, Done (Ok, Failed, Expired), and a late Delivery Failed the only path whose outcome names its command; its doses are two-step, computed and capped on the controller between prepare and commit AndroidAPS SMS no allowed number, one-time password and PIN 5 min to confirm the message thread an SMS reply outside the hub

What in this table bears on the rules:

  • A late failure after success. AndroidAPS reports Done Ok when the pump queue accepts a bolus and Delivery Failed if the pump later fails it; Trio replies "initiating bolus" before it enacts and may reply failed after. CM9 as written refuses a report after succeeded (§9).
  • One command, part enacted. Trio's meal command stores the carbs before it validates the bolus, so a refused bolus leaves carbs entered and the reply says failed. A single final state cannot say which part happened (§9).
  • No controller computes a payload hash (CM10); each checks its own authentication instead.
  • No released controller de-duplicates by a hub's command id (CM21). Loop's bolus and carbs are single use through the one-time password, stored across restarts; its overrides are de-duplicated in memory only, so a replay after a restart starts the override again. Trio refuses a bolus when boluses since the command's own time reach 20 % of it, refuses a meal when newer carbs exist, and has no check for overrides or temporary targets; its dev branch carries a command_id it does not yet check. AndroidAPS client control's per-client counter must strictly increase and is stored, which already meets CM21. The unreleased Remote Commands 2 controller stores the ids it handled, as CM21 asks, without pruning them (read at Loop v3.14.9, Trio v1.0.2, AndroidAPS 4.0.0-rc1, 2026-10-18).
  • Expiry is not uniform. Loop checks an expiration only when one is sent; Trio checks a fixed window around the sender's time; AndroidAPS's validUntil is unbounded unless the sender sets it; Remote Commands 2 records carry none. CM3 requires one of every command.
  • Today's push paths stay as they are. Loop's and Trio's APNs paths, through /api/v2/notifications/loop or straight from a follower, and AndroidAPS's settings documents carry their payloads outside the hub command record. CM17–CM20 and CM26–CM31 do not change them; a controller keeps them beside the hub path, or alone when a hub has no commands member (CM31).
  • Sender authentication is end to end. Every controller that accepts a remote dose authenticates the sender itself; a hub forwards that material and is not trusted with it.

docs.title: 9. Open
docs.text:
1. Choices for the maintainer:
  2. How a capability document marks a listed other role as proposing (CM12), and as an agent's (CM14). Today it lists role names only; nothing says which listed role may propose, or which belongs to an agent.
  3. The command's expiry after an approval (CM13 proposes the proposal's expiresAt), or a new one set at approval within the proposal's.
  4. Refusing a stale approval (CM15), or only showing the approver that the state version changed.
  5. Recording refusals at routing (CM1) as not-routed commands, or answering them only.
  6. Who may approve (CM14): today anyone who may send the command; a grant could narrow it (authority §7).
  7. A command that expires within its destination's fetch bound (CM30) is accepted and flagged mayExpireUnfetched. Refusing it instead would stop a sender relying on a signal that may not arrive; flagging keeps the hub out of judging an expiry (CM5), and such a command, if never fetched, expires with nothing enacted (CM3).
  8. A controller check before approval. The proposal lifecycle drew propose → validate → (evaluate) → approve; CM11–CM16 send nothing to the controller before approval, because no controller offers a dry run of a remote command except AndroidAPS dev's two-step prepare and commit, which computes and caps a dose on the controller before it is committed.
  9. The payload grammar. No definition declares the shape of a command's payload; the hub stores it unread, and an approver's display has nothing to render its units or product from (UCA-PROP-004). A plan made of elements, and an approval that accepts some of them, is specified in plans; the maintainer chose (2026-10-18) that the approval names each accepted element by id and hash and the command carries one hash of the accepted subset, with approver signatures as the next step, since only a signature lets a controller detect a hub that built the wrong subset (partial acceptance prototype).
  10. Outcomes that change after a final state: a late delivery failure after success (§8), and a command enacted in part (§8). Either a further state (failed after succeeded, with the record keeping both) or an outcome per part (UCA-CMD-011, UCA-CMD-013).
  11. The grant that lets a person approve for someone else, and auto-approval: authority §7.
  12. The registration contract per tenancy mode (SPEC-REG-MODES).
  13. Found by the control-loop analysis:
  14. A second command or approval while one is outstanding (UCA-CMD-001, UCA-PROP-007). CM24 shows the sender and approver what is outstanding, and nothing refuses a second one. The state version changes only when the controller's records arrive (A12), so two approvals in that window both pass CM15. The remaining choice: refuse a second approval on a channel while a command from an approval is not final, or include outstanding commands in what CM15 compares.
  15. The definition at approval (UCA-PROP-008). CM11 records the destination's definitionId; CM13 refuses destination-changed only when the instance differs, so an instance that renewed under a new definition receives a payload approved under the old one.
  16. Proposal volume (UCA-PROP-002). Nothing limits the open proposals one instance holds on a channel.
  17. Required reviews on a moment proposal. Plans name reviews an approval waits for (plans PN6); a proposal for one command has no such member.
  18. Who acts for the person (CM14). The owner sets the mark (decided 2026-10-26); whether more than one subject may hold it is open.
  19. A process holding the destination's credential (UCA-CMD-014). CM7 and CM18 check the subject, not the process: under single every holder of API_SECRET is one subject, so another app can fetch a command, which moves it to fetched and out of the controller's next fetch, or report its outcome.
  20. Approving at once (UCA-PROP-013). CM13 lets only an open proposal change, and approve-approved-proposal shows a second approval refused; that the change from open to approved is atomic under concurrent approvals is not stated.

  21. The operator's limits (UCA-AUTH-006). commands.maxExpirySeconds bounds every expiry (CM3) and has no bound of its own.

  22. The address for a platform push. A platform push signal (CM20) needs the destination's device address for that platform; where an instance gives it is not specified. Instance labels cannot carry it (registration §10), and the tenant's credential for the platform has no place in the capability document, which describes the deployment.

  23. The effect link (CM7). Where the identity of the record that shows an enacted command's effect lives: an effect[] list on the report, the commandId on the record, both with disagreements flagged, or a separate reconciliation record (item 4 overlaps it). The effect-link prototype measures each against the same scenarios, with its cost and failure modes.

docs.title: L0–L5 Compatibility: what each app does with a hub today, and what it sees from one that implements the specifications
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-26 at a31885f18.

Contributor-facing. Living specification table, current at main 8cb0b5ed (2026-10-18). Covers layers L0–L5 of the platform index; terms are in the glossary. Queue: SPEC-COMPAT-APPS.

A companion to the eight specifications in the reading order, read after them or beside the one a reader's app touches. Expect, for every app the corpus holds, what it does at each layer today and what it sees from a hub that implements the specifications without the app changing, an overview by layer, the cells where an answer changes, and what the table does not cover.

Each specification has a compatibility section that says, in general, what an older client sees from a newer hub (registration §17, sync-transport §7, commands §8, plans §8). This page names the apps. Every today cell is read from the app's source at the ref named, through the per-client files of the 15.0.9 consumer-impact survey and the controller notes behind commands §8; nothing was run. Every with a hub that implements the specifications cell cites the rule that decides it.

Status: evidenced for today, read from the specifications for the rest, which are proposed or specified and not implemented.

docs.title: 1. Files
docs.text: file holds specs/sync/compat/{ios,android,uploaders,readers}.yaml one entry per app, per layer: today, with a newer hub, the verdict, the rules and anchors; format in specs/sync/compat/FORMAT.md tools/nsschema/compat_tables.py writes the tables in §3 and §4 from the files tools/nsschema/test_compat.py the checks in §7 reports/consumer-impact-15.0.9/clients/ the per-client files each entry cites

docs.title: 2. How to read the verdicts
docs.text:
verdict means unchanged the app behaves as today; nothing it sends or reads changes gains the app benefits without changing, from the rule named opt-in a capability exists for it, which it uses only if it changes (typed writes, registration, the command record, plans) affected something it does today answers differently; §5 lists each one none the app does not touch this layer

L0 identity, L1 records, L2 definitions and instances, L3 state, intent and commands, L4 change and sync, L5 authority, as the platform index defines them.

docs.title: 4.1 L0 Identity
docs.text: app today with a hub that implements the specifications verdict rules AndroidAPS The v3 client never sends _id; it keeps the identifier from the POST reply and PATCHes and DELETEs by it. The 3.4.x v1 socket client reads _id from the dbAdd reply and sends it back on dbUpdate. v3 creates, edits and deletes by identifier answer as today, and the reply adds _id and matchedBy beside the identifier it reads (I4, I5). The v1 dbAdd reply still carries a 24-hex _id (I2), and a 3.4.x treatment dbUpdate whose _id is the UUID of a v3-created record is moved to identifier and matched to that record (I9, I5) instead of the exact-string _id match it gets today. gains I2, I4, I5, I9 AndroidAPS client control Each message is a v3 settings document under a fixed identifier (aaps_clientcontrol_hello_, cmd_<type>_, ack_, progress_, offer_ plus the client id), overwritten in place; the document date is a constant placeholder because API v3 refuses a changed date on a re-sent identifier. One identifier names one document and is compared exactly, so each slot is overwritten in place as today (I6, I5). The v3 refusal of a changed date is an open decision, and the constant date is unaffected either way (identity §5). unchanged I5, I6, identity §5 Loop Posts override treatments with _id set to the override's upper-case UUID and deletes them by that UUID; posts doses with syncIdentifier and no _id, so a re-send is matched by created_at + eventType; caches the 24-hex _id of carb treatments from the POST reply for later PUT and DELETE. Treatments match on client identity (syncIdentifier) before created_at + eventType, so two doses of one type at one time stay two records; the override UUID is moved to identifier as today and recorded as quirksApplied, and the upper-case DELETE still matches exactly (I6, I9). gains identity §3, I5, I6, I9 oref0 Sends no _id or identifier; re-sent pump-history treatments rely on the server's created_at+eventType upsert, which replaces the stored treatment, and ns-dedupe-treatments.sh reads _id back to delete duplicates. A re-sent treatment matches on created_at+eventType among records without client identity and is merged, not replaced, so fields added in Nightscout that the rig does not send are kept (identity §3, T2). The dedupe tool's deletes by _id find every stored form of the id (I2). affected identity §3, T2, I2 Trio Sends its own upper-case UUID in a plain id member, which the hub does not read, and deletes carbs and insulin by find[id][$eq]; on 15.0.8 a re-send without identifier is matched by created_at + eventType alone (QUIRK-TREATMENTS-007). Treatments match on client identity (id) before created_at + eventType, so two records of one type at one time stay two; id is still not identifier and gets no mapping (Q4a). gains identity §3, I5, Q4a cgmsim-lib Sends no _id or identifier on any upload and makes no PUT or DELETE by id. Its writes match on each collection's natural key as today and are answered with both ids (identity §3, I4). unchanged identity §3, I4 DiaBLE Posts sgv entries without _id and reads no id back; it posts only readings newer than the newest it read. A re-send matches on date + type as today (identity §3). unchanged identity §3 glooko-nightscout-eu Sends no _id; each treatment carries glookoGuid, and de-duplication is a client-side set of guids saved to disk. glookoGuid is not a client id the hub reads, so a re-send matches on created_at+eventType among records without client identity, as today (identity §3). unchanged identity §3 glooko2nightscout Makes no Nightscout request: it writes Nightscout-shaped entries to a local JSON file. Nothing. none — minimed-connect-to-nightscout Sends no _id; de-duplication is an in-memory recency filter on date and created_at, and API v1 devicestatus has no key, so a devicestatus sent twice is stored twice. An identical devicestatus re-sent with the same created_at and device is answered unchanged instead of stored again; entries match on date+type (identity §3, T2). gains identity §3, T2 nightscout-connect Copies records from a source hub with the source's 24-hex _id. On the 15.0.9 candidate a devicestatus or profile re-send that collides with a stored string copy is refused as a duplicate key, and the persist fails until that record leaves the window. Its in-process writes go through the one write step, which keeps a 24-hex _id as the ObjectId and matches every stored form of it, so such a re-send is answered with the stored ids, never an error (T1, I2, I4, identity §3). gains T1, I2, I4, identity §3 nightscout-librelink-up Sends entries without _id; on API v3 the hub computes a UUID v5 identifier from device and date. It sends only readings newer than the newest stored entry. A re-sent reading matches on identifier, then date+type (I5, identity §3). unchanged I5, identity §3 share2nightscout-bridge Sends entries without _id (device: 'share2') and relies on the server's entries upsert for re-sent readings. A re-sent reading matches on date+type and merges (identity §3, T2). unchanged identity §3, T2 tconnectsync Sends no _id on POST and keeps pump_event_id as its own key. It reads _id back to DELETE a treatment, and in profile replace mode PUTs the profile with the _id from profile/current, which 15.0.8 stores as a second copy when that profile was stored with a string _id. A PUT or DELETE by _id finds every stored form of the id, so replace mode updates the profile in place (I2, identity §3). pump_event_id is not a client id the hub reads, so its re-sends match on the natural key. gains I2, identity §3 xDrip+ Sends its own 24-hex _id (derived from its treatment uuid) on PUT /api/v1/treatments and deletes by it; on 15.0.8 a treatment stored with a string _id by an earlier release gets an ObjectId copy on the next PUT, and the DELETE misses the string copy. The 24-hex _id is kept as that ObjectId, and an _id matches every stored form of it, so the PUT finds the existing record and the DELETE removes it, as #8758 does on dev (I2, identity §3). gains I2, identity §3 xDrip4iOS Sends a random 24-character alphanumeric _id on entries and some treatments, which the hub moves to identifier or drops; reads treatment _id back for PUT and DELETE; counts a 500 whose body has code 66 as a successful duplicate. A duplicate is answered with the stored ids, never a 5xx, and xDrip4iOS counts that as success too (I4); the moved _id is recorded as quirksApplied and matched first on a re-send (I5, I9). affected I4, I5, I9 LoopCaregiver Writes no v1 records, so sends no _id; its experimental Remote Commands 2 option keys on a record _id from a route the hub does not implement. Nothing it reads on implemented routes changes (I2). unchanged I2 LoopFollow Writes no records; reads _id only from the subjects reply, to derive its token. Nothing it reads changes (I2). unchanged I2 nightguard Posts treatments through API v3 without _id or identifier, and keys its local cache on identifier, falling back to _id. Every reply carries both ids, and a projected document keeps one identifier and _id across reads, so its keys stay stable (I4, I8). unchanged I1, I4, I8 GluPredKit Writes nothing and reads no ids; sums insulin, carbs and temporary basals client-side from what it downloads. A record re-sent by an uploader is stored once on every write path, so it is counted once (I5, T1). gains I5, T1 GlycemicGPT Writes nothing; pages entries with find[_id][$gt]=<24-hex>, a cursor whose order is the _id's time. Every legacy _id is 24 hex, an assigned one carries the receipt time, and a projected document gets an ObjectId at its typed write, so the cursor reaches every new record (I2, I3, I8). unchanged I2, I3, I8 nightscout-cgm-skill Writes nothing; keys its SQLite cache of entries on _id and sums insulin and carbs client-side. Every legacy _id is 24 hex (I2), and a record re-sent by an uploader is stored once, so it is summed once (I5, T1). gains I2, I5, T1 nightscout-reporter Writes nothing; reads treatment _id as an opaque string and drops adjacent identical treatments and enteredBy == 'sync' before summing. A re-send is matched on identifier, then _id, then the natural key on every write path, so a treatment re-sent by an uploader is stored once and summed once (I5, T1). gains I5, T1, I2 oref-digital-twin Writes nothing; drops records with a repeated _id across its windows. A record re-sent by an uploader is stored once on every write path, so the replay's inputs carry no second copy under another _id (I5, T1). gains I5, T1, I2 nightscout-roles-gateway Reads and writes no records. Reads and writes no records. none — Nocturne Measured at 89dcaf1dd (tools/lab/nocturne-parity) - serves a 24-hex _id on v1 and v3 and sets v3 identifier equal to it, replacing a client-sent identifier (a read by the client's identifier answers 404); a v3 re-send is answered 200 with isDeduplication for entries and 201 without it for treatments, devicestatus and profile, and a treatment re-send is stored once. Read at 42275c81 - v1 by-id routes accept 24-hex and 32-hex (UUID v7 without dashes) ids, and look up by GUID, then by exact LegacyId, then by GUID prefix. It would serve a 24-hex _id on v1 and none in v3 reads, keep a client 24-hex _id in lower case on v1 and refuse a client _id on v3 with 400 (I2), answer each write with both ids and matchedBy (I4), and match a re-send on identifier, then _id, then the natural key (I5). opt-in I2, I4, I5, I8 babelbetes Makes no Nightscout requests. Makes no Nightscout requests. none — GlookoServiceKit No Nightscout traffic: it uploads Loop or Trio data to Glooko. Nothing at this layer. none — Not read not read not read none — openaps Makes no Nightscout request; a rig reaches Nightscout through oref0's ns device. Nothing; what a rig sees is under oref0. none — trio-telemetry Makes no Nightscout requests. Makes no Nightscout requests. none — xdrip-js A Bluetooth library for Dexcom transmitters; it makes no Nightscout request on master or dev. Nothing. none —

docs.title: 5. Where an answer changes
docs.text:
The verdicts describe a hub under TENANCY_MODE=single, the one every app reaches today. Two cells answer differently there:

  • oref0, L0. A re-sent pump-history treatment without client identity matches on created_at and eventType and is merged into the stored one instead of replacing it, so fields added in Nightscout that the rig does not send are kept (identity §3, T2). On 15.0.9 the rig's malformed count read is refused, and it then re-posts a day of treatments every loop, which makes this merge the common path (consumer impact §2.1).
  • xDrip4iOS, L0. A duplicate is answered with the stored ids instead of a server error (I4); the app counts both as success.

Under TENANCY_MODE=multi every app reaches its tenant with its tenant's credential: there is no deployment-wide secret, tokens are signed with the tenant's key, and subject tokens are re-rooted on the tenant's credential (AU3). Each L5 cell says what that means for the app. Three apps meet more than a new credential:

  • LoopFollow, L4 and L5. The load cycle's dataUpdate is withheld under multi on the seam branch (commands §3); LoopFollow slows its polling while its socket is connected, so it would refresh less often with nothing to trigger a re-poll (sync-transport §8).
  • LoopCaregiver, L3 and L5. The /api/v2/notifications/loop relay sends with the deployment's push key and looks devices up across the process (commands §3); CM20 allows only a tenant's own push credentials, so the route it depends on has no tenant-scoped form until a hub gives one.
  • nightscout-roles-gateway, L5. The secret it inspects with and every stored policy token must be its tenant's.

For a hub, the right-hand column is what it would serve to implement each layer: Nocturne's cells name the rules and the differences state and intent §6.2 measured on shared cases.

docs.title: 6. Open
docs.text:
1. Today's credential forms under multi: whether a tenant's root credential is accepted as the hashed api-secret header and the v1 socket's secret that apps send today (authority §9 item 7).
  2. The v1 socket's events under multi (sync-transport §8 item 7).
  3. Not read: the maintained nightscout-reporter (Angular), python-nightscout (GluPredKit's entries and treatments calls go through it), Sugarmate, Spike, closed-source apps, and xDrip+'s direct MongoDB uploader.
  4. Refs. Each row names the ref it was read at; the 15.0.9 survey read the apps on 2026-09-23, and the controllers' command paths were read at their releases on 2026-10-18. A row is re-read when its app releases a version that changes a cell.
  5. Well-known registrations exist for Loop, Trio and AndroidAPS only (specs/sync/registrations/); every other writer's L2 attribution rests on registration §11 and §17.

docs.title: L2–L5 Control loops: what each mechanism controls, and the unsafe control actions its rules prevent
docs.text:
Living document, last changed 2026-10-18 at baa67a88f.

Contributor-facing. Living specification analysis, current at main 85c645c8 (2026-10-18). Covers layers L2–L5 of the platform index; terms are in the glossary. Decisions: D18 and D19. Queue: SPEC-STPA-PLATFORM.

An analysis across the eight specifications in the reading order; read it after commands, or after all eight. Expect the losses and hazards, the control structure the specifications set up, one section per control loop with its unsafe control actions and the rule that prevents each, the patterns that apply to the proposed mechanics, what the analysis found, and the checks that hold it to the specifications.

This page applies STPA (System-Theoretic Process Analysis) to the mechanisms the platform specifications propose. STPA models a system as controllers that issue control actions and receive feedback, and asks, for each control action, how it could be unsafe: provided when it should not be, not provided when it should be, provided too early or too late, or applied for too long or too short. Each answer is an unsafe control action (UCA). The specifications' rules are then read as the constraints that prevent them. Where no rule prevents one, the analysis names the gap and the specification lists it as open.

Status: the loops are drawn from the specifications, which are proposed or specified and not implemented. Of 103 entries, 68 are covered by a rule and a case, 11 are the controller's responsibility (D18), 3 have a rule and no case, and 21 are gaps, each listed in its specification's open items.

docs.title: 1. Files
docs.text: file holds specs/sync/stpa/platform-control-loops.yaml losses, hazards, loops, control actions, every entry with its hazards, severity, constraints, verification and status, and what was considered not hazardous for each STPA type tools/nsschema/test_stpa.py the checks in §8 tools/nsschema/stpa_tables.py writes the tables in §4 from the file docs/STPA-USAGE-GUIDE.md the ecosystem's STPA method, severity scale (S1–S4) and id conventions traceability/stpa/cross-project-patterns.md the controller-side unsafe control actions (UCA-BOLUS, UCA-CARB, UCA-REMOTE, UCA-SYNC) this analysis meets at the hub

docs.title: 2. Losses and hazards
docs.text:
loss LOSS-1 Harm to the person with diabetes from insulin delivered or withheld (hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia, ketoacidosis). LOSS-2 Loss of the ability to say afterwards what was asked, by whom, and what was enacted, for care, incident review or regulatory review. LOSS-3 Disclosure of health data, or of control over therapy, to someone the person did not authorise. hazard losses HAZ-1 Insulin delivery, or a therapy setting, that the person or someone they authorised did not intend at that time, including the same change enacted twice. LOSS-1 HAZ-2 A therapy change someone intended is not made, while the people relying on it believe it was. LOSS-1 HAZ-3 A person, controller or agent acts on a picture of delivered insulin, active therapy or a command's fate that differs from what happened. LOSS-1, LOSS-2 HAZ-4 Control over therapy, or health data, reaches someone not authorised for it, such as another tenant or a reader promoted to an actor. LOSS-1, LOSS-3 HAZ-5 The record cannot show what was asked, by whom, what was enacted, and when. LOSS-2

Losses and hazards use LOSS- and HAZ- so that they do not read as the layers L0–L5.

docs.title: 3. The control structure
docs.text:
Solid arrows are control actions; dashed arrows are feedback. Every box is a role, not a product. The drawing's source is tools/structure-diagrams/inputs/3-platform-control.yaml, rendered with tools/structure-diagrams/render.py.

Two observations follow from the drawing.

  • The hub has no control action on the pump. D18 puts every dosing decision in the controller, and the structure shows it: the hub's control actions are routing and delivering what a sender asked, and the controller validates before it acts. A second path reaches the controller as well: treatments other clients wrote, which a controller that accepts them (S10) acts on with none of a command's record, expiry or outcome (§4.4). The pump has more than one controller upstream of it (the person, the algorithm, each caregiver and agent), and only the controller arbitrates among them (state and intent S1).
  • The hub is in the feedback path of every other controller. A caregiver decides whether to send a bolus from the hub's history, its active state and its command states; an agent bases a proposal on the hub's state version; a controller that downloads treatments acts on records the hub stored. So the rules about what the hub reports (the command states, the active-state rules A1–A13, the sync rules T6–T10, re-send matching I5) are safety constraints, although the hub never doses.

docs.title: 4. The loops
docs.text: Each loop lists its control actions and feedback, then its entries. Prevented by names rules and sections; status is covered (a rule and a case), uncased (a rule, no case), controller (the controller's own validation, D18) or gap (no rule; the open item named).

docs.title: 4.1 A remote command
docs.text:
Commands §2, §4, §5 and §7. The sender sends a command (CA-CMD-SEND), or would cancel one (CA-CMD-CANCEL, not specified); the hub records it and delivers it in a fetch, which a fetch-now signal may prompt (CA-CMD-DELIVER); the controller validates and enacts it (CA-CMD-ENACT) and reports an outcome, which the hub shows the sender as the command's state (FB-CMD-STATE). The sender's process model is the command's state; the hub's is its record; only the controller knows what the pump did.

flowchart LR
  sender["Sender"] -- "CA-CMD-SEND" --> hub["Hub"]
  hub -- "CA-CMD-DELIVER" --> ctl["Controller"]
  ctl -- "CA-CMD-ENACT" --> pump["Pump"]
  pump -. "delivery status" .-> ctl
  ctl -. "outcome report" .-> hub
  hub -. "FB-CMD-STATE" .-> sender
id type unsafe control action or feedback hazards severity prevented by status UCA-CMD-001 provided A sender sends a second command for the same intent while the first is pending, fetched or unconfirmed, and both are enacted. HAZ-1 S4 CM3, CM4, CM24 gap: commands §9 UCA-CMD-002 provided A retry of one request is treated as a new command. HAZ-1 S4 CM4 covered UCA-CMD-003 timing A command is enacted long after it was sent, when the sender's reason for it no longer holds. HAZ-1 S3 CM3, CM10 covered UCA-CMD-004 provided A command reaches an instance other than the live device holder of the channel's command sink, such as a lapsed former holder, the newest instance, or a simulator. HAZ-1 S4 commands §2, CM1, CM2 covered UCA-CMD-005 provided A command reaches an instance on another tenant, or a signal for one tenant is sent outside a request bound to it or with another tenant's or the deployment's push credentials. HAZ-4, HAZ-1 S4 CM6, CM19, CM20 covered UCA-CMD-006 provided One command is delivered more than once, by fetches that return it until the controller reports (CM26), and the controller enacts it each time. HAZ-1 S4 CM18, CM21, CM26 covered UCA-CMD-007 provided The payload a controller receives differs from the one the sender sent. HAZ-1 S4 CM5, CM10 covered UCA-CMD-008 not-provided A fetch-now signal or a fetch reply is lost and the destination never receives the command, or the sender reads the signal as delivery. HAZ-2, HAZ-3 S2 CM17, CM26, CM27 covered UCA-CMD-009 timing A command is signalled or fetched at or after its expiry. HAZ-1 S3 CM3 covered UCA-CMD-010 provided A controller enacts a remote command that its own limits, or a recent local action, should have refused. HAZ-1 S4 CM5, CM10 controller UCA-CMD-011 provided A controller enacts part of a command, such as storing a meal's carbs and refusing its bolus, and reports one final state. HAZ-3 S3 CM9 gap: commands §9 UCA-CMD-012 timing A controller enacts a command past its expiry because the hub's clock and its own differ. HAZ-1 S3 CM10 covered UCA-CMD-013 not-provided A controller does not enact a command it reported as succeeded, such as a bolus the pump later fails. HAZ-2, HAZ-3 S3 CM9 gap: commands §9 FB-CMD-001 incorrect A command that was handed over reads expired or undeliverable, and the sender sends it again. HAZ-3, HAZ-1 S4 CM2, CM3 covered FB-CMD-002 incorrect A command reads succeeded because a subject other than the destination's bound subject reported it. HAZ-3 S3 CM7 covered FB-CMD-003 incorrect A command reads as done because it was signalled or fetched. HAZ-2, HAZ-3 S3 CM7, CM18 gap: commands §9 UCA-CMD-015 not-provided A sender cannot cancel a pending command after the reason for it went away, such as a meal not eaten. HAZ-1 S3 CM3, CM25 covered

docs.title: 4.2 A proposal and its approval
docs.text:
Commands §6 and authority §7. A proposer proposes (CA-PROP-PROPOSE), anyone who may read it may evaluate it (CA-PROP-EVALUATE), and an approver approves it (CA-PROP-APPROVE), which creates a command that then runs the loop in §4.1. The approver's process model is the proposal's payload, its basedOn and what the hub shows as active (§4.5); the approval is a control action taken on that model, and every check CM13–CM15 makes is a check that the model still matches the hub's record.

flowchart LR
  agent["Proposer"] -- "CA-PROP-PROPOSE" --> hub["Hub"]
  evaluator["Evaluator"] -- "CA-PROP-EVALUATE" --> hub
  hub -. "proposal, evaluations, state version" .-> approver["Approver"]
  approver -- "CA-PROP-APPROVE" --> hub
  hub -- "command (§4.1)" --> ctl["Controller"]
id type unsafe control action or feedback hazards severity prevented by status UCA-PROP-001 provided A credential or tool that may only read proposes a change. HAZ-4 S3 CM12 covered UCA-PROP-002 provided A proposer floods a channel with proposals, and the approver approves from habit rather than reading. HAZ-1 S3 CM11 gap: commands §9 UCA-PROP-003 provided An approval creates a command whose payload differs from the one the approver approved. HAZ-1 S4 CM13 covered UCA-PROP-004 provided An approver approves a payload whose meaning they misread, such as its units or which product it is for, because nothing declares the payload's shape for a display to render. HAZ-1 S4 CM5 gap: commands §9 UCA-PROP-005 provided An approval reaches a device other than the one whose state the proposer read. HAZ-1 S4 CM13 covered UCA-PROP-006 provided An approval is given after the controller's reported intents changed from the ones the proposal was based on. HAZ-1 S3 CM15 covered UCA-PROP-007 provided Two proposals on one channel are approved before the controller reports either, so both pass the state-version check and both are enacted. HAZ-1 S4 CM15 gap: commands §9 UCA-PROP-008 provided An approval is enacted under a different definition from the one the proposal was made against, after the destination instance renewed under a new definitionId. HAZ-1 S3 CM11, CM13, S12 gap: commands §9 UCA-PROP-009 provided The proposer approves its own proposal. HAZ-1, HAZ-4 S3 CM14 covered UCA-PROP-010 timing A proposal is approved after its expiry. HAZ-1 S3 CM13 covered UCA-PROP-011 provided An evaluation changes a proposal's state or approves it. HAZ-1 S3 CM16 covered UCA-PROP-012 provided A dose proposal is approved after the person dosed locally, because the state version covers intents and not doses or carbs. HAZ-1 S4 A12, CM15, CM22 covered UCA-PROP-013 provided Two approvers approve one proposal and two commands are created. HAZ-1 S4 CM13 covered

docs.title: 4.3 Which instance receives commands
docs.text:
Registration §8 and §9, authority §4 and §6. The hub grants and keeps a command-sink role (CA-ROUTE-GRANT) from each instance's renewals; the owner moves a product or a role (CA-ROUTE-REBIND). The controlled process is the routing table: which instance a command for a channel reaches. Feedback is the renewal reply (a changed etag, a 412) and the owner's listing.

id type unsafe control action or feedback hazards severity prevented by status UCA-ROUTE-001 provided A device command-sink role goes to an instance not bound to the product, such as another subject's development build. HAZ-1, HAZ-4 S4 authority §6 covered UCA-ROUTE-002 provided Two instances, such as an old and a new phone, both hold a channel's device command sink and both enact. HAZ-1 S4 registration §9 covered UCA-ROUTE-003 provided A lapsed or dropped role passes to the newest instance without its own claim or the owner's transfer. HAZ-1 S3 registration §9 covered UCA-ROUTE-004 not-provided The instance now attached to the pump cannot take the command sink, because a former phone still renews it. HAZ-2 S2 authority §4, registration §9 covered UCA-ROUTE-005 provided A former holder keeps routing commands to itself after its lease lapsed. HAZ-1 S3 registration §8 covered UCA-ROUTE-006 provided After the owner transfers or releases a product, commands still reach an instance of the former binding. HAZ-1, HAZ-4 S4 authority §6 covered UCA-ROUTE-007 provided An owner moves a command sink and nothing records who did it or when. HAZ-5 S2 authority §8 gap: authority §9 UCA-ROUTE-008 duration A phone that no longer has the pump keeps the command sink until its lease lapses, and commands sent in that window go to it. docs.title: 4.4 Records written, matched and read back
docs.text:
Identity §1, sync-transport §2 and §4, records §2. The hub stores, matches and merges what controllers write (CA-SYNC-STORE) and serves it back as history pages and socket events (CA-SYNC-SERVE). Every reader's picture of delivered insulin is built from this loop. A controller that accepts treatments other clients wrote (S10) acts on what the hub serves it (CA-SYNC-DOWNLOAD): a careportal carb entry works as a command with no record, expiry or outcome.

docs.title: 4.5 What is active, as the hub reports it
docs.text:
State and intent §6. The hub derives which intents are active, and the state version, from the records it holds (FB-STATE-ACTIVE). It controls nothing; it is the sensor on which caregivers, agents and approvers act.

HAZ-3 S3 A7 covered FB-STATE-002 incorrect A duration is read in assumed units, so an intent is shown active for the wrong length of time. HAZ-3 S3 A11 covered FB-STATE-003 incorrect The hub composes overlapping intents into an effective value that the controller does not use. HAZ-3 S3 S1, A9 covered FB-STATE-004 incorrect What was requested is shown as what was applied. docs.text:
Registration §5 and §7, authority §5. The hub accepts a registration, a definition or an element (CA-DEF-ACCEPT), and every reader interprets stored records by it.

docs.title: 4.7 Credentials, permissions and delegation
docs.text:
Authority §2, §3, §4 and §7. The owner grants a credential or permission (CA-AUTH-GRANT) and blocks, retires, frees namespaces or pins a version (CA-OWNER-ADMIN); the operator sets the hub's limits and tenancy mode (CA-OP-CONFIG). The hub enforces them on every other loop.

HAZ-4 S4 AU3 uncased: authority §9 UCA-AUTH-002 provided An agent that holds the permission to send commands sends them directly, with no proposal or approval. docs.title: 4.8 A plan, approved once and run by the controller
docs.text:
Plans §3–§7. A proposer proposes a plan (CA-PLAN-PROPOSE), the person or a delegate approves its elements (CA-PLAN-APPROVE), the proposer confirms an occurrence under the plan's grant (CA-PLAN-CONFIRM), the person or a delegate approves an occurrence of a per-occurrence element (CA-PLAN-OCCURRENCE), the person, the approver or the proposer skips an occurrence or ends the plan (CA-PLAN-STOP), and the controller runs each occurrence (CA-PLAN-RUN). The hub's mirror is the feedback (FB-PLAN-MIRROR). This loop adds a level above the moment: the decision to dose is taken days ahead, and every check the moment loses has to be recorded with the plan and made again by the controller when the occurrence runs.

flowchart LR
  accTitle: The plan loop
  accDescr: A proposer proposes a plan and confirms occurrences; the person or a delegate approves the plan and per-occurrence elements, and can skip an occurrence or end the plan; the hub records and mirrors; the controller holds the plan and runs each occurrence on the pump after its own checks, and reports to the mirror.
  prop["Proposer"] -- "CA-PLAN-PROPOSE<br/>CA-PLAN-CONFIRM" --> hub["Hub (mirror)"]
  appr["Person or delegate"] -- "CA-PLAN-APPROVE<br/>CA-PLAN-OCCURRENCE<br/>CA-PLAN-STOP" --> hub
  hub -- "plan, confirmations,<br/>approvals, skips, end" --> ctl["Controller"]
  ctl -- "CA-PLAN-RUN" --> pump["Pump"]
  ctl -. "holds it, occurrence reports" .-> hub
  hub -. "FB-PLAN-MIRROR" .-> appr

docs.title: 5. Control-loop patterns in the proposed mechanics
docs.text:
Several mechanics in the specifications are control loops in their own right, and STPA's vocabulary says what each one has to get right.

mechanic as a control loop what STPA asks of it where Instance leases a heartbeat: each renewal is feedback that the instance is alive; a lapse removes its roles a lease is minutes long, longer than moving a pump to another phone takes, so a command sent in that window reaches the old phone; what holds then is routing once, the old phone's controller reporting failed, and the owner's transfer-role; a lapsed holder is never a destination registration §8, UCA-ROUTE-005, UCA-ROUTE-008 The state version optimistic concurrency, like an etag, on the hub's record of what a controller reported it is a sensor reading with a lag of one upload cycle; it covers intents, not doses or carbs; commands approved and not yet enacted are outside it A12, CM15, UCA-PROP-007, UCA-PROP-012, FB-STATE-006 The command states the hub's model of an actuator it cannot see a state must never say less than the hub knows: a command that was handed over is unconfirmed, never expired, because a sender acts on the state commands §4, FB-CMD-001 Delivery by fetch, prompted by a signal or by the cadence one actuator, two triggers a fetch returns a command until it is reported, so delivery is at least once and duplicates are expected; the receiving controller decides each command once (CM21) CM18, CM21, CM26, CM27, UCA-CMD-006 Prepare and commit feedback before action: the controller computes and caps a dose, then a second message commits it, as AndroidAPS dev does a controller check before approval would give the approver the controller's own model, not the hub's commands §9 item 2 Several controllers of one pump the person, the algorithm, caregivers and agents all act on one controlled process conflicting actions are resolved by one arbiter, the controller; the hub reports overlaps and never resolves them S1, A9, FB-STATE-003 Reconciliation (from Kubernetes) a controller drives its registration and instances toward what it declares; the hub records what it granted reconciliation stops at the hub's records: the hub never reconciles therapy toward a desired state platform index, D18 Plans a loop above the moment: a decision taken days ahead, an occurrence run later by the controller the checks the moment would make (doses since, live data, who approves) are recorded with the plan and made again by the controller at the occurrence; a plan's grant to confirm never releases a dose; the person can always stop it plans, UCA-PLAN-001, UCA-PLAN-013, UCA-PLAN-020, UCA-PLAN-024 Process models each controller acts on what it believes; process models draws believed and actual designs the feedback rules in §3 are what keep a caregiver's or agent's belief close to what the controller did §3

docs.title: 6. What the analysis found
docs.text:
21 gaps, each listed in its specification's open items:

  • Commands (§9):
  • a sender or approver sees a channel's outstanding commands (CM24) but nothing refuses a second command, or a second approval inside the controller's upload lag (UCA-CMD-001, UCA-PROP-007);
  • an approval does not check that the destination's definition is unchanged (UCA-PROP-008);
  • another process holding the destination's credential can fetch or report a command (UCA-CMD-014);
  • nothing limits open proposals (UCA-PROP-002) or the operator's maximum expiry (UCA-AUTH-006);
  • no definition declares a payload's shape for an approver's display (UCA-PROP-004);
  • a late failure after success, and a command enacted in part, cannot be recorded (UCA-CMD-011, UCA-CMD-013).
  • State and intent (§8): a treatment a controller downloads and acts on has none of a command's record, expiry or outcome (UCA-SYNC-DL-001), and an edit after the controller acted changes the record and not what was enacted (UCA-SYNC-DL-003).
  • Identity (§5): §3 stores a re-send of a deleted record again, which can bring back a dose the person deleted (UCA-SYNC-STORE-003); two distinct doses with one created_at and eventType and no identifier are merged (UCA-SYNC-STORE-007).
  • Authority (§9): an owner's move of a command sink is not recorded (UCA-ROUTE-007); blocking or retiring a product can pass its shared-channel command sink to another product (UCA-AUTH-005); an agent holding command permission sends commands with no proposal (UCA-AUTH-002); grants carry no expiry (UCA-AUTH-003); reads are neither scoped nor recorded (UCA-AUTH-004); revocation does not reach open socket subscriptions (UCA-SYNC-SERVE-005).
  • Plans (§9): whether two agents run by one operator review each other independently (UCA-PLAN-010); nothing on an intent names the plan occurrence that started it (FB-PLAN-004).

3 rules have no case: the owner never edits a registration's content (UCA-DEF-004), AU3's per-tenant credential root (UCA-AUTH-001), and the socket's permission check (UCA-SYNC-SERVE-006).

11 entries are the controller's: validating a remote command against its own limits and recent local actions (UCA-CMD-010), assigning identifiers that are unique per record (UCA-SYNC-STORE-002), acting on its own state where the hub's lags (UCA-SYNC-SERVE-004, FB-STATE-006), its age limit for downloaded treatments (UCA-SYNC-DL-002), failing a command it cannot deliver to a pump (UCA-ROUTE-008), and, for plans, never dosing on a confirmation alone (UCA-PLAN-013), checking doses since at the occurrence (UCA-PLAN-019), evaluating the withdrawal criteria with fresh data (UCA-PLAN-024), running each occurrence once (UCA-PLAN-025) and nothing after the end date (UCA-PLAN-026). These meet the controller-side constraints in the ecosystem's earlier analysis, such as SC-REMOTE-002 (refuse a remote command after a recent local action) and the de-duplication constraints behind UCA-BOLUS-003 and UCA-CARB-001.

docs.title: 7. Open
docs.text:
1. Severity. Each entry's severity (S1–S4) follows the usage guide's scale and was assigned by the analysis; S3 and S4 ratings need review by a qualified clinician before they are used to prioritise anything. The scale is clinical; entries whose hazards lead only to LOSS-2 or LOSS-3 are rated by their worst effect on care, and need their own review.
  2. Loss scenarios. STPA's fourth step, the causal scenarios behind each unsafe control action, is written only as notes on the gaps.
  3. The usage guide's other fields. Likelihood, causal factors and SC- constraint ids are not assigned; the specifications' rule ids stand in for constraint ids. Feedback flaws use the prefix FB-, which the guide does not define.
  4. The controller side. Each controller's own loops (its algorithm, its pump driver, its handling of a command) belong to an analysis of that controller; this page stops at the command it receives.
