(packaged by D21 as nightscout serve <roles>, 2026-10-26) {C} §2, {DB} §6 D6 Change feed = replication slot (spine) + NOTIFY (latency) + bounded aggregate poll (backstop), with NOTIFY emitted by the slot reader, never by a trigger {DB} §8.5, §9.4; measured in T4.1 D7 The platform-admin plane gets its own entrypoint on its own network interface, ORY-style, secured by unreachability rather than a credential. Tenant admin stays on the consumer interface under RLS. A deliberate departure from Nocturne maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §2 D8 API v3's closed operator set is the query contract; v1 is bounded by corpus evidence. mingo is the differential-test oracle maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §3 D9 Base the work on chore/nightscout-modernization, not dev maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §5 D10 Tenant slug is globally unique per deployment, and is a host label — the resolver maps Host → slug by a configured rule with one capture group, so both foo.user-content.apex.org and foo-user-content.apex.org name tenant foo. Store the label only maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §2.5 D11 devicestatus gets almost no generated columns. Only its indexedFields; the body stays JSONB. The answer to its 182 nodes is decomposition into normalised time series driven by registered controller descriptions, not a wider column list maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §2.6 D12 rag-nightscout-ecosystem-alignment carries the tooling, documentation, evidence and QC; cgm-remote-monitor stays pristine maintainer, 2026-09-14 — §2.7 D13 In TENANCY_MODE=multi there is no deployment-wide secret on any interface. API_SECRET is a single-tenant bootstrapping mechanism and does not exist in multi mode; each tenant holds its own root credential, stored with its configuration. The platform-admin plane remains credential-free (D7) maintainer, 2026-09-15 — §2.8 D14 Per-tenant JWT signing key, stored with tenant configuration. Tenant resolution runs before any credential is examined, so the correct key is known at verify time; cross-tenant token reuse becomes a signature failure rather than a claim-check failure maintainer, 2026-09-15 — §2.8 D15 Configuration source diverges by entrypoint. single reads the process environment; hosted entrypoints read per-tenant configuration from the database, administered by the tenant owner. Env-sourced configuration must not reach the multi path maintainer, 2026-09-15 — §2.8 D16 Three listeners, three audiences — consumer/data (ns-api, plus single), tenant-owner configuration (ns-tenant-admin), platform operator (ns-admin). Prerequisite: tenant resolution and credential verification extract into one module before the third listener exists maintainer, 2026-09-16 — §2.9 D17 The auth plane splits by audience, not by build-versus-buy. Adopted: devices and the data path keep a native per-tenant credential permanently; Hydra is deferred; D7 is unchanged. Adopted in principle, gated (2026-10-12): human identity via one cohort-wide Ory Kratos pool, hosted-only; cookie scope E (apex behind a hardened edge, 2026-10-12); no real identities until the edge's production conditions are measured over https and the compliance question has an owner. D14 holds either way: Nightscout mints its own per-tenant token after authentication. Amended 2026-10-27 (maintainer): the identity provider is interchangeable ("bring your own auth": Kratos, Clerk or another provider), behind Nightscout's own token exchange, to keep in-house human-identity security surface small maintainer, 2026-09-16 — §2.9 D18 Controller registration has two tiers. Well-known declarations ship with the hub, so legacy writers are described with no controller change (backwards compatibility). Controller-owned registrations are dynamic and typed: a controller declares its own definitions — intent kinds, states, transitions, initiators, effect fields, command contract — and the hub offers typed API for them, so controller-unique features have a home other than untyped devicestatus. Adoption follows the WHATWG pattern: specify what happens now, leave room to extend; the controller owns its registration's lifecycle. Roles: the hub (Nightscout, Nocturne) is responsible for observability; the controller is responsible for sending data accurately and for syncing and reconciling. The hub records a controller's composition and reconciliation results; it does not compute dosing state. Addendum (2026-10-12): every extensible field is typed; the grammar is must-ignore with typed, namespaced extensions, open vocabularies, per-kind versions, declared horizons and hub/controller negotiation, so neither side releases in lockstep maintainer, 2026-10-09 and 2026-10-12 — §2.6.1 D19 A registration separates the definition from the instance. A definition says what a controller's data means; it is immutable, identified by the hash of its content, and many coexist under one (vendor, product). An instance is one connected copy of a controller (phone, simulator, lab rig, agent): it names the definition it runs, holds a lease, declares a provenance (device or simulated) on each channel role it plays, and carries typed labels. Among device-provenance instances each channel role has one source of record, handed off by release, lease lapse or owner transfer; an overlapping writer is flagged, never silently resolved, and a command has one destination. Registered instances write typed records only for accepted elements; older readers get a declared, read-only view in today's shapes. The hub still decides nothing about dosing. (corrected 2026-10-15: reverse-DNS, dev.nightscout/ — the well-known label prefix of rule 7; specified 2026-10-15, SPEC-REG-INSTANCE, hub-sync design §3.6) maintainer, 2026-10-14 — §2.6.2 D20 Quirks are scoped to the versions that produce them, and identity has two fields under one rule. A quirk names the (vendor, product, versions) it affects, for stored documents and for declarations alike; versions released before registration get their mapping from the catalogue, newer versions declare it themselves, the hub records each mapping it applies, and a quirk moves to historical and then retired as measurement shows the affected versions gone. identifier is the sync identity the client assigns; _id is the storage key the hub assigns and returns; in single-tenant legacy mode _id is an ObjectId. (amended 2026-10-16: every legacy surface serves 24-hex _id values; the opaque option is dropped — §2.6.3 walk-through) maintainer, 2026-10-16 — §2.6.3 D21 One executable, and roles are served by nightscout serve <roles>. bin/nightscout.js (Node, not a shell script) is the container ENTRYPOINT and dispatches subcommands, as Consul and node-multienv's start_container.sh do. nightscout single is today's server, and every existing way of starting it (Procfile, npm start, server.js, iisnode's web.config, start.sh, the image's CMD) stays equal to it (D1). Hosted roles — D5's api, evaluator, realtime, vcpool and D16's tenant-admin and admin — are started as nightscout serve <role>[,<role>…]; several roles may share one process, and each listener has its own bind address, so admin stays off the consumer interface (D7), as Ory's serve public|admin|all does. Subcommands an operator runs against a deployed site (diagnose data, healthcheck, version, env, later migrate) live in the same dispatcher; developer tooling stays in scripts/. The dispatcher selects the bootstrap and keeps D15's split. Reorganising the repository into packages ({C} §3) is a separate, later track. Open: whether a composed serve of every role is part of the multi target or only a small-hoster convenience maintainer, 2026-10-26 — §2.12

Amendment carried with D13, true however D17 row 2 lands: credentials are per-tenant, identity is per-cohort, authorization is per-tenant. Isolation rests on the authorization layer and RLS, not on the authentication layer (§2.9).

docs.title: 2. D7 — the admin plane, and the decisions that followed from it
2.1 Two privilege planes that get conflated
docs.text:
plane who examples where it lives tenant admin a person administering their own site settings, subjects, roles, credentials, their own export consumer side, authenticated, RLS-scoped — Nocturne's Controllers/V4/TenantAdmin/*; under D16 the ns-tenant-admin listener platform admin the hoster create/suspend/delete tenants, provisioning, cross-tenant export separate entrypoint (bin/admin.js, ns-admin)

Only the platform plane moves off the consumer interface. Tenant admin is an authenticated, per-tenant request and must stay where RLS can bind it.

docs.title: 2.2 The ORY pattern, and why it is stronger than an admin role
docs.text:
ORY (Kratos, Hydra) exposes a public API and an admin API on different ports, and the admin API carries no authentication of its own — it is secured by being unreachable. An admin credential can be phished, committed, logged or reused; if no such credential exists, none of those failures is possible. The cost is an operational contract — this port is never routed from the internet — auditable in one place (the listen address, the firewall) instead of in every authorization check.

This departs from Nocturne, which puts admin behind controllers with authorization inside the same application (PlatformAdminBootstrapService, IsPlatformAdminToSubjects). Nocturne's approach is defensible; ORY's gives a smaller blast radius for a hoster running strangers' data, which is D1's target.

docs.title: 2.3 Design
docs.text:
bin/admin.js
  binds ADMIN_BIND (default 127.0.0.1), ADMIN_PORT (default 1338)
  no API_SECRET, no JWT, no shiro — authorization is network reachability
  REFUSES TO START if bound to a non-loopback address unless
    ADMIN_INSECURE_BIND_ACKNOWLEDGED=true is set explicitly

It is the only component that writes the tenants table, and — like the slot reader and ns-evaluator ({DB} §8.6) — it is cross-tenant by construction and cannot be protected by RLS. Its correctness is enforced by code review rather than by the database, which argues for keeping it minimal.

Endpoints. Built (T3.2): tenant create / list / get / suspend / activate / delete, and per-tenant export (lib/admin/platform-store.js:386 exportTenant, a streaming server-side cursor in one repeatable-read transaction that emits the covered-table list before any row; D1's requirement, {M} §11 Q6). There is no import counterpart (register CAP-02). Export sits on the platform plane, so a tenant cannot self-serve an export; a user-facing promise that they can is wrong until a tenant-admin route exists. Argued against and not built: quota get/set (nothing enforces a quota — §6 T3.2). Health reports only what has a producer (slot lag and pg_notification_queue_usage(), the two things {DB} §8.3 and §9.4 say must be alerted on, arrive with Phase 4).

docs.title: 2.4 Schema
docs.text:
Adapted from Nocturne's TenantEntity / TenantMemberEntity:

CREATE TABLE tenants (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  slug            text NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- host label: slug.example.org
  display_name    text NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
  is_active       boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true,   -- inactive => 403, not 404
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_reading_at timestamptz                      -- signal-loss detection; ingest updates it
);

CREATE TABLE tenant_members (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  subject_id    uuid NOT NULL,
  permissions   text[],            -- shiro strings, as today's auth_subjects carries
  label         text,
  last_used_at  timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, subject_id)
);

tenants is not RLS-protected — it is the map used to resolve a tenant, read before a tenant context exists. tenant_members is.

As built in lib/admin/platform.sql (T3.2), which differs from the block above: slug has a CHECK (writes only); tenant_members has ENABLE/FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and a policy; tenants.id has no DEFAULT. Owed (T3.0 / T32-REM): subject_id's type is wrong for the subjects it names — specs/nsschema/auth_subjects.model.json records auth_subjects._id as types:["string"], and a 24-character hex ObjectId does not fit uuid — so the fix is an ALTER on a shipped table, not an added REFERENCES. The table has no configuration, secret or signing key (D13–D15).

docs.title: 2.5 D10 — the tenant slug is a host label
docs.text:
Globally unique per deployment. Two independent hosters may both have alice, because nothing joins their tables.

The slug is a label inside a hostname, and hosters disagree on where the boundary falls:

shape example slug subdomain of a content domain foo.user-content.apex.org foo prefixed label on one domain foo-user-content.apex.org foo path prefix (fallback, {M} §5.2) apex.org/foo/api/v1/... foo

So tenant resolution is a configured rule, not a hardcoded "first DNS label" — a pattern with exactly one capture group, which covers all three shapes (T3.1).

Constraints on the schema:

  1. slug stores only the label, never the full host. A deployment that moves from foo.a.org to foo-a.org must not rewrite its tenant rows.
  2. The label charset is the intersection of DNS and a safe path segment: lowercase alphanumerics and -, not starting or ending with -. Validated on write in bin/admin.js, the only writer of tenants, and re-checked on read by the resolver.

Deferred: two hosters sharing one deployment and wanting the same slug — under D10 a per-deployment uniqueness question.

docs.title: 2.6 D11 — devicestatus is a decomposition problem, not a column-selection problem
docs.text:
The question "which of devicestatus's 182 nodes get generated columns" is retired rather than answered, because it assumed the document shape is the thing being stored.

The direction: devicestatus is decomposed into idiomatic, normalised time series, and what it decomposes into is declared by a registered controller description rather than hardcoded (controller descriptions §5):

documents:
  - collection: devicestatus
    discriminator: {path: loop, test: is-object}   # structural, not the device string
    decomposesTo: [ApsSnapshot, PumpSnapshot, UploaderSnapshot]

A known catalogue ships with Nightscout; a controller may publish or correct its own. The decomposition is data, not code, so it does not become another drift-prone list beside the OpenAPI spec, indexedFields, the nsschema model and the walker (§3.4).

What it decides for T2.1:

  • Emit only devicestatus's indexedFields — created_at, NSCLIENT_ID and one compound. The remaining 179 nodes stay in JSONB.
  • Do not widen the column list to anticipate decomposition. The normalised series are separate relations with their own schemas.
  • Decomposition must sit above the seam, like coercion (§3.4). The record rules are maintained in the records specification. The 56-of-166 dropped-path finding that motivates it ({M} motivation (a)) is a fidelity problem; fixing it in the multitenant backend only would leave single-tenant behind, which D4 forbids.

docs.title: 2.6.1 D18 — two-tier controller registration
docs.text:
D11 says what devicestatus decomposes into is declared by a registered controller description. D18 says who may declare it and what a declaration may carry. The contract that implements D18, D19 and D20 is maintained in the registration and identity specifications.

tier who writes it purpose what changes for the controller well-known the hub, generated from measurement (specs/sync/registrations/) backwards compatibility: today's writers are described as they are nothing controller-owned the controller, per release extensibility: typed definitions for features unique to that controller, and the hub API derived from them publishes a registration when it wants typed support for a feature

What a registration has to be able to declare is measured across Loop, Trio, iAPS, AAPS and both hubs in intent and workflow across the landscape §9: definitions with stable ids, intent slots and which coexist, states and end reasons, the wire carrier for today's documents, requested vs applied, the controller's composition result, its initiator vocabulary, its command contract, and which hub-originated intent it accepts.

The role split decides one open design question. Overlapping intents are combined by a controller-specific rule (Loop, Trio/iAPS and AAPS each differ, and the rule depends on algorithm settings), so the hub records the result the controller reports and never derives it. A hub-side composition rule, such as the override composition in conflict-resolution.md of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals, is outside the hub's role.

What D18 supersedes: controller descriptions §4 ("static descriptions, not CRD-style, no new endpoints"). The well-known tier keeps every property §4 lists; the controller-owned tier is the addition.

docs.title: D18 addendum — an extensible grammar (maintainer, 2026-10-12)
docs.text:
Goal. A controller adds a setting, an algorithm input, an intent kind or a new version of a data model without the hub shipping a release first, and an older or newer hub and controller still interoperate. Every extensible field is typed: the hub accepts controller-specific data only together with a declaration of its type, never as an untyped bag.

Where the grammar stands (specs/sync/controller-state-model.schema.json, e9634479). A new intent kind needs no hub change: stateSpans[].category is open and endReasons maps a controller's own term onto a shared value. Everything else is closed: every object sets additionalProperties: false, apiVersion is the constant nightscout.dev/sync/v1, x- fields are stripped before validation, settings.fields and replayInputs name a field without typing it, endedEncoding, command transport and replayInputs[].status are fixed lists, versioning is per registration (metadata.versionRange), and cadence is one value per controller. The settings document (controller-settings.schema.json) is already open and partly typed (x-source, x-algorithm, x-status-today); the registration does not reference it.

Rules.

# rule what it removes 1 Must-ignore, plus typed extensions. Within a major grammar version a hub ignores grammar fields it does not know (kept, not interpreted, not served as data). Controller-specific data goes under extensions, keyed by a reverse-DNS namespace the controller owns; each extension carries a type declaration (rule 2) and is stored, validated and served as declared. An extension without a type declaration is rejected. lockstep on new declarations 2 Typed field declarations. settings.fields[], replayInputs[] and extension fields are objects: a type as a restricted JSON Schema fragment, unit, range, horizon (rule 5), sensitivity label and evidence. The hub derives validation, indexing and query from the declaration. A field with no sensitivity label falls under the existing unlabelledPolicy: withhold. untyped settings and inputs 3 Open vocabularies. Every closed list a controller may need to extend takes a shared value, or other with the controller's own term, as endReasons does now. A hub renders an unknown term as "other: term" instead of rejecting the registration. lockstep on new encodings 4 Per-kind versions. Each intent kind and each extension has its own version. A registration may declare several served versions and one stored version, and optionally a lossless mapping between two versions. Without a declared mapping the hub serves each version as written and never converts. lockstep on model changes; side-by-side migration 5 Horizons. Each document, kind and field declares its horizon — cycle, span, effective-dated, definition or aggregate — with its own cadence and retention. availability gains experimental: the hub stores it as declared, gives it no well-known mapping and makes no long-term promise. one cadence per controller; no place for derived or trial models 6 Negotiation. The hub publishes the grammar versions and capabilities it supports at a .well-known address; the controller submits its registration; anything the hub does not accept, the controller writes as its well-known carrier (stateSpans[].wire). lockstep in both directions

The roles do not change. Typing tells the hub how to store, validate, index and render a value, not what it means for dosing. The hub still records what the controller reports (D18).

Compatibility.

older hub newer hub older controller today's documents the well-known tier describes them newer controller falls back to its well-known carriers (rule 6) typed registration, extensions and versions

Status. Rules 1–5 are schema and generator work in this repository, queued as SCHEMA-REG-EXT; its proof is the three generated registrations still validating plus an unfamiliar test registration that uses every rule. Rule 6 is specified as SPEC-REG-NEGOTIATE (capability document, submit and fallback contract, conformance fixtures); the API a hub derives from a registration is HUB-REG-CRM for cgm-remote-monitor and HUB-REG-NOCTURNE, a shared-contract proposal to Nocturne. All three follow SCHEMA-REG-EXT. (2026-10-12: rules 1–5 are in the schema and generator; "where the grammar stands" above describes the grammar before them, and the hub-sync design §3.1 lists the result.) (2026-10-12: rule 6 is specified — hub-sync design §3.5, specs/sync/hub-capabilities.schema.json (served at /.well-known/nightscout/sync), specs/sync/registration-submit.schema.json and 21 conformance cases under specs/sync/conformance/, checked by tools/nsschema/test_registration_negotiation.py. Authorisation follows D13–D17 where they settle it; ten points they do not settle are listed there as open questions.) (2026-10-14: the ten questions are decided — hub-sync design §3.5, "Decisions" — and question 6 became D19, §2.6.2; the spec and cases are amended under SPEC-REG-DECISIONS.) (2026-10-15: SPEC-REG-DECISIONS is done — the hub-sync design §3.5, the submit schema (the capability document is unchanged), the grammar's dualWriteLink and 53 conformance cases now carry first-to-claim namespaces, binding to the creating subject, the owner's actions on ns-tenant-admin and the blocked state, the recorded credential kind, carrier views, and the load-versus-definite rule for refused typed writes. The D19 parts of questions 7 and 9 remain SPEC-REG-INSTANCE's.) (2026-10-16, maintainer, on HUB-REG-CRM's scope: "HUB-REG-CRM should start in single-tenant and create a sufficient backlog to help ensure multitenant and singletenant remain compatible with a future roadmap." So HUB-REG-CRM is built on origin/dev, which has no TENANCY_MODE, storage interface or tenant scope (measured at official dev fade2299; those exist only on the local seam chain, "Where things stand"), with MongoDB and the owner's actions by API_SECRET on the one single listener. The backlog that keeps the two modes compatible is SPEC-REG-MODES (what the contract says per mode: storage key, credential kinds, owner listener, capability document scope, legacy id form), HUB-REG-CRM-SEAM (the store on the seam, checked in single on MongoDB and PostgreSQL and in multi by one harness), HUB-REG-CRM-ADMIN (owner actions on ns-tenant-admin), SPEC-REG-COMMANDS (command delivery in both modes) and SPEC-REG-MIGRATE (registration state across a site's move into a tenant, and back).)

docs.title: 2.6.2 D19 — definitions and instances (maintainer, 2026-10-14)
docs.text:
D18 registers what a controller's data means. It does not say which copy of a controller is connected. Several copies on one site are expected, not exceptional: a development build or simulator beside the phone that doses, a lab rig, a phone migration with old and new phones both running, and later cooperating agents acting as controllers of different kinds. Keying one registration per (vendor, product) per tenant makes those copies overwrite one another. D19 separates the two.

layer what it says identity lifecycle definition what the data means: kinds, settings, inputs, extensions, versions, carriers (D18 and its addendum) the hash of its content; many per (vendor, product) immutable; written by the controller instance which copy is connected, which definition it runs, which channel roles it plays opaque, issued by the hub or supplied by the controller a lease the instance renews; it lapses without housekeeping

The earlier draft. docs/proposals/agent-control-plane-rfc.md, part of the earlier draft in cgm-remote-monitor's docs/proposals (read at official b5ddd662), splits ControllerKindDefinition from ControllerInstanceRegistration, with lastSeenAt as liveness, and plans agents as a later phase. The hub-sync design §5.2 maps it. Instance identity does not come from the free-text devicestatus.device, which is recorded only as an observed alias (control-plane supersession map §3.3). D19 takes that split with that identity rule, and says what happens when two instances write to one site; the supersession map names the specification rule proposed to supersede each object of the draft.

Rules.

# rule 1 Definitions are content-addressed. A definition's id is sha256: and the hex SHA-256 of its RFC 8785 canonical JSON. Any number coexist under one (vendor, product); ten simulators on one build share one definition. Namespaces (§3.5) belong to (vendor, product), so releases of one product never clash. A definition whose kind is exactly a well-known kind references the catalogue kind and version instead of copying it, and gets the hub's native storage and the catalogue's carrier mapping. 2 Meaning conflicts are rejected. One kind at one version has one meaning (addendum rule 4). A definition that types an existing kind and version differently is rejected as version-conflict; a different meaning is a new version. Definitions that agree but cover different versions coexist. 3 Read selection. Writes need no selection: each instance names its definition. A view chooses a version per kind by this order: the operator's capability document limits what is accepted at all; the tenant owner may pin a version for the site's default views, or block (§3.5 question 5); otherwise the newest version a live device-provenance instance uses; a lab or development view selects its own instances by label. 4 Instances. An instance names its definition, renews a lease whose length the hub states in its capability document, and lapses when it stops renewing. It carries no hardware identifiers; anything identifying is a typed, sensitivity-labelled field (addendum rule 2). 5 Roles with provenance. An instance declares the channel roles it plays: source of a channel (a kind, slot or document it writes) or command sink (hub-originated intent it accepts, acceptsFromHub). Each role carries a required provenance, device or simulated, because one instance can mix them (a development build with a real CGM and a simulated pump). Only device-provenance data is therapy data in default views and exports. Role types are an open vocabulary (addendum rule 3), so roles such as proposing versus acting can be added for agents. 6 One source of record per role. Among device-provenance instances each channel role has one holder. A second claimant is refused that role (role-held) and writes the well-known carrier, and the hub flags the overlap on the owner's views (the warning GAP-SYNC-030 records as missing). The role passes by release, lease lapse or owner transfer. simulated roles never compete with device roles. A command channel therefore has one destination. The hub decides only which instance is the typed source of record; it never stops, directs or composes dosing. 7 Labels. An instance carries labels: string keys and string values, keys in reverse-DNS form as extensions are, with a few well-known keys under dev.nightscout/ (purpose, build, migration group; the values are set by the spec). Labels distinguish, select and filter instances. Provenance, not a label, decides what is therapy data. (corrected 2026-10-15: reverse-DNS, dev.nightscout/; it read nightscout.dev/, which is not reverse-DNS form. The keys are dev.nightscout/purpose — therapy, development, lab, research —, dev.nightscout/build — release, dev — and dev.nightscout/migration-group, an opaque string; hub-sync design §3.6.) 8 Older readers. A registered instance writes typed records only for accepted elements. The hub serves older readers (v1, v3 and their consumers) a declared, read-only view in today's shapes, from the catalogue's mapping for well-known kinds or the definition's wire carrier; each projected document is labelled as projected, is never stored as a source, and carries the ids of the entities decomposition already assigns. A view for older readers is not a conversion between typed versions under addendum rule 4. Writing both typed record and carrier, linked by (instance, the controller's record id), is for an element with no declared carrier mapping, or while an app moves over. Prior art: Nocturne's V4ToLegacyProjectionService (read at 42275c812) already serves its v1–v3 reads from V4 records — glucose to entries; boluses, carbs and device events to treatments. 9 Retention. A definition is kept while any stored record references it; each record's declared horizon retention decides when the record goes. Ageing out means a definition is no longer current, never that it is deleted while data depends on it.

The roles do not change. The hub records which instance wrote what and in which role; the controller still owns what it declares and how it doses (D18).

Status. Specified as SPEC-REG-INSTANCE; the hub work (HUB-REG-CRM, HUB-REG-NOCTURNE) follows it. (2026-10-15: SPEC-REG-INSTANCE is done — hub-sync design §3.6, specs/sync/controller-instance.schema.json, the capability document's instances, the grammar's wellKnownRef, and 86 cases under specs/sync/conformance/instances/, checked by tools/nsschema/test_registration_instances.py. Rules 1–9 are specified as written, with the label prefix of rule 7 corrected; the choices the item made beyond them are listed in §3.6 for confirmation. The generated well-known registrations declare no kind versions, so their kinds cannot yet be referenced by wellKnownRef; slot names, which become shared channels, are free strings in the grammar with no shared list.)

docs.title: 2.6.3 D20 — version-scoped quirks and the two-id rule (maintainer, 2026-10-16)
docs.text:
D18 paves the cowpaths: the hub specifies what controllers do today and leaves room to grow. The cowpaths include quirks — behaviour particular to some releases of some apps — and a reader has to handle them for as long as those releases are in use. The quirks registry records them per collection and per project, with prevalence measured over the corpus, but not which versions produce them or how an entry is retired once those versions are gone. D20 adds both, and applies them to the two places they are needed now: slot names, which become shared channels under D19 rule 5, and the document _id.

Why _id. In single-tenant Nightscout, where the API is coupled to a thin MongoDB driver, _id must be an ObjectId. That was the one hard rule, and it was unwritten; many apps sent other values, which produced undefined behaviour and the quirk handling that followed (write contract §2.3 rule 1, UUID_HANDLING, and the twin records BF-117 resolves). The intent was always that the data store assigns it. Separately, controllers gain from assigning a record's identity on the phone, so a record created offline or re-sent after a lost reply syncs without duplicating. Those are two jobs. Today's controllers, read-derived from the client id analyses and the UUID identifier backlog, not re-checked against source: Loop sends no _id and caches the ObjectId the server returns, so a lost cache duplicates on re-send; Trio sends a UUID it generated in _id, which UUID_HANDLING moves to identifier; (corrected 2026-10-16: Trio does so for carbs and temporary targets; its general treatment model sends the UUID as id, and Loop sends a UUID _id for overrides — read at Trio e41c9db37 and LoopWorkspace f8412858; QUIRK-TREATMENTS-006 and -007) AAPS keeps the server's _id as its nightscoutId and reads _id with identifier as a fallback.

Rules.

# rule 1 Quirks name the versions they affect. A registry entry may carry affects: [{vendor, product, versions}], a range over the vendor's own version strings. It applies to stored documents (today's registry) and to declarations (a registration's slot names, units, vocabulary). Entries without it keep their project-level attribution; the member is additive. 2 Catalogue for older versions, self-declared for newer. Versions released before registration existed get their mapping from a catalogue entry scoped to them, so they need no change. A newer definition declares the mapping itself — for a slot, sameAs naming a slot in an optional shared slot list in the well-known catalogue. Equal shared slots contend for roles (D19 rule 6). Two slots are never treated as one because their names look alike. 3 Mappings are observed, not silent. The hub records which quirk mapping it applied to each record or declaration, so a reader can tell a mapped value from a declared one. 4 A quirk has a lifecycle. proposed → active → historical → retired. An entry becomes historical when measurement shows no live instance and no recent write from an affected version, and retired when no stored record depends on its mapping. Each move is measured (make schema-quirks), never asserted. 5 Two ids, one rule. identifier is the sync identity the client assigns, stable across retries and devices; in the typed API it is the controller's record id. _id is the storage key the hub assigns. Every write reply returns both. Re-sends match on identifier first, as the write contract's keys already order it, so a client needs no cache of server ids. 6 _id is an ObjectId in single-tenant legacy mode. A hub declares its legacy id form in the capability document, objectId or opaque. cgm-remote-monitor in single-tenant mode declares objectId. (amended 2026-10-16, walk-through rows 1 and 2: every hub's legacy surface serves 24-hex _id values the hub assigns, on either store; nothing is declared and there is no opaque form) 7 Today's _id handling becomes a version-scoped quirk. A non-ObjectId _id moved to identifier (UUID_HANDLING) is recorded as a registry entry with the versions that send it; it becomes historical as those apps send identifier instead. Its behaviour does not change. 8 Projected records follow rule 5. On an objectId hub, each projected document (D19 rule 8) gets an ObjectId the hub assigns when the typed record is written and stores with it, so it is the same on every read; its identifier is the typed id. An opaque hub may use the typed id for both. (that sentence withdrawn 2026-10-16, walk-through row 2)

The roles do not change. The hub records which mapping it applied and which ids it assigned; the controller still owns its declarations and its records (D18).

Status. To be specified as SPEC-REG-QUIRKS; HUB-REG-CRM, HUB-REG-NOCTURNE and PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS follow it. Rule 8 replaces the hub-sync design §3.6 choice of the typed id verbatim in v1 _id, for objectId hubs. The contents of the shared slot list are not decided here: which slots mean the same thing is evidence for the controller authors to confirm (PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS). (2026-10-16: SPEC-REG-QUIRKS is done — hub-sync design §3.7, specs/quirks/quirk.schema.json, QUIRK-TREATMENTS-006 and QUIRK-ENTRIES-004, specs/sync/shared-slots.yaml, the grammar's sameAs, the capability document's legacyIdForm, wellKnown.slots and wellKnown.mappings, the write reply's ids, and 29 cases under specs/sync/conformance/quirks/, checked by tools/nsschema/test_registration_quirks.py. Rules 1–8 are specified as written. Rule 6's objectId declaration is scoped to single-tenant mode on MongoDB; single-tenant on PostgreSQL is open (SPEC-REG-MODES) (no longer open: decided 2026-10-16 in the walk-through below, rows 1 and 2 — the shape is 24-hex on either store and the declaration is removed). Rule 8 changed the instance case project-served. "Recent" in rule 4 is 365 days before the newest snapshot. The shared slot list ships override, loopMode and temporaryTarget, the names already used identically; the candidates are in §3.7. Two statements of the "Why _id" paragraph differ from source read for this item: Loop sends a UUID _id for overrides (LoopWorkspace f8412858), and Trio 1.0.1 sends its id as id, not _id (Trio e41c9db3); no rule depends on them. The choices made beyond the rules are listed in §3.7 for confirmation.)

Decided in the 2026-10-16 walk-through (maintainer). These settle open points of §3.5–§3.7 and of the compatibility backlog; SPEC-REG-AMEND applies them to the contract and cases.

# point decision 1 single-tenant on PostgreSQL objectId names the shape — a 24-hex value the hub assigns — not MongoDB's native type, on either store. UUID_HANDLING already runs above the storage seam (lib/server/treatments.js, read at crm-write 239f8c25), so a site keeps its ids across stores 2 legacy id form Every hub's legacy surface (v1, v3) serves 24-hex _id values the hub assigns. The opaque option of rule 6 and the capability member legacyIdForm are dropped for now: Nocturne's legacy surface already coerces its UUIDs to 24 hex (read at 42275c812, §3.7). A hub's own newer APIs may use other ids; the sync identity is identifier. Rule 8's "an opaque hub may use the typed id" is withdrawn 3 an assigned ObjectId's time the hub's receipt time, as for every id the server generates today; readers take a record's time from created_at/date 4 "recent" in rule 4 365 days, a declared measurement parameter 5 equal slot names A slot is shared only through the shared list or sameAs. Equal unlisted names from different products do not contend; the hub records an observation (same slot name as another product) on the owner's listing, for the catalogue to act on 6 Trio's id member recorded as a measured, version-scoped registry entry with no new mapping: Trio's treatment model sends its UUID as id (NightscoutTreatment.swift:62, Trio e41c9db37), while its carbs and temporary-target models send _id (CarbsEntry.swift:29, TempTarget.swift:50); cgm-remote-monitor matches such treatments by created_at + eventType (treatment-fallback-key). Whether Trio should send identifier goes to PROPOSAL-REG-CONTROLLERS 7 command-sink roles A command-sink role goes only to an instance created by the product's bound subject, or one the owner transfers it to (transfer-role); otherwise refused not-registration-owner. Source roles stay open to any permitted subject, so development builds keep working 8 the delivery deadline removed (it was added 2026-10-15 without being asked for). A typed write answered 5xx is retried with backoff until it succeeds; it is never re-sent as its carrier, so a write the hub stored before failing cannot appear twice. A definite 4xx refusal still sends the carrier at once (§3.5) 9 a released registration binds to its next permitted writer, as specified; the binding event and credential kind are shown on the owner's listing 10 loop-status exclusivity left unspecified: devicestatus is not a channel until its decomposition is typed 11 HUB-REG-CRM stays one item 12 migrating an api-secret binding binds to the tenant's root credential, a new credential kind (SPEC-REG-MODES, SPEC-REG-MIGRATE); the etag changes with boundTo

Decided 2026-10-17 (maintainer), on four choices SPEC-REG-AMEND made beyond the table above; SPEC-REG-AMEND-2 applies them.

# point decision 13 an unlisted slot the product's own channel (<vendor>/<product>/<slot>): instances of one product contend on it, as built 14 a command for an unshared slot the hub infers the product when exactly one product on the site declares that slot; when more than one does, the command is refused as ambiguous (the owner's slotNameObservations shows why) and naming the product resolves it. The inference is never a guess between candidates 15 simulated command-sink claims exempt from row 7's binding rule: any permitted subject's simulator may hold a simulated command-sink; it never receives commands routed to the device holder 16 a rebind when a product's boundTo changes, device command-sink roles held by instances that no longer match it are dropped at once, except roles the owner granted by transfer-role; a command sent before the new instance claims the role is refused no-command-destination

(2026-10-16: SPEC-REG-AMEND is done — rows 1–9 applied to the hub-sync design §3.5–§3.7, the schemas, the reference and the cases: legacyIdForm and the two opaque cases removed; a slot shared only through the list or sameAs, with slotNameObservations on the owner's listing and two new cases; QUIRK-TREATMENTS-007 for Trio's id, re-measured at 55,939 treatments on one site, and the Trio client-id analyses corrected; command-sink roles refused not-registration-owner without the binding or a transfer, with three new cases; the delivery deadline and its case removed; bindingEvent on the stored registration and registrations on the owner's listing, with one new case. The choices made beyond the rows are listed in the queue item.)

(2026-10-17: SPEC-REG-AMEND-2 is done — rows 13–16 applied to the hub-sync design §3.6–§3.7, the submit schema, the reference and the cases: row 13 stated as decided; row 14's inference and the reason code ambiguous-command-destination, with four new cases; row 15's exemption, with instance-create-other-subject back to accepted and one new case; row 16's drop on a change of boundTo, with a transfer-role grant recorded on the stored role as grantedBy: transfer-role, §3.5's release and transfer modelled as instance-case requests, and eight new cases. 103 instance cases. The choices made beyond the rows are listed in the queue item.)

Decided 2026-10-18 (maintainer), on how an agent is recorded as initiator (D18's initiator vocabularies; intent landscape P5).

# point decision 17 an agent as initiator no agent value is added. An agent initiator is written in the open-vocabulary form {value: other, controllerTerm} (addendum rule 3), as the registration specification §9 does for an agent's roles. No controller records an agent as initiator today. The registrations are built for needs that are latent but measured and demonstrated — in the corpus, in controller source and in the labs — not only for what apps send now; the open form lets a controller, simulator or lab record an agent initiator today, and a shared value can be named once the corpus or a lab shows one in use. The grammar's initiators.values take strings in each controller's own vocabulary, with no shared list, or the other form (state and intent S8). Map: agents in the ecosystem

docs.title: 2.7 D12 — what each repository is for
docs.text:
repository role rag-nightscout-ecosystem-alignment tooling, documentation, evidence, experiments, alignment exercises. Verification harnesses live here (tools/seam/, tools/qc/, tools/mt-bench/), as do all findings cgm-remote-monitor kept pristine. Shipping code and its tests, nothing else
  • A benchmark, differential oracle, census script or probe belongs here, even when it exercises code there; harnesses require() the shipping module by path so the two cannot drift.
  • A commit to cgm-remote-monitor reads as ordinary upstream work — no scaffolding, no research artefacts, no fixtures that exist only to support an experiment.
  • Findings are written up here and referenced from there, never pasted into code comments.
  • node_modules is tracked in neither; a manifest plus a lockfile makes a tool reproducible.

docs.title: 2.8 D13, D14, D15 — the credential root, and where configuration comes from
docs.text:
Why. One deployment API secret, one signing key and tenant separation by inspecting a claim are properties of single-tenant Nightscout, true only because there is one tenant to read the environment for. In the hosted target, per-tenant settings, plugin credentials and secrets come from the database, where a tenant owner administers them; the process environment is the single-tenant bootstrap. That is also why D5's entrypoints are separate: different bootstrapping, not only different process topology.

What the built code assumes (measured 2026-09-15 on 239f8c25; re-resolved on crm-seam 81a1f6ce):

site assumption lib/authorization/index.js:169-173 a matching api_secret grants shiro ['*'] (authorizeAdminSecret → env.enclave.isApiKey → the one secret armed from process.env at boot). No tenant dimension on this path lib/server/tenant-middleware.js:139-143 (tenantClaim) and the call at :346 (enclave: env.enclave, resolved once at construction) one install-wide key signs and verifies every tenant's tokens lib/server/enclave.js:29-30 the JWT key is read from the file node_modules/.cache/_ns_cache/randomString, so it is per-install, survives setAPISecret's scrub of process.env.API_SECRET, and appears in no environment census. Two deployments sharing an install directory share a signing key today lib/server/enclave.js:54 setJWTKey exists and has no caller in lib/ or bin/ — dead code or T3.0's injection point lib/admin/platform.sql no settings, secret or plugin configuration; tenant_members.subject_id references nothing — the subjects it names are still process-wide, which is BF-25's cause lib/server/tenant-context.js (T3.3) builds the mechanism for per-tenant settings (deriveEnv, validated overrides) and takes the overrides as a parameter; nothing supplies them

D13 — no deployment secret in multi mode. The ['*'] grant path becomes unreachable under TENANCY_MODE=multi; isApiKey becomes tenant-scoped. Consistent with D7: the platform plane already needs no credential. A tenant owner administers their site with their own credential, which is what makes the tenant-admin surface something a tenant can hold. D13 also reaches subject access tokens: enclave.getSubjectHash (enclave.js:71-76) hashes secrets[apiKeySHA1], so every subject's token derives from the deployment secret. Executed: with no API key set it throws a TypeError, and the isApiKeySet() guard above the call site turns the throw into silence — every subject loads with no digest, accessToken or accessTokenDigest, and the first lookup dereferences undefined. So D13 means re-rooting the subject hash on the tenant's own credential.

D14 — per-tenant signing key. T3.1 resolves Host → slug → tenant id before any credential is examined, so the tenant is known when a JWT is verified; a token minted for tenant A fails the signature for tenant B. D14 closes the signed-JWT vector completely but not BF-25 on its own: BF-25's vector is an opaque token in the request body, which carries no signature. Closing the class needs D14 and scoping the subject store under RLS. Needs key storage and a rotation story, which land with the configuration schema. BF-66: every JWT is minted with the payload {accessToken} and no tenant claim, so under multi with the default requireTokenClaim the deployment's own tokens fail its own tenant check (fails safe). T3.0 chooses the payload, so T3.0 fixes it.

D15 — configuration source diverges by entrypoint. Saying so is what stops env-sourced configuration leaking into the hosted path by default.

Bootstrap and rotation — direction set, evidence owed. The hosting operator mints a tenant's initial credential through bin/admin.js on the unroutable port, and the tenant owner can rotate on demand. An IdP binding on the tenant row is in scope as an alternative to a local secret (see trusted identity providers). The impact of operator-assigned-then-rotated credentials, and what the alternatives cost, are unmeasured — the first half of T3.0.

docs.title: T3.0 · Configuration surface and credential root
docs.text:
Queue: T30-RESEARCH, T30-SCHEMA-CRED, T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG, T30-WIRING; amends T3.1, T3.2, T3.3 (T31-REM, T32-REM, T33-REM). Specification: tenant-owner configuration surface.

  1. Research — delivered as the specification above. Findings it rests on:
  2. Nightscout's configuration variables have no common prefix. There is no SETTINGS_* family: across lib/server/env.js, lib/settings.js and README.md the string SETTINGS_ occurs once, inside MONGO_SETTINGS_COLLECTION (env.js:215). The measured union is 247 names from four sources; the specification's reconciliation puts the surface at 277 including names no regex can see.
  3. Three families are invisible to a readENV census: the eleven API v3 names read straight from process.env (BF-46, one family of which deletes stored documents), WEBHOOK_* (BF-48), and the hosted entrypoints' ADMIN_* / FEED_*, read through injected readers. A census scoped to lib/ describes the single entrypoint only.
  4. Dead names: SECURE_HSTS_HEADER_INCLUDESUBDOMAINS has two spellings and the settings dictionary produces the one nothing reads, with four more dead keys (BF-49); MONGODB_COLLECTION is documented and read by nothing (BF-50). A tenant-admin UI generated from the settings dictionary would offer five settings that do nothing, one a security header.
  5. Schema — add configuration and credential storage to lib/admin/platform.sql: the per-tenant root credential and signing key, device/uploader credential tables, and what subject_id references (T30-SCHEMA-CRED, claimable); the per-tenant settings table and human-identity columns (T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG). The specification's DDL has never been parsed, and two of its constraints are wrong on paper: a ?| proto guard that tests top-level keys only while the code recurses, and a threshold CHECK that a partial override satisfies because SQL NULL is not FALSE. Do not write human-identity DDL until T30-ORY-PROOF resolves. The amendment must also touch lib/admin/platform-store.js:45 (PLATFORM_TABLES, which drives ensureSchema's completeness check) and :51 (NOT_TENANT_DATA, or exportTenant streams every tenant's wrapped credentials).
  6. Wiring (T30-WIRING, which also carries D16's extraction prerequisite) — supply T3.3's deriveEnv overrides from storage and make isApiKey/verifyJWT tenant-scoped:
task site that must change T3.1 the call at tenant-middleware.js:346 (enclave: env.enclave, resolved once at construction) and the file-sourced key at enclave.js:30. tenantClaim at :139-143 is the reader, not the site T3.2 platform.sql (subject_id type ALTER; configuration, secret, signing key) plus platform-store.js:45 and :51 T3.3 the frozen list PER_TENANT_ENV_KEYS at tenant-context.js:143, the copy-loop guard at :278 (if (PER_TENANT_ENV_KEYS.includes(key)) continue;), and the explicit assignments in deriveEnv at :265-300. (:137 is the doc comment stating the rejected reasoning) pre-programme lib/authorization/index.js:169-173, from if (data.api_secret && authorizeAdminSecret(...)) through const result = { shiros: [admin] };

Blocked by: nothing for the credential half. Register entries owned: BF-46, BF-48, BF-49, BF-50, BF-66, and BF-25's subject-store half. The measurements, tests and isolation evidence of T3.1–T3.3 stand; only their credential assumptions are superseded.

docs.title: 2.9 D16, D17 — the auth plane
docs.text: Research: the auth plane: Ory Kratos/Hydra against building it ourselves. Queue: T30-AUTH, T30-ORY-PROOF.

docs.title: D16 — three listeners
docs.text:
Adopted whole, including the prerequisite. The argument is asymmetry of regret: merging two listeners later is a routing change; splitting one later means re-deriving which routes were ever safe to expose against a codebase that by then depends on them sharing a process. Separation also decouples the auth question from the data path — a separate listener can be fronted by Ory, by a native credential, or by nothing but unreachability, without touching the consumer API.

Three listeners for the whole deployment, not three per tenant. Tenancy is multiplexed inside each listener by Host → slug → id (D10) and bound by RLS. This axis is audience, orthogonal to D5's workload axis. Nothing in either decision splits per tenant — D2 rejected database-per-tenant on 47 WiredTiger files and 3.7 MB of RSS per empty tenant, and the auth research rejects Kratos-per-tenant on the same grounds.

listener audience authn authz tenancy ns-api + ns-realtime (and single) devices, clients, viewers native per-tenant credential, tokens shiro Host → slug → id, RLS ns-tenant-admin the tenant owner native today; D17 row 2 if it lands owner role Host → slug → id, RLS ns-admin the hoster none, by D7 none — reachability cross-tenant by construction

ns-evaluator and ns-vcpool accept no inbound connections — neither carries express ({C} §2) — so they are D5 entrypoints, not D16 listeners.

Open: is ns-tenant-admin its own process, or a second bound socket inside ns-api? D16 decides the boundary (the tenant-owner surface does not share a listening socket with the data path) and is silent on process topology. A second listen() in one process gets the routing separation and the extraction prerequisite at no extra process; a separate process adds its own failure domain, bind address and resource ceiling, which is what makes ns-admin worth a process under D7. D7's argument does not transfer automatically, because ns-tenant-admin is credentialed and RLS-scoped where ns-admin is neither. Decide before the third listener is built. (Decided 2026-10-16, maintainer: a second bound socket inside ns-api, on its own bind address, sharing tenant resolution through T30-WIRING's extracted module. The boundary is the socket, so it can move to its own process later without changing the contract. Built by T30-TENANT-ADMIN.)

The prerequisite. lib/server/tenant-resolver.js and tenant-middleware.js are the one module for the consumer path; the admin plane deliberately does not use them because it is cross-tenant. The tenant-owner plane is the first surface that is per-tenant and not the data path, so it is the first real consumer of that extraction, which must exist before the third listener does. It lands on T30-WIRING.

docs.title: D17 — by audience
docs.text:
The rules that follow from D13–D17 for registrations, owners and commands are maintained in the authority specification.

audience decision status devices and uploaders native per-tenant credential, never Ory ADOPTED. Forced by D1 — an uploader cannot run an OAuth flow tenant owners and caregivers Ory Kratos, one cohort-wide pool, hosted-only ADOPTED IN PRINCIPLE, GATED (maintainer, 2026-10-12): T30-ORY-PROOF held 23/23. Cookie scope: E, the apex cookie behind a hardened edge (cookie variants, 21/21 measured). Four production conditions: the edge strips the Kratos and CSRF cookies before any tenant backend; it refuses cross-origin writes, WebSocket upgrades included; every path to a tenant backend (API, socket.io) goes through it; and it is measured over https. No real identities until those hold and the compliance question has an owner. Host-only with a hand-off (H2) needed an origin check in every tenant and logout propagation, because tenants under one domain are same-site third-party apps Hydra deferred ADOPTED. Nothing needs delegated access today; deferring costs nothing platform operator D7 unchanged ADOPTED

Amendment, 2026-10-27 (maintainer): the identity provider is interchangeable. Row 2's direction stands (an external identity provider for people, never for devices), but Kratos is one provider, not the design. A hoster should be able to bring its own: Kratos, Clerk or another hosted identity service. The reason is the security surface: password storage, recovery, MFA and session handling are complex, need customising and need updates in the wild, and Nightscout should not grow its own. What makes this possible is already measured: T30-ORY-PROOF found that tenant isolation is held by our nsjwt exchange (Host-first tenant resolution, tenant_members, a per-tenant key, a client-id check), not by Ory. So the seam is that exchange: a provider adapter turns a provider's authenticated session or OIDC token into a subject, and Nightscout mints the per-tenant token (D14). Owed: the adapter interface, and which provider properties a hoster must supply (issuer, audience, cookie scope; scope E was chosen for Kratos).

Why row 2 is held. Every Ory claim behind it is read-derived — no Kratos or Hydra instance has been started — and a shared identity pool is effectively irreversible once identities exist. T30-ORY-PROOF (about a day): stand up Kratos 1.x and Hydra 2.x, register two tenants against one pool, and confirm a session for tenant A cannot be exchanged for a Nightscout token on tenant B — with a control: the same session against A's own host must succeed, or the test only proves that everything fails.

The bridge is nsjwt, and it is ours under every outcome. Kratos says who the person is; a policy says what they may do on this site; Nightscout mints a per-tenant token (D14) the data path already understands. That is externals/nightscout-roles-gateway's design (a working Kratos + Hydra + Nightscout RBAC gateway, 31 migrations, 2022-era dependencies, one cohort-wide identity pool plus one Hydra client per site, joined_groups.subject as the seam) and its unfinished half. Letting Hydra issue the token instead would abandon D14 for the human path: OSS Hydra signs with its own keys and has one issuer.

What "lean on Ory" buys: no password hashing, credential recovery, MFA enrolment, session invalidation or OIDC federation handshake of our own. What it does not buy: multi-tenancy, the authorization model, the token exchange, the device path, or freedom from maintaining the native path. Adopting Ory means the auth seam carries two backends permanently — the same standing cost D4 imposes on storage, counted as maintenance, not migration.

docs.title: The amendment to D13
docs.text:
One cohort-wide identity pool makes the authentication plane shared infrastructure by construction: one identity, one session, one login spanning every tenant — which is also the feature, because a mobile app can log in once and select which Nightscout it may reach.

D13 is about secrets and stays true: each tenant holds its own root credential. D13 says nothing about identity, and reading it as "nothing is cohort-wide" would rule out the only workable topology. So:

Credentials are per-tenant. Identity is per-cohort. Authorization is per-tenant.

Isolation therefore rests on the authorization layer and on RLS, not on the authn layer. The failure mode to design against is a cross-tenant identity bug shipped on the assumption that the authn plane was isolated. This holds whether or not row 2 lands.

docs.title: Corroboration: Nocturne reached the same split with no Ory
docs.text:
Measured 2026-09-16 against externals/nocturne@d9e14309 (read, after the decision — corroboration, not basis):

measurement SubjectEntity : IEntityTimestamped — not ITenantScoped, so no RLS policy and no tenant query filter (NocturneDbContext.cs:137) likewise PasskeyCredentialEntity, TotpCredentialEntity, SubjectOidcIdentityEntity, SubjectRoleEntity, RecoveryCodeEntity, RefreshTokenEntity, OidcProviderEntity — none tenant-scoped, against 57 entities that are ix_subjects_access_token_hash UNIQUE, with no tenant column TenantMemberEntity TenantId + SubjectId; unique on (TenantId, SubjectId) and (TenantId, Username) — the seam per-tenant authorization TenantRoleEntity, TenantMemberRoleEntity, unique on (TenantId, Slug) federation Controllers/V4/TenantAdmin/OidcProviderAdminController.cs:25,27 is [Route("api/v4/admin/oidc-providers")] under [Authorize(Roles = "platform_admin")], and OidcProviderEntity is not tenant-scoped — configured once per deployment by the platform operator, not per tenant

Nocturne's identity plane is deployment-scoped, its authorization plane tenant-scoped, joined by a membership table. It goes further than D13 allows (its access token is deployment-global). It has no D7 — platform admin sits on the consumer API behind a platform_admin role — so on the admin plane it is what D7 departs from. Agreement between two read designs is not evidence that either is safe.

docs.title: 2.10 What "declared safe" means, and what suspension means
docs.text:
The declared-safe gate is deliberately not written yet (maintainer, 2026-09-15). Every tenancy finding carries the qualifier "high, within TENANCY_MODE=multi, which is not yet declared safe." The anchor that qualifier rests on is reachability, measurable today:

mechanism effect lib/server/env.js mode: readENV('TENANCY_MODE', 'single') opt-in; defaults off tenant-middleware.buildRegistry throws unless the storage URI names postgres lib/server/socket-tenancy.js refuses to boot on a path-only rule lib/server/socket-tenancy.js logs WITHHOLDING per surface when it does boot

TENANCY_MODE=multi is developer-only until declared otherwise, and that declaration is the gate. Nobody reaches it by upgrading — it takes a deliberate variable, a PostgreSQL deployment, and ignoring a boot-time error saying alarms are off. fromEnv()'s boot message should name what is outstanding rather than saying "not safe" generically.

The checklist is deferred on purpose. {M} §5.2's eight cross-cutting requirements are the basis, extended by four found since (process-wide authorization.storage.subjects; the per-tenant credential root, D13/D14; process-wide language/levels, BF-31; per-tenant ddata). Roughly 4 of 12 are met; items 4, 5 and 7 — per-tenant plugin instances, fairness/backpressure, quotas — have not started, and acceptance criteria written for unstarted work get rewritten when it starts. Write the gate when 4/5/7 have owners.

docs.title: Suspension is two verbs
docs.text:
is_active = false is a total blackout: tenant-middleware.js:233 answers 403 to every request — reads, writes, the API and CGM ingest — and tenant-registry.js:25 keeps no cache so it takes effect immediately. platform-store.js:321 requires suspension before deletion.

Decided 2026-09-15:

verb meaning suspend total blackout, as built. Abuse/ToS, and the pre-deletion state the delete gate requires pause ingest continues; the UI and reads are blocked. A billing lapse or an owner-requested pause never costs the person their data

The delete gate requires suspend, not pause.

docs.title: The socket gap is a display problem
docs.text:
is_active is checked at the Socket.IO handshake and never again. A suspended tenant answers 403 to everything new while an already-open tab keeps its socket and shows a live-looking chart that will never update.

Decided: disconnect, and make the page say so — keep the last data visible and plainly marked stale, using Nightscout's existing staleness vocabulary (the clock and time-ago going red). Blanking the screen does not help someone mid-decision; a display that silently looks current is the failure to design against. A silent disconnect leaves the same frozen chart, so the disconnect alone does not close this.

docs.title: 2.11 Deployment metadata: a recommendation, not a decision
docs.text:
Operator-supplied deployment metadata, such as a support contact, is not yet decided. The recommendation: two fields with different owners, never merged into one.

  • A platform-level value is required, and it must be servable with no tenant binding. A support contact is needed exactly when something is broken: an unknown slug, a suspended tenant, a database outage, the boot-error page. Those are the cases where a tenant record cannot be read.
  • A tenant-level value takes precedence when present. Under single the one value comes from the environment, unchanged (D1). Under multi, D15 rules out env-sourced configuration, so the platform value is a deployment row and the tenant value is a tenant row.
  • Render both, labelled. "Ask the person who set up your site" and "ask the company hosting it" are different actions, and someone whose glucose data has stopped arriving needs to know which is which.
  • A tenant-supplied contact is often a private person's contact details, for example a parent who runs a site for a child. Treat it as tenant-controlled personal data: not on any unauthenticated endpoint by default, not in logs, and not in any export that crosses a tenant boundary. The platform contact is an organisational address and carries no such constraint.
  • It is a low-risk first consumer of the per-tenant configuration table (T30-SCHEMA-CONFIG), because it is tenant-administrable but not a secret.

Wherever this metadata is rendered (a boot-error page, a suspended-tenant response, a push notification), the text is user-facing. It must say plainly which party to contact and for what, and it must not suggest that contacting anyone replaces the person's own care team when the problem concerns their therapy rather than the software.

docs.title: 2.12 D21 — one entrypoint, serve <roles> (maintainer, 2026-10-26)
docs.text:
D5 decided the roles and D16 the listeners; neither said how an operator starts one. The components document sketched one bin/ script per role ({C} §3). D21 replaces that sketch with one executable and a subcommand per role, the pattern Consul uses for its agent and tools, node-multienv uses in start_container.sh (multienv, resolver, runner, inspector, …), and Ory uses to turn its public and admin listeners on and off (serve public, serve admin, serve all).

subcommand what it runs configuration (D15) nightscout single today's server: one process, ctx.ddata, the cache, every listener the process environment nightscout serve api express and storage; no bus, no ddata per-tenant, from the database nightscout serve evaluator change feed, plugins, notifications; no express per-tenant, from the database nightscout serve realtime socket.io and the change feed; no storage writes per-tenant, from the database nightscout serve vcpool connector actors and the egress proxy per-tenant, from the database nightscout serve tenant-admin the tenant owner's configuration listener (D16) per-tenant, from the database nightscout serve admin the platform operator's listener, on its own interface (D7) the deployment's own settings nightscout serve api,realtime several roles in one process, each listener on its own bind address as each role nightscout diagnose data, healthcheck, version, env operator tools against a deployed site as single, or as the role named

Rules that follow:

  1. No start path changes. node lib/server/server.js stays the implementation of single; the dispatcher require()s it in-process (no child process, so SIGTERM reaches the server directly). A test boots the app both ways and compares them.
  2. Listeners are named and bound separately. A role that serves HTTP takes its own address and port; admin refuses to share the consumer listener's address.
  3. A subcommand is something an operator runs against a deployed site. Build, test and analysis scripts stay in scripts/ and package.json.
  4. An unknown subcommand prints the list and exits with status 64 (EX_USAGE); help lists the subcommands with one line each.
  5. The image's healthcheck is nightscout healthcheck, so the image needs no curl.

Work items: PLAT-ENTRY (the dispatcher with single and the operator tools, no behaviour change) and PLAT-SERVE (the hosted roles, carved one at a time from bootevent's factory chain, starting with api) in queue/work-queue.yaml and the next-gen platform plan §4.4.

docs.title: 3.1 v3 is closed, v1 is open
docs.text:
operator surface where API v3 closed — exactly 9: eq ne gt gte lt lte in nin re lib/api3/generic/search/input.js:111 API v1 open — pass-through on origin/master (15.0.8) lib/server/query.js:157

On 15.0.8, v1's create() builds the filter with traverse type-coercion and injects a date constraint, then returns it to the driver with no operator allowlist — {M} §6.5's ReDoS/full-scan finding stated as a translation problem: you cannot write a complete SQL translation of an open pass-through. v3 is smaller because someone wrote the list down, which makes it the contract to implement first.

origin/dev now carries a v1 operator allowlist (BF-04, #8743, merged 2026-09-18, not released): $expr and the pipeline parameter are refused, $type is allowed (so the seam's filter AST owes a $type node, or v1 narrows by one operator when the seam lands). The unauthenticated $regex cost defect, BF-72, is open on 15.0.8 and dev; see the register.

docs.title: 3.2 Strategy
docs.text:
1. Implement v3's nine operators natively. Closed, enumerable, testable exhaustively.
  2. Bound v1 with evidence. The corpus census (T2.4) says which operators clients send; support that set and reject the rest with a documented 400. This is also the §6.5 security fix.
  3. Keep the shape backwards compatible. Same URLs, parameter encoding and defaults (ENTRIES_DEFAULT_COUNT, the two-day deltaAgo in query.js). A client that sends an operator in the evidence set must not notice.

docs.title: 3.3 Libraries
docs.text:
package version use here mingo 7.2.4 The differential-test oracle. Evaluates Mongo queries against in-memory objects, so a translation is checked by running the same query both ways — the technique PR #8733 used with 636 randomised fixtures. Limit: mingo applies JavaScript truthiness, MongoDB does not (it reads {$exists: NaN} as true — T0.5), and its regex engine is V8 where MongoDB's is PCRE2 (T2.3) sift 17.1.3 a second oracle if a mingo disagreement needs adjudicating mongo-query-to-postgres-jsonb 0.2.19 candidate for the v1 long tail, not for the v3 nine FerretDB ghcr.io/ferretdb/ferretdb Rejected for the multitenant target: connects as a single role and cannot do per-transaction RLS binding, which is D3's point. Possibly a migration bridge or single-tenant-on-Postgres option

Write the nine operators by hand, and use mingo as the oracle.

docs.title: 3.4 Type coercion belongs above the seam, not in mongoose
docs.text:
On 15.0.8, v1 coerces query values through a hand-maintained per-collection allowlist (walker), not from any schema:

collection walker source entries 7 fields, all parseInt lib/server/entries.js:186 treatments insulin carbs glucose → parseInt; notes eventType enteredBy → regex lib/server/treatments.js:260 profile {} — empty lib/server/profile.js:97 devicestatus, activity, food none —

Run against lib/server/query.js (15.0.8 behaviour):

treatments insulin $gte=1.5                  {"insulin":{"$gte":1}}      <- truncated
treatments carbs   $gte=7.5                  {"carbs":{"$gte":7}}        <- truncated
entries    sgv     $gte=120                  {"sgv":{"$gte":120}}        <- correct
entries    delta   $gte=1.5                  {"delta":{"$gte":"1.5"}}    <- still a string
devicestatus uploader.battery $lt=50         {"uploader.battery":{"$lt":"50"}}  <- still a string
  1. Over-coercion gives wrong answers. insulin and carbs are parseInt although specs/nsschema/treatments.model.json declares both number. A query for boluses ≥ 1.5 U returns boluses of 1.0 U.
  2. Under-coercion gives silently empty answers. A field with no walker entry stays a string, and MongoDB orders BSON types before values, so a numeric field never matches a string bound; every numeric filter on devicestatus and activity matches nothing and returns 200.
  3. The walker is a fourth drift-prone list beside the OpenAPI spec, indexedFields and the nsschema model ({M} §7.6).

T0.5 (bf/coercion, #8737, merged, not released) replaces the walker with a schema-derived table.

Why not mongoose. It would fix (1) and (2) in the wrong place: mongoose is MongoDB-only and D4 makes two backends permanent, so Postgres would need its own coercion and the drift problem moves up a level. The job — "HTTP query string → typed value" — is backend-independent and must happen before the repository interface is called; otherwise the interface's contract is "accepts strings or numbers, the backend decides". specs/nsschema/ already distinguishes the broken case (treatments.insulin: ['null','number'] against entries.noise: ['integer']), and five emitters already consume those models.

A coercion-table emitter is the sixth emitter, feeding one table used by the query parser above the seam, for both backends. Mongoose keeps the role {M} §7.6 scoped it to — write-path validation inside the MongoDB adapter.

Compatibility: fixing (2) is user-visible — queries that returned nothing start returning rows. It belongs in release notes.

docs.title: 4. D4 — what "MongoDB stays" costs the seam
docs.text:
The seam carries two mature backends permanently, not one plus a migration path:

  1. The interface is the intersection, not Mongo's shape. If it exposes driver semantics it is not a seam ({M} §2.5's complaint about mongo-storage.js).
  2. Both backends stay in CI permanently. Every storage test runs twice.
  3. specs/generated/mongoose/ is the single-tenant validation path — mongoose scoped to the MongoDB adapter, schemas generated from specs/ ({M} §7.6). It is for write-path validation, not query coercion (§3.4).

docs.title: 4.1 The write contract belongs behind the seam
docs.text:
Measured 2026-09-27 against official/dev 295f1177. Queue: WRITE-CONTRACT.

§3 puts the read rules (operators, coercion) in one place above the seam. The write rules have no such place. 15.0.9 added four modules that decide what a stored record looks like, and each write path calls them itself:

module lines added by decides files that call it lib/server/object-id-forms.js 169 #8758 which _id forms name a record; the twin left by a string _id 12 lib/server/srv-dates.js 222 #8775 srvCreated / srvModified, which API v3 history reads 11 lib/server/soft-deleted.js 53 #8775 that isValid: false is a delete 7 lib/server/treatment-fallback-key.js 67 #8780 the identity of a treatment re-sent without one 2

Eighteen files under lib/ call at least one of them (git grep -l "srv-dates')\|soft-deleted')\|object-id-forms')\|treatment-fallback-key')" official/dev -- lib). Beside them, the fields the server derives for memory (mills, endmills; ddata.processRawDataForRuntime) are derived at 18 call sites in six files, seven of them in lib/server/websocket.js.

Three write paths call these rules separately: the v1 server modules (lib/server/{entries,treatments,devicestatus,profile,food,activity}.js, which in-process callers also use), the API v3 generic operations over lib/api3/storage, and the socket path (lib/server/websocket.js, {S} §5). {S} §4.4 records that the three already deduplicate differently, per collection. Defects from a rule that one path applied and another did not, all in the register: BF-122 and BF-144 (srvModified and v3 history), BF-141 and BF-143 (treatment re-sends), BF-146 (mills on v3 writes held in memory), BF-135 (an isValid: false delete still counted), and BF-109, 110, 116, 117, 130, 136, 140, 142, 145 (_id forms and twins per path).

What the seam owes. One write step at the storage interface, applied to every write from every path, for both backends:

  1. the stored _id form and the handling of twins (object-id-forms; OID-STORAGE-HELPER is this rule alone);
  2. srvCreated / srvModified (srv-dates);
  3. soft delete (soft-deleted);
  4. the identity used to recognise a re-send (treatment-fallback-key, and {S} §4.4's table for the other collections);
  5. one change event per write. Under single it carries the runtime-derived copy, so the in-memory cache, v3 history and the socket consume one emission instead of each path emitting its own. Under multi the change feed (D6) is that event, and ns-evaluator derives on its own slice (§7b).

What stays where it is. Runtime-derived fields are not stored (the BF-146 fix derives on a copy). Query coercion stays above the seam (§3.4). Mongoose validation stays inside the MongoDB adapter (item 3 above). The in-memory cache stays for single (D4); the hosted evaluator holds none (§7b).

This is a behaviour change, not a refactor. Item 4 unifies re-send handling that differs by collection and by path today, so a client that relies on one path's behaviour will see another's. It needs a semver decision (at least minor), a consumer-replay arm and the existing regression nets:

docs.title: 8758's CRUD-by-id matrix, tools/qc/write-arm.js and tools/lab/rc-soak.
docs.text:
Measured 2026-10-07 on dev 43289dde (write-contract spec, tools/qc/write-contract-matrix.js). The counts above re-measure as stated. The paths are four, not three: in-process ctx.<collection> writes behave differently from v1 HTTP in some cells. Stored state differs between paths in 33 of 66 collection-and-form groups (47 on 15.0.8), and a record created through one path and re-sent without _id through another is stored twice in 38 of 66 path pairs. None of the v1, socket or in-process writes reaches the API v3 storage socket (BF-164). The spec proposes the step's interface, the re-send rule and the gates; its §6 lists the six decisions it needs.

The Postgres loader (BFQ-CAP02) runs imported documents through the same step, with OID-MIGRATION's rules for twins, so that an imported record and a written one cannot differ.

docs.title: 5. D9 — base branch
docs.text:
Base the work on chore/nightscout-modernization. At the decision (2026-09-14) it was 0a4109f6, 495 commits / 573 files / +107,596 −14,872 ahead of origin/dev a8888f0d. It closes {M} §3.1's shared-alarm-state blocker (commit 9e869662) and carries the Playwright suite and the Node 22/24 floor; rebasing that many commits underneath this work later would be worse than starting on top of it.

Measured 2026-09-27: official/chore/nightscout-modernization is b1bdaca0, 206 behind / 498 ahead of official/dev 295f1177 (git rev-list --left-right --count official/dev...official/chore/nightscout-modernization); its last merge of dev is e3b22034 (2026-09-21). The seam chain has not been refreshed onto it (SEAM-REFRESH): seam/t1-2-storage-interface 81a1f6ce is 68 behind / 50 ahead of b1bdaca0 with 19 conflicting paths (git merge-tree --write-tree --name-only official/chore/nightscout-modernization seam/t1-2-storage-interface) — three of them add/add supersessions from BF-04's upstream allowlist, which wins; sixteen content conflicts across the v1 API and server storage modules, cost unmeasured. Against official/dev 295f1177 the seam is 271 behind / 545 ahead with 49 conflicting paths (the same two commands with official/dev). Whether the seam refreshes onto the modernization branch or onto dev depends on how the release train reaches dev: by merge, decided 2026-10-12 (§5.1, queue RT-PROPAGATION), so the seam refreshes onto the modernization branch. D9 stands.

Caveat: #8605 (the modernization integration PR) has zero human reviews across its production lines, all by one author. That blocks shipping the stack, not developing against it. This plan does not constitute a review of it.

Refreshing the seam, when it is done. The chain is 16 linear branches, which is the nearest thing to an irreversible operation in this programme.

  • Before starting, record every seam tip in a committed file: git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(objectname)' refs/heads/seam/. Rollback is git reset --hard <recorded tip> per branch. ORIG_HEAD does not survive a multi-branch rebase, and reflogs expire.
  • Decide per-branch rebase or squash before starting. A squash discards the per-branch history that explains why each conflict was resolved the way it was. If squashing, tag the pre-squash tips first.
  • lib/server/query.js carries two fixes for the same $exists operand defect: the seam's coerceExistsArguments() (e0564167) and dev's schema-driven lib/server/query-coercion (#8737, BF-32). Measured 2026-10-07 (propagation rehearsal): dev's covers the ordering the seam's handles; they differ only on '' and ' false ', which the seam reads as false and dev passes to MongoDB. BF-04's operator allowlist sits in the same output path; removing its call turns its test from 79/0 to 65/14, so a resolution that drops it is caught.
